It was very high stock-based comp, which is common in software companies and particularly in the Valley in America. But it was elevated.

And so, you know, I did what I've commonly done where I identified something early and sold early, but made a very good return. But it was all based on fundamentals. There was a lot of free cash flow generation into a valuation that made it attractive on an EV to free cash flow basis. When I was buying the company at a 20 billion EV, you know, again, against the forecast I was able to generate, the business was extremely attractively valued. And I definitely sold it far too early. But I guess as Rothschild famously said, you can make a fortune or he said, I've made a fortune by selling things too early.

早期 Alpha vs 晚期 Alpha

And just on that point, Ethan, I think something that doesn't come out in spreadsheets is that like the alpha in situations is different. So if you have someone who generates 100% in a situation and it's a stock that goes from price of 100 to price of 1000 and they get the last bit, the kind of run from 500 to 1000. That is the riskiest part of the move before the stock tops, but it doesn't jump out on a spreadsheet. You know, it's the risk premium that's attached from the early alpha.

The early alpha is the best alpha, in my opinion, because it's where the valuations are lowest, the risks to equity are the lowest. And so even though it doesn't jump out when two people have made 100%, those returns can be extremely different. And the amount of risk that was taken, even if you're not looking in financial leverage terms, just fundamental valuation terms, and on a per share risk per unit of return.

Yeah, I generally try to be sizing larger where on a valuation basis, you're early in the move and then I'm pulling capital out as expected values declining as the equity is rising. And yeah, that way you're able to protect capital a lot easier. So as expected value goes up, as the expected value comes down and variance of return is going up as a stock is appreciating, very quickly pulling the capital back.

十二、AI 大交易的当下格局

Ethan: I think the only obvious question from there is what are your thoughts on the AI trade as it stands today?

Joe: No, I'm not sure. I mean, I see lots of risks. Things I'm thinking about are that from a regulatory perspective, there's a lot of concern on cybersecurity risk. There are increasing incidents taking place, which the companies are volunteering, whether it's the Hugging Face incident or there is some, there's a spectrum of, I guess we could call them mishaps.

But it's kind of undeniable at this point that whether you like it or not, you are exposed to this thematic in today's market because, you know, a statistic I read recently was that 40% of S&P earnings are now explicit or derived from AI. If you look in the credit markets as a percentage of issuance, whether it's the bonds from Meta or Google or SoftBank who hit the headlines two days ago, issuing a very high yielding bonds. AI is very represented in the credit markets now.

And yeah, I mean, there's a bear case, there's a base case, and there's a bull case. And each of them is going to have disproportionate risk for the market.

房东策略：数据中心 REIT 的低风险角度

I think I think what we think about is the sustainability of the capex that these hyperscalers are able to deploy and how you can participate in that as an equity investor without taking silly amounts of risk. So there are listed securities that are selling into this where you could be a landlord of a data center with a contract where you retain first liens on the property, your capex per megawatt is capped, the client is taking a ton of the risk, and you're effectively a landlord trading at a yield on cost in the teens, and there appears that are REITs or otherwise that are trading at cap rates in the single digits. And those are very attractively priced situations. And without naming them, unfortunately, I'm not able to give you those while we're trading them.

But yeah, I mean, we are active in the space in equities where we can see a very good return without taking a ton of risk.

OpenAI/Anthropic 的脆弱性

I mean, in terms of the cash flow burn and the financial position of these lease commitments on a take or pay basis, I think, you know, people are going to be keenly reading these S1s when they come out. You know, if these companies execute to the ball case and revenue keeps growing, they're going to be in a position to satisfy these obligations. And they're going to be very, very, very valuable companies. I'm speaking here mainly about OpenAI and Anthropic.

But to the extent you've got very high cash burn, very high obligations that aren't on balance sheet yet, that will come on balance sheet as that critical IT load is delivered, uh there is there is an outcome where the financial position becomes yeah uh fragile let's let's put it like that.

So uh you know ai as a technology is phenomenal uh we use it every day it's been extremely helpful to our process you know i don't i'm not one of these doomers who you know things it doesn't add value or things it's like redundant i think it's transformational.

分解 AI 价值链

But the actual, as a consumer of the product and then being an investor of the businesses is a completely different proposition. And, you know, accretion to equity value through that entire value chain, where at the top on the GPU side, you've got Nvidia. On the frontier lab side, you've got OpenAI Anthropic and a host of others beneath them that you alluded to in the private markets as well. The kind of Neo cloud space, you've got, the nebbiases, the coolweaves, the iris energies. In the Powered Shell players, you've got a host of listed players, or you've got fully fledged REITs like Equinix, Digital Realty. There's a host of these previously Bitcoin miners that have migrated over to AI, high performance compute. Then you've got memory.

So this is a very large value chain. It's a very large industry structure. And, you know, the whole thing sums to, you know, easily north of 20, 30 trillion of market cap. And it's a very, very big trade. And I think it's going to be very dangerous for the market if it doesn't work out.

供给侧瓶颈：吉瓦与 NIMBY

And I guess analyzing demand is one thing, but something we do a lot of is analyzing supply as well. And if you look at the gigawatts that are forecast to come into the market, even in the U.S. market, if you just look at the top five states, so like markets like Virginia, Texas, Pennsylvania, California, there's been a lot of headlines recently about it's becoming a political issue because you're running into nimbyism. People don't want a gigawatt monstrosity in their backyard.

You know, to the extent that permitting becomes an issue, like you saw in New York, there was a pause and, you know, permitting's been halted, perhaps indefinitely, we'll have to see. You know, there's discussions in ERCOT right now in Texas. There are lots of state elections happening. This is a big political football that people are kicking around. And if it wins votes, you know, politicians are going to campaign on it.

And that creates risk to consensus, because if the market is pricing that there's 200 gigawatt speed being delivered next year and that number misses by 25 percent, the earnings are going to miss accordingly for lack of delivered infrastructure.

芯片世代与冷却约束

So, very bullish on the technology and its potential. The trade has become incredibly large, even if there is risk to earnings and there's other technological aspects like something that is happening as Nvidia comes out with these generations of new chips is that the cooling requirements from thermal power design or thermal design power, which is effectively the amount of watts that are required or emitted from the chip and required for cooling.

So you've gone from like Hopper to Blackwell to Rubin, Rubin Ultra, and then you've got Fineman coming after that, which should be the next generation. And just the chips are so much more powerful. And, you know, there is the amount of packages put in per chip rises, the amount of heat that they're emitting goes up. And so, you know, ultimately NVIDIA has, you know, developed a low power mode as a just in case for this being delivered.

But there are many cooling solutions that are being worked through in the market right now, but they're not there yet. And that's another form of risk. It's like, well, you could be building these world class chips at the frontier and ultimately, you may go from single-phase cooling via liquid cooling to cooling in-chip, which may then become an NVIDIA product.

技术乐观 + 结构警惕：ASML 的类比

So there are so many technological risks. There are regulatory risks. There are permitting risks. But the truth is that the potential of the technology is so big. And people said these things about ASNL like 10, 15 years ago. They were like, EUV lithography will never work. And Nikken and Canon and the others just fell away and ASML kept betting on it. They made the breakthrough and it's the most valuable company in Europe today.

So the potential is there, but there's a lot of risk. And our job as investors is to dissect that value chain, understand all the technology constraints, regulatory, political, etc. and then find the most asymmetric attractive part of the value chain, both long and short, and position accordingly.

十三、言行不一致：隐藏的 AI 多头

Ethan: Yeah, I mean, what's also so funny about AI, not really funny, but just it's a cool fact, is that you'll have these people or, you know, an example is, say, a college student. And he watches something on YouTube and he says, "AI is a bubble, AI is a bubble." But his career, the way he's recruiting, the bets he's making with his personal decisions are all extremely correlated to the AI factor. Or people who make calls about, say, the US, another example, and then with their careers are extremely long the US. It's like these incongruencies that I find very funny.

十四、最大的个人 Edge：产业结构研究

Ethan: And I guess final question, talked about a lot during this podcast. Out of all the parts of your process, what would you say is the most important that lots of other hedge fund managers, lots of other investors could learn from?

Joe: I think it's a pretty self-aggrandizing question. I'm not sure I could teach these you know, great fund managers much, but I think probably if I could twist your wording slightly where I think my process maybe has a large amount of edge, if you allow it, is I think the work that we do on industry structure yields a lot of alpha.

AI 价值链例证

I guess I'll give you a couple of examples to bring it to life because it's just more fun when you bring it down to a stock. So we just went through some of the AI value chain there. So starting at the very top, you've got chip manufacturers, you've got like Nvidia, you've got the TSMCs, you've got the AMDs, the Intels and all those people. You've got then in memory, you've got Micron, Samsung Hynix. On the lab side, you've got OpenAI, Anthropic, a host of others. In the Neo cloud space, you've got the CoreWaves, the Nebiuses, the Iris Energies, etc. And then going back through PowerShell, you've then got a host of data sensor providers. There's four different products even within that.

And to cover like 50 names, and you don't have to go into molecular detail, but you do have to understand their business model. You do have to understand their position in the value chain, how much of the industry's profit accrues to them, and then how industry structure can change over time so that their share of the profit may go up or down, their share of the revenue and cash may go up or down. What is that industry growing at? So are these, is this pocket of the industry taking market share or losing it?

And so, yeah, an area I was quite early to was the PowerShell players within the AI value chain. You could buy those businesses on enterprise values of $1 million per megawatt on their secured power portfolios. And they're trading you know at three to four having gone to seven to eight at peak and the good ones did more than that. I'm giving you like sector statistics.

风电案例：Cadeler 与价值链转移

So yeah, I think doing industry understanding industry structure as a stock picker an equity investor and a buyer or seller of companies is very valuable, but it's very time consuming, which is why a lot of people don't do it. And I understand that, but there is a big ROI on that work.

You know, another one, I mean, there's several really, where industry structure has led to not just an individual great opportunity, but great long, short opportunities. A few years ago, it was in the wind space, where you effectively have developers who are the owner-operators of wind farms. You have the turbine makers who provide the equipment that goes into those wind farms. You have cable manufacturers that are manufacturing the export cable that goes from the substation onshore out to this offshore wind farm. You have the turbine installation vessels, you know, that ultimately are these fleets of self-propelled jack-off vessels that jack down on the seabed. They have a Hussmann crane attached to them. They're phenomenal assets and they're very bespoke. You know, you can't replace it and retrofit an oil rig to do this work.

And, you know, there's a company in particular that I used to be a shareholder of called Cadala, which by taking out an entity we were long of became, frankly, a monopolist of this profit pool and disproportionately attracted economics relative to the rest of the industry at a very, very low starting valuation.

So, yeah. So yeah, we, you know, through the evolution of this industry over time, back in 2017, everyone in the wind space was making very attractive returns because they were being remunerated on a feed-in tariff basis. And then there was a pivot to auction, which basically drove a lot more competitive pricing. That led to more competitive bids from developers. They pushed that deflation down into the value chain. So pricing per turbine per megawatt came down. And then they pushed that through their supply chain. Everyone got squeezed and the economics were terrible.

You know, the business effectively went from generating low double digit operating margins and making good returns to having some very lean years and having multiple profit warnings. Meanwhile, Cadla was sat there filling up a backlog and their share price did extraordinarily well.

But it's understanding how all those parts of the industry speak to each other and not just looking at one in isolation saying, "Okay, this is growing, it's cheap, I'm going to buy some." If you know how all those moving parts talk to each other and you're meeting all of those companies at conferences and you're doing the work, you can you can have a far better kind of ability to to cover risks that can be coming and also see upsides before other people see them.

So probably that's the thing that's been the most helpful. And yeah, it's it's a lot of work, but it's it's worth it understand and the structure of industries there's alpha there.

结束

Ethan: Thank you Joe for coming on the pod. This was awesome.

Joe: Ethan, thank you and uh yeah well done on the growth of the show. I've uh I've got value from the episodes and hopefully I've given a bit of value back so yeah well done.

Ethan: Absolutely man, thank you.

item.description:
## 一、最意外的观察：他其实在"反向使用"扑克——不是赢得牌局，而是**选择不去的牌桌**
大多数人读到"扑克手优势"会立刻想到：读心、心理战、虚张声势、GTO 策略。但 Walsh 几乎完全不谈这些。他承认自己"甚至没进过前百分位"，却靠扑克赚到钱——**靠的是选桌而不是打牌**。
这里藏着一个被整个投资行业系统性忽视的真相：**绝大多数"选股方法论"书籍都在教你如何打牌，但顶级 Alpha 来自于拒绝坐上某些牌桌。** 他对冲基金的核心框架不是"我能比谁更聪明"，而是"**在哪个时间尺度上、哪个流动性区间里，聪明人已经退场了？**" 他明确说：3-6 个月视角的欧洲工业股——那是多策略平台的屠宰场，不去；流动性 1000-3000 万美元/日的名字——他们因杠杆约束进不来，所以我去。
这是一种**负向定义的 edge**：不是"我强在哪"，而是"**对手弱在哪、或根本不来**"。换个说法——他的 Alpha 不是技能溢价，而是**结构性缺席套利**。
## 二、跨领域连接：Walsh 的"时间尺度套利"与生态学的"生态位分化"是同一个数学结构

item.title: [a16z] What Happens When AI Agents Can Spend Your Money?
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

从"旁观者"到"行动者"：代理商务的本体论转变

Terry 用了一个极其克制但意义深远的词：代理从 spectator 变成了 actor，而让这个转变成立的不是智能提升，而是一张能支付的卡。这是整个访谈最被低估的洞察——智能并不等于能动性，能动性来自于"能让你损失钱"的权力。一个能推荐却不能付款的 AI 本质上和一本百科全书没有区别；而一旦它能从你账户中划出资金，它在法律、伦理、经济上都变成了一个新物种。这意味着整个"AGI 什么时候到来"的辩论可能走错了路——AGI 的真正门槛不是 benchmark 分数，而是支付凭证的信任边界。有趣的跨界联系：这与"法人"的诞生惊人相似。现代公司之所以成为公司，不是因为它有多聪明，而是因为它能签合同、能被起诉、能持有财产。代理商务正在悄悄地让 AI 获得类似"法人"的功能性人格。

拉斯维加斯三步验证法：代理时代最被忽略的债务

Alex 顺手讲的一段"珠宝店-拉斯维加斯"类比值得单独放大。传统交易验证有三步：卡是真的吗？人是卡主吗？人神志清醒吗？ 代理商务已经解决了前两步（network tokens + agent registration），但第三步——是否神志清醒——在 AI 语境下变成了"是否幻觉"。而这里有一个几乎没人指出的结构性问题：赌场的"神志清醒"判断由商户承担（没让醉汉付款是商户的责任），但在代理商务里，"幻觉检测"的责任目前完全没有被分配给任何一方。这不是技术缺口，是法律真空。可以预测：未来 12-24 个月，代理公司将不得不像保险公司一样，为自己的"错单"自掏腰包赔付，这会催生一个新品类——代理错误保险（Agent E&O Insurance），并最终把"幻觉率"从一个研究指标变成一个精算指标。

Amazon 封杀 Muse 泄露的秘密：企业对代理的态度，暴露了它真正是什么

这是整段对话里最有爆点但两人都轻描淡写处理掉的洞察：Amazon 之所以敌视代理，不是因为它是零售商，而是因为它根本不是零售商——它是一家广告公司。代理没有眼球，所以不能被变现。换句话说，一家公司对 AI 代理的接纳程度，是检测它真实商业模式的试剂。热情拥抱的（Shopify 下的 SMB）靠商品差价赚钱；犹豫的（Walmart）既靠差价也靠流量和会员订阅；敌视的（Amazon）主要靠注意力贩卖。这个诊断方法可以反向使用：下一个值得做空的，是那些声称"我们是科技公司"但对代理高度敌对的 SaaS——它们大概率在用"科技"包装"广告"。跨界联系：这与达尔文"检视身体结构即可反推生态位"的做法一模一样——鸟喙的形状暴露它吃什么，公司对代理的 API 政策暴露它真的卖什么。

隐形崩塌：返现、里程、信用卡积分的"保险精算基础"将在三年内瓦解

Terry 几乎是以脚注方式提到了一个会震动整个消费金融行业的事实：信用卡的高额返现之所以存在，是因为"breakage"（破损率）——持卡人错配、遗忘、未优化。而代理恰恰消灭 breakage。一旦我的代理永远给我用对的卡、在对的类目、在对的促销期——那张"餐饮 5% 回赠但其他 1%"的卡在精算上就无法成立。这不是边际调整，这是整个 reward 经济学的塌陷。类比：这与 ETF 对主动管理基金的侵蚀一样——不是击败了对手，而是抽走了对手赖以生存的信息不对称。预测：三年内会出现"反代理化"信用卡产品（例如需要人类生物认证才能解锁高额返现），银行会以"保护用户"为名实际保护自己的毛利。

不对称红利窗口：你现在正站在"2005 年的高频交易员"位置

Alex 自己几乎意识到了但没有点破：早期代理用户正在剥削一个尚未部署代理的世界。所有的"代理帮我省钱"的爽文，都来自于交易对手还在用人类节奏运转。这与 2005 年前后 Renaissance 和 Citadel 面对手工做市商时的处境完全同构——不是因为他们更聪明，而是因为对面还没升级。当 Comcast 也用代理接电话、当航空公司用代理动态定价压制你的升舱代理，这个套利窗口就关闭了。所以现在听这期播客的人，正站在一个历史性窄缝里：你能用代理占便宜的时间，可能只有 18 个月。

📝 转录文本

开场：从旁观者到行动者

"In the last 3 months, we've had this huge leap from agents being what I would call spectators to agents being actors because they effectively have arms and legs, which are payment credentials. Amazon recently blocked Muse and there are many reasons for this. You can either be antagonistic to agent commerce or you can be highly receptive. What's happened with the rise of, you know, Muse and Instinct is once they have access to payment credentials, their utility increases. So, we sort of have kicked off what I kind of call the wallet wars where every wallet is now rushing to connect to the agents. Everybody who's listening to this podcast, I almost guarantee you have a credential that's stored at VGS."

"The largest online merchants, the largest neo banks, and the largest frontier labs all use VGS to secure payment credentials. It's a really formidable position to be in. Where do you think VGS is going to go? I think we are."

嘉宾介绍

Alex Rampell: Hi everyone. I'm Alex Rampel, partner at Andreessen Horowitz, and I'm here joined by Terry Angelos, and I'm very excited about being joined by Terry because Terry and I started a company called TrialPay in 2006. Um, long long time ago, 20 years ago.

Terry: 20 years ago. Alex looked very different.

Alex: Yes. Uh, you look the same. So I think you're insulting me and I'm complimenting you, and hopefully not the other way around. But today — this is the really cool part — one of my first investments here was a company called VGS, which stands for Very Good Security. And some people might not get that that's actually a pun or a joke, because one of the most famous cryptography companies was called PGP, which is Pretty Good Privacy. And obviously, it's very good priv — it's not just pretty good privacy, it's incredible privacy. It's unbreakable privacy, because it's very hard to factor very large composite numbers into their primes. And "pretty good privacy" is actually very good. So that was kind of the original name for Very Good Security.

So I led this investment a long time ago. TrialPay got bought by Visa. Visa under your leadership invested in VGS, and now you're back and you're the Chief Strategy Officer and board member alongside me at VGS.

Terry: Yeah. It's been a very fun and incredible journey. And I think if you look at VGS today, it's a payment infrastructure business. We secure credentials for about a third of all e-commerce by GMV. And we have the largest online merchants, we have the largest neo banks, and the largest frontier labs — all use VGS to secure payment credentials. And I think today, part of the reason why we want to talk about Agentic Commerce is because VGS is involved in helping agents get those credentials, helping wallets hand those credentials to agents, and also to merchants who have to receive these credentials. And so we're sort of in the middle of these really interesting conversations and handovers between credentials.

什么是 Credential？VGS 的核心业务

Alex: But maybe we should dig into what a credential is. "Credential" is a fancy way of saying a credit card for most lay people. It gets a little more complicated than that when you really dig into it. But you work with — I don't know which merchants I'm allowed to say that you work with. You work with all the big ones. Why don't we take an example merchant that you work with kind of pre-AI, pre-agentic commerce, and just explain what you do — like, why do they use VGS? What do they use you for, and how pervasive is it?

Terry: Yeah, let's assume we're working with like a very large online ordering platform. And so we have that company — effectively — has to store your credit card every time that a new customer comes onto that site and hands over a credit card. That company doesn't necessarily want to be exposed to that card number. And so VGS is involved in capturing that card, securely vaulting it and storing it. And every time that the online ordering service wants to transact with one of its processors, it goes to the vault and retrieves the information in such a way that the online ordering company never actually has to touch the payment information.

Now, one of the things that I think has made VGS a lot more interesting since the days that you first invested — it's been a decade of becoming sort of the most trusted vault online — is that the card networks have also introduced a form of tokenization. So, in our days back in TrialPay, we would actually store a 16-digit PAN, and we would encrypt it.

Alex: A PAN is a Primary Account Number.

Terry: A PAN is a Primary Account Number.

Alex: — credit card number. It's the 16-digit number that you have on your card.

Terry: We would encrypt it and vault it, and then when it came time to charge someone, we might unencrypt it and give it to, I think, Chase Paymentech back in those days. Today, that doesn't happen. Today, instead of storing that 16-digit card number and using that, you actually go to the network that issued it — so, Visa, Mastercard, AMX, Discover — and you say, "I would like another version of this card that's actually domain-bound just to my merchant domain." Which is safer, because if there's ever a problem, the only number that I have only works on my merchant domain, and I am going to use this when I send it to Chase Paymentech.

So VGS as a company vaults all these credentials on behalf of the merchant, also gets all of the network tokens — which is the primary way that these credentials are passed to the payment processor and to the network. And that's what we do today.

多处理器与账户更新

Terry: And so, because of that complexity of interacting with the card networks and doing this across multiple processors — actually, here's a question for you, Alex. If you're a merchant with over a billion dollars in GMV, how many payment processors do you have on the back end?

Alex: Well, it depends. There are plenty that just have one, but you are better — I mean, this goes to the use case of VGS, which is rather than being locked into one payment processor, you'd rather unbundle that and you'd rather be able to pick and choose which payment processor you use. But also, if you have a kind of shared infrastructure that is storing credentials — what if one credential goes bad?

Like, I just had a Capital One card. Great example. Capital One bought Discover Card — Discover Network — and then my fancy Capital One cashback-rewards-1.5% Visa card became a Discover card. And every week I get notifications from very sad merchants: "We are unable to process your card." Why are they unable to process my card? Because that old card number doesn't exist anymore, even though I still have a relationship with Capital One. I just got a new card number from them. Granted, it's a little bit complicated — it's on a new network. There's also the possibility — like, merchants can't just say, "Oh, we've seen, we know that this card became that card." One merchant cannot do that.

Terry: Yeah.

Alex: But a large vault can do that. And then the actual networks themselves — like Visa and Mastercard, and actually Discover too — they have these Account Updating tools.

Terry: Yeah.

So we might have, in the case of Chase and open banking, it was much more a case of security and control. In the case of Amazon, it might be: "I am an opinionated API. I have an opinion on what you should buy, Alex, based on many data points about you." And then my agent may have an opinion about what I want. And so that's going to be a fascinating battle, or communication. And in the end, I think consumers probably win, but we don't know what that's going to look like going forward.

被高估与被低估的

Alex: Right. Well, maybe on that — like, what do you think is overhyped versus underhyped in terms of everything that's happening? I mean, in general, my rule of thumb is that Silicon Valley overhypes things, but then the rest of the world underhypes things. You know, everything here, every conversation is AI. And it feels like you go to Iowa, nobody's talking about AI, but then you show it to them like, "Holy — how is this real?" Because they tried it three years ago.

Like — I just bought a new Tesla, and I remember I had an old Model 3 (I think this is a good metaphor for what we're talking about). Like, I had an old Model 3 in 2017 — self-driving didn't work at all, it was a joke. Eventually got a different car, and now it actually works. But I was skeptical, because I was used to the 2017 thing. And I feel like a lot of that is playing out with AI right now — where if you had tried ChatGPT with all the hallucinations and everything in 2022, you're like, "Oh, it's a cute toy for writing poems — or doing my homework in English class or something. This is not going to actually buy things for me, this is not going to write code." It does all these things right now.

So, I guess, what do you think is underhyped versus overhyped in terms of everything that's going on?

Terry: Yeah. So, maybe I'll start with overhyped.

Overhyped: I don't think we're going to get a bank run on savings deposits where agents are going to maximize yield and move my money around between different accounts. A perfect example: I am a very happy Mercury personal account customer. I'm also a Chase customer. And ideally, I should put all my savings in Mercury, where I get a very good savings rate — and then at the last moment, when I have to make bill pay — pay bills, I'll move the cash over to my existing bank, Chase. But their bill pay just works better, and it has more integrations, and I have more kind of setup. So I think there's enough friction in the world where we won't see some of the crazy volatility in financial services.

Underhyped: There is a lot of demand that is unmonetized. And this is both at the sort of part of the world where you could expect more GDP. An example of this: we actually have a group cycling WhatsApp group, and we have a person on that group who — every six months, when our friend Seth comes up with a new recommendation for what tires to get, because he looks at rolling resistance — every time he does this, I'm like, "Oh, I should remember to buy those tires, because they're safer." But I only buy it every two years. If my agent was in that group chat, I would be buying tires every time Seth makes a new recommendation. You're dramatically under-monetized on your bike equipment, Alex. If the agent could find things that could help you with cycling and just bought them for you, there's more GDP coming out of Alex on cycling.

That is underhyped. At the same time, agents are going to save us money. There's probably many places where I have some subscription and it's just been a hassle to cancel, or I did some trial and I forgot about it. So I think agents will simultaneously save us money — maybe use that savings to help us buy new items.

So, I think we have yet to experience the always-on nature of these agents. And as far as I can tell, human desires and needs are infinite. So there's always something else that I will want.

不对称红利：7 点订餐与升舱技巧

Alex: Maybe on this kind of antagonistic versus consiliatory (or whatever the opposite of antagonistic would be here) — I mean, a lot of what people are very excited about with the agents is: it gets something for you that is intentionally hard, and is not really subject to the laws of economics. The laws of economics are like, the cure for high prices is high prices. If it's really hard to get a restaurant reservation because you have to call at 7 a.m. — well, now everybody has a tool that calls at 7 a.m. And therefore the first five people that have the tool — now they have an amazing tool. The last five people [say], "No, no, no, no — it's so crowded nobody goes here anymore," kind of thing.

So, how do you think the world changes? Because it feels like right now this is the weird position that we're in — is that a lot of the early wins, if you will, the consumer successes, are around, like, "Oh, it saved me money, it did this," because of the asymmetry. A very small number of people have the tool. The merchant or the counterparty has no idea what's going on.

I can't wait — you know how, like, as a consumer, I've been trained to say, "No, no, I want to talk to an agent," or "press zero"? Or it's like, "You can look up: how do you get out of the stupid phone tree?" I can't wait for the other side to say, "No, I have to talk to Terry. I ain't talking to Muse." Right? Like, wouldn't that be funny? You call Comcast — "I hate you, you suck, your service is terrible, you went down 10 times." This is — I do this all the time. And of course I actually do this with Codex because it turned out Comcast is blocking Muse. They know the IP addresses or something, so it won't let you log in. So I just have ChatGPT, you know, Codex, Astra — login on my computer, does everything. But I'm waiting for the day when Comcast says, "We know this ain't you, put Alex on the line, because I'm not giving something to his agent."

And that's going to — because right now, again, that's what I mean by the asymmetry. The small number of insiders have this tool. But you know what? You can't scale that infinitely, because the world is going to adapt.

Terry: Although I do have news for Comcast — the GPT, Astra, and Alex are about the same sort of foe. So, be careful if you get them on the phone.

I mean, I think you're pointing out something that we have yet to appreciate, which is: what happens when you actually read the terms and conditions and go to the edge of what is allowed and disallowed? So, an example: the other day I was looking at flights. I wanted to buy a flight that was on the edge of the price that I could pay that would get me an upgrade. And that's kind of a hard thing to do — sometimes I overshoot it. My agent did that perfectly.

Or, any case where it's very difficult to uncover the terms and conditions. Like, a good example might be: what happens to rewards? Like, rewards on cards are only there because I get this very big headline reward on dining, but then you also spend it on fuel. And if agents are intermediating all of our transactions, and I'm only using the card where I get points, the whole points-reward ecosystem falls apart. Many of these things — anything with a breakage model in it — is going to start to fall apart, and then we will have to have new terms and conditions. So, maybe that's better, maybe that's worse — I don't know, but it'll certainly be different.

VGS 的三个时代

Alex: And maybe — what are you with all of these themes — like, where do you think VGS is going to go? Because, again, I find it so interesting, because it's the world's most boring business around. It's this giant vault that stores all of the payment credentials for everybody who's listening to this podcast — I almost guarantee you have a credential that's stored at VGS, because you interact with the merchant that uses VGS for storage of credentials. So that's a really formidable position to be in, and it's been growing remarkably — just because every merchant needs to store the credentials of the consumers that they work with. But where do you think is the most exciting of everything that we've talked about for VGS's future?

Terry: Yeah. So, I think there's sort of three eras of VGS that are kind of overlapping and compounding.

Era 1 — The Vault: You talked about the first era, which is the vault. This is 10 years of becoming the most trusted store for credentials across the internet. Very hard business to execute on, but that's the privileged position that the company's in.

Era 2 — Information Flow: The second era has been what you talked about — sort of information going into and out of that vault. So, a third of those credentials have to be updated. That's become very interesting and complicated, because each network has their own standard for how you update their credentials, and each network has created multiple network tokens that represent the vault. If you were just storing the information, that would be one thing — but you have to store it, and get a series of tokens from the networks, so that the data is effectively refreshed.

Era 3 — The Network Era: The third era is what we call the network era — which is this role of brokering the credentials among multiple parties in a way that makes sense according to the rules, and that adds value to all of the ecosystem players. And we're sort of starting to do that now with Agentic Commerce. There are other cases where VGS is actually working with the banks on the tokenization front. So, if you're tokenizing the cards and you're storing the cards, you're on both sides of this ecosystem — which allows you to do some of the information swaps that you talked about earlier.

And all of these combine — we'll continue to be a vault, we'll continue to add services, and as we add more services on more merchants and more issuers, we continue to get this network effect, where you can broker credentials among the parties. And I think Agentic Commerce is just fuel into that ecosystem.

结语

Alex: Well, Terry, this has been fun down memory lane. One of these days we should do — did we ever — I think we actually did a history of TrialPay one, a long time ago.

Terry: Yeah, I think we should redo it. It was one of the first podcasts that we did — the studio wasn't as nice. But I think what's consistent between that first podcast and this one is: you should be buying more flowers for your wife.

Alex: Yes. I think that's a great idea. All right, well, thank you very much.

Terry: Thank you for having me.

## 从"旁观者"到"行动者"：代理商务的本体论转变
Terry 用了一个极其克制但意义深远的词：代理从 **spectator 变成了 actor**，而让这个转变成立的不是智能提升，而是一张能支付的卡。这是整个访谈最被低估的洞察——**智能并不等于能动性，能动性来自于"能让你损失钱"的权力**。一个能推荐却不能付款的 AI 本质上和一本百科全书没有区别；而一旦它能从你账户中划出资金，它在法律、伦理、经济上都变成了一个新物种。这意味着整个"AGI 什么时候到来"的辩论可能走错了路——AGI 的真正门槛不是 benchmark 分数，而是**支付凭证的信任边界**。有趣的跨界联系：这与"法人"的诞生惊人相似。现代公司之所以成为公司，不是因为它有多聪明，而是因为它能签合同、能被起诉、能持有财产。代理商务正在悄悄地让 AI 获得类似"法人"的功能性人格。
## 拉斯维加斯三步验证法：代理时代最被忽略的债务
Alex 顺手讲的一段"珠宝店-拉斯维加斯"类比值得单独放大。传统交易验证有三步：**卡是真的吗？人是卡主吗？人神志清醒吗？** 代理商务已经解决了前两步（network toke

item.title: [Lex Clips] Trying the famous Taiwanese oyster pancake | Lex Fridman and Jensen Huang in Taiwan
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、黄仁勋的"反向明星经济学"：当CEO成为地理坐标

最出人意料的观察是：这段视频表面是美食纪录片，实则记录了一个"人即地标"的奇特现象。摊主说"黄仁勋一两天前来过，很多人是因为他才来的"——注意这里的因果链被颠倒了：通常是名人去打卡网红店，而这里是一个CEO把一个夜市摊位变成了朝圣地。

这与硅谷常见的"名人效应"有本质不同。扎克伯格、马斯克去哪里吃饭，媒体关注的是"他们"；但黄仁勋在台湾，关注的焦点被转移到了他身边的供应链、工程师、台南小吃上。他成了一个"注意力转发器"——把全球对AI的关注，重新路由到了实体世界的毛细血管里。这是一种罕见的反向名人经济学：明星不是终点，而是渠道。

二、"愚蠢惊人"的语言失效时刻——与量子物理学的隐秘共鸣

Lex两次说"Stupid amazing"，然后承认"你无法解释这个（You can't explain this）"。这个瞬间比视频里任何技术讨论都更有哲学分量。

跨领域连接：这与物理学家费曼谈量子力学时的态度惊人一致——"如果你以为你理解了量子力学，你就没有理解它"。真正的巅峰体验（无论是夜市小吃还是物理现象）都有一个共同特征：语言在它面前失效，而失效本身成为验证。

更深的隐藏模式是：黄仁勋带Lex吃的不是"最好的食物"，而是"最无法被工业化复制的食物"——牡蛎煎、刨冰、现场的油烟与喧哗。在他本人正在建造一个4000人的AI硬件大楼、把世界推向极致可复制的时代，他却选择在"不可复制性"中招待朋友。这是一种潜意识的工程师悖论：造标准化的人，最珍视非标准化的东西。

三、"包装工程师"的禅意——被你忽略的那句最深刻的话

全程最被低估的一句话，是黄仁勋平静地列出：

"供应链。很多系统工程师。运营工程师... 包装工程师，测试工程师，运营工程师。"

西方科技媒体永远在谈"AI研究员"、"芯片设计师"，但黄仁勋在台湾的一千人团队里，特意点名"包装工程师"。这不是口误——这是台积电—英伟达联盟的真正密码。

让我把这个连接拉到意外的远处：日本的"职人文化"里有一个概念叫"地味な仕事"（朴素的工作）——寿司店里剥虾、磨山葵的人往往比捏饭团的师傅资历更老。台湾的半导体封装产业就是这种"地味な仕事"的工业规模化：全世界都盯着7纳米、3纳米的光刻机，但真正把一颗GPU从晶圆变成能装进服务器的东西，是无数"地味"的工程师。

真正的洞察：黄仁勋在夜市排队吃牡蛎煎的姿态，和他列出"包装工程师"时的语气，本质是同一件事——对"看不见的中间层"的尊重。这才是英伟达为什么是英伟达，而不仅仅是"AI浪潮中最幸运的那家公司"。整个供应链文明，正在以一种食物的、烟火气的方式，被这段视频无意间揭示。

📝 转录文本

偶遇与"限量版"衣柜

Lex: Going back out there for some shaved ice. Once more to the breach.

路人/粉丝: HEY, THAT'S ME.

[laughter]

Lex: YOU HAVE A VERY LIMITED WARDROBE.

Jensen: Limited suggests there's more than this.

Lex: More than one.

黄仁勋效应——"他本来就是这个地方的一部分"

Lex: Jensen was here I think a day or two ago, and a lot of these folks came here because he was here a couple days ago. And now they're like, I did— we didn't expect you to also. He comes with the place basically.

Jensen: First time?

Lex: That is incredible.

Jensen: Stupid amazing, right?

Lex: Stupid amazing is right. Yeah, yeah.

[laughter]

Lex: I know. You can't explain this.

Jensen: No.

Lex: People tried to explain it to me. Not even close. Not even close. Beyond amazing. This is joy.

台湾的工程军团：一千人与一栋新楼

Lex: Is there— is there a lot of engineering team that's local to Taiwan?

Jensen: A thousand. A thousand. Supply chain. A lot of systems engineering. Operations engineering.

Lex: Did you try this one?

Jensen: Our family.

Lex: It's— it's really mild flavor.

Jensen: Packaging engineers, test engineers, operations engineers.

Lex: So, all those super legit hardware folks.

Jensen: Yeah. We're going to build a building. Just like the building you were in.

Lex: Mhm.

Jensen: Almost a replica.

Lex: Mhm.

Jensen: Except— so down here. A piece of land. That building will hold 4,000 people. So, 100 million dollars worth of—

刨冰、脑冻与一份意外的礼物

Lex: Wow. Brain freeze.

Jensen: Yeah.

Lex: Given the heat outside, it's nice.

Jensen: Mhm.

Lex: Oh my goodness.

Jensen: This one's a gift.

Lex: Oh wow. This is very good. Pineapple with guava. No wonder they— no wonder they get the doctors to us.

Jensen: They wanted you to try something new. They're sampling. They're expanding the market.

[laughter]

Lex: I think. Yeah.

终极目标：著名的台湾蚵仔煎

Jensen: This is— this is the famous oyster pancake. Thank you. Oh. Crazy good, right?

Lex: So good.

Jensen: Yeah. They're all in there. Two oysters in there.

Lex: Did you oyster— did you do it oyster?

Jensen: Yeah.

Lex: Okay. Amazing. I'll go in for seconds. Oyster— famous Taiwanese oyster pancake. Amazing.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [Bg2 Pod] Jensen Huang | Does AI Revenue Justify Capex, '27 AI Bottlenecks, Singularity, Open vs Closed & more
item.dc:creator: Bg2 Pod
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、容纳框架：黄仁勋把婴儿床变成了AI安全学

最打破常规的洞察藏在他讲"围栏"的那段话里。他说AI安全的核心不是"完美对齐"（那是永恒问题），而是容纳（containment）加带外监控（out-of-band monitoring）加零信任扩展——听起来像前沿安全工程，但他亲口承认：这就是你带一岁孩子的方法，就是你雇新员工的方法，就是你养宠物的方法。

真正让人意外的是：这个"从零信任开始，随置信度扩展边界"的算法，在生物进化中已被独立发明过数十亿次： - 胸腺对T细胞的阴性选择（先关在"游戏围栏"里，确认不攻击自身才释放） - 信用卡公司给你5000额度而不是50万（随还款行为扩展） - 公司试用期（权限随信任递增） - 甚至蜜蜂新工后的分级任务（先在巢内清洁，再出巢采蜜）

黄的隐含主张极其激进：对齐学派在哲学上找新答案，但进化已经解决这个问题几十亿年了。我们不需要新哲学，我们需要抄生物学的作业。 这解释了为什么他对末日论者如此不耐烦——不是因为他不在乎风险，而是因为他认为对方在重复发明轮子，而且是方的。

二、"可替代性教义"：黄仁勋真正的护城河不是CUDA，是选择权本身

表面上他讲TSMC、CUDA、生态——这些大家都知道。但真正令人震撼的是他对"fungibility（可替代性）"的反复强调，这其实是把马科维茨投资组合理论偷偷搬进了半导体经济学。

他的论证链条是： - 专用化是可替代性的敌人 → 定制ASIC是集中押注 - 可替代性是风险的敌人 → Nvidia是指数基金
- 低风险 → 可出租性 → 生产力 → 可融资性 → 最低TCO

这是个翻过来的论证：当你花500亿美元买基础设施，你买的不是性能，你买的是面对未知工作负载时的期权价值。模型架构从Transformer到SSM到Diffusion到混合体——你押不准，但CUDA全跑。

跨领域联想——这其实是塔勒布的凸性原理（convexity）在硅片上的体现：在一个波动性递增的世界里，保留选择权的价值随着不确定性平方增长。所以黄说他的护城河"在扩大"——不是因为技术差距在扩大，而是因为未来变得更难预测，期权价值因此升值。这是真正反直觉的：规模越大、技术变化越快，Nvidia越难取代。

同样的逻辑解释了TSMC为什么拿到他100%的订单——他把自己对TSMC做的事（给我五年的产能可见性和敏捷调整），拷贝到了自己对CSP客户的关系上。这是价值链上的协议传染。

三、"管子里的奶酪"：被低估的美国移民飞轮引擎

这是整场对话里最被忽略的政治经济学观察。黄仁勋讲他父亲1960年代被派去纽约参加Carrier的培训，带回了巧克力和"管子里的奶酪"——然后说"我们应该搬去那儿"。

但请注意他把这件事和当代"五分之六的台上人出生于美国境外"直接并置。这暴露了一个被政策讨论完全忽视的事实：美国的长期人才吸引力，不主要由大学、创业环境或资本市场驱动，而由"文明丰裕感"的实物痕迹驱动——那些能装进行李箱、能带回家乡展示的"未来证据"。

跨领域连接：这与人类学里的"货物崇拜"（cargo cult）有着镜像结构，只不过方向相反——人们不是因看到飞机投下罐头而建假跑道，而是因看到罐头而真的建造前往罐头源头的生命路径。1960年代的奶酪管触发了黄仁勋的移民，这个移民造就了Nvidia，Nvidia造就了AI基础设施。

让人出一身冷汗的问题：今天AI时代的"管子里的奶酪"是什么？ 哪个国家的青年打开手机看到的东西，会让他五十年后把一个万亿美元公司的总部放在那里？如果答案不再是"美国制造的消费品"，而是"中国制造的消费电子+抖音算法+DeepSeek的开源模型"——那美国的人才飞轮引擎可能已经在不知不觉中改变了方向，而政策讨论还停留在H-1B签证数额上。

四、凯恩斯悖论的AI复现：你永远等不到15小时工作制

黄仁勋对凯恩斯1930年预测的回应极其精彩——凯恩斯预测对了经济增长（8倍），预测错了人类（本该15小时周工作制，实际我们工作80小时）。

但这里有一个他没明说的、更阴暗的推论：AI的生产力红利不会给你休闲，它会提高进取者的边际回报，从而让勤奋者更勤奋，差距更大。

这其实是凡勃仑式"炫耀性闲暇"反转为"炫耀性进取"。在零成本智能的世界里，不用AI的人闲下来了，但用AI的人工作更多——因为AI让他们每个决策的杠杆放大了100倍。1小时的高杠杆工作创造的价值超过80小时的无杠杆工作，所以理性选择是继续工作80小时的高杠杆版本。

跨领域呼应：这与Transformer架构本身的历史完全同构——注意力机制没有减少计算需求，反而让计算需求爆炸性增长，因为每个性能提升都解锁了更多"值得解决的问题"。人类认知似乎遵循同样的定律：解锁的智能越多，看到的问题越多，野心越大。

最意外的推论：如果黄对了，那所有关于"AI会让大家失业从而有闲暇"的焦虑都搞错了方向——真正的危机不是失业，而是进取心的两极分化：有野心的人进入一个无止境加速循环，没野心的人被甩开到无法追赶的距离。这不是失业问题，是存在意义问题。

五、被遗忘的四分之三：AI叙事本身被严重扭曲

一个几乎被所有报道忽略的黄仁勋承认：Nvidia的算力中，只有约四分之一服务于前沿实验室（OpenAI、Anthropic等）。另外三分之一是"经典计算"（分子动力学、风控、推荐系统、模拟），还有三分之一是数千家垂直领域初创公司。

这意味着整个关于"AI泡沫"的讨论，是在用全部资本支出的担忧，去质疑其中25%的收入模型。这是一个认知比例错配——好像有人看到一座城市，只看见市中心的三栋摩天大楼，然后争论"这三栋楼支撑不起全城的房价"。

跨领域联想：这与18-19世纪铁路泡沫叙事高度相似——人们记得泡沫破了，但忘记了铁路本身没破；破的是对特定几家铁路公司的估值，不是对运输网络本身的需求。黄仁勋在重复提醒投资者的，本质上是：不要用对OpenAI估值的担忧去评价对计算基础设施的需求，这是两个独立问题。

I might choose one or two or three of them, roll them out, prune the rest of it, and then you just keep on doing this.

And you know, people — we do this. That's the reason why we say great strategists love strategic optionality. You don't want to prune things too fast on the one hand, but you also have to optimize your resources. Well, AIs are doing that. They're keeping their strategic optionality. They're rolling things out. They're reflecting, they're pruning, and so on and so forth.

The first part of it is — they say some people say that AI is uncontrollable because it's impossible to align perfectly. Alignment means this, for all the audience: you tell somebody, "I want you to do this." And so the mission is clear. The mission is clear, and it's clear to you because you said it in English.

It could be, "I want you to solve this quadratic equation." And so the mission is to solve the quadratic equation. The alignment is: how do you do it? There are many ways to do it. For example, you memorized it. The answer is, whatever it is. Or you saw the answer in a textbook, so you looked it up. You referred to a reference. Or you went to a drawer, and that drawer had all the answers. You open a drawer, you picked out the answer. Some people call that cheating. I call that opening the drawer and retrieving the answer. And that's what computers do.

There's a lot of different ways you could solve that problem. Now of course that one is very explicit. Here's another one: "Be successful in life." The mission is easy to say, and in fact we say it to each other all the time. We say it to our children. We say to our friends: "Let's do our best to contribute to society."

Well, now the question is how. There are so many ways. How do you reasonably align? And everybody's culture and background — some people think that contributing to society means to be generous, to be kind. Some people might mean that contributing to society means make a lot of money and then be philanthropic. Some people might think that building a company alone, or doing something alone, is a sufficient contribution to society. Creating a beautiful piece of art, or — all of it is true. And so the question is, what's the alignment? It just depends on your background, your culture, maybe something to do with where you live, where you came from. There's just infinite number of ways.

And so my point is this: alignment is going to be a forever problem. If we depend on perfect alignment in order to ensure safety, then we're never going to get there.

And so the answer is this. The way we treat — the way we think about babies, and when we're raising kids, and we have pets, or employees — you start with containment. You give them the rights, the access to tools, the access to information, the access to whatever responsibility, capabilities that they have, funds, resources. You give them access based on the job that you ask them to do.

You start out with zero trust. When you hire somebody, you start out with zero trust. When you have a baby that's one year old, you put them in a playpen. You assume zero trust. You give them minimum rights, and you expand that boundary as you learn more.

And so whenever we have a new AI, we have to assume the same thing. Whenever you're testing an AI: zero trust, minimum boundaries, minimum rights, and you expand it as you test and give yourself confidence. So containment, very tight containment, is really important to any autonomous system.

The part that people are trying to extrapolate — the $100 billion of ARR or $125 billion where they are, they're trying to extrapolate — is a small part. Not a small part — it's just a part of the overall infrastructure buildout. For sure.

And so the question is: are people going to continue doing shopping online?

Brad： You know, that third of the buildout — let's call that a third. You say it's a third of your business.

Jensen： Take that to the bank.

Brad： Right. Like that's not even a debate. So a third of the —

到十年末：每年 3-4 万亿基础设施

Jensen： I said a couple years ago that as we exit this decade, infrastructure buildout will probably be somewhere between 3 to 4 trillion a year. Obviously, it's closer to four than it is closer to three. Per year. By the end of the decade.

And if you said that one and a half trillion of that was just compute — just compute. Now, why is it going to be so big? Well, it was half a trillion before AI started. And if I told you that over the course of some six, seven, eight years, it became one and a half trillion because the world's just consuming more compute — I mean, that's not illogical.

On top of this, remember, Moore's law is over. There was a time if you want to get twice as many transistors, you just wait one year. And if you want twice as many transistors, get another — wait one year. Same price. But if you want twice as many transistors now, doesn't matter how long you wait, you have to pay twice as much. Because Moore's law is over.

And so whatever computing capacity that the world wants, every single year, if you want twice as much, you're going to pay twice as much. And so on top of that half a trillion dollars that was growing just naturally because the world just used more and more digital, you're going to have to effectively give it an X factor just to account for the fact that Moore's law is over.

And so without AI, the semiconductor industry was on its path to become the largest industry in the world. And I've mentioned that long ago. Just people forgot.

Brad： It's just one of those things that I said. Yes.

Jensen： I just said that two years ago. And so that's just one part. And then — don't forget, because we're in a new computing platform shift, there's going to be a whole lot of startups. Innovation is part of the economy. New companies. And we said it's accelerating.

If you go back to Moore's law, general-purpose compute, $5 billion per gigawatt. Today it's 50. For a Vera Rubin. So the question is: is Vera Rubin delivering 10x more valuable in the world?

So the punch line is: I don't think it's necessary to extrapolate any of the labs into multiple trillions of dollars. Unnecessary to do that.

两个实验室无需承担万亿压力

Brad： It's an important one, because I think — we just saw yesterday, even in the market, some chatter about: was OpenAI's revenue 70 billion or 50 billion? I think you and I —

Jensen： They're going to be insanely successful companies.

Brad： Correct. But you saw the pullback in a lot of the infrastructure companies on the fear that: oh my gosh, OpenAI doesn't have the money, won't have the money in order to pay for the infrastructure. I think the point that you're hammering home is that when we look at the 40 gigawatts of infrastructure buildout next year, at least a third of it is just going to right general-purpose compute replacement — the basic stuff out of the hyperscalers. A third of it's going to kind of neo-cloud sovereigns, enterprises, everybody else who's using this, all the startups. And a third of it's going to not two labs, but many labs, including Grok and Thinking Machines and all the others.

Jensen： We're putting way too much pressure on two labs. I'm delighted to partner with them and support them. They're going to be two of the most consequential technology companies ever built in history. They're going to be magnificently successful. But they don't have to be anywhere near a trillion dollars in revenues to be successful.

And I think we're putting way too much pressure on that. And then the rest of the industry — we still do have to build out a few trillion dollars of computing infrastructure.

小插曲：话梅

Brad： Just to keep going — let's shift a little. How good is this, you guys? By the way, what are these called?

Jensen： These are dried plums.

Brad： Dried plums. The old dried plums.

Jensen： Yeah. This one particular store in Taiwan is one of my favorites.

Brad： Kind of a licorice-y.

Jensen： There is licorice. A little licorice-y. Salt, sugar, cinnamon.

Brad： Has a little twang to it.

Jensen： Yeah. You got it.

订单簿：需求远超供给

Brad： You said as to next year, demand for Nvidia's chips well over 100%. You guided to 70% revenue growth. You gave a year-forward look because you said supply's constrained.

Jensen： That's all I had at the time.

Brad： That's right. You said, "I got 18 months to work here."

Jensen： Right.

Brad： You said you were very confident.

Jensen： Don't come to work every day —

Brad： You said very confident and plenty of time to work with the supply chain to do even better. You expected to do even better and to not disappoint customers. So are things going even better? And has the order book continued to grow? Because the other part of that is right, you took a snapshot at a moment in time, and of course people are continuing to place orders. So do you think there's enough slack in the supply chain, you can squeeze more out, and is the order book continuing to grow as more of these capabilities are unlocked?

Jensen： The first — let me tell you why I told everybody. The challenge that we have is we had giant order books. Every single CSP, every single NCP, every single OEM had already placed orders on us. Startups, big companies, small companies, they already placed orders on us. And the reason for that is because we work with them on — depending on the size of the customer, at least a year, for the largest ones, two years forecast. And so we already have a very large order book. And because I was in the process of allocating, and what I was allocating to all of our customers is a lot less than they wanted — if I didn't publicly say what we had, everybody would be second-guessing: "Are these short-changed, are we being...?" And so it was my way of essentially handling every single conversation where I'm disappointing people.

Um, so pretty much every customer would buy more from you if you could deliver more.

Brad： By far.

Jensen： And then since then, of course, we have new orders almost weekly and daily. In addition, however, we're getting more supply. And some of the supply that is limiting us is land, power, shell downstream.

Brad： Correct.

Jensen： And so a couple weeks ago we announced 2 gigawatts in Australia. That's a very big deal. 2 gigawatts to us is like $80 billion. Huge. And then I'm hoping when I go to Europe with UTC, we'll be able to announce some new partnerships there and unlock more land, power, shell.

下游与上游的双重约束

So this land, power, shell is clearly one of the obstacles, and this is an area where Nvidia has a huge advantage. Based on what we build, if there's a neo-cloud, and this neo-cloud like CoreWeave or EBS — they would like to scale out their business — Nvidia has the entire full-stack complete AI infrastructure. And so we could support them as their scale out. And so we could build in places and we can build with partners and customers that nobody else can.

I think this gives us a lot more resilience. But nonetheless, as we continue to increase supply upstream and downstream — one of the critical areas is substrate. Substrates are getting larger and there are more chips. And so it's working against them in two ways. Every single chip that's being shipped uses more of the weight of the material. And so these organic materials are really hard to make at the precision that we need, because the packages get larger — the coefficient, the thermal coefficients, and the way we stack things make it really hard to handle things like warpage and various manufacturing defects. At the scale that we do, we have to be very precise, and we need really great partners.

That's supply constraint. And just — those are just some examples. Silicon photonics is supply constrained. So everything is supply constrained. We're going to keep working on — I have 18 months to do so. Every single week that goes by we increase. But nonetheless, every — we keep increasing more supply and the order book keeps going up. And so it's going to be hard to close that gap for a few years.

共识预测的大幅低估

Brad： Take a look at this chart.

Jensen： This is like a deposition. No, right? Excuse me now. Usually goes like this: "Mr. Monk. Ex, please please. Now examinate. Please. Now look at exam —"

Brad： Good deposition. Okay. So the gray line, this was the consensus at the start of 2025. This was the consensus for Nvidia at the start of 2025. The blue line was Altimeter's forecast way back then. So we were a lot higher than the consensus line is now, where the new consensus is based upon your guidance. And so one of the things that blows my mind about this is the 25 people who get paid to just forecast what this company is going to do. Their consensus of all their ideas was off by a couple hundred percent. Right? Just at the beginning of 20—

Jensen： Oh, no. This time last year —

Brad： This time last year, not even 25.

Jensen： 25 line.

Brad： Yes, that was the consensus at this time last year.

Jensen： One year ago.

Brad： Last week.

Jensen： Okay. So in a year, the consensus forecast has shifted up by 100 to 200% for this company. Extraordinary. In my 20-plus years of doing this, you don't often see consensus being off by that much. And yet the stock's only up 20%. Okay? You literally doubled what the revenue forecast was and the free cash flow forecast was for the company. You're now trading at 13 to 14 times earnings, depending upon who you're looking at.

So what do you think the market is saying about Nvidia or about the confidence in the expectations of the market to cause that to be the case? Because usually if you see it shift up by that much, the stock would have shifted up by a lot more.

规模与护城河同时扩大

Jensen： First of all, for a company to be as large as us gaining share tells you something about the resilience. And the size and scale of our advantage. And —

Brad： Is that advantage increasing or decreasing? Is your moat increasing or decreasing?

Jensen： Increasing.

Brad： Increasing. Increasing.

Jensen： Your competitive moat is increasing at scale.

Brad： Yeah. Let me give you an example. Let's just do a thought experiment right now.

Jensen： If you had to hand somebody a $100 billion dollar check to place a purchase order right now for a next-generation — if you want to get in line for Vera Rubin Ultra, it's close to placing order time. Sight unseen.

Brad： Wow.

Jensen： Right. But they have the confidence. So let's say there's — you got to place $100 billion on somebody. How do you know it's going to be any good? But because Nvidia builds it, you know it's going to be better than Vera Rubin. And Vera Rubin's awesome. And the reason why — the reason why everybody had confidence in Vera Rubin is because Grace Blackwell was awesome.

And in the world of computing, the workloads that these computers do are so complex, you can't just have, like, measure one benchmark. You know, it's $50 billion. And the number of technologies that have to come together to deliver the performance is insane. And so the question is: sight unseen, who can you place a $50 billion order on? We're literally the only one.

Now, back when it was place a PO, a billion-dollar PO, that was challenging enough. But if you had placed a $100 million PO and the system is sitting right in front of you, you could just benchmark the chips. How do you benchmark these systems? Just building it is a miracle. So if somebody wants to do an evaluation, I'm happy to support it, but you're going to need to give me a giant data center and we're going to need a couple years to retrofit it. And so you can't even benchmark these things anymore.

为何 TSMC 拿到 100% 订单：五年可见性

Brad： Interesting.

Jensen： And so it's exactly what happened with TSMC. The reason why we give 100% of our business to TSMC is because they're the only company in the world that I can plan five years out and know, sight unseen, that transistor is going to be really good, because it's better than that one, better than that one. And that they will have capacity for me, and that they know how to work with my business team, that they have the agility to handle all of my ups and downs. For example, to deal with the fact that I went from gray to blue to green.

Brad： Exactly.

Jensen： They have to be big enough to go help me go from gray to blue to green. There's no other company in the world that could help me do that.

Brad： That's right.

Jensen： And to have all these different process technologies — from silicon photonics to logic to memory, to push-pull packaging. The number of things that we do is so dynamic. And so how do you possibly do that with a company that is one-tenth their size? It's impossible.

基础设施公司的信任溢价

And so I think the big idea is this: because we're building infrastructure for the planet, and Nvidia has become an infrastructure company, and because these infrastructures cost so much money and they're moving and technology is moving so fast — we're practically — the combination of the trust, the fact that we run everything. So it started out with some GPT models, but look at the flash attention mechanisms that were invented. The way that we parallelized the models and sharded across MVLink 72 and how all of that changed changed. And now people are talking about transformer-diffusion models that are hybrid SSMs that are transformers hybrids — all these different technologies. The evolution of all that, we know that it all runs on CUDA.

It is the only — we don't know whether you need to do more pre-training, post-training, or just agentic inference. Well, it turns out we run it all anyways. And so you could build a $50 billion data center and know that the fungibility of the work — and if something were to happen, for whatever reason unknown, you wanted to, if you will, sublease half of your capacity to somebody — Nvidia is completely fungible.

So we're fungible in workload, we're fungible in models, we're fungible across customers, and we're deployable everywhere in the world. You start a company in Europe, you start a company in United States, but guess what — you want to serve customers in Europe, you want to serve customers in Japan. Well, turns out we're already there. Nvidia's infrastructure is already there. So OpenAI wants to go to Europe — we'll take them there in a heartbeat. If they want to go to India, in a heartbeat. If Anthropic wants to go to Japan, Korea, in a heartbeat — we're already there. All of these architectures are already there.

And so I think if you take Nvidia as a whole, and then you come back and you say: "Okay, I want to do the thought experiment. I want to place $100 billion dollars on somebody" — how do you do it?

可替代性教义：专用化是耐用性的敌人

Brad： A year ago we were sitting here, and the consensus forecast was that you were going to be flat or shrink in 2027. Now the consensus forecast you're going to grow 74%. Okay, so you know — I just want to let that sit in, because a lot of people follow these consensus forecasts, and it was really wrong.

Jensen： Did they go back and listen to your podcast from last time?

Brad： Right. You told them.

Jensen： Yeah. I explained everything. Listen, ladies and gentlemen, I did explain everything.

Brad： And so I look out at 2029 —

Jensen： There was an ROI question. And then there was this custom — yeah, custom versus general purpose. The reason why Nvidia is general purpose is so I can have all this fungibility.

Brad： That's right.

Jensen： The benefit of fungibility is low risk. And low risk really comes into play when you're placing big dollars. When you're building out $50, $100 billion worth of infrastructure, you need to know that that infrastructure is going to be really good for a long time. No matter what.

So specialization is the enemy of fungibility. Specialization is the enemy of durability. And so, so long as I can prove that our performance is extraordinary — and we prove that every single day — the moment we can prove that, then fungibility and durability translates to rentability, which translates to productivity and financeability. And therefore financeability which leads to the lowest TCO.

Brad： Right. Exactly.

两条新成长曲线：软件授权与收入分成

Jensen： Well, now, you're buying back the largest amount in history. On my math, you could probably buy upwards of 10% of the company back within the next two years. At Goldman, you called Nvidia the first growth-value company.

Jensen： Is that right?

Brad： Yeah.

Jensen： Or more.

Brad： Yeah. Or that they could return the capital.

Jensen： It worked for sure.

Brad： It worked. Went from — at the time $30 to 300. 300-plus.

Jensen： And in a lot of ways, we're going through a similar transition. For example, the thing I did — I forgot to mention, and Brad, I think you were about to ask me about that — most of our investment and financing partnership strategies is trying to set up two new business models:

软件授权

One business model we've been working on for some time and will be accelerated in the near future is software licensing. The body of software that we have in our company is just extraordinary. And that data center is so large. Imagine all the software that runs in it. And we provide the entire stack. Our entire stack is completely industrial strength for the CSPs. They want to run their own stack. And so we license — or we give them our software open source, and then they take it and they modify it and they integrate into theirs, and then they operate their services.

But for a lot of the world's companies, they don't have the IT department, they don't have the software department to do it. So they need me to maintain it. And so because AI in the last several years was largely focused on training, but now they're moving into deployment, they need to operate these as factories, and they need to know that I'm on the hook. I'm on the SLA to support it and maintain it, keep it secure, keep it safe for as long as we shall live. And so software license for enterprise business will be very, very large.

And so if our software license is just roughly — for simple math — a couple of thousand dollars per GPU per year, and we have millions of GPUs. We ship 20 million GPUs, say, a year. I'm growing. And so half of it goes into world's enterprise. It adds up.

Okay. And so I'm fairly certain this is going to be a very big part of our business — software license.

收入分成

And then of course there are some clouds that rely on Nvidia for our full stack. They rely on us for our offtake, our ecosystem. They also rely on us for maybe as an investment partner in helping them secure their financing and capital. They've secured land, power, shell. They're regional champion. They got all kinds of stuff working in their advantage. But these three areas they need our support on.

And so in those kinds of relationships, it's very likely that we'll move to rev-share. And so we'll make an investment. We'll get the benefit of the sale up front, but we'll also have the benefit of rev-share going forward. And so we're not a cloud service provider, but we're going to be providing offtake and providing software support for them for four, five, 10 years. And so we ought to get some economic return on that. And so rev-share.

Notice I just described two new growth vectors independent of the hardware sale of our company, and it's much more related to the install base of our platform. What's the benefit of software licensing if you have no install base? And how could you have rev-share if there's no offtake?

回购与投资：现金流的分配

Brad： And so the install base element, the richness of our software stack, the offtake, the richness of our offtake and the ecosystem that we have around the world — that's going to fuel that.

One of the ways — so we're talking about this trading at 13 times. You know, when Tim and Luca went to see Warren Buffett, one of the reasons that Buffett has said he doesn't like technology companies is they have this hit, they produce an enormous amount of free cash flow, and rather than ever giving any of it back to the shareholders, they go and spend it on something else. And oftentimes the something else isn't as good as the thing that caused them to generate the cash flow in the first place.

You guys are now spending over 50% of your free cash flow buying back your stock, effectively returning it to shareholders, while you have this exponential growth at the same time. As we've already discussed —

Jensen： We said 50. I think this last quarter we did 60-some odd.

Brad： Correct.

Jensen： Yeah. We're going to increase. We invest in really high quality companies as you guys know. And the last couple of years, whoever Nvidia buys from — whoever Jensen's buys from — you got to invest in that company. That's right. And now the new word on the street is: whoever Jensen invests in, you invest in that company. And it's true.

And the reason for that is because, like you, we're in the ecosystem. We're in the flow of information. We know those investments together. And we know a lot of smart people, and we want to back these people when they want to do something great. So we're kind of in on the inside. We have a lot of information. And so our investments are well-informed. And not to mention, Nvidia is also in the ecosystem, and so we could help them succeed. That's right. So there's a lot of different reasons why the investments turn out great.

But as a percentage of our total cash generation, it's going to decline very rapidly, partly because OpenAI and Anthropic isn't going to come around again. That opportunity is not going to come around again, frankly. And then secondarily, our cash flow generation is growing quite fast.

耐用性：重新架构全球计算

Brad： And to that point, it seems to me that if you're buying back that much, and the durability of the revenues — I think as you've described here today — is longer than people expect. And I think that's the one place people are still hanging too much on. "This is only going to last as long." Ezra asked you this on the pod the other day: "How long until the bubble bursts?" And I think you said something about 2 to 3 years. You have good visibility that the demand is there, and who knows kind of after that. And I heard some people saying, "Oh, it may only be two years before this bursts."

But when I look at this, like, this is fundamentally a rearchitecture of all global compute forever.

Jensen： Forever. So unless there's a global depression — then every single year people are going to have to consume an enormous amount of Nvidia compute. And so the way to think about that is — we were running — the CSPs were running about half a trillion. The whole industry, the whole world is running call it a trillion dollars of buildout each year. And every year more gets built, and every 5 years or so some gets depreciated or turned off and taken offline, and some of it lasts longer.

So that old world was in the retrieval way of doing computation. In the new way of doing computation, I've predicted that going out of the decades. So three, four — let's say four, let's say five. And my sense is that we're going to continue to grow from there. If you told me that the annual capacity building, infrastructure building, refreshing — combination of new and old refreshes — runs around $10 trillion dollars, I'm not even a little bit surprised.

Brad： Just again for people listening — you think $4 trillion of annual spend by the end of the decade, because every time you consume tokens, every time you use intelligence, you have to run the machine, the factory has to run. And I think you've described that's about 50% — if you assume that $50 trillion of global GDP is related to knowledge work, if we get a 20% productivity gain over 5 years on that, like you've seen inside Nvidia — you've seen much bigger productivity gains inside Nvidia — but if we see that sort of productivity gain, then if we get $10 trillion of incremental economic activity by 2029-2030, that seems very reasonable. And you're just saying we'll spend half of that on capex, on the intelligence to produce it.

收尾：乐观的未来与人类的能动性

And so maybe that's a good place for us to take a bit of an offramp. You've been incredibly generous. I could go on forever. But I kind of want to wrap where we started.

Jensen： If this was one of those eating-drinking podcasts, we could keep going.

Brad： We could keep going. But it wasn't so long ago that the human condition was described as "nasty, brutish, and short." Was that last week? Innovation has really driven all human progress mostly in the last 200 years. More time with family, longer lives, less time doing drudgery that humans really didn't want to do. Safer.

Jensen： We're the first generation where 63 years old is considered young.

Brad： Exactly. Exactly. When people still got, you know —

Jensen： People call me young man.

Brad： Safer, better lives. All of this despite all of these concerns that you and I hear out there. By the way, those same concerns were expressed at the beginning of the industrial revolution.

What's your level of confidence that in 5 years from now, we will have made the right decisions and the world will be that much better place, that we describe, because of the investment and all that we're doing? Are you more confident as we sit here today than you were 12 months ago?

Jensen： I'm 99.99% — just in honor of a good friend, not using zero and 100 — I'm 99.99% confident that too many of us care deeply that the outcome turns out well. That we will dedicate our might, our intellect, our resources to ensure we get there responsibly and optimistically.

And so there's just so many people doing the right things. Oftentimes there are people who pontificate about these things, and they're informed by several things, and they don't realize that there are a lot of people, industries, incredible researchers and engineers outside of their sphere of information that are doing amazing things all by themselves, independent of them. Just because they didn't say — they didn't say — doesn't mean a lot of smart people are doing smart things.

And I say this all the time inside the company: even without my leadership, without strategies, the company is doing smart things all by itself. Smart people do smart things. They do more impactful things when you organize them, but amazing people are doing smart things all by themselves.

And so when somebody tells me that you're worried about — it's good that we worry. And we should express our worries. We should express our concerns. But we shouldn't predict the end of the world. Because they're underestimating the human condition. They're underestimating the human capacity. And they think, for some reason — maybe it's just hubris, maybe it's arrogance — that unless they do it, it won't get done.

The fact of the matter is this company is doing amazing things whether I say it or not. Okay. And I, you know, I get all the accolades and the blame — but in both cases, I'm fair, especially the accolades. The reason for that is, when you surround yourself with amazing people and you create the conditions by which everybody wants the same outcome — the good outcome, the good version of it — and I think most people do. That's the reason why I say we need to hold ourselves accountable and responsible. But we should express a future that's optimistic. For sure.

And I am 99.99% certain, that surrounded by all the amazing people in the world, we're going to get there together.

Brad： Yeah, agreed. It's a — I think you're a national treasure. We're lucky to have you helping to lead the charge. The nation's indebted to you for getting everybody together, getting us all on the same page, building the framework. There's going to be more work to do. But as a father of two — and I know you have kids, you're going to have grandkids — we don't care about anything more.

Jensen： That's right.

Brad： Than actually building a better world for them. We could easily stop. But if we stop today, we lose. We lose the opportunity of that better world. So we'll wrap it there. Thank you, Jensen.

Jensen： Thank you, guys. And Brad, thank you for — I've never met a greater patriot, somebody who cares so much about the industry — but even more so the country — and your gift, your enthusiasm, and just tireless energy in coordinating, pulling together a lot of people in order to do something great like what you did. Incredible.

Brad： As a reminder to everybody, just our opinions, not investment advice.
