item.description:
## 一、容纳框架：黄仁勋把婴儿床变成了AI安全学
最打破常规的洞察藏在他讲"围栏"的那段话里。他说AI安全的核心不是"完美对齐"（那是永恒问题），而是**容纳（containment）加带外监控（out-of-band monitoring）加零信任扩展**——听起来像前沿安全工程，但他亲口承认：这就是你带一岁孩子的方法，就是你雇新员工的方法，就是你养宠物的方法。
真正让人意外的是：这个"从零信任开始，随置信度扩展边界"的算法，**在生物进化中已被独立发明过数十亿次**： - 胸腺对T细胞的阴性选择（先关在"游戏围栏"里，确认不攻击自身才释放） - 信用卡公司给你5000额度而不是50万（随还款行为扩展） - 公司试用期（权限随信任递增） - 甚至蜜蜂新工后的分级任务（先在巢内清洁，再出巢采蜜）
黄的隐含主张极其激进：**对齐学派在哲学上找新答案，但进化已经解决这个问题几十亿年了。我们不需要新哲学，我们需要抄生物学的作业。** 这解释了为什么他对末日论者如此不耐烦——不是因为他不在乎风险，而是因为他认为对方在重复发明轮子，而且是方的。
## 二、"可替代性教义"：黄仁勋真正的

item.title: [No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups] Revolutionizing Cybersecurity and AI-Driven Science with OpenAI President Greg Brockman
item.dc:creator: No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"美学过滤器"：当AI的证明比人类更"人性"

Brockman 几乎顺带提到了四色定理——那个数学界的"丑证明"：机器穷举、人类看不懂、问题"解决"了却毫无美感。但他对当前这波数学突破的描述反而是"令人惊讶的洞见"、"为什么把这个结果用在了那里"。

这里藏着一个反直觉的现象：相比上一代计算机辅助证明（更"机器"），今天的 LLM 产出的证明反而更接近人类审美。原因很简单却很少被点破——GPT 的训练数据里包含了几百万份人类数学家的"品味梯度"（哪些证明被反复引用、哪些被当作典范教学、哪些被誉为"优雅"）。换句话说，神经网络正在把人类的美学偏好作为搜索启发式在用。

这与 AlphaGo 的"第37手"故事构成一个奇妙的对称：当年人类觉得丑，后来重估为美；今天 AI 产出的数学让领域专家惊呼"妙"。一个合理的推论：AI 不是在摧毁数学的美感，而是在把数学的美感"规模化生产"——这是一个几乎没人在讨论的角度。

二、"软件趋零 → 验证成为全部价值"：一条跨行业的通用物理学

Brockman 抛出了一个会被很多人误解的论断：网络安全支出应该"远远超过"软件支出。听起来像在推销自家 Daybreak 项目，但这其实是一条跨领域的经济规律：

  • 有机食品：生产成本只占售价的小部分，认证/溯源成本才是溢价来源
  • 大宗商品市场：铜就是铜，LME 仓单的可信度才是定价锚
  • 2008 金融危机：次贷本身不是问题，MBS 评级/验证机制崩溃才是
  • 疫苗研发：分子设计成本持续下降，临床验证成本却占了 93%（他自己提到的 15 亿美元药品开发中 14 亿在临床）

一旦生产的边际成本趋近于零（AI 生成代码/药物/内容），可信度（trust layer）就吸走了几乎全部价值。所以 Brockman 不是在说"要买更多安全产品"，他是在说一条物理定律：可复制性越便宜，不可复制的那部分（信任、可验证性、合规）越昂贵。

有趣的二阶推论：OpenAI 自己的商业模式最终会不会从"卖智能"转向"卖对智能的担保"？ 这个方向他没明说，但 Daybreak、formal verification、"25% 工程师停工搞安全"的叙事，都在悄悄给这个转向铺路。

三、"iMac 把手"隐喻：Brockman 不小心承认了 Agency 已经是心理建构

他引用了乔布斯给 iMac 装把手的故事——"让人觉得他们能控制机器"。但请注意他的措辞："feel that they could control the machine"。

把手从来没有真正提高过人对电脑的控制力，它只是让人感到有控制力。Brockman 用这个比喻来谈 AI 和人类 agency，相当于不经意间承认了一个尴尬的事实：当 AI 全面超越人类认知能力后，"人类坐在驾驶座"将主要是一种心理设计，而非技术事实。

他接着的类比更直白——"人类会变得更像 CEO 或董事会成员"。但任何做过顾问的人都知道，董事会的信息完全由管理层筛选和建构，所谓"监督"在信息不对称下常常是仪式性的。

跨领域连接：这与算法交易中的"human-in-the-loop"合规要求惊人相似——监管要求人类审批每笔交易，但交易决策的真实窗口是毫秒级，人类点击"批准"按钮早已是一种合规剧场。AI 时代的"人类主导"可能会沿着同一条路径演化：从真实决策权，退化为规范性仪式。

四、一个几乎没人注意的角度：Dots 是"外化的执行功能"，不是生产力工具

Dots 被描述为"主动的、永远在线的代理"。但真正激进的变化不是任务自动化——那是上一代。它真正做的是接管了人类大脑最昂贵的部分：前额叶的执行功能（会议冲突检测、未完成承诺追踪、时间估算）。

这与五千年前文字外化记忆、算盘外化算力是同一量级的事件，但针对的是"决定做什么"而非"做某事"。

一个很少被提出的问题：当"决定做什么"也外包后，人类的身份锚点在哪里？ Brockman 的答案（"是否快乐、是否你想要的"）其实是把身份锚从能动性转移到了偏好表达——这是一个从"行动者"到"消费者"的身份降维。这或许是整个访谈里他最未被追问的那句话。

📝 转录文本

Revolutionizing Cybersecurity and AI-Driven Science with OpenAI President Greg Brockman

Cold Open

Greg Brockman: To ensure AGI benefits all of humanity — we think that humans should be firmly in the driver's seat, should have control over the future, and this technology should amplify human agency.

When I look at the world we're going to be in, where software in some ways is becoming like... the barrier to entry is becoming so cheap. You don't just want software, right? You want software that is reliable, that is secure, that you can believe in. And so cyber spend, security spend should actually vastly outstrip software spend.

I think that people have not yet really internalized how much the physics around cyber security are going to change. I think there's an opportunity to end up with a much more secure world.

Intro

Hi listeners, welcome back to No Priors. Today I talk with Greg Brockman, the co-founder and president of OpenAI. We discuss OpenAI's latest math results, Astra, and why Greg believes AI can now generate genuinely new knowledge. We get into drug discovery, Dots, and his case for why security spending should actually vastly outstrip software spending — which is quite a claim. Here's our conversation with Greg Brockman.

Host: Greg, thanks so much for doing this.

Greg: Thanks for joining us. Thank you for having me.

What's Most Exciting Right Now

Host: So, every week in AI feels like a year, and a lot's happened this week for OpenAI. You rolled out GPT-6 to over a billion people, which is pretty amazing. There's some really exciting news that you have on the math side. There's all sorts of things undoubtedly that are happening internally. What are you most excited about that's happening right now, both at OpenAI and in the broader AI world?

Greg: Look, I think that in AI I have this belief about how OpenAI operates — that there's this cycling quote of "it never gets easier, you just go faster." And I think that's very much what happens: there's just so much activity, and every time you think you're at kind of peak impact and how things are happening, you realize that there's actually another level that's possible.

And it's not just about any one company. It's not just about any one technology. It's really about we as a world and society all coming together to adopt this technology, get the most out of it, to improve everyone's lives.

The Math Milestone

So I think to me the math results this week represent a real milestone. It's a real moment where — if you think about the fundamental driver of human quality of life improving over past thousand years — it's technology, right? It's scientific advancement. And I think that we now have the ability to massively accelerate scientific discovery.

There's always been this question of: is AI actually able to come up with new knowledge? And at this point, it's just impossible to deny. It is definitively yes, possible. Now, there's still more to go. I think we're not yet coming up with whole brand new theories, but we are able to resolve these hundred-year-old math problems.

And to me, the thing that's very exciting is it's not just about the machine just sort of giving you an answer. It's really: what can a human equipped with these tools achieve that was unthinkable before? The leverage of humans to do whatever you want to do — it's going way, way up.

If you have a math problem you want to go solve, you can solve it. But what about taking that same capability, applying it to biology? What about if you're a small business owner and you want to be able to operate your business? Well, that level of intelligence tuned for that domain — it's just going to mean that almost these sort of unthinkable results that are aligned with your goals, with your desires, is now going to be within the reach of everyone. And that to me is so exciting.

Communicating Advanced Results to Humans

Host: The rate of progress has been pretty amazing too. If I look at it, you used to have problems with arithmetic in early models — I remember people complain, "oh, why can't it do basic math?" And now you're solving these advanced theorems.

As these things continue to advance and this starts to really impact areas of math, physics, materials, etc., is there some need — if these models get so smart — to focus on how to communicate that effectively to people? Because if you look at any field of math, only a very small number of people can ever really adjudicate a theorem that's produced by a person.

Greg: Yes.

Host: Right. And so you kind of have this specialization that happens.

Mathematical Beauty, Invented or Discovered

Greg: Well, and this by the way is something that has always been — I came from a math background, I thought I was going to be a mathematician, and I was very inspired by mathematicians like Galois or Gauss. These people who are working on like a 100-, 400-year time horizon.

I think there's something deeply beautiful about mathematics being about understanding the structure of the universe. And there's always these questions about: is math invented or discovered? In my mind the beauty and the meaning of mathematics — it's not something that is objective in some sense. It's in the eye of the beholder. It's something that appeals to us. And there is some math that's like kind of physical laws — it's about simplicity, and compression theory, complexity theory, and all these things that are maybe more physics. But there's something that is also importantly human about it.

Beyond Incomprehensible Proofs

So to me, a lot of the conversation about mathematics is not just about "here's a proof, no one understands it, great, we resolved the problem." It's really about: what are the insights that are derived?

The thing I think we will see — and I think that there's promising signs of life on — is that there's beautiful insights within the work that these AIs have done. We published about almost 400 very important open problems that are now resolved, and the mathematical community is going through all of that to look for insights.

If you read some of the things that people have posted — domain experts in these particular problems — they say that there's these almost like very surprising ways of applying ideas. "Why did they use that result over here?" What's coming out is not these incomprehensible theorems or proofs — which by the way, there is a history of incomprehensible proofs in mathematics. The four-color theorem is a perfect example of this: it's like, okay, we just had the machine check a bunch of cases.

Host: Like there's no beauty in that.

Greg: And so I think we're into a different phase of machine discovery.

Theory of Mind and the Rising Tide of Understanding

Host: I have some optimism that as models also get to better theory of mind — the ability to figure out what we as humans know, and how to get us to follow them on the path to new understanding — will also be paved. For example, I'm a math person, but at some point in school I stopped learning math. And then I did Math Academy, and then I did ChatGPT to help me learn new math. So I just feel like the expectation for the rising tide of knowledge, what you can expect people to understand, will also be there.

Greg: I think that this is a really important point, and one of maybe the underappreciated benefits that I expect from, and hope for, and we're starting to see from this technology — is helping people know more, understand more, understand each other better, understand the world better.

Debate and Iterative Amplification

There are technical mechanisms that can underly this: you have an AI that's able to go and solve these problems, see all the connections between domains — but how does it actually communicate to you? How do you understand it?

And actually there's even connections to AI safety and alignment on having AIs that we're able to understand what they're doing. So there are techniques that we've been talking about since 2017, such as debate and iterative amplification, which are kind of two sides of a similar coin.

You really think about: if you have AIs that are solving problems that are just too hard for humans to check. For example, summarizing a book is a task that's really hard to check — it's really hard to know, is the summary any good, unless you've read the whole book. So if an AI just gives you a summary of a book and says "this is the summary," is it a good summary or not a good summary? It's pretty hard — unless you have another AI who is trying to prove that the summary is a bad summary.

If that AI comes back and says, "hey, here's this paragraph from the book that I found; it's got clearly a very important plot point and that does not represent this summary" — you don't have to read the whole book to be like, "oh yeah, that's actually a very good argument."

And so you realize there are ways to train the AI that are actually very aligned with having humans be able to have oversight, to be in the driver's seat — which is a fundamental value, a fundamental thing that is important for the future from OpenAI's perspective. But also very much aligned with: can you make the results of an AI be something that means you learn something that is really tuned for the human, rather than just knowledge for some abstract knowledge sake?

From Math to Science: What's Next

Host: For most people, advancements in math theory are still somewhat abstract. Then also, you know, "AI for science" — there's a claim or a belief that it could solve all disease in some number of future years. How do you look forward one step in terms of what we might see in advancements in between?

Greg: Well, I think that we've had a number of years and iterations of this technology to see the shape of what to expect. When you have an AI that is capable in a certain dimension, and if you understand why it got capable in that dimension, then all other fields of human endeavor that have similar properties, you should also expect similar results.

Why Math Worked

So in my mind — why is mathematics something that we've managed to really transform, in the way that we've had such incredible results? Part of it is that our AI is now at a certain level of capability and raw intelligence. Part of it is that you could think of it as: mathematics is checkable. But that's not quite true anymore.

We really started with very checkable problems: here's an arithmetic problem, there's some numeric answer, and so you have an AI that you can train to just check if it got the answer right. But for a proof — different proofs are very hard to check. Formalized proof: okay, yes, that is checkable. But natural language proof, which is what we're really producing here: much, much more difficult.

The Core Insight: Data

But the thing that actually I think is the core insight is really about data. You can get lots of data in mathematics. You get lots of data in theoretical physics. Can you get lots of data in biology? That's obviously something very data-bottlenecked, very difficult.

Now fortunately we also have been working on lots of techniques to be able to work with less data. If you think about what that means — okay, we now have smart models that if there's something where there's a lot of data (and this is the fundamental physics of deep learning: compute, data, algorithms equals capability equals results), we're able to do it in these hard domains where people have spent hundreds of years of our smartest people all trying to solve the problem, and now the AI can solve it. Amazing.

Transferring to Biology

When you transfer that over to biology — and clearly what we want is drug discovery, all these things that are fundamental changes in biology and our understanding of it to improve quality of life — the question will be, and this is not yet resolved: do we have the data? Do we have the ability to get the data?

So what will happen is that we will take these models — these same techniques — and apply them in the biological domain. There are some areas that will fall quickly: we'll just see massive acceleration of things that used to be incredibly painful, now incredibly easy. But there will be other bottlenecks, and there'll be a question of: well, how do we alleviate those bottlenecks?

Some of these, by the way, are not even really about deep biological theory. For example, regulatory filings — huge bottleneck. It takes like a year to write up your whole case for clinical trial and all these things. You can write those things with an AI much more easily.

We're going to have to look at every step of the drug discovery process, and there are going to be places where the fundamental data just does not exist. So then innovations on wet labs, innovation on how you actually do simulations — all of this will become incredibly important. We will see these breakthroughs coming, but it's important to know there are things that are shared with mathematics about scientific discovery, and things that are very different in terms of where the data comes from.

Drug Discovery Deep Dive

Host: You mentioned biology, and I think that's a great example where a lot of the early research — AlphaFold and things like that — were really focused on designing a molecule, or understanding how something binds to each other. And to your point, it takes 15 years to develop a drug. It's $1.5 billion. $50 million or so tends to be preclinical mouse studies — the molecule — and then $1.4 billion-plus tends to be the clinical trial. And so it's also 2–3 years versus another 12 years.

A lot of the early emphasis of these models has been "can the thing mine," versus what are all the other things we have to worry about downstream to actually turn it into a productive thing for human endeavors. How do you at OpenAI currently stack-rank the different areas of scientific endeavor in terms of where you're focused, or where you want to generate more data or more results or more capabilities that others can benefit from?

Why Drug Discovery Is #1

Greg: Look, I think that drug discovery is the most clear and obvious area, if you get to pick one that you want to fully revolutionize — just a place where you're going to really uplift everyone's quality of life. That is just so purely important, and maybe the top one application of AI that everyone's been kind of thinking about for a long time. We clearly got to do it.

And to your point, there's this whole pipeline — it's just so long. I think we're going to find that humans are incredibly bad at biology, incredibly bad at drug discovery. If you think about it, there's this property where for humans, natural language, we're very well suited to it. It's something that very clearly it's very human — it's very well tuned to how we have interacted with the world. Whereas biology, it's totally foreign.

A First-Principles Argument

But for a neural net, I don't really think there's any reason to believe it should be better at natural language than it should be at biology. So the fact we're seeing such incredible results with neural nets in natural language — you're just like, from first principles, you should be able to really crack the language of biology.

So to me, that is number one. It's like, first principles, it should work; in terms of what we're seeing, we're so close on so many axes.

Host: Yeah, it's really exciting.

Greg: I think you can massively increase the parallelism. I think you can decrease so many of these steps in terms of their duration. And by the way, there are many dimensions to drug discovery — for example, N-of-1 diseases. There's even lots of people where the drug to cure their particular condition exists, it's just that it's out there somewhere in the literature. There's a paper, and if you can find that one paper that is relevant to your condition, then you'll be able to cure the person. There's plenty of precedent for it, and this can massively scale up those kinds of operations. So I think that impact in the short run is actually very possible.

But material science — another example. And I think there's a long tail of other domains where we should just see real changes in what is possible for humanity to accomplish.

Regulation and the Physics of Drug Discovery

Host: It seems — just, we think about why a drug might take 15 years to go to market. Part of it is you're doing successively more expensive trials that have a different set of safety considerations, resulting in large-scale human trials. And then these trials today are ordained by regulation, right, for good reason.

It feels like one of the limiting factors — if you believe the technology will work and parts of the data can be acquired or generated — is going to be convincing regulators that we should change the expectations around what drugs are accepted and what the steps are.

Greg: I think there is a moment here. And there's more work to be done to reach this point. But if you can really prove that the physics of drug discovery have changed, then of course it should trickle through to every part of the system.

The Self-Driving Analogy

Even just take a very different example. Think about self-driving cars. So much of how roads operate, and safety, and all these things that are really tuned for human drivers. If you reach a point where self-driving cars are 10 times or 100 times safer than human ones — you've reached that point where AI is actually able to deliver the results in a domain that just are so unambiguously the thing that you want — of course, you should then say: okay, how do we rethink the whole transportation system? Maybe you should have regulation that says you only are allowed to have self-driving cars in certain areas.

There are a lot of potential changes to the way that you think about what is even trying to come out of a system, that needs to trickle back into regulation as well.

Regulatory Arbitrage

And of course regulation is not uniform across the world. There's very different regulations in Australia versus the US when it comes to clinical trials. You're already seeing a lot of people moving their trials to places where the regulatory environment makes more sense for how they want to pursue — what people think is efficacious for them.

Exactly how things should change, I think will depend a lot on what we actually can prove. Is it the case you actually reach the point that you can get better results from a neural net than from actually running a clinical trial? We're not there, yes. But you could imagine we will get there.

Host: But if they were more predictive on efficacy or tox or something, then obviously you should change it.

Greg: Of course. And I think there are areas where I think society should — and I hope will — be very leaned into: what is possible has fundamentally changed, and let's very quickly then reorient around it. And again, you have to really think through all the consequences and all the implications.

If you're thinking about long-term studies of people, the question of "is this neural net actually, in terms of what's predicting the simulation, actually accurate for long-term outcomes" — it's pretty hard to not have at least had one long time tick to correspond to that. But I think that we will see like 80% of what is possible come to fruition very quickly.

Dots: Proactive Agents

Host: You're a little ways out from the Astra release and Dev Day now. Is there anything in terms of how people internally or externally are using some of the new products or capabilities that surprises you?

Greg: Well, I think Dots has really changed how many of us work. And the thing that Dots represents is —

Host: Can you describe Dots briefly?

Greg: So Dots is a proactive agent. It's always on, always working. You stop working, it keeps working.

What My Dot Does

The kind of thing that my Dots does: I have a Dot that's looking out for work that I was supposed to do — like messages I was supposed to send, things I said I would do that I haven't gotten to yet. And I always wake up in the morning, there's like a list of things that I was like, "oh yeah, this is my to-do list."

And it often notices things that I never even asked it to notice. If there's a conflict on my calendar in terms of scheduling, it'll point that out. If it's like, "hey, you actually need to leave this meeting earlier in order to get to the other thing." So it's so contextually aware. It knows what I'm doing with my day. It understands the projects we're working on. It knows what's in my inbox. It knows what's in my Slack. And it's able to integrate across these. And it knows the questions I've been asking about, so it knows what areas are most top of mind for me.

A Change of Form Factor

In some ways what Dots is, is a change to the form factor, not the capability. It's an Astra-level model. It's got its own cloud computer. But that change in that form factor, in a workplace setting, with this level of intelligence — it's a game changer.

Host: And do you have multiple Dots running, or you just have one that's sort of covering all your background tasks?

Greg: I've got one. It's a little owl, is the icon — you can change the icon. And I just sort of do everything across my work life.

Consumer vs. Enterprise Assistants

Host: OpenAI obviously has research efforts, and then a consumer and an enterprise and developer business, platform business today. Do you think there's going to be a separation between, let's say, assistants that help you at work like Dots (which is how I primarily think of it), and then consumer assistants, like the Instincts, Muses of the world?

Greg: I think these things are going to converge, no question. And I think that there are some pressures that are very different in different environments.

The Cost Axis

For a mass market consumer product, really figuring out how to scale and to provide things for free or at very low cost is very important. Whereas in the workplace — if you're a productivity, busy executive, individual contributor, whatever your role is — then it is much easier to say "peak intelligence," and really as long as you're getting returns to paying more, it's worthwhile to throw more compute.

So I think that is the main distinction — it's really around cost. We've seen this in ChatGPT: we put in a lot of effort to have the largest-scale free tier, and bringing things like memory to all of our free users was an incredible endeavor, a real huge engineering effort. It's just very easy to implement the same functionality at much higher costs for a very small number of people.

What we're seeing in the personal assistant workspace is that there are going to be these different market segments where different amounts of compute are going to be expended fundamentally. And sometimes when there's different levels of compute, it then means the product can look a little different. There's just more functionality that's embedded in one versus the other.

Different Use Cases, Same AI

And there's of course different use cases. You think about things like payments and travel and things like that — much more for the consumer. But I don't think there's any fundamental difference. It's really just an AI that's doing things, and it just happens to be like a slight pressure in one way or another.

One of the strengths of OpenAI is the fact that we have 1.2 billion consumers on ChatGPT, and we have also a leading coding and enterprise business. And no one else has both in-house. A lot of our strategies to say "let's unify these" — so we're not competing on two fronts, it's really competing on one front.

I think that this is also the general direction of travel of AI: to blur the distinction between what is consumer, what is enterprise. We're going to have this renaissance of entrepreneurs — we're already seeing it. I imagine you're seeing this very concretely. I know people who are quitting their job to go start companies, who say, "I never would have done it if I didn't have an AI that I knew I could rely on. It could take care of so much of the normal barriers to entry." The distinctions have held for so long — I think they're going to change.

The Future of UI: No UI

Host: So one of the things that traditionally has separated the enterprise and consumer world is how you think about UI. Obviously there's your point on cost and underlying ability to deliver something for somebody at a certain level of fidelity, but the other part of it is just the user interface — often very different in an enterprise setting from a consumer setting. To your point, you're looking towards unifying these layers. You've also been thinking quite a bit about dynamic UIs — that's always been one of the things people have talked about quite early: how do you just dynamically generate a UI that's useful for a user, or in some cases these things kind of move into the background, it's just part of your chat. How do you think UI will evolve for these different use cases?

"The Best UI Is No UI"

Greg: First of all, I think that the best UI is no UI. And I think in AI, that is where we're going. You just want a thing you can talk to. You can speak to it verbally, can talk to it over Slack, iMessage, any of the surfaces. You can call it. And that's literally what you can do with Dots — literally today.

Enterprise Complications

But there are some fundamental differences between a personal setting and a workplace setting. In a workplace, you have an admin. You have kind of your company security team. You have just more stakeholders. It's not just an AI that's for you, that's representing you, that you own and you own its outcomes.

So I think that is the main distinction I see between the enterprise and the home use case. And of course, this leads to product differences as well. Sometimes there are very small things — for example, when we release a new feature, enterprises want control over when it's introduced. So we have admin controls and toggles, and so you can have an experience where there's just less functionality available to you as a result of the fact that it is in the workplace.

That does then change the "well, we need some way to surface that to you." And this comes back to: well, the whole point was that there was no UI. So what does it mean for there to be functionality that's missing, and how do you even surface it and let people know that that's the case? That's an ongoing challenge, and I think that will not magically go away — you need to lean into that complexity.

From Text Box to No Text Box

But yeah, to me fundamentally it's kind of crazy and beautiful if you think about it. The ChatGPT text box — that's where it started. It was a text box. And what we're heading to, there isn't even a text box. That is the AI we were promised.

Levers for Making a UI-less Product Better

Host: When I think about what might make a product that doesn't have a UI better, there's — you tell me — but I think there's: how much compute can I spend on it? How good is the model itself? There's a memory system. There's I-don't-know decisions about behavior. How good are models at being calibrated on how hard they should think about something?

Thinking Fast and Slow

Greg: That's something we're getting very good at. With the release of GPT-6 to everyone, we have the ability now for the AI — if it's going to go think hard about a problem, it actually can give you a quick answer, and then keep thinking, and then give you the more wholesome answer.

Generative UI

And also to the point of "no UI," and to the thing you were saying earlier too: we introduced intelligent UI. So now the AI can do generative UI on the fly. So even though there's no fixed UI, there's no buttons, there's no menus to learn, having an AI that can actually craft the result to be visually exactly what you want —

Like you think about even something like flight booking: you want kind of a complex UI there, so you can see all the different options. For any question you might ask, like "how do I assemble a bicycle" or something, you might want some very bespoke app that normally a person would have gone off and written for a month. And of course you're never going to hire someone to write a one-off app for you to help assemble a bike, but totally fine for an AI to go do that for you in real time, in the moment you need it.

So we're now in a world where the AI is molding itself much more to you. The user interface is becoming exactly the thing you need at the moment you need it. And that is a lot of our focus — we're doing that across every aspect of how we think about the product.

Cybersecurity: The Defender's Window

Host: One of the biggest shifts in the discourse around AI recently has been around cyber, and how do you build secure systems that are resistant to AI-driven cyber approaches. I'm just a little bit curious how you're thinking about that — how are you building guardrails, or how are you approaching the different aspects of cybersecurity?

The Changing Physics

Greg: Well, first of all, I do think the physics of cybersecurity are changing, and we're in what we call the defender's window.

The way that I think about this window is that we have peak frontier AI capabilities that can help defenders secure themselves. They're not broadly diffused yet. But the broadly diffused capabilities are ratcheting — you can see this from each model release to model release, from providers across the world. The capabilities on cyber that are available to everyone are going up.

You're starting to see the leading edges of some of the impacts. For example, in South Korea there were some high-profile hacks of banks that were driven by different models.

Daybreak and Responsible Access

The picture that is so critical is that defenders need to use this time. And so we have been working very hard to be able to responsibly give access through our Daybreak program to defenders, to be able to use our peak intelligence, to use very capable models, to find and fix vulnerabilities in their systems.

One thing that is very important to realize is these flaws have existed. Every line of human-written code, in some ways, you have to ask: is this secure? Was the developer trained in the right way? And you just start to realize that the way in which we built systems were kind of fundamentally insecure, and we always knew it. There's never been a CISO who's been over-resourced.

Host: Yeah. I mean, you can look at XKCD, in the comic of like all the world's infrastructure reliant on like one open source project written by one dude in his basement. Or Heartbleed, or anything that predated all these AI issues.

Tech Debt Comes Due

Greg: Exactly. And I think very importantly, it's very important to realize that these are really human issues. These are the way that we chose to build the internet. Security got kind of bolted on, right? And we had high-profile incidents — you think about early worms and viruses, and then people started to realize, "well, we need virus-scanning software." And "we need encryption for requests over HTTP, should be over HTTPS." All of these mechanisms were ones where I think we kind of took the slower route in order to add security on afterwards. The internet's really been built for resilience, not necessarily for security.

What we're going to see now is a moment where a lot of that debt, a lot of that tech debt, is going to come to the surface. It's time for us to pay it down.

OpenAI's Billion-Dollar Commitment

And as a company, we are really leaning into trying to help with this moment. For example, we have a billion-dollar commitment that we've made to help frontline defenders get access to our models and utilize them for defense, that we're studying and trying to find different vulnerabilities out there. And then thinking about: how do we help the world respond? How do we coordinate incident response? How do we work with government? How do we work with the community in order to land these as well as possible and to help people navigate through?

A More Secure World

I think people have not yet really internalized how much the physics around cybersecurity are going to change. I think there's an opportunity to end up with a much more secure world.

You think about the fact that AI lets you pay down your tech debt in a way that was just previously unthinkable. The fact that you could do things like formal verification of software — these models are obviously great at proving things. Why not prove security properties of software? That's something that the technology has kind of been there, but —

Host: Exactly. No one does it for anything significant.

Greg: So I think all of that can change.

Saturating Vulnerabilities

The world we're moving to right now — and we've done this internally within OpenAI — is: every time a new model drops, you need to apply it to secure yourself, find your vulnerabilities, and then saturate.

For example, we took about 25% of our production engineers and said, "all of your projects are on hold. You are just securing now." Took our peak intelligence model at the time, had it poke at all of our infrastructure, red-team a bunch of things, built some tools so that it's easy to do it again over time. And we found a number of issues, we fixed it, and at some point we saturated the issues that this model was capable of finding.

That's a very good story. The thing to realize is that we're going to have a next model, we're going to have to repeat that process, and that will continue. But at some point — if you think about the code that's being written, so much of it is now AI-assisted — we can actually train these models (and we are training these models) to write secure code from the beginning. So I think we can have fundamentally more secure systems through the use and applications of these AI models in the right way.

A Transitionary Period

Host: So it sounds like basically there's going to be a period of time where maybe we're going to see more of these cyber attacks, more incidents, etc., as humanity, or as people, sort of catch up in terms of their code bases getting more and more secure, using more AI-generated code that's sort of preset to be more secure. And so we'll probably end up with some transitionary period over time where we'll have more offense and defense, and then defense will catch up. I mean, that's kind of the consensus I've been hearing in the industry in general.

Greg: Seems like the most likely forward case, at least.

Host: Yeah.

Greg: Look, I have a lot of optimism about how we can navigate this moment. I think it does require a coordinated response. It really requires defenders to internalize how the physics of cybersecurity are changing — that there is this window; that window is not going to last forever. You should think about: we're shifting to this world where the security of an organization is related to both the fundamentals that they've gotten right (which is kind of one-time investment), but also the level of cyber capability they've used to defend themselves.

As we shift to that world, I think we can be in a world where defenders are able to outstrip attackers. But it is going to take a lot of change — a change in terms of how we think about every organization operating, and how we collectively think about critical infrastructure, and resourcing those that have not had those resources to date.

Security Spending > Software Spending

Host: Your description of this is like "let's say like internet-wide tech debt," and then your response to it internally is a really good one. Because I'm like, okay, I've been part of companies where tech debt is very painful to address, and to say "we're going to take 25% of the engineers," or god forbid, "we're going to do a feature freeze for a quarter until we fix some stuff that really needs to be fixed" — that doesn't feel like the state that the world has decided on quite yet.

When you think about where the entire world is from a security investment perspective, traditionally it's thought of as like, "oh, maybe it's like low-single-digits percent of the IT budget." Like, what do you think it should be at this moment of time? And is it all of this other stuff that you were investing in from a cyber tooling perspective — network, endpoint, traditional corporate security — is less relevant, or we just need to go spend twice as much?

The Big Claim

Greg: I have a feeling that cyber spend, security spend, should actually vastly outstrip software spend. I really think that that's a statement.

Host: Yeah.

Greg: I really believe it. And I may not be right, but when I look at the world we're going to be in, where software in some ways is becoming like the barrier to entry —

Host: Exactly. It's freeish.

Greg: Exactly. It's becoming so cheap.

Host: And so of course —

Greg: You don't just want software. You want software that is reliable, that is secure, that you can believe in. So to me, the resilience of that software is —

Host: That's the value.

Greg: That's going to become even more important.

Fixing the Supply Chain

So I think that we have this moment, we have this opportunity — to your point of the XKCD, with the little block at the bottom of some open source maintainer — that never made any sense.

Host: Mhm.

Greg: The reason we had that world was because of some of this physics, right? Of kind of how hard it is to write software and to write reliable software, and that everyone has this supply chain, and so few companies audit their supply chain. We've seen this with supply chain vulnerabilities, where someone uploads a malicious package and a number of companies get hit.

All of that needs to change, and it was totally impossible to change with human software developers because there's so few people who have this expertise in this very obscure thing — knowing different packages and different security —

Host: Third-party software now, like Socket and others, who will do this. As an example, they'll scan through your open source supply chain and try and find vulnerabilities and identify them for you. Or there's the human element of it, where maintainers would suddenly take over a project and then install something that would be malicious relative to people who are using that package. So it's really interesting to see that shift in terms of the third-party ecosystem as well developing to support the efforts that OpenAI and others are doing in terms of this market.

Coordinated Response

Greg: Exactly. I think it's so important. We're doing this with the community. We partner with companies like CrowdStrike. I think that it is a coordinated response, but we really view it as a core priority for OpenAI to lead — for us to really [lean in], because we have the frontier model, we have the peak intelligence model. Certainly in cybersecurity, we think that there is transformative potential for the good possible.

But that means that we as a company — and we've been going through a security transition. Over the past couple months, we've talked about safety, security, alignment of our development process. But we're also thinking about that for the world: of how to really help the world become more fundamentally secure, and help people through this whole period.

Human Agency and the iMac Handle

Host: One of the things about OpenAI is that it's always been very pro-human and very pro-human agency, human progress. Let's use AI to better everyone. I think the original premise of OpenAI was: let's have something that can counterbalance other companies, in terms of creating AI that can be used very broadly and universally in a positive way. Has that ethos continued at OpenAI, or how do you think about that in the context of the AI community?

Mission and Humanity

Greg: I think that ethos is very core to our mission — to ensure AGI benefits all of humanity. And the humanity there is very key. We think that humans should be firmly in the driver's seat, should have control over the future, and that this technology should amplify human agency, even as models surpass humans in capability.

I think this is absolutely critical. These models are very jagged — there are places where obviously these AIs are more capable than anyone today. Even GPT-4 knows far more than any person.

The Steve Jobs Handle

But the thing that is so important — and I'm reminded, for example, of the story of why Steve Jobs put the handle on the iMac. So that way people could feel that they could control the machine. That you can always pick it up and throw it out the window.

I think that the same spirit needs to apply to AI. The spirit of: humans are in the driver's seat; human judgment, human values. And maybe you should think of how humans will operate in certain fields, in certain dimensions in the future — whatever it is, we become more like CEOs, or like board members. But it's important that we have that level of agency.

Humans as CEOs

We're going to build machines — just like, you know, if you're a CEO, you're clearly going to have domain experts, you're clearly going to have teams that are going to have knowledge across so many things, and maybe even better ideas than you on many different axes. But fundamentally the question is: are you happy? Is this what you wanted? Is this what makes your life better?

That to me is something that we should all collectively — it's not just about AI, it's about technology. Technology is to lift up human civilization. It's the single most fundamental driver of improvement of quality of life. And that is what we should be seeking from AI. That is the belief of OpenAI.

Outro

Host: Thank you so much for doing this, Greg.

Greg: Yeah, thanks for the time.

Host: Thank you both. Appreciate it.

Outro: Find us on Twitter at @NoPriorsPod. Subscribe to our YouTube channel if you want to see our faces. Follow the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you listen — that way, you get a new episode every week. And sign up for emails or find transcripts for every episode at no-priors.com.

item.description:
## 一、"美学过滤器"：当AI的证明比人类更"人性"
Brockman 几乎顺带提到了四色定理——那个数学界的"丑证明"：机器穷举、人类看不懂、问题"解决"了却毫无美感。但他对当前这波数学突破的描述反而是"令人惊讶的洞见"、"为什么把这个结果用在了那里"。
**这里藏着一个反直觉的现象**：相比上一代计算机辅助证明（更"机器"），今天的 LLM 产出的证明反而**更接近人类审美**。原因很简单却很少被点破——GPT 的训练数据里包含了几百万份人类数学家的"品味梯度"（哪些证明被反复引用、哪些被当作典范教学、哪些被誉为"优雅"）。换句话说，神经网络正在把**人类的美学偏好作为搜索启发式**在用。
这与 AlphaGo 的"第37手"故事构成一个奇妙的对称：当年人类觉得丑，后来重估为美；今天 AI 产出的数学让领域专家惊呼"妙"。一个合理的推论：**AI 不是在摧毁数学的美感，而是在把数学的美感"规模化生产"**——这是一个几乎没人在讨论的角度。
## 二、"软件趋零 → 验证成为全部价值"：一条跨行业的通用物理学
Brockman 抛出了一个会被很多人误解的论断：**网络安全
