item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：这是一场"沉默创造神话"的完美闭环实验

真正让这个故事变得诡异的，不是 Elizabeth Holmes 做了什么，而是她因为"过度守规矩"而放弃了唯一能救自己的武器——声音。

Billy 反复强调：Elizabeth "maniacally follows rules"，法官一句"案件在法庭里打，不在媒体上打"，她就彻底闭嘴了七年。而讽刺的是，Billy 自己也承认——"her power was in her voice"。

这就形成了一个几乎只有在博弈论课堂上才会出现的病态均衡： - 她的核心能力是叙事（这是她从 19 岁就能融 1 亿美金的本钱） - 她面对的指控本质上是"叙事性指控"（manipulation、deep voice、turtleneck 都是叙事符号） - 而司法程序恰恰剥夺了她使用这项能力的权利

一个靠语言生存的人，被规则关进了语言的真空。她越遵守规则，公众越觉得她在隐瞒；她越沉默，Bad Blood、The Dropout、Carreyrou 的叙事就越像唯一真相。这是一个"守法者被守法本身定罪"的案例——比她被指控的任何罪名都更值得社会学研究。

二、跨领域连接：Theranos 案与中世纪"异端审判"的结构同构性

一个让你意外的平行：Theranos 的审判，在信息结构上，和中世纪宗教法庭对女性神秘主义者（比如圣女贞德、Marguerite Porete）的审判惊人相似。

三个结构性相似点：

  1. "异质语音"即罪证——贞德的"听见上帝之声"被当作精神错乱的证据；Holmes 的"低沉嗓音"被当作操纵的证据。两者都是对一种偏离规范的女性声音形态的集体不适，被包装成了理性判断。

  2. "沉默义务"的致命性——中世纪被告在宗教法庭上没有辩护权，只能通过书记员转述；Holmes 在 gag order 下只能通过律师发声。审判程序本身消除了被告的主体性，而公众恰恰把这种"缺席"读解为"心虚"。

  3. "叙事考古"倒推因果——Carreyrou 式的调查新闻，和宗教裁判官的"审查提问清单"工作方式一致：先假设有罪，再从一个人的全部人生中捡出符合该假设的碎片。Billy 举的那个精彩反例：同样的 45 分钟拿到 1 亿承诺，男性是"深刻的愿景领导者"，女性是"骗钱"。叙事框架先行，证据只是填空。

更深的洞察：硅谷创业史的"伟大叙事"（Jobs 的扭曲现实力场、Musk 的 Mars 承诺）本质上都是允许一定程度的 reality-stretching 的——因为风险投资本身就是对未来叙事的定价。Theranos 并不是因为跨越了"虚构-现实"的边界被惩罚，而是因为跨越这条边界的那个人恰好是她。这条边界，在男性身上有弹性，在她身上是绝缘的玻璃。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：这是一次"媒体-司法反馈循环"的教科书案例

真正值得科技-法律交叉学界研究的，是本案司法量刑中的一个被忽略的闭环：

  • Carreyrou 的 WSJ 文章 → Walgreens 违约 → 收入目标未达成 → 收入虚报指控成立
  • 换句话说："虚报收入"的事实构成，部分是由揭发报道本身触发的违约造成的

Billy 提到的那个细节极其关键：Walgreens 800 家店、每店 100 万美元合同，是真实签约的；Theranos 没有达到这个数字，不是因为"编造合同"，而是因为合同对方因负面报道违约了。但在起诉书的叙事里，这个数字差被包装为"欺诈证据"。

这揭示了一个系统性盲点：当媒体披露成为司法事实链条的一部分时，谁来评估媒体报道本身对"损失金额"的因果贡献？损失评估决定量刑点数，而损失是媒体部分制造的——这是一个闭合的因果环，但法律系统假装它不存在。

更隐蔽的是 Rupert Murdoch 作为"受害者"被追加到量刑中——而 Murdoch 恰好是揭发 Theranos 的 WSJ 的所有者。一个人既是报道机构的所有者（受益于报道的影响力），又是量刑中的"受害投资人"（受益于更长的刑期），这里面的角色冲突，没有一个媒体敢于深挖。

这不是在为 Holmes 开脱——她很可能确实有罪。但11.25 年的量刑逻辑里，有一部分是循环论证的产物，这件事本身比"她是否撒谎"更值得被看见。

一个附赠的意外观察：Billy 在采访中接到 Elizabeth 从监狱打来的电话，在 500 人面前让 Dave 跟她打招呼——这个 15 秒的现场，比整部纪录片预告片都更有"去神话化"的力量。因为真正的"操纵者"永远不会允许自己在这种时刻显得真实。真实本身，就是最好的辩护——而这恰恰是七年沉默里，她从未被允许展示的东西。

📝 转录文本

开场与引入

Billy Evans, who is Elizabeth Holmes's partner, the subject of the forthcoming documentary — you can see everything, has had an unconventional love story with her fiance Billy Evans. The couple first connected as federal authorities were investigating Holmes for fraud and conspiracy connected to her failed blood-testing startup Theranos.

A new documentary is offering an unprecedented look into the life of Elizabeth Holmes, the tech CEO turned convicted felon — at the center of a massive multi-year fraud.

Elizabeth Holmes was sentenced today to 11 and a quarter years in prison, four counts of criminal fraud. The disgraced tycoon and her fiance Billy Evans…

Please welcome Billy Evans.

Billy: What's up? Hi everyone. Host: Have a seat. Have you ever done a live interview like this? Billy: Dude, I've never done an interview. Host: You've never done an interview. Billy: Thank you guys all for being the guinea pigs here. I appreciate it — and apologies.

初次相识：被介绍为"Elizabeth Holmes 的丈夫"

Host: You're Elizabeth Holmes's husband? Billy: That's typically not how I love to be introduced. Um, yeah, my name's Billy Evans and yes, Elizabeth Holmes is my wife and best friend and partner.

Host: You and I met at a party. Billy: Yeah. Um, a year and a half ago, I think. Around F1, I think. Honestly, yeah, that's right. And we started talking and that kind of got us chatting about Elizabeth and the case and the history.

I think I came up to you when I said, "David, my name's Billy Evans. You guys talk about my wife a lot on your podcast. And you've got a lot of the story pretty fundamentally wrong. So if you're ever interested in learning some more details, I'm happy to read you in."

Host: I'd had a couple drinks. I'm like, "Sure, I'll hear the story."

And one thing led to another — we talked on the phone, and I ended up getting on a plane to Texas. I went and visited Elizabeth in prison. I spent the day with her and her parents, and the kids — going quite deep into the whole thing. And there was a lot more to the story than what I think had been portrayed.

I was aware of the documentary. I had heard in Hollywood that this documentary was happening.

Host: But it was a pretty well-kept secret. Billy: Yeah, but I know people. Host: Look at the crowd.

关于缄默令：为什么 Elizabeth 一直不说话

We're not going to litigate the Theranos case today. That's Elizabeth's story to tell when the time is right. And she was under a gag order until last April. So from the time that the DOJ began their investigation, Elizabeth was under a gag order through the trial and through the appeals process, which ended last April, I believe.

Billy: One thing for people to know about her, which might shock you, is that Elizabeth follows rules maniacally, like to a T. So when the judge said that we are going to litigate this in the courtroom and not in the media, she held true to that. Host: But she never spoke to the media. Billy: No, for the entirety of the process. She remained silent. Host: A lot of articles being written. Billy: Yeah, and movies being made and podcasts.

第一次见面：旧金山屋顶上的 Fleet Week 派对

Host: How did you and Elizabeth first meet?

Elizabeth and I met at a Fleet Week party in San Francisco on the roof of some venture capitalist. He was trying to hire me and date her. I was going to be there for like maybe 5 minutes — I had 100 people coming over to a house I lived in with four other guys, and we were going to throw a big Fleet Week party.

He called me when I went out to go grab ice, and he said, "Billy, you know, are you coming by our event today?" I said, "Of course." I'd totally forgotten. So I drove over to his place, I parked my car in the red, I went up the elevator, and a few minutes later, he introduced me to Elizabeth. And that killed my whole afternoon.

The next two and a half, three hours, her and I just spoke, and we started a conversation that really has never ended. I don't know if I can say I fell in love with her in that moment, but she was just incredible. Her ability to listen and really care about everything that you're saying. She made you feel so seen. She was infinitely curious about the smallest things that nobody else really cared about — or was too, you know, cool to pretend like it mattered.

As the planes flew overhead, she was just amazed by them with this childlike wonder. And when I first met her, I didn't know she was Elizabeth Holmes. She was just Elizabeth. She was wearing a big floppy hat and dark sunglasses and had a band-aid on her face because her puppy husky had just scratched her.

Somewhere through the middle of the conversation, it turned to where we worked, like physically. And I told her that I worked on Page Mill Road. She said, "Oh, no way, where?" I said, "The 1891." And she said, "I'm 1790" or something. She was two doors down — and then that's when I really put it together.

2017 年 10 月：Theranos 风暴中心

Host: What year was this and what was the state of the Theranos story at that point?

Yeah, so this was October 7th of 2017 that we first met. It was peak like bad.

Host: This was after the DOJ case? Billy: It was before she was indicted. Host: The Carreyrou article machine had started. Billy: Hundreds of them. Those were already out there.

So she had this reputation — a horrible reputation. Fraudster, all this sort of stuff.

Host: When you first met her, it was her, who she is, that you engaged with — not the story of Elizabeth Holmes — and then you found out it was her. Billy: Yeah, I mean, it's like the 30 people that I've spoken to while I've been here, where I know nothing about their story. I'm just seeing the person in front of me.

Host: So, then when you found out who she really was, you didn't just shut down? Billy: Pretty hard to grok. It was like a hard thing to come to terms with, because you get to know this person separate and apart of how you're supposed to feel about them. And then you invariably go back to this idea of like, "this is who I've been told this person is." And those two things were so radically different from one another. It was really challenging.

从邻居到朋友：六个月的遛狗期

We didn't just start dating. I was looking at renting her building, because we were right next door, and our business was kind of doing this, and hers was doing this at that time. So we were looking at renting the Theranos HQ, and that was kind of the context under which she gave me her business card — and she crossed out her cell phone number on it, and wrote "personal cell." Like, "Huh. Maybe this just isn't business." And that's how we originally…

When I first met her, she told me that she had this husky. And I told her I had a dog. I didn't really have a dog — it was my roommate's dog, but he was like mine. The first times that we hung out, we'd just go on walks. And I was really curious about the circumstance.

Host: You're curious to understand what's going on. Billy: I think I was most curious to understand the difference between the person that I experienced and the person that I was told existed. And they were so different. I was really curious, and I was interested in her, and she made me feel good, because she listened so intently.

Basically, we were friends for 6 months. We'd go on walks with her dog and my rent-a-dog that was my roommate's.

从友谊到爱情：三周后被起诉

Host: And then there was a romantic turn.

Yeah, and it moved super quickly. I was traveling a lot at the time. I was working for a company that built LiDAR, and we were selling to car companies around the world. So that year I spent maybe 12 trips to Germany.

Host: What was your role? Billy: I was just solving the most important problems the CEO didn't want to solve. Kind of like a startup special projects type — everything from sales to big automotive manufacturers, to hiring executive team members, to raising capital at times. Just really anything that needed to get done. It's a startup — there's a lot of problems that need to be solved, and I was just really willing to say yes.

Host: So you guys kind of this becomes more serious, becomes emotional, and she's going through this court case. The indictment started? Billy: Yeah, I think like 3 weeks after we started dating, she got indicted. It's one hell of an experience to fall in love with somebody so quickly and then immediately come to terms with — like, I didn't even know what an indictment was. I was really unfamiliar with the entirety of this whole thing.

Host: [She was] through a period of crisis in her life during this courtship period? Billy: She is like cool as a cucumber.

Host: While all the articles are coming out before the indictment, she didn't feel super phased? Billy: There's certainly things to be freaked out about, but you have to put yourself in her mindset. I don't want to speak for her, but I can share with you the perspective that I saw — which is this is somebody that fundamentally believes in their innocence. And was being told at the time prior to the indictment, "You're never going to get indicted. You did nothing wrong. The company did nothing wrong." I know that's hard for you guys to comprehend and believe, but yes, this is what was going on behind the scenes.

So I think at each of these chapters in which, you know, shitty thing after shitty thing happened, we're kind of perpetually surprised.

Host: It wasn't supposed to go this way. Billy: Yeah, I think that's a good way of describing it.

被起诉之夜：与岳父岳母初次见面

Host: And then she gets indicted. How was that? Billy: That's the first night I met her parents. Tough way to meet your in-laws.

Host: How was she? There was a lot of articles and press about this. Billy: Infinite press. But she wouldn't read it. I've seen maybe an episode and a half of The Dropout — for reason maybe some of you guys will understand in the future. Host: You didn't watch this. Billy: No. I skimmed Bad Blood because my lawyers told me to for other reasons. But otherwise, I really didn't consume any media on the subject.

Host: How was this for your relationship at this point? Billy: I was three weeks into a relationship with somebody. But we were so close already because we'd spent six months really being friends. It was intense, man. If I knew what I know now — how painful the process was — I probably would have responded differently at the time. But I was in new territory. This was 2018. I was like 26, 27 years old.

审前漫长等待：八个月的 RV 旅行

Host: Then the trial began. Billy: Well, it took a while for the trial.

We had a long period of time in which there was this impending thing, and there was an enormous amount of time spent with lawyers, and her working late into the night to go through hundreds of thousands of records and try and piece together a story that she didn't fully understand that was being told about her.

So it was a really intense time — but there's also some really beautiful moments in there, too. One thing that nobody knows, but I guess you guys are the first to know: Elizabeth and I spent 8 months traveling the country in an off-road RV. We had our dog, Balto — he's a husky. And if you've never seen a husky in the wild, it is a sight to be seen. Because that dog lived.

We just went to trailer parks, and we went to national forests where you're allowed to stay and park your car for 14 days without moving it. We would just hike all day and work at night, sit around the fire, and just be together.

At that time I had already left the business and was starting something else, so I was kind of working for myself.

Host: "Let's go be free, get away from all this." Billy: Part of it was the enormous attention by the media when we were in San Francisco. I've got an entire collection on my phone. Here's how the situation works: we'd go into a restaurant, and within 30 seconds six people would pull out their phones. Some were sneaky; others were pretending like they were taking a photo of their friend — but it was obvious. It was so uncomfortable.

We couldn't go anywhere without immediately being recognized, immediately being judged. We'd go to a restaurant for a friend's dinners celebrating their anniversary or their engagement, and then we'd have articles written about how Elizabeth Holmes is gallivanting around San Francisco. It's hard to know how to act when every action that you take and every decision that you make and every place that you go is being judged through the eyes of a thousand angry journalists.

关于黑色高领与低沉嗓音的叙事

Host: There was this period of time when everyone talked about Elizabeth Holmes being manipulative — wearing the turtleneck and talking with a deep voice, having this character she played. The idea was: if she's playing a character for everyone around her, clearly she's playing a character all the time, and that might be the origin of the fraud, the manipulation.

A lot of things have been said about that. If you just look back with as much clarity as you can muster, and try and disassociate "Elizabeth Holmes" from the situation as much as possible — if you just say some of it, it's pretty crazy. That she would manipulate people with her big blue eyes, and that her deep voice would immediately have people give her $100 million. It was like she was like a man. I mean, it's incredibly sexist.

You'd never say that about a man. Liz would have a meeting with somebody — like, not insert name here, but think like one of the biggest family offices on Earth. It would be a 45-minute meeting. They'd commit $100 million by the end of the meeting. And any guy that did that, people'd say, "Wow, what an incredible ability to tell a story. What an incredible ability to have deep conviction in the thing that you believe in — that this person wants to support your mission and your vision." And when it's Liz, it's, "Wow, she fleeced that person in 45 minutes."

关于"误导"与收入目标

Host: But then there's these stories about things that were misrepresented — the machine does this and then it doesn't do that. Was there any experience you had where Elizabeth stretched the truth, where she was pushing the boundaries, where the imagination in her mind maybe became the reality?

That's a good question. Where the imagination became the reality… Liz is somebody who so deeply believes — and until you've met somebody like her, it's really hard to understand what that's like.

A lot of the things most litigated in the press, this is not the machinations of a single person. This was hundreds of employees working tirelessly for 16 years to solve a really difficult problem.

One of the things largely described as fraudulent behavior was missing revenue numbers. "She missed her revenue numbers. She should have known that was going to come." If you look at where that comes from: they had contractual obligations with Walgreens to pay them that amount of money. And then when bad press came out, they defaulted on those obligations and then the business didn't fulfill those revenue obligations. So they missed it by a large number — but it wasn't a made-up number. This was a number obligated to be paid by a company that they had a contract with.

Host: How many Walgreens stores? Billy: About 800 Walgreens stores. A million dollars per store. Host: They had done this contract to do that. Billy: Yeah, and they did. Host: And Walgreens stopped doing that after the Carreyrou article came out. Billy: That's right.

怀孕、COVID 与庭审

Host: You guys then start going through this process of preparing for the trial. Is that when you got pregnant? Billy: Uh, well, she did. Host: Sorry — I don't know the right term. Did she get, you know… it's always like "you guys got pregnant." I'm like, I didn't really do… Billy: I'm always about five words away from being canceled. So I'm going to watch myself. My X-File says "already canceled."

Our son was born on July 10th of 2021. The trial was supposed to start well before, but this was COVID. It was a really weird experience because we were all masked going into the courtroom.

Host: You settled down and had a kid knowing there was this trial coming up. Was that ever a debate? Billy: Not like a planned and decided thing, just to be clear. Sometimes God gives you gifts that are unexpected. And it's been the greatest experience that I'll ever know.

We have two children. My son is now five. And my daughter's three.

带着婴儿打官司：挤奶、Uber 送奶

Host: How was it going through the trial with these little kids?

It was so gnarly. Many people say the reason she did this was to get sympathy. Tell you what — first of all, the jury had no idea that this was happening. Elizabeth was militant about not letting people see her in a place of weakness at this time.

We would wake up at 4:30 every morning with the baby — Wills is his name. Liz would feed him, we'd change him, we'd get him ready, then we'd put him back down, and she would start getting ready. Liz isn't very good at doing her hair, and I bought a Dyson Airwrap and would help her with that after watching YouTube videos. We'd get all prepped and get into the car with our family — typically her mom and myself and sometimes my mom, and our closest friends — to go to what felt like war.

She would pump milk all the way down with these mobile pumps, because our son was 3 months old when the trial started, and he needed milk throughout the course of the day. She bought a special diaper bag that wouldn't look like a diaper bag, so people wouldn't be able to say anything about it.

During breaks in court, she would go to the bathroom and pump more milk. I would collect it at lunch and send it up in an Uber up to the house, and then my mom or Liz's mom who was at the house would feed it to her son. It was crushing to spend the first two months away from this thing that you love more than everything in the world without the ability to hold them all the time. It was a really tough timing.

判决与量刑：13 项指控的真相

Host: You guys thought you were going to win the case? Billy: 100%. Yeah. 100%.

The basic math: there were 13 counts. Liz ran about 12 and a half million tests on patients at Theranos over an 18-month period. The government spent years investigating.

Host: 12.5 million blood tests on patients. Billy: It's not a small number. It's a pretty big number in a short period of time. The next year they were going to do 100 times more. They were going to be the third largest lab company in the country. Host: After Quest and LabCorp. Billy: And the year after that they would have been bigger than either of them.

Sorry, I lost my train of thought. Can somebody remind me where I was?

Host: We were going through the counts.

Oh, the counts. There were 13 counts. Of the 12.5 million tests she ran, the government brought forward four patients they accused her of defrauding with inaccurate results.

Host: Patient fraud. Billy: Yeah, patient fraud. "You gave this person a bad result, you knowingly gave them a bad result, and you were responsible for having done so." She was acquitted of those counts. There was no evidence brought forward that was convincing to a jury that there was any fraud associated with patients.

One thing really strange to me, as an inside and sometimes outside observer: diagnostics is an inherently inaccurate space. 90% accuracy for some tests is good; for other really inaccurate tests, 70% is really good. If you're running 12.5 million tests, four patients isn't statistically significant to show there were problems. But yeah — she was acquitted.

Host: She was convicted of financial fraud. Billy: She was convicted of defrauding three investors, and then colluding with her partner at the time to do so — so conspiracy. Host: And the conspiracy conviction is what gave the judge the authority to give her a bigger sentence. Billy: Yeah, that was insane. Host: Coupled with the fact that they brought in Rupert Murdoch as a victim after the case, enabling them to add additional time to the sentencing guidelines. Billy: Yes.

11.25 年与"量刑算术"

Elizabeth was sentenced to 135 months in prison — 11 and a quarter years. The way sentencing works, there are aggravating factors. They calculate this through a point system, depending on things like aggravation, the amount of financial loss. Elizabeth was convicted of three counts of defrauding those three investors — and I, and she, deeply believe in her innocence associated with those.

Host: Do you want to tell me why? Billy: What I will say — my lawyers would probably kill me — but in the next 2 weeks I ask you to read something we are going to put out. I'm not telling you what to think, but I'm asking you to spend the time to look at it and to think honestly about what it means. I think it's going to be pretty shocking. We have spent years trying to understand what the hell has gone on here.

为什么她不讲她那一面？

Host: To understand what's going on, one can get a story that's very clear-cut — the book Bad Blood, the articles, the awards given for the investigations. There's a lot of anecdotes that have painted a very clear picture for everyone: this person is guilty of fraud, should be convicted of fraud. Tell me about the side of the story she wanted to tell and why she didn't tell it.

Billy: I can tell you why she didn't tell it.

I want to be really specific, because a million people are going to pick this apart and clip it. Technically it was not a gag order. Technically, what the judge said to the trial team in pre-trial hearings — at the very beginning — is that this is a case that's going to play out in the courtroom and not in the press.

I think that was the single biggest mistake Elizabeth has ever made. Maybe Sunny's number one, but it's up there. Because her power was in her voice. Her power was in telling that story — and she did not, because she followed the rules of not going against what the judge had asked her to do. That case just ended a handful of months ago. It's been a long time in which she was silenced.

Host: She felt like she didn't want to risk going through the court process and winning there by speaking out of court. Billy: Yeah, she's a really idealistic person. She grew up in a house with a mom and a dad who both worked for the government. Her mom worked with Charlie Wilson, and her dad worked with the EPA and USAID doing water projects around the world. The conversations around the dinner table — we still have them, because her parents are helping me with my kids and they're in my house all the time. I've spent more time with Elizabeth's parents over the last few years… they lived with us throughout the entirety of trial. They're amazing people. But they're also very idealistic. The conversations were always around service — "what pain and suffering did you alleviate in the world today?" That was always what she was so focused on, because that was her upbringing.

现场插曲：监狱打来的电话

Host: I have to ask — why did she wear the black turtleneck and speak in a deep voice? I've met her — she doesn't… Billy: She's got a deep voice. But — why did she wear the black turtleneck? Tell me about the experience of being a young CEO…

I think this is probably her calling. Sorry.

Host: Oh, it is? Billy: I think the BOP would have something to say about that. Do you guys mind if I just say hi for one second? I can't call her back because she's in federal prison. Host: Are you allowed to put her on speaker? Billy: No, like really — she'll get sent to the SHU. That's the Solitary Housing Unit. Not a nice place to be.

[recorded prison call message: "To accept this call…"]

Billy: This is what I hear every time she calls me. I swear to God this was not planned. Billy (to Elizabeth): Hey baby. I'm on stage right now in front of a bunch of people. Can Dave say hi? You're not on speaker phone or anything, don't worry. I love you with my whole heart. Here's Dave. Sorry guys, thank you. Host: Not trying to get you in trouble. So the context is we've got 500 people here. There's thousands of people here. We're just talking to Billy. Okay, we'll talk soon. Bye. Billy: That's actually her. That was crazy. I miss you. We'll talk soon, okay, baby. Okay bye.

她入狱后的日常

Host: What's it been like since she's gone in — for the kids, for you?

I am not unique in going through the process of having your partner in prison. At Liz's facility, Bryan Federal Prison Camp — "it's a camp, everybody says it's super easy." Let me tell you, it is not. It's in College Station, where Texas A&M is. There are 800 women there. Elizabeth has been there for 1,205 days. Every single day has been incredibly painful.

But I recognize I'm not unique in that. There are 130 million Americans who have a family member that will be incarcerated. The incarceration rates are insane. It's really hard to do this alone. I have a newfound really deep respect for the moms out there who do this by themselves, working and raising a family.

It's impossible to have your best friend in the world — and the person… I knew I wanted to marry Liz, or like have her be my soulmate, when I genuinely knew that I wanted my kids to be more like her than they were like me. And it's hard knowing that they're spending a lot more time with me than they are with her.

Host: What do you tell them? Why is she there, and why do we go to prison every Saturday?

It's kind of a mix because one's five and the other's three, and they have different comprehension of the situation. My son knows where she is. But to start, it was just "this is mommy's work." He was 22 months old when she went to prison. How do you describe that to a two-year-old?

Our rule is really simple: when they ask questions, we tell them the truth regardless of how complicated or uncomfortable the conversation is. We want them to understand what's really happening. But it's hard. It's really hard. Because I'm building a business, I'm trying to free my wife from federal prison, and I'm raising two kids.

入狱那一天："现在我们自由了"

Host: Was there a moment when she went in and said goodbye to the kids?

My kids weren't there. We thought it would be too emotional for them. I flew out — a friend very kindly paid for a plane to fly us out to Austin, and then we stayed the night. We did some filming with Nathan and Lance.

We were told all these things about prison that just turned out to be totally wrong. We were told she was allowed to bring New Balances — that's not allowed. You pay these prison consultants who supposedly know the system, and you're just woefully unprepared.

What was it like? It was one of the hardest things I've ever done. We drove her to the prison. I got out of the car — there are three parking spots right in front of the facility. She got out wearing these new ridiculous New Balances and this little sweater that was a gift from a friend. I hugged her and I said, "I love you more than everything." And she looked at me and she said, "Now we are free."

关于 Nathan Fielder 的纪录片

Host: Tell me about the documentary. How did it come about? Billy: Pretty crazy, huh? Have you guys seen this thing? Host: Everyone's seen the trailer. Billy: Why did we do it? For context: I also have not yet seen it. So I can't pretend to know more than I do.

Host: What was the context going into this?

Elizabeth is facing an 11-year sentence. She's been prevented from speaking publicly in any way, shape, or form. This would come out after that period in which she's now allowed to talk. There's been a lot of media produced on her, a lot of people who have told her story, and that narrative is pretty ossified. The whole idea was: here she is — see her and make up your own mind.

Host: They don't talk about the case in the documentary? Billy: Practically at this time she wasn't allowed to talk about the case, so she again was going to follow the rules and not talk about the case. It's a personal life. It's a reality context of your lives.

One of the most stressful times imaginable. Liz had given birth in February to our daughter Ivy — shortly after she had gone through IVF. And she was going to report to prison 2 months later.

Host: You guys chose to do this to give an opportunity to tell the story of who she is differently?

It was to have people see who she is. I've gone through a really consistent experience with the people who love me most — everybody from my grandmother who's my idol, to my best friends who are backstage right now. They'd hear that I knew this person, or that I was falling for this person, or now we're going to have a kid. In the beginning every single one of these people were like, "Billy, you are crazy. What are you doing? Do you know who she is?"

I'd tell them, "I understand why you feel that way. But just meet her." And those people would meet her, spend time with her, see her in a totally natural environment — going on a hike, or helping a friend. And every single one of those people's opinions of her would radically shift. It wasn't because she convinced them of something related to Theranos or some specific detail. The intention of the film is to help scale that up and allow other people to sit with her and make up their own minds.

Host: How do you think it went? Billy: I haven't seen it yet. I might think this is like the dumbest thing I've ever done.

Host: This guy's a pretty unique guy to choose to do this show with. And it's been 3 years. Why is it taking so long? Billy: It was supposed to come out within a year of the time they first started shooting. Yeah, it's a long time, man.

Host: Are you worried about it? Billy: About what part? Host: The whole show. Are you worried that they've edited in a way that doesn't showcase who she is? You look at the trailer — she looks insane. It's reinforcing the narrative: this is a manipulative narcissist. It feels like, "whoa, she's bad." Billy: It's pretty intense. Well, especially the music. Host: The music makes it. Billy: Am I nervous? I've been through so many intense, surreal experiences that it takes quite a bit to raise my blood pressure. This one — there's certainly concern. But ultimately it's our decision.

刑期倒计时：First Step Act 与半程居所

Host: What's the status with Elizabeth in prison? How much longer till you guys can be together?

It's a really confusing process understanding what they call "the calculator." Prison numbers 101: you've got your sentence — how long you're supposed to be under the watchful eyes of the Bureau of Prisons altogether. Then you have the amount of time that you actually spend in the facility itself — in the four walls of that prison. Then you've got some time at a halfway house, and some time at home confinement.

President Trump in his first administration passed the First Step Act, which has been one of the most incredible pieces of legislation that helps bring my wife home sooner. She can earn 16 days off her sentence for every 30 days she's there if she's doing programming — things proven to reduce recidivism, your likelihood of going back to prison.

Short answer: as of now, the expectation is that she could be at a halfway house in Q2 of next year.

4.35 亿美元赔偿与"受害投资人"的真相

Host: One of the most remarkable things for me was when I went to visit in prison — when you send money for commissary to her, 70% gets taken away because how much does she owe to the victims of the financial fraud? Billy: $435 million.

And of that — which is important to note — less than 100 million… I mean, she would like to know the exact math, but that number is made up of 10 investors. From my perspective, what it looks like is the people who did the sentencing basically said, "Who are the 10 biggest investors? Let's add them all on, because then that increases the sentence length."

Host: So her original sentence, without these additional investors — that she was never convicted of, that she was never proven guilty of having done anything to — was arbitrarily increased? Billy: With the conspiracy charge, they were able to bring them in. That raised her sentence from something like 4½ or 5 years to 11. Two things it did: it increased the loss amount, and it was now fraud of 10 or more victims.

One really interesting thing: recently we got a 1-year sentence reduction for Elizabeth because they changed the sentencing guidelines. And at that time, even the government argued there was no evidence that any of the investors who lost money faced any financial hardship from this.

Host: These are people like the DeVos family, the Waltons, the Niarchos…

She can't buy food and stuff at the commissary — it's difficult. We spent the whole afternoon together buying trail mix at the vending machine. She's like a squirrel, she eats like… I spent all the money I had on vending machine trail mix.

I've never been to prison before. When you see prisoners, it's easy to dismiss criminals, but you go through this and you always have to feel something for people being punished for their crimes.

The saddest thing to me: there are 800 women in the facility, and on a given weekend, maybe 30 of them will get a visitor. It's just crushing. You see these little kids crying, saying goodbye to their mom, screaming at the door.

Haemanthus：不是 Theranos 2.0

Host: The press has been reporting that you're running Theranos 2.0. What is the business you're building today, and why is it not Theranos 2.0? Host: Is it an Elizabeth thing you're doing for or with her? How did this come to be for you?

My background's in the photonics space. I helped build a company called Luminar — we built lidar for autonomous vehicles using lasers. So I've got background in photonics. I did that for a handful of years, and I found Elizabeth's mission incredibly compelling, as I hope you all do — the idea that diagnostics are broken today, they're way too expensive, and we want to make it more accessible and cheaper.

In the wake of Theranos failing, very few people have tried to do something incredibly ambitious in that space.

My company is called Haemanthus. We are building a new layer of sensors to better understand biology. We use a technique called Raman spectroscopy, in which we shine light through biological samples. It creates a scattering effect where the light changes color, and then you interpret what chemical structures are within that sample. This is a really well-known technique — people do it in research labs around the country. The problem is these devices are millions of dollars, many feet long, super complicated to use.

I'm taking a lot of the learnings from my work in the photonics space to make these cheaper and widely distributed, so we can give artificial intelligence really rich and deep data sets for biology. Today, most things are built for human doctors to understand — we're trying to create really deep data sets that artificial intelligence can use to create correlations between all these disparate signals.

It's a chemical detection platform that can be used broadly in a bunch of different techniques.

Host: So the Theranos 2.0 story may be a bit of a press… Billy: What sells more? "Billy builds technology — Raman spectroscopy devices"? It doesn't exactly drive clicks. It's a lot easier to make it seem like Elizabeth Holmes is El Chapo, running a diagnostics cartel from prison, than it is to say "Billy's building a nerdy company."

结尾

Host: I appreciate you being with us today, Billy. We've talked a lot over the last year and a half to start to share your story. There's a lot more of your story and Elizabeth's story still to come. Is there anything else you want to say before we wrap up?

Gosh, you know, there's so many things that I want to say — but I just want to say thank you guys for listening. I really appreciate it.

Host: Thanks for being here. Billy: Thank you, bro. Appreciate it.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：这是一场"沉默创造神话"的完美闭环实验
真正让这个故事变得诡异的，不是 Elizabeth Holmes 做了什么，而是**她因为"过度守规矩"而放弃了唯一能救自己的武器——声音**。
Billy 反复强调：Elizabeth "maniacally follows rules"，法官一句"案件在法庭里打，不在媒体上打"，她就彻底闭嘴了七年。而讽刺的是，Billy 自己也承认——"her power was in her voice"。
这就形成了一个几乎只有在博弈论课堂上才会出现的病态均衡： - **她的核心能力是叙事**（这是她从 19 岁就能融 1 亿美金的本钱） - **她面对的指控本质上是"叙事性指控"**（manipulation、deep voice、turtleneck 都是叙事符号） - **而司法程序恰恰剥夺了她使用这项能力的权利**
一个靠语言生存的人，被规则关进了语言的真空。她越遵守规则，公众越觉得她在隐瞒；她越沉默，Bad Blood、The Dropout、Carreyrou 的叙事就越像唯一真相。**这是一个"守法者被守法

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一场感官的"对抗生成"——榴莲作为大脑的 GAN

Jensen 那句 "My brain can't make sense of it" 几乎是神经科学教科书式的自白。嗅觉走的是边缘系统（杏仁核、海马），是情绪与记忆的直通车；味觉信号则经过丘脑中继，更接近"客观评估"。榴莲恰好在这两条通路里给出完全相反的分数——这不是"矛盾"，而是大脑第一次遇到一个无法降维到标量的输入。有趣的是：这正是 Jensen 这辈子都在做的事——GPU 的本质就是拒绝把高维信号强行压成一维。他吃榴莲时露出的那种"坏掉的笑"，和一个工程师第一次看到 CUDA 跑出诡异正确结果的笑，是同一种笑。

"Nature played a trick"——其实大自然在做精准投放

Lex 说"自然开了个小玩笑"，但榴莲不是玩笑，而是植物界最精明的 B2B 营销：它那股硫化物臭气在半公里外就能被红毛猩猩、象、麝猫闻到，而这些动物恰恰是种子传播效率最高的渠道。对人类而言臭，对目标客户而言是信号。这里藏着一个让人意外的观察：榴莲是"反大众产品"策略的始祖——它主动排斥 90% 的物种，只为深度绑定那 10%。Nvidia 二十年前做 CUDA 时市场反应其实一模一样："又贵又怪，谁用这玩意？"——只有少数研究员闻到了香味。榴莲和 CUDA 的早期曲线如果画在同一张图上，几乎可以重合。

"Acquired taste"是认知系统升级的隐喻

"后天习得的味道"这个词组被用得太轻巧了。它背后其实是一次神经可塑性事件：你的嗅觉皮层需要重新给同一个分子打标签，把"威胁"重标为"奖励"。这个过程和一个人从"看不懂数学符号"到"觉得公式漂亮"是同一套机制——Hebbian learning，连接强度随共激活而调整。所以当 Jensen 边皱眉边说"it tastes really good"的时候，他的大脑正在当场完成一次微型 fine-tuning。更挑衅一点的推论：所有真正的技术突破在第一次相遇时都"闻起来像榴莲"——反直觉、让人想躲开、却在舌尖留下无法否认的信号。能分辨"难闻但正确"和"难闻且错误"的能力，可能是比 IQ 更稀缺的职业资产。而这段 3 分钟的街头小插曲，刚好把这个能力演了一遍给镜头看。

📝 转录文本

Street-side greetings

Lex: Thanks for the mark. Thank you, guys. Away from the front of the car.

Vendor: Thank you.

Lex: No problem.

Trying the powder-coated fruit

Lex: So good — the powder. Oh, sweet and sour together with the pear. Sweet-and-sour powder. Oh, incredible. Have you had the red one?

Jensen: Mhm, not yet. Not yet. Not yet. Not yet. Thank you. Thank you.

Vendor: The powder.

Jensen: It smells good.

Enter the durian

Vendor: Durian.

Lex: This is amazing.

Vendor: Oh, you should eat this.

Jensen: Mhm. What is it?

Lex: Yeah, what is it? What is it?

Vendor: Durian. Durian.

Lex / Jensen: Durian. Durian.

Vendor: Durian.

[laughter]

Lex: Yeah, my favorite. I love durian. I mean —

Jensen: You'll love it and you'll hate it.

Lex: Okay.

Shh, shh, shh, shh.

Vendor: Durian. Durian.

Jensen: Durian.

The dare

Lex: They dared me to eat durian. It's an acquired taste, apparently.

Jensen: What?

Lex: Mhm. It smells — it's sweet, but it's… it's good, but it smells. It smells really bad, but it tastes really good.

Jensen: It's — well, exactly. It smells grotesque.

Lex: Mhm. Okay.

[laughter]

The paradox

Jensen: I get it. I get it. But it tastes really good. Which is fascinating. I don't know — my brain can't make sense of it, 'cause it tastes really good, but it smells really bad. Nature played a little trick.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [Zhang Xiaojun Podcast] 154. 对Dyna创始人Lindon的3小时访谈：机器人世界的迷雾、分歧与抉择，修心、《沉思录》与王阳明
item.dc:creator: Zhang Xiaojun Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

迷雾中的三个反直觉洞察

一、"产品研究派"的隐秘发明——他其实在造一个"数据炼金炉"，而不是机器人

表面上看，Dyna 是一家折叠餐巾的机器人公司；但如果把 Lyndon 的叙述解构一遍，你会发现他真正在构建的，是一套"场景即测温计"的研究系统——每一个 workflow 不是终点，而是一次对智能体天花板的精密校准。

这里有个让人意外的观察：他挑折叠作为第一个场景，根本不是因为折叠本身重要，而是因为"折叠的容错率特别高"——咖啡拉花洒了就毁了，但毛巾折错了可以再折一次。换言之，他不是在选"最有价值的场景"，而是在选"能最大化给模型纠错反馈而不摧毁商业回路的场景"。

这是一种极其隐蔽的反向工程逻辑：大多数创业者问"这个场景能赚多少钱"，Lyndon 问的是"这个场景能让我以多低的代价知道模型哪里坏了"。前者的 KPI 是营收，后者的 KPI 是认知密度。

二、跨领域连接：他的创业论和自身的"强直性脊柱炎"是同一套操作系统

这是整期访谈最惊人也最少被捕捉到的隐喻——Lyndon 得的是强直性脊柱炎（他说周杰伦也有），一种自身免疫系统攻击脊柱的疾病。他说突破不是症状减轻，而是"把疼痛当作一个实验"。

把这句话放回他的创业方法论，你会发现完全同构：

疾病经验 创业方法论
身体攻击自己的脊柱 市场/投资人"攻击"自己的判断
把疼痛当实验，调整饮食、作息 把失败当强化学习，调整策略
不是消除疼痛，而是改变与疼痛的关系 不是消除风险，而是改变与风险的关系
10年身体实验找出规律 10年创业迭代找出 workflow

这不是巧合——他的身体就是他的第一个 Dyna。 他在自己体内已经验证了一套"长周期、低反馈密度、高噪声环境下，用自我观察代替外部指标"的方法论，然后把它移植到了机器人公司上。这解释了为什么他对"修心"、《沉思录》、王阳明如此痴迷——那不是文青式的点缀，而是他已经验证过的操作系统。

三、最违反直觉的判断：他说"大脑是下限，身体是上限"

整个行业的叙事都是"大脑是上限，身体是下限"——Figure、PI、特斯拉都在押注智能是天花板。Lyndon 反过来说："大脑决定能不能做，身体决定做得多好。"

这个观点藏着一个被忽视的产业预言：当大脑能力曲线趋于饱和时，竞争会突然切换到"身体精度 × 单位成本"的较量——而这恰好是中国供应链的主场。

所以他的"中美双团队"根本不是运营决策，而是一个十年期的战略对冲： - 短期（1-3年）：大脑是瓶颈，所以研究团队在美国，靠近 scaling law 前沿； - 长期（5-10年）：当大脑收敛、身体定胜负时，供应链在中国的团队就从"后勤"变成"主力"。

最让人意外的推论：如果 Lyndon 对了，那么现在所有把"身体"当成外包、把"大脑"当成核心壁垒的公司，10 年后会突然发现他们建的壁垒在错误的那一面。就像 2015 年的智能手机行业——所有人都在卷芯片和系统，直到突然发现制造精度、供应链韧性才是真正的护城河。

一个额外的"啊哈时刻"：他说"B2B 比 B2C 需求更大，因为人的欲望是无限的"——这是极少见的用经济学第一性原理反转行业共识。大家都把家庭机器人当圣杯，但 Lyndon 的推理是：劳动力成本下降 → 商品变便宜 → 消费欲望爆炸 → 企业需要更多产能 → B2B 需求爆炸。家庭机器人只是替代一个阿姨，而 B2B 机器人是在给整个消费社会的欲望涡轮增压。

📝 转录文本

对 Dyna 创始人 Lindon 的 3 小时访谈

机器人世界的迷雾、分歧与抉择，修心、《沉思录》与王阳明

开场

Hello everyone, I'm Xiaojun. Today our guest is a co-founder of Dynarobotics, a US company. He is the founder and CEO of Dynarobotics, Lyndon. He is very different from the previous guests. Dynarobotics has gone on a product research journey.

The global robot industry is still far from the end. This is a very long long run. You can't see the end. Sometimes you can't see the surroundings. How do each founder make decisions? How to set a route? And how to find yourself in the maze? Lyndon gave his answer.

If you like our show, please like and subscribe to our channel. And expect to make progress together with AI in 2026.

预告金句

Very few entrepreneurs give up their business even after hundreds of times of preparation. I told my teammates that we were cockroaches. We were cockroaches. We couldn't die.

At that time, when we lost our strategy for a while, this was the biggest difference. As a team, our identity was very impactful.

Some people said, "We have to do this." Others said, "We have to do research."

Do you think there's a difference between being able to smell money and being idealistic? No. I'm a very idealistic person. I came to be a robot not to make money. I think being able to smell money is a way to survive. My dream is to reach the stars, but my path requires a lot of ground.

一、来到上海：中美机器人产业的分歧

Hello, I'm Lyndon. Say hello to the audience. Hello, I'm Lyndon.

How do you feel about coming to Shanghai? How long have you been to China? I've been here once or twice a year. We have a team in Shanghai, so I come here sometimes. I think the feeling of coming to Shanghai — it's a fast-growing robot industry. Everyone is talking about robots.

What's the difference between the robot industry and the antitrust industry? I think both sides are pretty boring. There are a lot of releases every day. Every company is releasing something new. Every company wants to raise more money. I think basically everyone is more or less the same.

But I think that in essence, I think that the Gui Gu and the domestic strategy for robots for a long time is still a certain different understanding. How do you say? In fact, it is divided into brain and body types. Brain type is actually the United States thinks that the brain is the only problem, the body will solve it itself. China thinks that supply chain is the only problem, the brain will solve it itself for a long time. So these two groups are still quite prominent in China and the United States. But I do know China. Recently, they have also started to set up on some model layers.

Are you a brain or a body type? We are a full-time type. Full-time type. Yes.

二、少年创业与成长底色

Before we talk about Dynas, let's talk about you as a continuous entrepreneur, your previous entrepreneurial experiences, your growth and entrepreneurship.

I was born in China. I went to the United States when I was 11 years old. Actually, the environment I grew up in was I was more entrepreneurial. People around me would do small businesses. So I would do small businesses early on. When I was 14, I did my first business. Many people would say it was a start-up. But I thought it was just a hustle in English. Making a little bit of money.

Were you in junior high or junior high at 14? Junior high. I was playing games and I thought it was easy to make money in games. So I sold accounts and equipment. I created a platform and made some money. What platform? It was a business. You could buy and sell on this platform. Or I go to someone else's platform or forum. Sometimes, you can also sell on the forum. So that's the way to sell.

How much did you earn in the first round? About $10,000. $10,000. How did it end? The business was on the rise. Then I sold the website.

当时做生意的这段时间其实不是一段 — 我只在做这一件事情 — 其实零零散散的是非常非常多的 — 所以说比如说今天我会卖游戏，明天我会卖软件，然后后天我会卖 shoes.

Actually, the atmosphere I grew up in was very common. Actually, people around me were doing the same. Maybe I grew up in a very different environment from elementary school. So people around me actually like to make money. So I was influenced by this atmosphere. And I also followed them. I was chasing the trend and learned how to make money.

Is it hard to make money? It's not hard. Making money is very... for me, it's very... It's not very simple. I like it very much. I don't like money itself. I like to do something right and get rewards.

三、大学时的珠宝生意：从 2C 到 2B

How about your career? I don't have a particular focus on my career. I'm not a typical person. How did you start your second career?

I was also in the business mindset. I started doing jewelry sales when I was in my second year. At that time, I found that there were some jewelry stores in different places. They didn't really want it, so they wanted to melt the jewelry and then restore their metal. I was thinking about buying your pants and selling them on eBay. I was selling pretty well when I was in my second year of college. Then it gradually became a business.

Was this company born? This company actually became a self-managing business. I didn't have to spend too much time. I could make money on my own. I was managed by a family member. This business was done — it's been almost 10 years. But it's still there? It's not there anymore. I don't want to spend an hour on it. I used to spend 3-4 hours a week, and earn a few hundred thousand a year. I think it's quite a good deal. But I don't think it's worth the time now.

So he ended it? Yes, I ended it myself.

How did you end up with jewelry? First of all, it was because of my family. Then there were also my friends' reasons. Then there were also China's domestic market. Through my family and friends, I got to know the Chinese jewelry supply chain. Through some friends in the US, I got to know the demand for jewelry. I turned the jewelry 2C business into a 2B business. Because when selling jewelry, I had to pack my things every day and get feedback from my clients. I was still in college and had to do my internship. I didn't have much time, so I turned it into a to-be business. The to-be business was actually selling jewelry to jewelry designers. There were a lot of designers in the US. They needed to find their own supply chain or factory in the US. And it was very expensive.

So you went on to study business as a business student? Yes. Did you have other choices when choosing a major? I think my education path is very free. My parents didn't care much about me. They let me go. So I chose what I liked. I started with medicine. At the University of New York Medical School? Yes. Their hospital was very good. Yes, actually my parents wanted me to study medicine. But after two years, I didn't want to study it. So I studied finance.

Why did you not follow the path of investment? In fact, investment was a bandwagon. The Business School of New York University was also very good. Everyone wanted to invest. When I first started to study finance, I didn't know what investment was. But I knew everyone wanted to do it. So I knew everyone wanted to go, so I wanted to compete with everyone. So I went. I think it was a pretty good experience.

How many years have you been in the investment industry? More than two years. More than two years. And then you started your own business? Yes.

四、第一次正式创业：KBR 与 YC

What experience do you have from the beginning of your investment career to now? No, I started my own business directly from the beginning. And then you became a robot. My first startup was with a half-robot. You had another startup experience before DaYin. Yes, it was called KBR. Oh, KBR. Okay.

KBR... It's actually very interesting. Keeper is a non-profit company. Non-profit companies were very popular in 2017. Amazon launched a product called Amazon Go. Anyone can enter a store. The store has no revenue. You can take any item and leave. It will help you pay your own bills. This concept is very new and cool. It allows people to imagine 了一下这个购物体验会是什么样子的。

然后我，所以说当时其实国内国外可能有，也数不清了，当时可能跟机器人，The track is still alive. We have more than 50 companies. We are the only few survivors in this industry.

Our concept of product was very different from everyone else's. At that time, everyone wanted to renovate the entire store. They would put all the sensors and fusion in the — I put the camera on the shelf and did a self-checkout.

I brought this concept to the supermarkets. I met 150 supermarkets' owners and asked them, "How's Amazon Go technology? I'll help you." What surprised me was that no one wanted it. I asked him if he wanted it for free. He said he didn't want it either. I was surprised. I asked him why. He said the price was not high. I didn't have ROI. He asked me to spend hundreds of thousands to help me raise a few salespeople. Actually, my salespeople weren't just doing sales. So they couldn't talk no matter what. And they had to do the decoration. After the decoration, the technology still needed to be maintained. So at that time, I found that the business logic of this product might not work.

So I changed the product. I put the sensor fusion and visual recognition into a shopping cart. It's the same problem. Because there are two problems when it comes to non-sale. One is who pays for it. The other is how much you have to pay. In fact, the same problem can be solved in a shopping cart. And the technology is much simpler. The one who pays for it is the one who brings you to the shopping cart. How much money do you pay for the goods you put in? In fact, we can directly identify these goods in the shopping cart through visual recognition and sensor fusion.

So at that time, and then slowly made it.

五、七千美金烧两年半：极限生存的融资经历

Was there a difficult period in the process? Yes, when we first started, we were very lucky. We got into YC the first time we reported it. After we got into YC, our mentor was also very famous. He was named after Sam Altman and Jeff Ralston. Both of them later became YC's president and CEO.

But after we came out of YC, we were ranked in the whole batch. From the financing perspective, we were ranked in the whole batch. We only had 300,000 people in total. So it was actually quite difficult. Because a very common problem is actually, what background do you have? Why do you think this will happen? And in fact, the US investment circle really doesn't like to invest in hardware. Because they felt that the hardware cost was very high and it was very difficult to distribute.

So when we only had 300,000 yuan, I told my other three partners, "Sorry, I only have 300,000 yuan. If you are willing, we can move into a house and I can live together. I can't pay you the salary, but we can pay the rent. We can pay for your car fuel and food. But we have to pay for the food ourselves." At that time, we lived together with four people. Plus one or two early employees. We burned 7,000 islands in a month. We burned for two and a half years. Then we got the first bucket of gold, Zhongzi Lun. The first bucket of gold was about 2 million.

Okay. Did you go through this difficulty? When you first started financing?

Actually, no. When we started financing, we encountered a very difficult point. Our products were very anti-competitive. Anti-competitive to the few brands that we rarely had in the market. Very, very few. When we first started, no one had ever thought of making this kind of product. So when I went to finance, everyone was like, "How can you compete with Amazon?" And there were so many other companies, they were all using Amazon technology, they were all doing so well and they were making so much money. Some companies would make more than $1,000 from YC. We had only a little bit of money and a little bit of people. We also took a shopping cart and told others. They said, "You will be eliminated if you take a shopping cart." So it was actually quite difficult to raise money.

We had to hold the seed wheel. I emailed a friend — 一个人一千多个天使投资人，最后 convert 了两个。 当时因为已经快死了，账户里可能就只剩下一两万了。 These two angel investors gave us about 50,000 yuan each. And we were able to survive.

When we started to go out and use the seed wheel, we had built over 100 institutional investors. We all gathered and lost one. It was the first round of capital. So it was not easy to survive.

And you asked about the process from the melting point to the A-level, which is also a very difficult process. Because the product development cycle itself is relatively long, plus the supermarket itself, their sales cycle is very long. So when we actually went to the ground and went to the point where it could spread, it actually took a lot of effort — in the first year and a half.

In 2019, when we were going to integrate A-Land, we wanted to integrate an A-Land with a 10 million-level financing. There weren't many institutional investors who could invest at a 10 million level. We also met more than 60 investors. Basically, they were all in the same boat. Finally, we kept looking for new investors and finally found Lux Capital. At that time, they invested about RMB1,000. This innovation was also sold out.

Yes, after the A round, we had a lot of traction in the B round. So in the B round, we got two term sheets and an acquisition offer. At that time, we had met them twice and then decided to sell them.

六、修炼心性：从被拒 100 次到自我觉察

When was the most painful time for you? Were you still holding onto your thoughts?

How did you know? I think I saw a report. I think that when you're in a low position, you need to practice. So I think the whole process is a process of practice.

Because you can imagine, I met 10 investors and I was rejected 10 times. I said, "Okay, I'll meet the 11th investor and the 12th investor." But after meeting 100 investors, you start to doubt yourself. You will think, "Is it my fault or the project is bad?" "It must be because 100 investors have rejected me."

So, actually, through this experience, I've improved my understanding of the world. I think it's about looking at things from a perspective. Every failure is a reinforcement learning for me. How to do better next time. So, it's actually gradually forcing me to grow. So, during that period, I grew the fastest, but also the most miserable.

You said you had a certain image of an investor. Did you have one since then? You've met hundreds of investors during that time.

Actually, no. I think because I didn't have a certain image of an investor at the time, I was rejected more than 100 times. I only cared about speaking, not listening. So I didn't reach the same level as the investors. It was very difficult to establish a resonance. This is something I discovered after a while.

How long did your startup last? It lasted for about six years. That's a long time. Yes.

How did you feel when you sold it? Did you suddenly feel rich? Actually, when I sold it, I didn't suddenly feel rich. I just realized that I was doing the right thing. Because at that time, I think I can do something bigger. So that was mainly the reason I wanted to sell, not really for money.

Which year was that? 2021. Oh, that was a good time. Yes. AI started to explode later. Yes. It should not be very obvious in 2021, right? Yes, it was only in 2022 that there was a very strong curve.

七、第一次创业的核心感悟：产品是根本

Count the two business you started before. What do you think you learned from it?

My strongest core view is that doing things should be the most fundamental. In the past few businesses, I've gone through a lot of twists and turns and done a lot of things that are not fundamental. The model's understanding of the world's nature, whether it's from physical property, the state of what's happening right now, or even the understanding of semantics, has a very strong awareness that it can know what we are doing now, what stage we are in, how we should proceed next, and then we can use these to understand and send out language commands for System 1.
  • System 1 is essentially a world action model. After receiving the language from the world action model, how do we convert language into action?
  • System 0 — we want to output the trajectory. How can we use better learning methods to achieve faster, smoother, and more accurate movements on the hardware?
