item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的真相：西班牙人的"胜利"其实是特拉斯卡拉人的赌局

传统叙事总把科尔特斯塑造成征服者，但转录中最耐人寻味的细节是：特拉斯卡拉人（Lash Collins / Tlaxcalans）才是真正的战略操盘手。他们打到僵局后"重新评估"科尔特斯，这不是失败者的投降，而是围棋高手看到了"借子攻杀"的机会。阿兹特克的"花朵战争"每年升级、盐路被切断——他们正处于被温水煮青蛙的状态。几百个西班牙人在他们眼里不是征服者，而是一枚可以用来反杀的活棋子。

这里有个令人意外的反转：真正的"征服者"心态属于特拉斯卡拉人，他们才是把西班牙人当工具使用的一方。只不过历史的黑色幽默在于——工具最后反客为主，吞掉了使用者。这与现代商业中"引入战略投资者却被反向收购"的剧本如出一辙。

二、跨领域连接：钢铁、马匹与"认知维度打击"

Jared Diamond 的"枪炮病菌钢铁"框架在这里被微妙地修正了——枪支几乎没用（装填太慢，土著很快识破了心理冲击），钢是真正的致命差距。但更深层的洞察来自科尔特斯的一个诡异习惯：他把阵亡者埋在屋子底下。

这不是军事行为，这是信息战。他在人工压制"损失数据"向敌方的流动——相当于现代公司向市场隐藏季度亏损以维持估值。战场成了感知管理的舞台，物理层的胜负反而次要。

而马匹的意义被低估到了荒谬的地步。想一想：马起源于北美却灭绝了。这是一个美洲大陆输给自己的生态悲剧——它曾经拥有改变文明轨迹的物种，却在冰河期尾声让它消失了。换句话说，西班牙人只是把一万多年前"美洲丢失的本土资产"又还给了美洲，然后用这个资产征服了美洲。这种"归还即摧毁"的历史回旋镖，几乎可以与引入澳大利亚兔子、把欧洲葡萄病寄回北美相提并论——生态记忆的断层比军事技术差距更致命。

三、系统性真相：被困住的霸权永远会邀请自己的掘墓人

真正打破常规的观察是：阿兹特克帝国的"花朵战争"制度，是它自我毁灭的内置程序。阿兹特克需要源源不断的俘虏来献祭，这就要求周边必须保留"永恒的敌人"——他们故意不彻底征服特拉斯卡拉，而是把它当作一个仪式化的"永久对手"。

这种"豢养敌人"的策略，在逻辑上和冷战的代理战争、科技巨头"扶植小对手避免反垄断"、甚至免疫系统刻意保留低水平病原刺激，都是同构的。但这类策略的致命弱点是：你永远不知道你的"宠物敌人"什么时候会找到一个外部变量。

特拉斯卡拉人就是那个"被豢养的敌人+外部变量"的组合爆发。阿兹特克的献祭经济学逼迫它维持一个不死不活的敌人，这个敌人在被压到极限时遇到了一支外来舰队——于是帝国的"稳定装置"反向成了点火装置。

启示：任何一个靠"保留弱势对手来稳定自身"的系统（无论是帝国、公司还是生态位），都在等待一次外部黑天鹅——因为它早已把反抗的组织结构、动机和地理条件都为对手准备好了。

📝 转录文本

一、科尔特斯深入内陆：与特拉斯卡拉人的初次交锋

Cortez begins to march inland and he enters the territory of the Lush Collins, who, like an autoimmune system, immediately rallied to defeat him, to expel him from their territory. But he fights them to a standstill for such a period of time. The Lash Collins and he arrive at a new kind of arrangement. The Lash Collins again appreciate his strength, his power, his potential. They swing over to his side and will then henceforwards serve as guides and reinforcements for his expedition deeper into the interior.

Okay. Can we pause here and talk about the numbers? So how many men had Cortez brought with him? Even the Tlaxcalans had much larger numbers than Cortez did. So even the standstill is an impressive military achievement, especially because he's fighting without native support. So what are the numbers even at this point? A few hundred on Cortez's side and multiple thousands on the Lashkullan side.

二、新旧世界的技术差距：枪、钢、马

It's at this point that the critical technological differentials from the old and new world really begin to come into effect. The classic text which got me invested in this whole scenario in the first place is Jared Diamond's book Guns, Germs and Steel. He enumerates in the title those critical advantages that the Spaniards had.

Guns in reality weren't so significant once the native people got over the shock value. They appreciated, given the very slow reloading times involved in firearms at that time, that they weren't so significant as assets on the battlefield.

But steel was critical. Local weapons were carved from wood and from stone and from obsidian — that volcanic glass which is razor sharp when honed to a point and quite dangerous as a slashing weapon. But against the steel armor and especially the steel helmets that the conquistadors were wearing, it was much less effective. And the conquistadors were drawing on military traditions of the old world that went back, incorporating long steel sword blades. They used those as thrusting weapons to take out indigenous warriors who were coming in with cut and slash weapons, which of course open up the side of the body to be taken out very early.

So the combination of the technology with generations of inherited military training and skill meant that the conquistadors had that critical edge on the battlefield.

三、心理战：科尔特斯掩埋尸体的细节

Now they weren't invincible. And Cortez, again playing those mind games — he was taking casualties, and he was careful to bury his dead underneath the houses that they were sheltering in, so the Lash Collins wouldn't be aware that they were even having some successes in hand-to-hand combat. It was as much a mind game as it was a physical game.

四、决定性武器：马、海权与战犬

And the ultimate weapon, of course, the conquistadors brought with them was their horses. I cannot emphasize or overemphasize enough how vital the horse was to the conquistadors once they entered into the interior of the American continents.

They had the external asset — they had sail power, which enabled them to land anywhere they wanted on the coast. But in the interior, the horse was decisive. There were no native equivalents.

The horse originated in North America, but it had subsequently died out. And the local peoples had not just no horses but no beast of burden generally that was integrated into their economies, into their ways of life, or into their military. The Inca — who we'll discuss in a moment — they did have one, which was the llama. And when they campaigned, their armies trailing for miles behind them would be these endless baggage trains of pack animals, llamas. The Aztecs had had no equivalent. Their only domestic animals were the turkey and the chihuahua.

And speaking of dogs, the conquistadors also brought these big war mastiffs — these fighting dogs which wore armor and were trained to take down men. Again, imagine the terrifying impact that would have for the indigenous people.

But the horse was the critical asset on attack. You could blast through any native formation which did not just have the weapons but the training or discipline to be able to stand up to massed shock cavalry. And if things were going bad for the conquistadors, they could retreat much faster than of course the enemies could chase them.

五、特拉斯卡拉人的"豪赌"

So Los Collins appreciate all these assets coming together, and they see this as their opportunity. They were the holdouts, the last remaining major entity in Mesoamerica which were still able to go toe-to-toe with the Aztecs. They'd been completely surrounded. The Aztecs were upping the ante every year with these ceremonial flower wars, which were becoming more and more obviously wars of conquest. And the Lash Collins had been cut off from the coast and from sources of salt. Right? So they were being pushed to the brink.

This is a Hail Mary for them: "If we ally with these outsiders, these strangers who are just few in number after all, we may have some potential way to break out of this strategic trap that we've had imposed upon us."

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、被忽视的真相：西班牙人的"胜利"其实是特拉斯卡拉人的赌局
传统叙事总把科尔特斯塑造成征服者，但转录中最耐人寻味的细节是：**特拉斯卡拉人（Lash Collins / Tlaxcalans）才是真正的战略操盘手**。他们打到僵局后"重新评估"科尔特斯，这不是失败者的投降，而是围棋高手看到了"借子攻杀"的机会。阿兹特克的"花朵战争"每年升级、盐路被切断——他们正处于被温水煮青蛙的状态。几百个西班牙人在他们眼里不是征服者，而是**一枚可以用来反杀的活棋子**。
这里有个令人意外的反转：**真正的"征服者"心态属于特拉斯卡拉人**，他们才是把西班牙人当工具使用的一方。只不过历史的黑色幽默在于——工具最后反客为主，吞掉了使用者。这与现代商业中"引入战略投资者却被反向收购"的剧本如出一辙。
## 二、跨领域连接：钢铁、马匹与"认知维度打击"
Jared Diamond 的"枪炮病菌钢铁"框架在这里被微妙地修正了——**枪支几乎没用**（装填太慢，土著很快识破了心理冲击），**钢是真正的致命差距**。但更深层的洞察来自科尔特斯的一个诡异习惯：**他把阵亡者埋在屋子底下**。

item.title: [Latent Space] Robots That Predict the Future: Dyna-2 & Physical AI — Jason Ma, Dyna Robotics
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、napkin 悖论：Dyna 最大规模的客户，不是在搬箱子，而是在折餐巾

一个让人意外的观察：当你以为"通用机器人"的杀手级应用会是搬运、组装这类"硬活"时，Dyna 规模最大的落地场景是——在鼎泰丰折餐巾。这不是降维使用，恰恰相反：可变形物体（napkin、towel、面皮）的构型空间是无限的，一块餐巾的"状态数"甚至比围棋棋盘的落子空间还大。Jason 一句话戳破了行业迷思——"专用机器人之所以难以替代通用模型，就是因为可变形物体根本没法用固定夹具和脚本应付"。

这里有一个被忽略的真相：机器人真正自动化的不是劳动，而是连锁加盟的一致性。Cheesecake Factory 的终极护城河是"每一克酱料、每一个国家都一模一样"；而 Dintyong 让 Dyna 跨城市部署的核心价值，是让洛杉矶、纽约、西雅图的餐巾毫米级一致。换句话说，Jason 卖的不是手，是一组可以 OTA 更新的"连锁 SOP 权重"。这是餐饮经济学长达一个世纪都在追求的东西，第一次以权重文件的形式交付。

二、Flow Matching 的"降级"在机器人身上反而变成超能力——跨领域的隐秘反转

在图像生成领域，flow matching 一直被视为对 diffusion 的"质量妥协换速度"：你牺牲一点点生成保真度，换来 4 步而不是 100 步的推理。可是在机器人上，这个"妥协"摇身一变成了架构级优势——因为机器人每秒要重规划 10～20 次动作，一次性的"完美输出"没有意义，持续、可预测、低延迟的输出才是关键。图像生成社区的"二等公民"，到了机器人世界成了"头等舱"。

这是一个漂亮的跨域反转：同一个数学工具，在不同的时间尺度下价值完全倒置。延伸一下你会发现这和"亚毫秒延迟"在金融 vs. 搜索引擎里的价值反转、"低分辨率传感器"在自动驾驶 vs. 医学影像里的反转，是同一个思想谱系——"约束"从来不是绝对的，它是场景与时间尺度的函数。

三、Dyna 这个名字——一次跨越 35 年的理论闭环，以及它暗示的隐秘赌注

多数听众只会把"Dyna"当作一个品牌。但 Jason 揭示了：它直接致敬 Richard Sutton 1990 年的论文《Dyna》——那篇论文的核心主张就是"智能体通过内部世界模型自我改进"。35 年后，Jason 让这个想法以一百万小时数据、一台半人形机器人、鼎泰丰里的真实餐巾，走出了论文附录。

这背后藏着一个更大的赌注：Jason 实际上在押注"预测即行动"这条路线。他对 VLA（vision-language-action）流派的质疑非常尖锐——"任何对世界做'抽象表征'的建模都隐含了人类偏见；bitter lesson 告诉我们，别抽象，直接预测最原始的像素流"。这是 Sutton 的 bitter lesson 原教旨主义应用在物理世界的产物。

但 Jason 自己也埋了一个"我可能错在哪"的伏笔，而这个伏笔非常值得你记住：如果视觉之外的模态（触觉、听觉）信息密度比视觉高一个量级，那么纯视觉世界模型会被"视觉+触觉"世界模型以 100× 的数据效率击败。这个假设如果成立，意味着机器人公司对"硬件 + 感知融合"的 know-how 将构成无法被视频生成大厂迁移进来的护城河——这才是他真正押的那张牌。

四、一个藏在采访里的产品哲学彩蛋："拉伤的肌肉"原则

Jason 讲为什么机器人需要四个自由度的腰部时，用了一个几乎没人注意到的类比：只有当你某天落枕、拉伤某块肌肉，你才会意识到你每天在无意识中用了多少个自由度。这是一句充满禅意的产品方法论：

约束揭示自由度，缺失揭示需求。

把这个原则拿去看任何领域都通用——Jobs 说"用户不知道自己想要什么"，神经科学里的"幻肢综合征"，经济学里的"直到停电才知道电有多重要"——都是同一条认知路径：人类对自己依赖的东西几乎是盲视的，你必须让它"断掉"才能把它看见。做机器人硬件设计的 Jason 事实上提出了一个所有产品人都该贴在墙上的句子："去设计那些用户肌肉拉伤之后才会想念的功能。"

📝 转录文本

开场：Dintyong 的餐巾工厂

Yeah. So if we want to learn a new task, uh, you know, we basically do a little bit of robot data collection, then the model...

— "What is 'a little bit'?"

Yeah. Like a couple of hours.

— "A couple of hours."

Yeah. Where in some of the tasks, like, just tens of minutes, right?

— "Yeah. And then..."

The chopping one was 45 minutes.

— "The 'open the fridge' was... and that's an interview. That's like an onboarding task for one of your engineers."

Our robots today fold thousands of napkins for many, many different locations, many different Dintyong locations in the United States. So that's actually our biggest scaled customer, right?

So I want to make a distinction here. Uh, today there's a lot of robotics companies talking about deployments, talking about pilots, but what's really hard is not putting your robot in one location or doing a pilot. What's really hard is that the customers believe or validate that your robot creates enough value that they want to deploy your robots across many of their sites. So that's what's happened for us with Dintyong — which, to the best of my knowledge, hasn't really happened for other companies doing similar general-purpose robots. So at Dintyong our robots fold thousands of napkins per day.

主持人口播：订阅请求

Before we get into today's episode, I just have a small message for listeners. Thank you. We would not be able to bring you the AI engineering, science, and entertainment content that you so clearly want if you didn't choose to also click in and tune into our content.

We've been approached by sponsors on an almost daily basis. But fortunately, enough of you actually subscribe to us to keep all this sustainable without ads — and we want to keep it that way. But I just have one favor to ask all of you. The single most powerful, completely free thing you can do is to click that subscribe button. It's the only thing I'll ever ask of you. And it means absolutely everything to me and my team that works so hard to bring the Inspace to you each and every week. If you do it, I promise you we'll never stop working to make the show even better. Now, let's get into it.

正式访谈开始：Jason Ma 与 Dyna Robotics

All right, we're here on site with Jason Ma, uh, co-founder, chief scientist of Dyna Robotics. Thanks for having us in your…

— Of course. Thank you for coming.

— Yeah, it's been a blast. So, we got to see — you'll see a lot of B-roll — but we got to see, uh, drinks being pulled, a lot of evils, robots with knives for the first time. Uh, so under the hood of all this, you have a world action model. What is that?

什么是 World Action Model（Dyna 2）

Yeah, so last month we released our world action model called Dyna 2. So, it's the first world action model trained on more than 1 million hours of data.

So going back to your question first: a world action model is a model that's able to predict the future video, the future state of the world. So hence the name "world model". But in addition, you could also use that future generation to also produce actions robots can execute in the physical world to control the robot.

So why do we do that? It's a very powerful architecture because, if you think about how humans act in the physical world, in our brain we are implicitly thinking about how the world will evolve based on our actions. So now we have a model architecture that's able to do that — to guide robot actions. So what we find is that by doing so, the model is much more dextrous, much more robust, and much more capable of generalizing to environments, to scenarios it's never seen before.

输入、输出与架构细节

— I want to prompt this question a bit. I think a lot of people hear "world model" and they think you're outputting video, or world, or 3D state. Um, you're also doing action. I think most people don't understand what models are under the hood of robotics. So what is input/output? What's the training data? What is the architecture? Give us all the details.

Yeah. Yeah. So, uh, for inputs the most important input is video, right? You know, you can think about videos that the robot is capturing with its cameras — video or images of the past many seconds. That's the input.

But for robots, what's really interesting is that the robot also has a lot of actuators, a lot of joint encoders on itself. So the robot also knows the angles of its joints. So those can also be inputs to these world models. That's something that's very different from just a pure video model that's only looking at videos, right? So that's the input. And additionally, for robots you want to be able to talk to it, to instruct it to do different tasks, right? So you can also feed it, like, language instruction. So those are what I consider the basic set of inputs that go into any robotics model, including world action models.

And once we have that, the output at the basic level needs to output actions the robots can execute on the hardware. But in the case of a world action model, what's really interesting is that in addition to the actions, you can also output future video, right? So basically you can almost output the future video or some representation of it first, and then use that to guide robot actions. So the way I think about it is this is kind of analogous to, you know, chain of thought — basically the models are reasoning in the visual, the physics space, and then outputting actions. So that's the key difference between world action models' outputs versus other kinds of robot models' outputs.

Diffusion Transformer 与 Flow Matching

— Um, you put out a good blog post around your model. I think a lot of people understand language models or transformers — next-token predictors. In this case, you shared quite a bit: there's diffusion, flow matching. You're predicting next world state plus action. Um, one thing you say is a million hours. How do you determine the architecture?

Yeah, so the mental framework to think about how we build models for robotics is that there are essentially a couple of things to look at. One is data, and the second is: how do we make a model learn as much as possible from that data.

So let's first talk about the model. The blog post we released is our Dyna 2 world action model. So under the hood it's a diffusion transformer. Transformer is essentially like the language model, you know — sequence-to-sequence, decoder-only. But what's really interesting is that in visual domains — if you think about generating images, generating videos, and in this case robots looking at images to generate actions — people have found the diffusion kind of architecture to work really well.

So what is a diffusion model? A diffusion model is a model that takes some random noise and, through iterative computation, can go from noise to something that's really high-dimensional, something really highly defined and have very fine-grain features. If you think about generating images, right, you want sharp edges, sharp corners, color contrast. And for robotics, even though you're not generating an image, you're generating actions that need to be very precise, very smooth, right? So it has kind of the same consideration as generating images. So that's why, from first principles, the whole field, not just us, has been using this kind of diffusion transformer architecture to train robotics foundation models. You need the transformer aspect because transformer is the thing that can just ingest the most amount of data, can learn — then diffusion helps you to refine the outcome to get to the smooth, precise, fine-grain motion you need to actually execute on the robot.

— And we've covered flow matching before on the podcast. It is mostly an efficiency speed-up. Like, let's say you normally would take 40 to 100 diffusion steps, you can reduce it to four.

Yeah, that's right. So with a diffusion model, one thing that's really hard in practice is that you need to tune the scheduler — like by how much you're converting the initial noise input into the final output. So flow matching is kind of like a special case of diffusion that makes the transformation much simpler. In practice, you don't have to tune as much and it works just as well. That is why, I think, about two to three years ago most generative modeling for image and video has shifted from a diffusion model to a flow matching model. But the concept is the same — flow matching is just a special, simpler-to-tune variant of diffusion.

— Yeah, it actually makes me think that — so flow matching obviously has trade-offs in quality. — Yeah. — But actually, it's very suited for action diffusion and robotics, because you get to re-evaluate in real time. Whereas in images, you're... it's basically one shot. — That's right. — Which is pretty fun.

通用基础模型 + 小样本微调

We got to mess with the laundry folding robot, like, you know, throw a random towel in. Um, the models adapt, right?

— I think one key thing about your models is that they're made to be generalist. So one foundation model, and you adapt them a lot. Uh, how does that work? Basically in 45 minutes of mapped data you can generalize towards — we saw an example of pulling drinks out of a fridge. What's the mindset there of one general model, and then how do you adapt to different tasks?

Yeah. So the way we think about it is that for robotics we need to build a very general, strong base model, and then — because if you think about how a human interacts and behaves in the physical world, right, we have very strong base knowledge, we can just readily do a lot of tasks. But if you want to become an expert at any given task, there's some amount of training that needs to happen. And I think to train a general-purpose robot like the one we're building here, the same principle has to apply.

So our approach is to first train a general model that's trained on as much data as we can find. So that is when our Dyna report — our model is trained over a million hours of human data as a starting point. And then, given that strong foundation, what we found is we can quickly make the robot (or make the model) do many, many different tasks with a very minimal amount of fine-tuning, to just tell the model, "Here's the task I wanted to do and here's a very few amount of demonstrations," and the model can readily do a bunch of the tasks that you have seen in the office.

数据策略：什么是"好数据"

— Um, we actually have quite a — to people who deal in data, who sell data — what is good data? What is bad data? What do you want to buy?

Yeah. Uh, I think these are all open questions. Obviously, the top important thing is egocentric data of humans doing tasks. Uh, what else would you modify on that basic statement?

So data is the most important thing in robotics today because, unlike language models, there is no internet, right? So every company that's building a model, building hardware, has to think about data. So there's roughly a couple different ways of operating here. One is that you can collect a lot of data yourself, which is what we are doing as well.

— You have employees here doing that.

I mean, that robots are everywhere in the office, right? But if you think about how much data you need for a robotic foundation model, I think the amount of data any individual company can collect by themselves is just nowhere near sufficient, right? It's kind of like you're trying to build an internet by just having Reddit or just having Facebook. There are great websites, a lot of users, but it's not enough, right? So, when we think about data, there has to be some sort of data acquisition happening, right? You buy data, you look at data that's already out there.

And then there's many different tiers, right? You mentioned data quality. I think data quality in robotics is a non-stationary problem, in the sense that what is high quality data for your model changes over time. Like when your model doesn't know anything, like when it's zero, any data is useful, right? You can use a lot of video data.

In the case of egocentric data, I think it's actually a very good way of pre-training robots, because human data is so diverse — it covers every single physical activity you can possibly imagine. And that gives the model such a strong prior on how the world can evolve around an embodied actor, a human. But the issue with human data is that, before your robot looks exactly like a human, there's going to be some gap between human actions and the robot actions. So just by training on human data today, it's not very likely you can just execute robot actions directly. So you still need some amount of adaptation using the robot's own data. But the robot's own data collected on a robot is going to be much more expensive and much harder to collect.

So the kind of recipe we're thinking about is: how do we take the largest source of data we have today, like egocentric data, to give the model a strong prior over everything physical manipulation can cover, and then combine that with a small amount of robotics data to make the robot, you know, master whatever task we're interested in.

So data quality and getting data in robotics is really — I think it's a fascinating multifaceted problem, but the reality is that there's not a single winning strategy. Like, "Here's one kind of data I'm only going to collect on that, which will give you a strong foundation model." You really need to think about: this human data covers this part of robot cognition; I need robot data that covers low-level reflex dexterity the robot also needs; and put them into one model. And I think that's what gives a really adaptable, really strong model at the end.

数据合作呼吁

— Yeah. I'll prompt you, uh, just for the people listening who want to work with you. Um, what data vendors do you want? Uh, this is your call for data.

Yeah. So in our Dyna 2 blog at the end, we actually have an email address called data-partnerships@dyna.co. Okay, so if you're a data vendor that has a lot of high quality — let it be egocentric data, uh, robot data, video data, or anything you think could help robots — send it to the email. Our team will take a look and we'll get back to you.

— Yeah. But at your stage, you're probably not buying any more egocentric data off the shelf, right? You probably want to be like, "Here's what I need." Is there a niche that's lacking?

If you really want to nail a task, having data from that task will certainly help you a lot, right? So for us, we still think, you know, just a million hours of data is not enough — it's just the beginning. We show the first model on a million-hour scale, but we need more than that. So we're still looking at a lot of just raw, diverse data that we can get. But we're also thinking about: how do we get more custom data, either collected in-house or by our partners, for really specific niche tasks? Because I think you still need that to get to excellence that any model needs to actually be useful in the physical world.

It's kind of like humans — you know, if Sean or me go work at Rosewood Hotel tomorrow, we're not going to be able to make the bed the way they want, right? We need a lot of training. So that kind of data — special data — it's kind of like what Mercor is doing today for language models. I think it will be very, very valuable for robotics as well.

— Yeah. So, hotels, you know, strap a GoPro on your employees' heads.

合成数据与 Sim-to-Real

So uh, so one thing that we discussed is like closing the sim-to-real. And what's very interesting is now you can basically fabricate environments on the fly.

— Yes. — Have you tried that with the frontier models? What's your experience? Are they good enough? Are you using any world-model robotic/world-model companies to generate these and train on them?

Yeah. So generating synthetic environments, synthetic data, simulation data for robotics is going to be one of the next frontiers, right? Because today people have looked at egocentric data, robot data — those are scaling — but I think synthetic data will be a new dimension of scaling.

So going back to your question — like, yeah, we have been exploring using frontier models to generate synthetic environments for us, on our environments that we care about. And surprisingly, I think now it's at a point where this technology is actually very much worth going really, really deep into.

So for some context: in my PhD, I primarily focused on simulation-based training for robotics. Back then simulation wasn't ready, but we had this paper called Eureka, which was the first paper taking a large language model (at the time, GPT-4, which just had come out) and had it self-generate environments, generate reward functions for reinforcement learning, and just do things in simulation. And at the end I think we had this really nice demo of the robot spinning pencils. That was really cool at the time, but that kind of thing was still very limited because back then the model didn't really have good vision capability, didn't have an innate 3D understanding, right? So it was basically just generating code and using very limited feedback from text to try to come up with new simulation environments.

But today, the vision capability of these frontier models is crazy. They can do real-to-sim CADing, there's 3D reconstruction, all of that. I think now it's at a tipping point where this technology could really accelerate robotics. And for us, we think about that as a way to accelerate our internal progress — because we're building models, we're building hardware. So if a frontier model can give us more data that way — like, generate really tailored data for ourselves — that's extremely useful for us.

And another thing we've been thinking about is, instead of using these models to generate 3D environments, we have also used our own world model — right, the world action model I was telling you about — because the model not only generates action, can also generate videos. The model can also generate its own training data. So that becomes a self-fulfilling flywheel that I think will also be powerful.

So overall I'm just really excited about this direction, because I think even though we have scaled to a million hours of data, we are deploying bunch of robots, and the robots are already starting to do very cool things — we're just at the beginning, just the tip of the iceberg for what is there to come.

推理约束：On-Device vs Cloud

— For those on the research side, we recently had Runway on the podcast. One of their things is robotic world models. So, you know, next people to look at it. Um, one of the questions I have about you making your own models is: what are the constraints you operate in?

So if you draw a parallel to language models, you see like GPT-OSS 20B is very fit for your average MacBook. Then there's a larger one that's fit for a single GPU. Do you work in the constraints of a robot model on-device, in cloud, a hybrid? And then how does that affect your scaling law of data? A million hours is great, but do we just scale up parameters, data?

Yeah. No, that's a great question. So I think what's really different about robots versus language models and other applications is that for coding agents, language models — it's okay if it has latency, right? Like, you know, today whenever I ask ChatGPT it takes like a couple seconds before it spits out anything. But for robots, the inference latency has to be very short. Like, the robot needs to act — it can't just hold a knife and not do anything for three seconds. That's going to freak people out, right?

— Yeah, we saw someone put their real hand…

And our model's pretty smart, so that's okay. But in general, if you think about very dynamic tasks — for example, you want your robot to hold a tennis racket and juggle the ball — this is very dynamic, very reactive. The physics, gravity, doesn't wait for you, right? So for that reason, a robotics model needs to be able to inference very fast. And the fastest way to do that is by serving on-prem, like on-device, right? Because if you call a model over a network, there's no guarantee…

— Drive a car.

There's no guarantee, right? Like, so for that reason, the model that gets deployed eventually has to be of reasonable size that can be served locally. But that doesn't mean that the initial model you train also has to be small. Like, in language models, people do distillation — the best way to make a small model very smart is by doing distillation, right? You train the biggest model, then you distill. So I think in robotics we're getting there, but I think that's what people are going to converge on.

— How about inference? You have your own inference stack, or a lot of this is architecture — you've pulled diffusion and whatnot. I'm guessing you can pull off of something. Anything you want to share?

Yeah, so we build our own inference stack for whatever model we deploy, because, like I was saying, latency is so important. So owning the whole stack is extremely important for robotics, right? 机器人领域的"Bitter Lesson"

— Anyway, the term that comes to mind is like sort of like bitter lesson for robotics, right? Instead of the specialized robots, which is a lot of industrial engineering, you build a generalized platform that can do a last-mile tuning. Give the expert add-on outside of your… what is more bitter lesson in robotics?

Yeah, I think there's several bitter lessons for robotics. One is that robotics is going to scale just like any other domain that machine learning has solved. So what does that mean? That means have as much data as possible. But in robotics, the one thing that's a lot harder is: what is the right data is much harder to figure out than in other domains. In language, it's text. In video games, just video game data. But for robotics, what sensors you choose determines what kind of data you have, right? But if you have the right set of sensors and just scale that data, I think you'll get predictable return on model performance. So in that way, robotics isn't so different.

So that's the bitter lesson. As a corollary of that: there's a lot of research in robotics that's coming up with very specific priors. Like, "we need to make the robot see objects as they are, draw some boxes that will give robots better perception." But I think the bitter lesson here is: just keep the algorithm simpler and scale the right kind of data, then generalization, better behavior will emerge. So that's not so different.

And the second — which is the main bitter lesson — is that at the end of the day, scaling will work. But in robotics, to scale and how to scale is just much harder, because there is no internet. You have to come up with your hardware, come up with the sensors, get all of those right, and then scale.

为什么选择迭代式半人形

— I mean, there's the argument that the world is very made for humans — it should be a human, right? As hard of a hardware problem as that is, think 10, 20, 100, 200 years down the line — can we make a really efficient human? But you have to be practical with what we have now, right?

Yeah. So the way I think about it is: yes, eventually, if you want to build a general-purpose robot — a machine that can be adapted to as many use cases as possible — I think human form factor will be the best one, just because that's what we have been doing for ages.

But I think the best way to actually build a human robot is to take an iterative approach, because robotics is so hard — the whole problem, the whole stack is so long. It's really hard to know a priori what's the right decision to make. And because hardware decisions are much more expensive, much more costly — just because hardware iteration is a lot slower — you actually want to take an incremental, iterative approach, not going all the way to the final form factor. Because the chances that the thing you build actually doesn't last, is not good enough, so you just end up scratching it anyway.

It's public news that, you know, Optimus has already gone through many, many iterations and they had to scratch their designs. And I think by iterating with a semi-humanoid form factor and actually putting them out to real customers and getting models really deployed, you get that feedback loop that you wouldn't get if you're just trying to build a warehouse humanoid and you spend 5–10 years building it. I think the iterative approach will actually get us closer to the final robot faster.

— Yeah. And I have a screenshot of the fridge demo, where there's agentic planning and tool-calling and all those things, so we can show that for listeners. I think that's an interesting side. Is this custom per use case, is it you have your own SDK?

Yeah. So I mean eventually we will have our own SDK, but the way we think about it is we want a general harness layer for robotics foundation models — today that is our own model, right?

The way I think about it is: for any real task, long task in the physical world, there's a lot of high-level decision-making you have to do. It's not just the robot only reasoning about the physical world in the action continuous trajectories, right? Because that's very low-level — the thing you're actually executing in the physical world. But that's not the intent that, you know, like when we are doing decision-making, we think about steps of a recipe. We think about: "oh, like I finished this, I need to do that; while I'm waiting for this part to finish, I need to go somewhere else to do something else." There's a lot of high-level cognition, decision-making that's happening.

And I think for robots to handle even, you know, the laundry task we are showing you, it has to have that capability. Because it needs to reason that, okay, the washer is running so I should go do something else while the washer is finishing. But now the washer is done, I should take the towels from the washer and put it in the dryer immediately. Because if not, then that becomes a bottleneck in the whole workflow.

So there's a lot of reasoning that needs to happen for robotics. And I think in theory you could just try to learn that with a low-level model that's outputting actions, but it would be extremely inefficient. So that is why having a hierarchical system — like putting a harness, like an agentic system, around our world action model — is what allows the model to compose different capabilities, different skills, to solve a much longer-horizon task.

It's very much like in language models, right? Like two years ago, three years ago, the model was only good at autocomplete. Humans had to tap-tap-tap to get the model to keep spitting out code. But today, agentic systems just carry the end-to-end task. And I think that's important, because in robotics today, people are still thinking about autonomy at the very task level, like a one-minute, 30-second task. But really the value is about tasks or workflows that go on, like unsupervised, for hours. And that's what we're building towards. And that's why we think about the robotics problem not just as a modeling problem, but rather as a system problem. You need a good agent, good harness, good engineer, good model, good hardware, everything. It's like how we think general-purpose robots ought to be solved.

Yeah. No, that's a great question. So I think robotics is the most exciting space today, and there's just so many amazing companies that I truly respect. They've been doing great frontier work like us, and it's very exciting.

And I think what we are seeing today is that there's still many different approaches to robotics. Like, we believe that hardware needs to be built in-house. We need to own the whole chain. We believe that scaling human data is extremely important. But there are companies that are betting on just scaling robot data. There are companies scaling some sort of intermediate data-collection devices. All of them are in play, and I think it's different approaches — we'll just see what happens.

I think right now it's still a bit early to tell, but we feel pretty good about the way we're building things just because, like, we as a company culture-wise, mission-wise — we're not here to just build a model. We're here to truly get robots deployed. So we deploy as much as possible, work on the hard problem, so we identify problems much earlier on. So then I think that really helps us identify what is the true bottleneck and then solve it. And I think for folks, for people who are only working at one part of the problem, it's kind of like fog of war — you don't really see the whole picture, and you might be building something that's extremely cool technologically but may not be what people need or want at the end. I think there's a whole graveyard of robotics companies, and I think all of them had very shiny, very cool robots. But just figuring out what people actually want — it's actually very easy to say, "build something people want" — everyone says that, but it's actually really hard to execute at a robotics company.

世界模型 vs VLA：第一性原理

— On the technical side, you have your world action model. Is that standard across industry? Is there other directions people are taking?

Yeah, I would say that's also not standard. So we're building a world action model on top of a world model. There's many companies building world models — you mentioned Runway, they're also getting to adapt video world models. There are also companies building vision-language-action models. So that's like taking vision-language models and adapting them to robotics.

So I think there's many different ways to go about it. But I think at the end of the day, what we call the models is less important than what we believe the model needs to be able to do at a first-principles level.

So I want to explain that a bit. I think for robotics, the most important thing is that you need to be able to predict the future. Robotics, any physical system, is fundamentally about: based on the information you have at the present moment and before, what should you do next? So it's really about predicting what comes next. So predicting robot action is like predicting what the robot should do next. But if you think about it, the robot is just a part of the world. The robot influences the world, but the world also influences how the robot should behave in that environment. So if you think about it this way, then the maximal, the most first-principles thing you can do is just predict as much of the world as you can possibly predict.

So that's why we believe predicting the future is extremely important. And today the instantiation is a world action model. VLA only predicts robot actions, or some more abstract representation of the world. But whenever you're predicting an abstract representation of the world, you're encoding your own bias into what's important to predict. And the bitter lesson tells you: let's remove human biases, let's just take the most raw representation, the camera inputs, and just predict all of that. So that's how I think about modeling for robotics today.

— So just to press you a little bit on this — you're basically saying your approach is better than the VLA, right? You're emphasizing prediction. I fully buy that, I like — you've sold me on it. If you were wrong, what is the most likely… be number two? [laughter] So someone else is doing — interesting question.

Yeah. So there's a caveat in what I've said before, and I think that's where I could be wrong. I said you need to predict the world as much as possible, right? But what that doesn't say is: does your sensor have everything about the world that you need to predict? I think I touched on this a little bit. If you train a world model that's purely based on videos, I think it'll be a very powerful world model, but it may not be a sufficiently rich enough world model, because you're missing critical aspects of the world — like sound, like touch.

So I think where we could be wrong is: okay, I have the best world model on vision — a vision-based world model — but tomorrow someone else comes out with a vision-plus-tactile world model that's 100× more data-efficient, just because vision is a very high-information, or like a highly-redundant, input. Every other pixel, they don't change that much. You can understand the world without perfect vision. But tactile, or other modality, might be much denser in information. So maybe having that, predicting that, would just allow you to use much less vision — so you can get to the same performance with much less compute, with much less data.

— I think you'll be able to adapt very easily.

No, exactly. There's also the level of how much data. The reason why I bring this up is because I think if a vision-tactile world model, or vision-tactile-audio world model, is the final thing that solves robotics, then I think robotics companies will be able to do that better than video-generation companies trying to pivot to robotics. The reason is: to understand sensing is actually very complicated. We've been building that since the company started. So we know the bottlenecks, we know how to combine them. But if you're just trying to adapt a video model to robotics action — if you were wrong, if video model is not enough — you don't really have the know-how to get tactile to work very well. But we have that.

— This is a side question, but I think it's a quick one. Heat seems very important. Is infrared just another color to you, or is that a…?

Yeah, it could be another color, another input to the model. Could be used in cooking scenarios, actually. Like, I know companies that are using infrared to know how cooked their food is, because that's really hard to tell from an RGB camera.

— My very naive pushback on your last point is: maybe we don't need to understand hardware — Cloud Code or Codex can just, you know, vibe-code it in. There's a lot you can do without understanding, but of course, it's just not in the distribution.

Jason 的个人经历：围棋、Penn、Nvidia、DeepMind、Dyna

— So I wanted to bring it a little bit to your personal story, or your background. We both went to Penn. I did not — I just found out today.

Yes. Yes.

— Uh, I — my big regret is I didn't join the DARPA challenge. Okay. And then I could have been like early Waymo or something.

Um. You were at GRASP, and then you've also worked at Google and Nvidia. What are the different focuses of, let's say, academia versus Google versus Nvidia? You've seen all these places, right? And then, like, that obviously caused you to say, "screw all that, I'm going to do my own thing," right? You could have joined OpenAI Robotics. Yeah. Uh, so can you just take us through chronologically, but also one thing you learned from each?

Yeah. So, chronologically — yeah, maybe it's useful to talk about how I got into AI in the beginning.

So, as a kid, I spent time in Japan and China. I grew up playing Go — you know, going AlphaGo. So when AlphaGo came out, I was a senior in high school, and I was mind-blown, because I've been playing this game for many, many years. It's so complicated. I think before AlphaGo came out, people were like, "okay, Go is one of the games that AI will never solve. The search space is larger than the total number of atoms in the world. How could you possibly search for solutions in that?" Then, you know, RL, reinforcement learning, just cracked it, right?

And I think that was how I got into AI initially. I was just really interested in models, systems, agents that can self-improve. So when I got to Penn as a PhD student, I just really wanted to work on reinforcement learning. So I was co-advised — both my advisors were interested in — at the time, one of my advisors was more in robotics, he did a postdoc at Berkeley Robotics Lab. So that's how I got into robots. At Penn, you know, we have GRASP Lab — I think one of the best places to do robotics. And so that's how I got into doing RL for robotics in my PhD.

And then I did a bunch of research thinking about how to connect reinforcement learning with human data, how to do reinforcement learning theory in a very rigorous way. And then I went to Nvidia. That's when GPT-4 came out. At the time we were very interested in just solving pen spinning tasks. I don't know why — like, uh —

— It's the dexterity limit, right? I mean, you can solve Rubik's cubes and then…

At the time I was working with Jim Fan, who you guys probably also know. We were just like, "okay, let's try to do dextrous pen spinning." The initial idea was learning it from human videos. We were trying to watch humans do it. But then I realized: okay, today we don't have a dextrous hand that can spin a pencil at all. So how would I even be able to evaluate the algorithm, even if learning from human worked at all? So I said, okay, we need to first try this in simulation. Then as soon as I tried to set up a simulated environment for a robot hand with a pen, I immediately saw what the issue is. The issue is: if I had to come up with the simulation environment, the reward function for reinforcement learning to solve pen spinning — that's impossible. I wouldn't be able to come up with all the terms that you need to get RL to learn the right behavior.

And then I was just thinking: what if a model that can write code can do that? That's what became the Eureka project. We basically — in my opinion — we had the first recursively self-improving robotic agent in simulation, because we really used that to solve a new task that no one has demonstrated before. And that allowed me to see the potential of using language models, using coding models, to really accelerate robotics.

So then I went to Google DeepMind, because at the time — I mean, even today — they have one of the frontier models in Gemini. So I was looking at how to use Gemini for robotics. But eventually I realized: I had a lot of fun doing academic research, but there was always a question in the back of my mind: does any of this matter? Like, when you're working on this kind of thing in the lab, you ask me, "how do we come up with so many interesting, fun tasks?" You're basically doing your own eval. You're grading your own homework. I wanted something more real. I wanted something that could actually be used by millions of people in the world. And I felt 2024 was when we started Dyna — like end of 2024 — that was the right time that we can take some of these technologies to actually putting them out in the real world.

So that's why I started Dyna with Lindon in New York. And fast-forward two years, we built our platform, our model, our robots are in Dintyong. Go check it out, and go eat.

— Yeah, go eat.

It's been a journey. But what still gets me really excited is a lot of the ideas that I temporarily abandoned when we started Dyna — because, you know, to build a company you have to be very practical. Like, I think simulation wasn't ready in 2024, but now with the new frontier models and what we're seeing internally, this might change. And that's very exciting.

公司文化：研究 + 产品

— Yeah. And so, then also let's talk about company culture. What principles are you building the company with? Obviously, you're responsible for the science and the research agenda. And it just seems like when we meet the engineers, they're very engaged and they have a lot of ownership. They have a lot of motivation.

— I'll say, it's interesting to see how many side projects people just work on. So some of the demos we've seen, it's just the engineers that work on it were like, "yeah, this seems fun, might as well do it."

Yeah. To your point on fun evals, right here, like 2 feet behind the camera —

— Can't talk about that.

No, I mean the thing is — the eval is just, there's highlighters for highlighters being rubber-banded together, right? It's like, who comes up with "ah, yes, we need to test putting rubber bands on highlighters"? It's just stationary. Fun stuff. People are very creative here.

— It's a beautiful space.

Yeah. I think culture — so let's first talk about how we run a company. We think of ourselves as, like, eventually, like a research-plus-product company. It's kind of like OpenAI, where you do frontier research but eventually all of them make their way into Codex, to ChatGPT. That's how we think about it too. We're not here to just do open-ended, whatever thing that interests us at the time. We're always product-driven. We want to deploy our robots, our platform, to a new customer. What are the technical problems we have to solve? We have to solve generalization. We have to solve whole-body control. We have to solve how to adapt quickly. We have to solve how to make the robots follow language. We have to solve dexterity.

So once all those problems are very clear, then — I mean, our engineers are very capable, they're very smart. So they just create instances of the task. They create tasks that would stress-test those capabilities. Like, the "grabbing a drink" task is just how we test language following. You can just specify what you want. If the model follows intent, follows instruction, you should be able to do it. So that's how we think about: at the top level, we identify what are the things we have to solve. Then we have a lot of bottoms-up projects to actually drive execution to solve them. And you hire the right people, and everyone here is super passionate about robots. They've been doing this for a long time, they love it, and we just create a culture where it just naturally happens. It's a really fun place to work.

— What's the split between technical research, software, versus hardware side of the company?

Yeah, we recently grew so much, so I don't have the perfect number, but I would say on the hardware side we have I would say probably like 30%-40% of hardware, just because hardware you need a lot more people. And then we have like around 10 people working on models. Then we have software engineers, robotics engineers. We have a lot of very talented people on the business side.

You know, the most fun thing about building a robotics company is: you see everything. Everything under the sun that could possibly be helpful will be helpful. And you just get so much exposure working with so many different people from many different backgrounds, who are all very passionate about robots. And it just has been really eye-opening for me as a founder. Because when I was a researcher at a lab, or a PhD student, I was talking to researchers every day — and that was great, that was really good, I still get to do that every day. But now I also get to learn from so many different people from different walks of life. Like, some of our people who collect data — they had no robotics experience, they were working retail, working in some other jobs, and they came here, and they also became very well-trained in robotics. And I think that's just pretty amazing to see. And I think of myself as, like, I'm still learning. You know, I think of myself as just always learning in the robotics space. And I haven't learned so much as I am now. You know, even though I'm not a student anymore, I'm here running a company, managing a lot of things, but I still feel like the day-to-day learning is just so much.

Dyna 这个名字的由来

— Um, and then just to close off — where is Dyna going? Two years, five years, what's the vision?

Yeah, I think our vision is to truly — the high-level mission is to truly bring robots and intelligence right into the physical world. Actually seeing our robots deployed, like, thousands of customers, even more, millions of robots. That's what we want to get to.

— What's the name — from Dyna, dynamic? Is there a story?

Yeah, there's many stories. So, I named Dyna. There was a lot of internal different options, but how the name came to be was there are two things.

One is: Turing-Award-winner Richard Sutton, who's like the pioneer of reinforcement learning, wrote a paper called Dyna many, many years ago. It's about basically an agent that self-improves in a world model. And I felt, even when we started the company — like we weren't doing world models yet — but I felt that's how robotics will get solved. And now our technology direction is converging to that. So I felt that was a really neat inspiration. Also because I worked in reinforcement learning, I have a lot of respect for Richard.

The second thing is a bit more personal: I grew up in Japan, and the year I was born there was just like a cartoon show. I don't know if you guys have seen it, like, Ultraman.

— Yeah, of course.

Yeah. The Ultraman that year was called Dyna.

— Oh. Yeah. So, yeah, it's a very subtle thing. Not people know, but I guess now everyone will.

The team is finding out too. [laughter]

But I think Richard would appreciate — I don't know if you've ever talked to him, but…

— No, I've seen him at RL conferences. You should just be like, "hey, this company…"

Yeah, I'll invite him. Come to you.

— Everyone knows Richard for bitter lesson, but, you know, also "bitter or less."

临别寄语：招聘与行业期待

— Okay. Any parting thoughts or calls to action?

Calls to action. Yeah. I think, um, I do feel like, as an industry, robotics is still very demo-oriented. I have done a lot of demos in the past in my lab. You know, even here, we had to show some demos. I think we need more people that are truly mission-focused, on doing whatever it takes to get robots deployed, get robotic foundation models truly integrated with hardware and seeing them at real customer sites. I think we are a pioneer in this regard, and I want to see more in this field.

And for the audiences watching: if this mission inspires you, if solving the hardest problems today is what makes you wake up every day and you want to contribute, you know, we're always hiring. And yeah, looking forward to that.

— Bay Area, anywhere else?

Uh, yes, just Bay Area today, but, you know, as the company grows, never say never to other locations.

Yeah, but that's what I want to say. And I want to see more robots in the world.

— Yeah. Cool. Congrats on everything. I mean, this is incredible progress for two years.

Yeah, amazing.

Yeah, I really appreciate it. Thank you for visiting us. I hope it's been fun.

— Yeah. I would say I don't regret doing this on-site, like, okay.

— Yeah, we do a lot of in our studio.

Like this was worth it.

Yeah. I think for robotics, you got to do it on-site. It just…

— For people listening in, you know, watch the video version. And we have fun B-roll.

Dyna 2.1 现场演示（一）：洗衣全流程

This is Dyna 2.1, our brand new hardware with a physical agentic harness around the world action model Dyna 2. So what Dyna 2.1 can do is to automate an entire end-to-end workflow in a real physical industry. So here what we're demonstrating is end-to-end laundry task in a real laundry room in a hotel. And behind me these are the researchers for this project. They're going to show you something really cool, a quick demo, and going to explain some of the technical details behind what made this possible. So, I'll pass it to George.

— All right. Um, I'm just going to show some quick steps in the entire laundry workflow. Just going to start the robot. This will be the task of transferring towels from the washer into the dryer. Let's take a look.

Yeah. So, this is actually an extremely hard task because you saw the robot has to really maneuver its body to stick the arms in to grab all the towels without colliding with the doors, right? But you see right here, it actually has to be very dextrous, and the motion is very smooth because it's a single model that's controlling every single joint in the body. So there isn't like a classical planning-versus-acting separation that makes the motion less smooth, right?

— Okay, cool. We can also — do you want to simulate it? Okay, we can also simulate the robot realizing a dropped towel. So I'm just going to drop my towel here. We'll see how it is able to see that the towel is dropped and then pick it up. So, after it's done putting the towel in the dryer, we'll see — and it also realizes that this towel is now dirty. So it goes and puts the towel in the dirty basket.

I think this is a perfect case to showcase why we need to build a whole-body robot like this, right? So it can access different parts, all of the corners of the workspace, that it can do everything that a human worker can do. Next, it will close the dryer door and turn it on. And it can also reason, based on tactile, in terms of what drying mode to put in.

— Yeah. The most impressive part to me is actually this part of turning the knob, you know, like actually operating a machine like a human would. And yeah, maybe it's worth getting a close shot, right? And making sure it's on the right mode and pressing a button to start the dryer, right?

— It's also important to realize that this is digital frames. So you really need more context to realize, because when you capture an image, the LED screen also blinks. So that's why it's important to realize that the robot knows how to start and realizing when the dryer has started. So, it's pretty cool.

Yeah. So, this is just one part of the whole laundry workflow. On Tuesday, we're going to drop the entire workflow. The whole workflow will take quite some time, as you can imagine. So, uh, you know, for this…

Yeah, folding, stacking, transferring, basket, everything, right? Really like Dyna 2.1 is about a robot for the first time becoming like a whole employee at a workplace doing everything. There's no need for a human or for any other machine to feed it items or help it with certain steps of the task. It's just going to take the whole thing and do it end-to-end. And I think that's a big breakthrough because historically we think about robots as machines, right? But this is for the first time, like, I think we can really see them working alongside humans to really improve and increase productivity, physical productivity in the world. Yeah. So we're super excited about it.

— Yeah. Go ahead. It will be the longest local dextrous manipulation demo. So quite proud of the work that we have done and, yeah, exciting.

Dyna 2.1 现场演示（二）：从冰箱取饮料

Yeah. So here's another demo we put using Dyna 2.1. So here the physical agent with our hardware is going to grab a drink for you based on whatever drink you select on this screen. So our researchers, me and Chad, who lead the project, we just give you a quick demo.

So in this case, they selected a vanilla shake drink, and the robot has received a command. So, it's going to go to the fridge, and then now use the world action model Dyna 2 that's controlling the whole robot to get the right drink for you and then retrieve it. And what's really interesting here is this is really to showcase the agent capability. So, the model is not just doing actions, it's also following language commands very faithfully, and can also navigate back to you to fulfill the order.

So, all right. So, got the right drink. It's going to nicely close the door. And I think it's switching, switching —

— Oh, yes. Gates.

Yeah. Switching mode, because here is the navigation part, which we can just have another high-level reasoning model to do, right? Also.

— Yeah. Yeah. Anything you guys want to add on what's happening? Anything cool you want to point out?

Yeah. So, this one has a reasoning layer and an action layer. So, it's a two-model architecture. Underneath, we are sending language prompts — basically, a few-sentence instruction to the reasoning model. And then the reasoning model is planning out what it needs to do step by step. First, go into the fridge and grab something, and then come back, and then hand it off to a human in sequence, and oversee the whole execution. And the lower-level action model is responsible for performing the manipulation and the dextrous task.

Yeah. On the action-model side, um, it also needs to be steerable. So you're telling it which of the six drinks you want to pick up. And then our video-action model sort of helps with imagining, like, understanding your intent. So you can imagine, like, what does it look like when this robot grabs a drink. And that sort of helps it really follow what you tell it to do. And then there's also some timing aspects to this: it needs to recognize when you've grabbed the drink, and then release at exactly that point. And you don't want false positives, you don't want to drop a drink on the ground. So there's all sorts of little things you just have to be careful about to get a demo like this working.

Yeah. And the model is quite good at this kind of dexterity, and very robust. So, like Chad was saying, it's able to just recognize and kind of imagine what it's going to look like if it grabs the right drink and then execute.
