item.description:
## 一、napkin 悖论：Dyna 最大规模的客户，不是在搬箱子，而是在折餐巾
一个让人意外的观察：当你以为"通用机器人"的杀手级应用会是搬运、组装这类"硬活"时，Dyna 规模最大的落地场景是——**在鼎泰丰折餐巾**。这不是降维使用，恰恰相反：**可变形物体（napkin、towel、面皮）的构型空间是无限的**，一块餐巾的"状态数"甚至比围棋棋盘的落子空间还大。Jason 一句话戳破了行业迷思——"专用机器人之所以难以替代通用模型，就是因为可变形物体根本没法用固定夹具和脚本应付"。
这里有一个被忽略的真相：**机器人真正自动化的不是劳动，而是连锁加盟的一致性**。Cheesecake Factory 的终极护城河是"每一克酱料、每一个国家都一模一样"；而 Dintyong 让 Dyna 跨城市部署的核心价值，是让洛杉矶、纽约、西雅图的餐巾毫米级一致。换句话说，Jason 卖的不是手，是**一组可以 OTA 更新的"连锁 SOP 权重"**。这是餐饮经济学长达一个世纪都在追求的东西，第一次以权重文件的形式交付。
## 二、Flow Matching 的"降级"在机器人身上

item.title: [Latent Space] How to kill your SaaS: what we learned replacing a $43K/yr tool with AI agents
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的发现：AI 评审完全失效，但正是这个失效揭示了"品味"的本质

这场比赛最令人震惊的数据点被低调地藏在中段：AI 评审 Top10 中有六个被人类判为"弱"，而真正的冠军在 AI 排行榜上排第 19 位。表面上看这只是"AI 不够聪明"，但真相更深——AI 评审在前七名里把分差压缩到 2.3 分（饱和），说明它只能识别"及格线"而无法识别"卓越"。

这与心理测量学里一个老问题同构：标准化考试能有效筛出差生，却无法筛出天才（信度在尾部坍塌）。所以 AI 评审在这场比赛里真正扮演的角色不是裁判，而是健身房的热身器械——帮选手爬坡到及格线，然后它自己就瞎了。更妙的是，赛会方其实知道这件事并故意保留——他们在找"有品味的编码者"，而品味按定义就是尚未被形式化的判断力。一旦品味可以被 rubric 捕获，它就不再是品味。

二、被忽视的产业史重演：SaaS 时代其实是软件史上的"工业化插曲"

大多数评论者把这件事读成"AI 杀 SaaS"，但真正的叙事更长。软件行业其实经历过三段：

  1. 1980s–90s 定制时代：每家公司雇佣程序员写内部系统（像裁缝）
  2. 2000s–2020s SaaS 时代：Salesforce、Workday 们把软件变成成衣（像 Zara）
  3. 2026+ 代理时代：非工程师用 agent 回到定制（但是裁缝现在是运营总监本人）

这跟 摄影对绘画的冲击非常像——摄影没杀死绘画，但杀死了"肖像画作为中产职业"。类似地，AI 不会杀死所有 SaaS，只会杀死中段商品化 SaaS（视频里反复强调的 "mid-tier"）。Salesforce 不会死，session board 这类会死。被压扁的正是"卖软件其实在卖维护合同"的中间层。

还有一个几乎没人提的隐藏结构：Marco 承认他 4-5 年前就写过这些 spec。换句话说，执行从来不是护城河，设计意图才是。SaaS 公司这二十年卖的其实是"把 PM 的 doc 翻译成代码"的服务。当翻译成本归零，剩下只有 doc 本身——而 doc 的拥有者本来就是客户。

三、"If you break it, you own it" 的真正逆命题，与政府分权的奇怪同构

Kelsey 那段"我没法让百万美元客户去清缓存"的抱怨，表面上说的是责任制。但更深的洞察是三位冠军都不约而同采用了"没有模型批准自己工作"的架构——Claude 规划，Codex 实现；或者两队 worktree 对抗验证。

这跟 孟德斯鸠三权分立的底层逻辑一致：没有一个 agent 能既是裁判又是运动员。Green Room HQ 的做法——Claude 队和 Codex 队在隔离的 worktree 里互相合并门禁——几乎就是宪法学意义上的 checks and balances。

这里有一个跨到生物学的更深连接：免疫系统的 T 细胞之所以要在胸腺里"自我-非我"筛选，就是因为同一个识别器不能既产生判断又验证判断。AI agent 对自己代码的宽容和对他人代码的严苛，本质上和人类心理学里的"自我服务偏差（self-serving bias）"同源。换句话说，我们不是在设计工程流程，而是在用软件架构模拟免疫学和政治学已经解决了数百年乃至数亿年的问题。

最后一个让人不适的推论：既然"拥有即责任"，那么过去二十年企业疯狂外包软件的真正原因可能不是"效率"，而是责任外包。SaaS 卖的不是软件，是"锅"。当 AI 让你养得起自己的锅厨，你会突然发现以前每年付 43K 美元其实是心理保险费——现在这份保险不再划算，因为锅也变小了。

📝 转录文本

开场：一场真实的 SaaS 刺杀实验

Every few weeks, someone on my timeline declares that AI killed SaaS. Then someone else replies that you can't vibe code your way out of a real business problem. Back and forth, back and forth. So over, so back. So at Latent Space, we decided to stop arguing and actually try killing a real-life SaaS and evaluating it on real business evals.

This is a special episode recording on that experiment. So let us know what you think.

"And you literally put it into an LLM and you walk away for like 2 hours, like 3 hours. You just get the entire thing pixel perfect built."

"Um, I'm normally the person who has to set up session board, and so I was the one actually having to suffer through our actual session board. I can't ask someone who's like, you know, at a multi-million dollar company to refresh their cache because something we did broke."

背景：为什么要杀 SaaS

So quick context, I run two businesses, Latent Space and AI Engineer. AI Engineer runs conferences for the AI industry. We're looking at event software like Session Board to manage our speakers. We buy a bunch of software all over from tens of dollars to hundreds of thousands of dollars to fit our various events and platforms and needs.

For this particular piece of software that we needed, they quoted us $43,000 a year for four events. For three grand is a lot of tokens. And when we buy a software off the shelf and file a change request, it often takes something like 3 months to 6 months — or never — for them to actually ship something that we want to use.

We've run seven AI Engineer events and we know how bad this category of software is. For years, I've had it written into our literal company founding contract — I can literally show you — that nobody could build internal software without my explicit approval, because it is so easy to get not-invented-here syndrome with the general running of a business, and it's so easy to get distracted into building commodity software that you can just buy off the shelf.

This year I changed my mind. I think agents are finally good enough for us to have personalized software, and I'm putting my real money to the test.

The other thing that we found in terms of buying software is: SaaS is usually a bundle of things. We use maybe a third of what this particular vendor was selling us, and there's no discount for the stuff that we don't use.

比赛规则："Kill My SaaS"

So on a whim basically I put up a challenge called Kill My SaaS. Anyone can sign up and I give them the specs — the jobs to be done — of this particular piece of software. And the hardest thing to get a real eval from: real buyers who aren't interested in how you implement things. They just want to get done.

And that's basically my events team. They're not technical. They don't care what stack you use, what agent you use, what model you use. They don't care if it's open source, closed source. They just care whether they actually buy it and use it.

So ultimately, 72 people or 72 teams ended up submitting. Most of them are still live and open source, and we'll link to all of them. So go poke at them yourself.

为什么比看起来更难

So why is this harder than it looks? I want to use us as a case study for exactly the kind of routine mid-tier business software. You know, it's not Salesforce. It's not something that you vibe coded in a day. It's something in the middle where there's billions of dollars of just crappy software that regular everyday people are using.

Our software is like still relatively complicated. I think it's easy for people who don't have any exposure to this kind of business to appreciate why it's hard to replace. So for example, here are some of the jobs to be done:

  • Speaker submits a talk.
  • Reviewers score the talk.
  • The review committee accepts the talk.
  • Now we need a speaker portal to upload a headshot and slides.
  • Speakers get reminders if they haven't completed some tasks.
  • We place them in a room on the schedule.
  • We move the schedule. They change their title. They have to show up correctly on the public agenda.
  • All sorts of stuff. They have to add co-speakers.
  • There are sponsors. We have to do it all again for invited speakers and sponsors and attendees.

And one individual person can have one or two or three roles at once. You might be a speaker and a sponsor and an attendee, or you might be an organizer, a volunteer, a vendor, god knows what. Sometimes we just make roles up on the fly just because of that particular situation.

Event people are very risk-averse and for good reason. If software pushes us a week past the deadline, people show up at the wrong place or the conference just doesn't happen. All of that has happened to us before. We have to pay rush fees or union fees — stuff that just is super ugly under the hood — and attendees just take everything for granted as just happening because they pay for a ticket. And nobody I know loves their conference app.

比赛机制

So here's how we ran the contest. Builders got a brief that I wrote, a walkthrough video of a real product, and 42 screenshots that I sent inside of that brief. And I put up $10,000 for the winner. And since nobody builds this on a $20 Claude whatever plan, we actually offered up to $500 in token reimbursement for anyone who made a serious attempt — because there were a few half-ass attempts.

The final call basically goes to my real events team. So it's not me picking, and that's basically a semi-blind eval.

三大绊脚石

Here's what they kept tripping over. There were roughly three things.

1. Portals

The first was portals. Speakers, invited speakers, and sponsors each need their own portal, and most submissions only built one kind of portal that was not very flexible.

"So, like immediately off the bat, I noticed a bunch of quality-of-life improvements, so I appreciated that. You were one of the few that actually was able to parse out the difference between a form and a portal, which I loved. The biggest detractor — and don't get me wrong, this is amazing for everything you've done — was: we have multiple portals. For instance the CFP portal, the sponsor portal, the invited speakers portal. Having the ability for an admin to set up those multiple different portals in different ways — that was also a feature we have in session board, but it was one of the few things I didn't notice in yours that everyone else had."

2. Drag and drop

The second thing people tripped up on was effectively drag and drop — one of the more complex elements of a UI that is hard for models to get across. What we tested was: does the section actually move when you drag and drop it, and can you tell whether it's confirmed or updated, or if it's ambiguous? Because obviously you can't have a single person in two sessions, or double book a single room at a single time slot for multiple sessions.

"But I did like the tooltips. It did tell you how to do the setup. The problem was like, the tooltips was not — it felt like an overlay over what it should have done. 'Oh, click here to do a session,' or 'click the top to do a session.' I'm like, why can't I just click the button to add a session there? I really did like your clean drag and drop with schedule. One of my criteria was: can you do drag and drop with the schedule? Because that made me able to say, hey, did they actually follow the instructions?"

3. Adding a talk without pretending to submit it

The third was adding a talk without pretending to submit it through the CFP form, which you need for an invited speaker or a VIP.

None of these three were well specified on our docs or Session Board's — but you do find them immediately if you use the product like a real person.

AI 评审：有用但不是裁判

During the challenge, we also published our own AI judge. It was not meant to pick the winner — it's just a sanity check for people to get their applications up and running. Basically an RL environment without the RL part — just a sort of environment for people to hill-climb.

So basically our eval was: we had Claude logging in as each role and clicking through 20 scenarios that we wrote as normal user flows. You can see a sped-up version here. And basically using Claude again to grade it. So you can get flexibility on what you name the button, where you put it.

If you ever run a competition like this, I highly recommend it. Record yourself clicking through the full application, turn it into scenarios, release them so people can hill-climb.

We ran 56 apps through these evals. 40 of them had enough coverage to rank. Top seven landed within 2.3 points of each other, which is basically saturation. And I think it was very successful overall.

So hill-climbing against an automated eval I think is a very useful initial bootstrap step. For example, we have some of these examples from Lectern to Curtain Call pointing their workers particularly at areas where they scored lower and just hill-climbing that really quickly. I think that is a good first task for people doing SaaS coding to do.

And that works for parts you can build independently. But we also found that you have to tie them into an overall app, and that's where a lot of people fell down. They would spend a lot of tokens and they duplicated features with no connection because they didn't really dogfood their apps, and then they submitted it.

真正的裁判：人类事件团队

So really, our real judging after the AI judge was our events team led by Kelsey, who is head of ops at AI Engineer.

The ratings had a pretty poor correlation with the AI judge. For example, six of the AI judge top 10 was actually rated weak by our humans, and eventually our winner was 19th on the AI judge leaderboard. So it's kind of weak. It has some kind of R-squared correlation but not perfect, and it was never intended to be.

Some of the correlation stuff was on purpose. We let people deviate from the spec based on their own taste — to encourage them to, because honestly this is also a hiring exercise looking for people who can code with taste. We want people who understand the job to be done instead of the specific spec, and instead of mechanically cloning a product, you can actually define what a good user experience looks like.

So really this competition is not objective. The rubrics are not well defined, the spec is not well defined. If there was a checklist, we could publish a checklist. So we did publish a checklist that can be cloned, but taste is what we really are looking for from humans that are manipulating the coding agents. And if that's you, we're hiring, of course.

One of our builders, OpenStash, actually told us: most of what they were proud of putting into the app wasn't covered by the AI judge at all. And they were right. And we found that because we had humans clicking through every app.

他们是怎么造的

So how did people actually build these cloned apps?

First of all, the good news for the SaaS killers: almost everyone shipped something substantial. The median public repo was 91,000 lines of code, and people ran agents for days on end.

Claude Code and Codex were basically tied. And more interestingly, 40 of the 66 submissions used both of them. Nearly everyone mixed model families. All three finalists use GPT-soul, but so did 50 of the other 66, and so there's no alpha.

How they split the work is what I find most interesting, because I don't really do it myself. I tend to keep one model per project so that all the context stays in one place. I want one Codex thread to cover everything to be able to discover the past stuff that I did. I want one Claude Code thread to also do the same thing for the task that I deem them to be most fit.

It turns out that a lot of these builders don't do that. They actually switch roles. And one interesting part of this whole process is that we had the builders commit their prompts and process docs to GitHub — a voluntary submission by them — so you can actually read exactly how they did it.

三种模式

Overall, we studied what they submitted and how they use these mixed model situations and we found three patterns:

  1. A smart model decides what to do and then a cheaper model is the slot cannon that writes what was specified. One example was Cboard HQ. They had Claude plan and review while Codex wrote most of the code.
  2. One model builds and a different one checks — and usually whichever is better at driving a browser or testing, that's the one that checks. I think right now that is GPT Codex.
  3. No model approves its own work. Green Room HQ ran a Claude team and a Codex team in separate worktrees, and neither can merge until the other one verifies it. That's just a principle of on-policy versus off-policy verification. Agents tend to be easier on their own work than they are on other people's work. And I think that's reflective of what humans do as well.

决赛选手：开始编码前的工作

So overall that is the process of cloning. We data-mined everything and we're sharing some of our initial findings. But now let's talk about the finalists. We interviewed all three of them, and they were so nice to come in for a recorded interview. This is the qualitative side of humans talking to humans about the process and understanding them. We also wanted to make sure that they were real before we award the prizes.

The first thing they all reported in common was how much work happened before any code was prompted or got written. They actually did a fair amount of preliminary exploration and spec writing.

Marco：先规划 8–9 小时

So Marco has cloned apps for clients before. His rule is to plan everything first.

"If the UX/UI is done, the only thing I do is I sit down for 8–9 hours and I, in the most granular way, I plan out the entire data schema, the business logic, and literally pseudocode. So it's kind of funny, because it's like, if you take these tasks that I did like four or five years ago and the design, and you literally put it into an LLM and you walk away for like 2 hours, like 3 hours, you just get the entire thing pixel perfect built."

Yazin：先爬整个帮助站

Yazin from Conferencer started with research. He crawls Session Board's entire help site before writing a spec.

"Yeah, the first step, sort of before even doing the direct prompting, was doing a lot of research. I took the Google Doc, I turned it into a markdown file, and then I also ran Firecrawl on — I think it was — they crawled the entirety of Session Board's help portal, as well as a few other sites that were kind of similar that popped up in the results. And yeah, I just tried to get as much information as possible."

Valentin：先造模板和护栏

Our third finalist Valentin put most of his effort into guardrails, and he turned them into a template that anyone can use.

"So I've made it a template rather than formalizing it. In many projects I have to redo this old work, and this was a perfect example where I hate-swap like everyone — and if you have to take over this project you want to be able to write on it like code. So I spent so much time putting the links, putting the whatever code reviews whatsoever, and now I just made it a GitHub template. So for each new repository I will clone from — system light — so I don't have to redo this whole thing. But I don't have a Google doc saying here's what I've done. Yeah, it's fully open source."

Then his agents mapped every flow in the product before he planned who works on what in parallel.

"Huge exploration of swiping everything on the internet. Basically, I just asked Codex, 'Hey dude, you must be able to draw me every single flow of every single feature of this app.' And amazing thing is — there was a bunch of YouTube videos. And so he took screenshots of frame by frame to be like, 'Oh, okay, here's what happened.' And then he had a huge markdown folder of markdown with the expectation of each feature. And only from that, then the goal was: okay, well divide that into things that can be done concurrently. Some features might overlap and so you might have to do it sequentially, but basically create a plan of what must start, how many agents can you do concurrently for each step, and then do everything. Once it's done everything, I did the manual process of everything — it works like, 'Oh wait, it's not perfect. Why?' Oh, why? Because I see that he's actually never launching the app locally. Okay, then the next step is to redo the whole process, but with the app running locally."

Marco 的 stack

Marco fed the walkthrough video and Session Board's API docs straight into Claude.

"I literally took the video that Sean shared. I took the documentation, the API reference from Session Board. I put it into Claude. I told it to use Convex and Next.js and my preferred stack, because obviously speed etc. is quite important. So the Convex just gives you a real-time database. It's a super simple — it will literally give you something that's highly performant and feels good without a lot of work."

So if you look at all of these clips, notice that nobody said they typed one prompt and walked away. Really the prompt was almost the last step that you sort of lead up to after building up a full knowledge of the problem and mocks and docs and specs and all this stuff. Most of the work was figuring out what the software actually does, and then they can deviate from there.

真正的狗粮：5 分钟测试

One other thing that all three finalists did was the unglamorous part. They used their own products as a real user over and over.

One of them wrote that the agent was very good at building but quite bad at noticing UX issues. For example, they had a headshot upload feature which saved a photo somewhere, but then the public speaker page would not even read from the same place because it was just coded independently.

Valentin's version of this was a 5-minute test. If you can't get through the product smoothly in five minutes, something is missing.

"So I just put myself in your shoes and be like, okay, if I have only five minutes to test the product, what will it be? And as long as the five minutes were not smooth, I would redo the whole process. Meaning okay, something must be missing. Either it's context about the product, either it's context about the expectation, or maybe it's not able to test what the current state of a product is. But my goal again was never to do anything manually of 'oh I don't like that' or 'oh I don't like this.' I would just, for example, give — okay, onboarding is... why the hell — and I would ask him to explore the traces to understand, okay, what comes from, is it because we gave no instruction about onboarding? And he would tell me something like, 'Oh well, this was just a title about onboarding, and onboarding is just supposed to onboard, but we have no idea about what's a good onboarding.' Okay, so I know that in the process it's not only about 'do an onboarding,' it's about okay, what defines a good path for onboarding, what defines a bad path. And so ask him okay — and redo the old step, the old flow, but include a step that is researching what defines a good onboarding."

Yazin 的 clickthrough

Yazin just kept clicking through and keeping a running list of fixes.

"And once it was done, it just sends me back these videos, and I have to sort of click through, and that's when I realized, okay, like it's actually really annoying to switch between the different views. So that's why I did the — yeah, there actually wasn't a way — you had to sign out and sign in, and then I'm like, where are the username and passwords? And then I had to add those. So that's when I kind of realized there were some obvious things that were missing. So the sign-in stuff, and then switching portals, and then I also added Resend support. And I kind of realized there were a few UX issues — just stuff that was kind of obvious. And I was looking through it and I was like, all right, let me fix those. So I just had like a running list just clicking through."

意外的 polish

And net care showed up in places we didn't actually ask for. Here's Kelsey on Conferencer's deliverables page:

"Your tweaks were great. Like, I showed this to our content manager and she's like, 'What? That's all in one page?' You don't need to click into the individual forms to see the statuses, and she's just like, 'That's amazing.'"

"Yeah. Structurally it looked okay after it was done. But then I was like, you know, it would just make so much more sense if the menu is reorganized and there were icons and things kind of logically came together. And I think that was one of the things where it just ended up doing huge changes to the deliverables page, and also the abstracts page — because that one looked, you know, it just looks very table-y, and then you're trying to make it seem like an actual UI."

反驳：AI 并不能完全杀 SaaS

So now it's time to push back on the idea that we can completely kill SaaS with AI. Cloning something that looks like it works is really the easy part. And we've proven that with so many submissions that were all honestly decent first-shot clones. But somebody still has to keep it running — take bug reports, fix it at 2 a.m.

Literally last night, Flo on my team was throwing a dozen Codex agents at our Token Billionaires program right before it went up, with a conference already running at AI Engineer.

If you break it, you own it. And now a lot of people talk about the other way around too: if you own it, you can break it.

Kelsey put it better than I can:

"So, we have multiple things connecting to each other that are hodgepodged together with certain APIs — some speak to another. Anyways, we want this all-in-one system where we want to be able to say registration data goes to the sponsor portal, the sponsor portal can immediately go to our schedule. Like, we're having problems with the piecemeal effect, and we know enough to basically say, hey, we want better. We could do this better. We need this better. But we don't have time. So we can't prompt the agents. We can't have that — you know, like, as soon as something breaks, we need someone to be able to go in, fix it, fix the error of it. So that's kind of like why we're having this."

And here's Kelsey again on what it's like when a sponsor hits a bug and the vendor's answer is to clear your cache:

"Our sponsor came to us and said, 'Hey, we have a bug, hey, I can't unassign these tickets.' And I had to go back to the chat support for this. And then, you know, do all of this. And then they had to go back to their engineers, and do all of this. And then their engineers came back to their chat support agent, which came back to me, and said, 'Hey, can you try refreshing your cache?' And I'm like, I'm not going to tell our sponsor to refresh their cache in order to fix the bug two steps away from this. And so this was one of those user-availability errors of like, I can't ask someone who's at a multi-million-dollar company to refresh their cache because something we did broke. So there's a level of accountability of — I don't care how you fix it, I need it to not break."

Which is why I told Yazin what I want to build first in terms of building up this new internal software tools team:

"We should probably replace our own software first, because I think that is something that will give joy to everybody. And then we can talk about other stuff. But, you know, I have non-stop ideas for the team. I just need people who know how to work with me on turning those ideas into things that people actually enjoy using."

"Yeah. So like, go deep, and then create software that's not sort of a small piece of the entire slice, but the entire thing. I think that would be so interesting — like, just seeing what the experience could look like if you were to build out the entire vision in a way that no, like, piecemeal software would be able to fulfill."

结果公布

Okay, the moment you've been waiting for — the results.

Five apps cleared our bar for something we'd actually adopt or seriously consider buying: three finalists plus two more. There are another 12 projects that we found ideas we'd probably steal even if we wouldn't use the whole app. Obviously all of them open source, so congrats to them.

第二名（$1,000）：Marco Kramer of TrackStage

We found that he had the cleanest drag and drop complex scheduling UI experience in the field, and also a really well-documented repo. If you want to learn how to run an agent fleet, go read it. And also check out Marco's main day job, Cortex, which is kind of a ChatGPT knowledge-base clone.

第一名（$5,000）：Yazin of Conferencer

By far the best click-through experience of just intuitively navigating the whole app — with every deliverable displayed on one page, which you heard Kelsey get excited about — and also real emails at every step of the speaker lifecycle. It made transactional email enjoyable, and that's a really hard thing to do, and we have some experience with that. And we came away pretty sure that Yazin puts that level of care into everything.

冠军（$10,000）：Valentin de Matas of OpenRostrum

He built a software factory, debugged the factory, shipped multiple portals and a schedule that our team actually wanted to use. And we'll probably be shipping to all of you guys for 2027's AI Engineer conferences. My team is so excited.

What we run in 2027 will probably be a mix of OpenRostrum and Conferencer plus ideas from the other 12. My team is so excited about this because now we know what event software built in 2026 can look like, instead of software built in 2006. And the fact that we can own that software and improve it based on real user feedback.

Like, my people that are coding the most on the team are not engineers. They're designers. They're domain experts. They're operations people — the people actually doing the work and reporting everything and getting minute-level turnaround on their bug reports and feature requests.

收尾：路线图

So just to wrap up, that's the overall story of how we killed our own $43,000 SaaS that we're about to buy. If you're renting a software that you don't love and will never own, that's actually a reasonable thing to do now, and we have published the roadmap to do that.

Cloning something — that piece of mid-tier software — probably costs a thousand dollars in tokens, let's call it, on subscriptions, and maybe another 10,000 more in AI engineering expertise. For which all of these people who submitted, probably you can hire some of them.

But then the trade-off is that from then on you own it, which also means you're responsible for maintaining it. That's not a trivial trade, but also it's not a negative in a strict sense, because agents make maintaining and customizing your own software for your team far more feasible than literally 12 months ago.

All right, to everyone who took part in Kill My SaaS, sorry it took so long to get back. It turns out that evals are hard. We were running two simultaneous conferences — I'm recording this at AI Engineer New York, and we have AI Engineer Code next month — and we did this on top of our regular day jobs. So the first time around it was a very chaotic process, but I think the next time we have learned a lot of lessons, and the next time I'm definitely planning this a lot better and not doing this by myself, so that we can get back to people and be more structured.

Our team has gone from skeptical about AI vibe-coded apps to now we're demanding it — and excited not about the cost savings. I mean, cost savings is part of it, but using the cost savings to fund actual software improvements that we've never been able to pay for. I much rather pay for tokens and use my time to build software that all of my attendees, my sponsors, my speakers actually enjoy using and deserve.

So if you want to sponsor the next Kill My SaaS, if you want to participate, I really appreciate that. All the repos we're going to link in the related post to this post, and congrats to the winners. See you next time.
