item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的发现：AI 评审完全失效，但正是这个失效揭示了"品味"的本质
这场比赛最令人震惊的数据点被低调地藏在中段：**AI 评审 Top10 中有六个被人类判为"弱"，而真正的冠军在 AI 排行榜上排第 19 位**。表面上看这只是"AI 不够聪明"，但真相更深——AI 评审在前七名里把分差压缩到 2.3 分（饱和），说明它**只能识别"及格线"而无法识别"卓越"**。
这与心理测量学里一个老问题同构：**标准化考试能有效筛出差生，却无法筛出天才**（信度在尾部坍塌）。所以 AI 评审在这场比赛里真正扮演的角色不是裁判，而是**健身房的热身器械**——帮选手爬坡到及格线，然后它自己就瞎了。更妙的是，赛会方其实知道这件事并故意保留——他们在找"有品味的编码者"，而品味**按定义就是尚未被形式化的判断力**。一旦品味可以被 rubric 捕获，它就不再是品味。
## 二、被忽视的产业史重演：SaaS 时代其实是软件史上的"工业化插曲"
大多数评论者把这件事读成"AI 杀 SaaS"，但真正的叙事更长。软件行业其实经历过三段：
1. **1980s–90s 定制时代**

item.title: [Business of Sport] “We had 10 Days to Rescue the Football Club” | The Torquay United Story
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的发现："旅游衰退"才是这家百年俱乐部真正的病根

表面上这是一个"烂摊子救援+财务翻盘"的故事，但真正惊人的是 Michael 轻描淡写地揭示的那条暗线——托基（Torquay）作为英国"里维埃拉"小镇，过去 20–30 年因廉价欧洲航班而被掏空。换句话说，这家足球俱乐部不是被老板搞垮的，而是被瑞安航空、被马洛卡的阳光、被全球化消费地理学慢慢杀死的。俱乐部进入管理清算只是最终的会计确认。

这就产生了一个让人意外的推论：他们买下的其实不是一支球队，而是一个社区的"最后一盏灯"。 Michael 原话——"如果足球俱乐部也没了，那还剩什么？"（what else is left?）这不是情感修辞，而是精准的宏观诊断。他们在做的，本质上是一场地方性反熵工程——用一个 125 年的符号，去对冲一个海滨经济体几十年的坍缩。

二、跨领域连接：他们正在把俱乐部从"娱乐业"迁移到"情感基础设施业"

这里有一个几乎没人点破的转型。Michael 在最后说出了关键一句——"We are dopamine providers（我们是多巴胺供应商）"。这句话一旦被你听进去，整个商业模式会瞬间重排：

  • 他们和 Netflix、TikTok、手游公司在竞争同一样东西——人的注意力和周期性情绪峰值；
  • 他们和教堂、工人俱乐部、大家族饭桌在竞争同一样东西——"共融"（communing）；
  • 他们和健身房、心理咨询、抗抑郁药在竞争同一样东西——在一个"没什么可高兴的生活里"稳定供给的那一下 endorphin。

这就是为什么他们的"最快增长用户画像是年轻家庭"——这个数据点非常反常识。按常理，低级别足球的新客应该是中年老球迷的回归，但事实是：没有历史包袱的新家庭在用 Torquay 替代那些已经消失的社会制度（教堂、大家庭、工人俱乐部）。这意味着俱乐部真正的护城河不是球场、不是球员，而是"每两周一次、三代人并肩站立、经济阶层被抹平的仪式空间"——这是 Spotify 永远无法复制的产品。

跨领域再推一步：这和日本"商店街复兴"、荷兰"社区花园运动"、底特律"城市农业"是同一种东西——都是在后全球化时代，用一个高度地方化的、不可外包的仪式性资产，重新编织正在解体的社区微结构。足球只是伪装。

三、隐藏的系统性真相："球员工资—名次"相关性是一种结构性集体幻觉

这是整段访谈最值得警惕的"啊哈"时刻。两位主席一边破除工资—成绩的直接相关性神话（把工资从营收的 70–80% 砍到 35–45%，还打进附加赛边缘），一边又承认这条相关性确实在统计上成立。听起来矛盾？不矛盾——因为整个联赛的所有俱乐部都相信它成立，所以它就成立了。 这是一个纳什均衡式的囚徒困境：没人敢率先退出军备竞赛，于是数据永远会"验证"相关性，构成一个自我实现的真理。

Torquay 的策略其实是一场"元博弈" ——他们没有否认这条曲线，而是选择"向下平移整条曲线的截距"：他们不是在相同工资下取得更好名次，而是用更低工资维持中游，然后把省下来的差额投入 commercial 和 academy，让收入曲线斜率上翻。两年把营收 top line 加了 100 万英镑，这才是真正的赢面——他们在换一条曲线，而不是在同一条曲线上刷分。

而这又连接到一个更隐秘的真相：全英足球金字塔的瓶颈不在球场，而在"学院许可（Academy License）"规则。Michael 冷静地指出——学院地位竟然和一队的联赛级别绑定，这意味着像 Ollie Watkins 这种本地天才被迫流失到 Exeter，Exeter 由此赚到 500–600 万英镑。这其实是整个英格兰低级别足球最大的"资源分配 bug"：越是急需 player trading 收入的小俱乐部，越被规则禁止培养自己的卖品。这在制度设计上和"大学排名决定科研经费"一样荒谬——用结果去决定造血资格，而非反过来。

四、给你的额外一击：Neil Warnock 的"方法论"价值大于"情感"价值

大家都在把 Warnock 当作可爱的吉祥物，但看他实际做了什么：他是在把 17–18 任董事会主席的隐性经验，反向传递给两位缺乏足球经验的新主席。Mark 说得极准——"他告诉我们好主席好在哪、烂主席烂在哪、为什么。" 这是管理咨询界价值最高的那种资产：高频样本下的因果反刍。一位做过 9 次升降级的老帅，相当于一个只专注"足球俱乐部治理"这一门课、带着 40 年数据的 McKinsey 合伙人——而他只收一杯茶的费用，顺便带去更衣室讲几个段子。 这才是 Torquay 真正偷来的那张王牌。

📝 转录文本

临危受命：10 天抢救一家百年俱乐部

开场：买下一家破产俱乐部，是在"盲买"

The trouble is when you buy a club out of administration, you're buying it essentially blind. We had 10 days in which to close the deal so we could scramble to make it to the National League AGM and keep our place in the pyramid.

Torquay's main industry is tourism hospitality and that's been on a precipitous decline over the last 20–30 years, and we felt if the football club goes that felt to us like the final nail in the coffin for the community.

We were only custodians of this football club. It's got 125 years of heritage. So therefore, we've got to make sure this football club is here for another 125 years. And we're not here for ego. We're here to support the club.

We've added a million quid to the top line of the business in two seasons. Fans have gone from being hostages to apostles. This is all new stuff that we've been allowed to create because the community's given us permission to do so.

Your academy status shouldn't be determined where your men's first team is in the pyramid. And famously we sit there and look at Ollie Watkins, who's a Torquay boy, born in Torquay, could have been a Torquay — and I wasn't a Torquay academy player, we shut the academy, went to Exeter, and Exeter have benefited to the tune of five–six million.

We want success, we want to get up to the next level, everyone knows that — but my god, we've come a long way.

I'm going to say two words: Neil Warnock.

第一部分：两位联席主席与"疯狂的足球世界"

主持人： Fascinating. Gents, delighted to have you in the studio. Firstly, for me, this is strange because it's two people on that side, one on this side. More often than not, it's actually the other way round, but to have both of you in the studio is fantastic. As co-chairs, we rarely get the opportunity. So, thank you for joining.

嘉宾： Our pleasure.

主持人： How has it been? I mean, that's probably the best way to start, isn't it? Firstly, working together, being co-chairs — that must provide its own entertainment. And secondly, getting into the mad world of football.

嘉宾（Mark）： Mad world of football, yeah. Roller coaster. Very close the last couple of years, obviously, to getting promoted, but very proud of the way the consortium has been put together. And that's been down very much to this gentleman to my left. He did a great job persuading me to get involved.

When we first heard about Torquay going into administration and we got the financial package, it was definitely too big a job for me. Not necessarily the finance, but the amount of time that was needed — hence the reason for co-chairs. And then there were various individuals that came forward who were lifelong Torquay United supporters, successful in their own right.

And very proud now to be at a level where we've got seven top guys, different skill sets — whether it be in marketing, whether it be in negotiation, whether it be in just management — and we've all come together, and yeah, we've created something quite amazing really in terms of where we are, in terms of building up the support again, building up the optimism, sponsorship, bringing the supporters' trust in, making a happy club. So yeah, it's fantastic.

第二部分：第一次接触——"周日那通电话"

The supporters' trust got in contact with me, said, "We've got this guy called Michael Westcott. Have you heard about him?" And I went, "No." So the first thing I did was went on a computer: who's Michael Westcott? And then I kept getting a phone call from Michael Westcott. And it was on a Sunday. I was like, "Oh god, stop phoning me up." I thought one time I'm going to have to answer it.

And then I answered it and he said, "D, can I have a chat with you tomorrow?" And I said, "Yeah." And then we had to get our proposition, our tender, in to Torquay — I think it was about 3:00, 4:00 in the afternoon on Monday. And Michael had done a lot of work on the budgeting, etc., what was required. And then literally within half an hour, three-quarters of an hour, it bit me. Couldn't let it go. Had to get involved in it.

I thought there would be a lot more people involved in terms of putting in tenders to the football club — and there wasn't. And when I felt that we were — we know we weren't the last chance saloon, but I felt there wasn't enough people behind it in terms of supporters, in terms of finance and investment for what that club needed. So we had to get involved.

第三部分：俱乐部的历史与社区意义

主持人： You said administration, you said last chance saloon — probably the perfect time. Michael, for people that may not know, can you just give a little bit of background as to what has happened?

Michael： Yeah. So if we rewind the clock to February 2024, the previous season — so in 2022 we lost on penalties at Ashton Gate to get promoted back into the EFL after a 10-, no, yeah, nearly eight-year absence. Two years later we dropped down another level. And on February the 24th — which is a date that will be emblazoned on my mind — the then owner put the club into administration and said he's no longer able to financially back the club. Brought in the administrator, Begbies, who then went about trying to find someone to take on the club. And it was at that point that we got involved with the process.

We were half a dozen individuals that were either contacted by different people within the club network, by the club itself, or by each other. And those are the first early days of the consortium coming together.

主持人： And just to be really clear, we're talking here about a club with huge heritage and value, not just to the community but to football in this country. 125 plus years, if I'm right.

Michael： Yeah. 125 years is right, of which 80 years was spent straight in the EFL. Torquay have always been really a League Two club, that occasionally flirted and had the odd year in League One and then back down again. And we were part of the furniture, really — part of the fabric of the EFL. We were most clubs' favourite away day because you'd have a weekend at the English Riviera. People will come down, and we're a quirky little club on the seaside.

I think when the club went into administration, it became really clear to us as fans how beloved the club was by the football fraternity, which I thought was really interesting. And we've had some high-profile players come and finish their careers with us over the years — you think of people like Chris Waddle and Bruce Rioch and people like that.

Growing up as lifelong fans — and particularly at that point — since the advent of cheap travel to the continent, Torquay's main industry is tourism, hospitality, and that's been on a precipitous decline over the last 20, 30 years. And we felt if the football club goes, that felt to us like the final nail in the coffin for the community.

As someone that grew up in Torbay in the 70s and 80s — and we all did — we felt that we lived in paradise, because it was by the sea, it was fantastic, it was booming. And it's been sad to watch its decline. And then if the football club went… like, what else is left?

That was one of my personal motivations: like, we can't let this die. It means too much to the community.

第四部分：盲买之后——账本"清洗"的一年

主持人： A lot of fans, if their football club is in trouble, would look at it and go, "I need to be able to do something." When you're in the position — or you think you're in the position — to do it, and the club's been in such significant financial trouble, how did you make the call that this was something, from a business perspective, financially, that you thought you could do?

Mark： It's really interesting that you say that, because the package that came in — the financial package of how things stood on the finances — was incorrect. And it's taken us a year to cleanse that completely to understand what those costs are. What actual ticket receipts did we get from those, or were they all freebies? How much money is actually coming to this football club? That took us a lot of time to cleanse all that process.

And we knew that we could invest in the football club. We knew that we had to get involved. I think I can say this for all members of the consortium: we're here for the long term. We're here to make sure that we get this club back to where we want to be.

On the first day that we came out of administration, we did a speech to Sky Sports and we said: we want to get this club back at least into the EFL, and that is our mandate. That's what we've got to do. We're moving in the right direction.

We've spoken about the investment that we've put in, but also we're going to use the skill sets of our business management to make sure that we bring that optimism on the ticket sales, that we have other options in terms of non-match day income, that we bring those sponsors into the football club, that we now have a system whereby we can bring in an academy or bring a player and we can get transfer fees for the football club if it's correct. So I think we've laid a lot of the foundations.

And I saw, when you interviewed Robert Smethurst — a lot of it is very similar to what he had to deal with at Macclesfield. When you come out of administration and you sign the final paperwork, you've got solicitors there and they've almost got a sign-off: those are the accounts and you just have to take them as they are. But what supporting evidence have you got here? How are you helping us out here? What happens if something goes wrong? "Hey, you're signing it as it is. That is what it is. That is how it is. You're signing to take over this football club."

So yeah — a lot learned, a lot of improvements. The efficiencies are much better within the football club. They can still be improved, but me, Michael, and all the guys in the consortium knew from day one that there was an investment initially to support the club, stabilize the club — but we're only custodians of this football club. It's got 125 years of heritage. So therefore, we've got to make sure this football club is here for another 125 years. We've got to make sure we lay that groundwork for other people. If there comes a point that they want to come in and they're the right people, good strategic investors to get us to the next stages, then we're more than welcome. We're not here for ego. We're here to support the club.

第五部分：真实的财务画像——1.1 百万年亏损

Michael： Back then the administrator gave us a set of numbers which said the club turned over about £1.88 million and was losing about £1.1 million on an annualized basis, and had done for the previous seven years.

主持人： 1.1 — those numbers, that's incredible.

Michael： Over five years, so revenues were about £1.88 million and they were on a P&L basis losing about £1.1 million on an annualized basis.

主持人： And where was the slippage? Where was the ill discipline?

Michael： The usual — two things. Playing budget completely, we think, out of whack, and vastly underexploited revenue generation. So the commercial operation was underinvested, moribund, and given the reach and the size of the club, we felt commercially it was super underexploited.

So we set about: how can we right-size the cost base? The playing budget clearly was over-inflated and we felt that the commercial performance was significantly underperforming. And so we started to set about a new model where, rather than the playing budget being 70–80% of turnover, it was closer to 35–40–45% of turnover.

And that's kind of where we are today. So we felt: can we recreate a more sustainable model?

The trouble is when you buy a club out of administration, there's no due diligence. There's no warranties given to you. You're buying it essentially blind. And the clock is ticking. We had a real deadline — we had 10 days in which to close the deal so we could scramble to make it to the National League AGM and keep our place in the pyramid.

主持人： Financially, when you complete that deal, what were they requiring you to show? Existing cash day one for both — buy and for the next three years. How detailed was it?

Michael： So they needed from us a cash flow forecast, a detailed P&L plan for the next three seasons, and they did their diligence on us. And obviously, through the CVA, we had to put cash on account, creditors in full. We had to provide proof of funds between us that we could fund the cash flow of the business going forward — not on the current losses, but on the revised business plan that we submitted. The three-year business plan that we submitted to the National League and their advisers — they diligenced that.

第六部分：破解"工资预算 = 名次"的神话

主持人： People would assume — and it's the big problem with football — that if you get your cost base on the playing side to 35 to 40%, that your performance is going to reflect that. They're going to think you're going to be 50% worse on the pitch because of this illness that we've created within football that just directly attributes excessive spend, careless spend, reckless spend, just because it's how the system works, to success. Debunk that myth by doing what you've done.

Mark： I think this is an opportune time to mention about Paul Wotton when he came in. Paul we acquired from Truro, and he came in and on the first day he had one player signed on. And he brought in all these players by the deadline so we could compete. And as you know, in the first season we lost out by two goals from going up. It was a tremendous achievement.

We were around about £650K, I think it was — if I'm correct — when we took over the club, not including scouts, management and everything, just the playing side. The players, it was about £1.3 million. So you can see — and they were struggling in National League South. They managed to just stay up. So it's an incredible journey to get to where we are.

And do you know what — that's one of the things that I would say I've learnt most about football, is the fact that any one of those teams in National League South, if they're at home, they can beat you. And they may have a budget of £400,000, £500,000, they might be PE teachers playing football, but every single club gives you a game. It is tough out there.

And I love the name "Business of Sport" that you use, because one of the things I said to Michael last night: we put ourselves down as "we don't know enough about football, or we don't know enough about what's going on within that football fraternity." We do. We're businessmen. At the end of the day, it is still a business and it has to be solvent and it has to be sustainable.

So, you've got to try to match the pressure that a manager is giving you. And bearing in mind, the manager has pressure because of his contract — he has to be successful. Managers get sacked all the time. So when they come in and say, "Oh, that team's spending this much money, that team's spending that much money" — we're part of a CEO group and chairman's group. And they'll tell you with us all. We talk about things. We talk about players. We talk about managers. And they'll tell you what their budgets are and what they're doing. And it's nothing like what some of those people are saying.

As I said, I'll call back to Macclesfield — Rob — what he said. It's not about what we're doing at the moment, and you know where the figures are right. So you've got to hold your wits, believe what you're doing, and make sure you've got a great manager who has the contacts and the pool of players that can bring them in. And Paul did a wonderful job with that, and we went close, as I say, in the first year, and the foundations were built in the second year as well, which Jimmy's now taken over.

Michael： But you're saying "debunk the myth" — is playing budget related, is there a direct line with performance? Well, obviously, yes. If you put the player wages budget against a league position, there are a few outliers, but they generally correlate — at our level, and especially when we're rescuing a business that was effectively bankrupt and trying to rebuild the cost base and fire up revenue channels.

The way for Torquay United to spend more on players is to increase the top line of the business. So 40% of £1.8m is a lot smaller number than 40% of £2.8m, which it is now.

Mark referenced Paul Wotton — why we recruited Paul Wotton as our manager in the first season. We knew that we needed to bring the wage budget down. We knew that he had geographic knowledge of the playing universe down in the Southwest, and so we could recruit locally and we could have a hybrid team of part-time and full-timers to keep a lid on wages while we set about growing the top line of the club.

Also, you wanted a coach — and a manager — that can recruit experience where you need it to make a difference, and be smart about recruiting down the pyramid where you could bring in young talent that you can develop on lower wages to make the numbers add up. So it's getting that balance right.

But the truth is — and this is the reality of football — there is a direct correlation between investment in player wages and performance in the league. Is it right? Not sure. But it is true, and it creates a problem for most of us. And that's why I think it's a system that's essentially broken.

主持人： So why are you all doing it?

Michael： Just because — he's right, I could go home. Football just gets a hold of you like nothing else does. It's mind-blowing because we're a group — we've got a diverse series of interests on our board and our group. You've got a guy that's a CEO of one of the biggest financial institutions in the world, publicly listed. This guy next to me has grown one of the biggest medical and testing laboratory businesses in Europe. I've got an extensive media background. Two guys that built huge businesses in the motor trade. We've got a guy that's built a huge music industry business — music tech entrepreneur of the year, and all of that.

So we live in these other worlds, right? And then we have these crazy board meetings, discussions where you look at these numbers and these decisions — like, why are we… in our world we would not make decisions like this, but why are we suddenly looking at each other, nodding like, "yeah, this makes sense"?

In the football world — and I don't want to sound frivolous, because the football club is so important to the community it serves, and I don't want to feel that this is a plaything, because it certainly isn't for us. But I bristle when people say, "Well, the normal rules of football, the normal rules of business don't apply in football." There's an element of that, but that's both its attractiveness and the downside of football for me.

第七部分：情感 vs. 商业——怎么做决定

主持人： It's weird. I'm very conscious when asking some of these questions — you sit down and have these conversations on the level of judgment that you ever seem to share when you talk about some of this from a business perspective, because it is so easy to sit outside of it and look with full impartiality saying, "Well, that's a mad decision. That didn't make sense from a business perspective." But as we all know, that's probably only 10% of the story.

Emotion versus sound business is why people get lost in the middle. Now, is that excusing bad practice? No. And we know the impact of owners who maybe don't have that feeling on clubs and do treat them more as a plaything. The one I was going to ask is: how do you make your decisions? How have you found making decisions where you don't get driven by emotion? Where you have to keep a head on you? Because football from a fan versus football as an owner is a very different place — or is it?

Mark： From a fan's perspective, they look for communication, transparency, trust, people they can rely on, and a football team they can be proud of and be successful. The figures almost are immaterial. Okay — long-term supporters, yes, stability, a club, etc. So, it's a different conversation to potentially coming in there from a business perspective and making it profitable, or at least break-even.

It's very tough. In my own business, I think my colleagues would say to me, "Oh, you're quite a tough negotiator." But then I could go up to the manager, go to training, he'd say "I want that player," and then immediately I walk out of there and go, "Have I given him a yes that he can go and get that player?" It's a very different type of emotion to a normal business.

Look, we sit back and we see the history of football. We see these clubs who managed to get success and move on to the next stage — be it an FA Cup run, etc. — and you dream of giving that to the fans. You think about how can you make this club be as successful as possible. And obviously, as Michael said, it does come down to finance sometimes and how much you can spend on playing budgets as well as coaching.

Don't put yourself down too much about that you haven't got the skill sets in football to be able to make those decisions, because I think you do get persuaded to do things that you wouldn't normally do in a business environment. The amount of times I've sat back and gone, "Why have we signed that player? Why have we done this?"

One of the successes we had in our first year with Paul — I mentioned it earlier about having one player signed on — we brought players in. It's impossible to bring 21 players in and them all to be successful. When we had four or five players that weren't delivering, we were able to loan them out and move them, bring other players in. So, one of the things they say in business — one of the best things about businesses and the way they grow — is flexibility. You're able to change decisions very quickly. And I think you need to do that with football clubs.

The one thing that I've learned is to try and remove that emotion from it. Somebody comes up to me who's a supporter and says, "I can't afford my season ticket," and everything else — I'll probably go in and buy it, mate. It's that difficult. But you do have to take it away sometimes and say, "we've got to move away from all this emotional side and get this back to normal."

主持人： You may have a few people coming up to you now going "£3,98…"

Mark： But it is a bit like that. On the first day when we came out, there was a guy who came to me and said, "I can't afford my season ticket, I've been here for so many years, is there anything that we can do on it?" And you take this personally. You want to give everyone the opportunity to come and watch the club. Especially in the current financial market, what can we do to help people to come to the football club? So it is very difficult. The responsibility is unbelievable for every individual with that football club — whether it be staff, players, manager, everybody, supporters. It's tough.

第八部分：Paul Wotton 的离任——"把船从礁石拉下来"

主持人： You mentioned Paul a few times and you clearly attribute a lot of the success that you've had in the last two years to him. But then — to the point that you've just made and disassociating some of the emotion from it — he's no longer your manager. When you have to make decisions like this and you're new to football ownership and you've still got that fandom, how do you do it? Because I'd imagine it is impossibly difficult. And yet from the outside you're often the ones that look like the bad guys.

Michael： The emotion of football — trying to park your fan head at the door and put your business head as custodians of a football club, knowing that 24 months ago that ship was steered onto the rocks and 125 years of heritage and being part of the community nearly disappeared. So we pulled the ship off the rocks and we're trying to set sail out to calmer waters and then sunnier waters.

Don't forget — the reason we were in a position to be able to help save the club was the fact that we've made good decisions in business along the way to allow us that opportunity to do that. And so your business head does kick in around discipline — and particularly, most successful businesses are built on the backs of founders being able to make good decisions about people. And we felt that we made the right decisions on people at the time that we needed it.

Then your business plan evolves, you start looking a bit further down the road. We're no longer looking over our shoulders thinking, "oh, we're going to get washed back on the rocks." We're out of the rip currents now, we're steaming towards the horizon because everything feels solid. And then you need to know what comes next.

Now we can feasibly contemplate building out other bits of the club: youth development, bringing the women into the club, contemplating what does life look like in the next league above if we can envision promotion. What does it look like in three to five years' time where we might be back in the football league? What type of people do we want in place that could take us on that journey?

Decisions around people in any business are important, but we need the right people at the right time to be able to take us on that journey. And I think that's why it's difficult — because football's very visceral, and particularly with probably the one position in the whole business, the football manager is the one that's the trickiest relationship to have, because they tend to look quite short-term. We're trying to look long-term, and there's always tension there.

It's always around, "well, the budget says this, but we also want to win on Saturday because we've got a few injuries," and the number of times we have those conversations — it makes me chuckle, because we just go, "hang on a minute. So we're having a conversation which to you says we need a centre-off on Saturday — to me, that's a £100,000 commitment over the next two years, right? And how have we gone from watching every penny to literally having, on the touchlines of a training ground, a £100,000 conversation which you expect an immediate answer? So what, how does that work?" It shouldn't.

We've learned a lot around discipline, around budget, how we should think about recruitment, and how we put every pound in the budget — particularly towards people and players — and how we get a return from that.

第九部分：预算的秘密——不押宝"杯赛彩票"

主持人： Can I ask about that budget? When I was having a look beforehand and saw what you were budgeting for, it looked like there was no inclusion in there of cup runs. It looked like there was no inclusion in there of transfer. So to me, that was straight away, "okay, that's the disciplined way to approach this."

Mark： If we're looking at really how to manage anything else — we call it the football lottery, right? It is brilliant and that can be hugely valuable for the club, but you can't rely on it.

If you look at the deficit that we have at the moment: so let's take it back to the beginning. We took over the club — £1.1 million. Second year, get it down to between £700–800,000. Then we're going to get down to closer to £400,000. So how do we get that figure to level of breaking even?

There are a number of factors:

  • People through the door — obviously getting attendances up. We're up to about an average last season of 36–37[00]. We started off the season with 4,300, 4,100. We'll probably be close, if we could be successful, to getting a 38[00] average again.
  • Season tickets up again this season.
  • Transfer fees — making sure that we can get feasible transfer fees if we are going to let players go.
  • Non-match day income is really important. We're starting to do more events now — sportsman's evenings, tribute bands, all sorts of things going on at the football club.
  • Sponsorship — when we came in, we've over-doubled sponsorship within the football club. It was around £230[K], we're about £500[K] now.

I spoke to you earlier about the hospitality proposal — our hospitality is exceptional, really really good at this level of football. All the away directors, when they come along, really enjoy coming to Torquay, etc. So all those things, if we can engineer and contribute to that, we can get very close to where we need to be. And I feel that this season, with the amount we've spent on the budget for players, we're in a good place. We've got good potential selling fees if players perform. We've got a good combination of experience, etc. So there's lots of really good seeds that have been put in place for this football club.

第十部分：信任——从"人质"到"门徒"

主持人： I want to just ask on this then, because it's the thread that's going to get us here. Trust. Day one — because of the previous relationship with ownership, doesn't matter who you two are and who the consortium is — you've got a lot of trust building to do with a fan base who is pretty scarred from previous experiences. You build that trust and you get that community value back. People come through the door. The attention turns positive in the club. That turns into better financials.

As a… you have the advantage — you said it's a disadvantage as well — but you have the advantage of a catchment area, a support of a community: if you're a Torquay fan, you're a Torquay fan. Your businesses — you're not going for the global payments platforms. The people that you want partnering with the club are still going to be local-ish businesses that are probably trading off that. That's your biggest early challenge, right? If you can rebuild that trust, you get the community back on side. The positivity feeds the appetite to come and partner with and sponsor and build relationships and have broader business — or you see the upside on the revenue. And we all know what happens after you see the upside on the revenue — you can invest more money back into the club.

Mark： And that's exactly what's happened in this year. More sponsors have come in, the suites are full, everyone's coming to the football club. To be honest, everyone knows us locally and they know — action speaks louder than words as well. Since we've taken over the club in two years, we've done our absolute best to communicate exceptionally well. Michael's involved in the media world. We regularly have chairman chats. We have forums. We're very very open. We've got a trust that's part of a shareholder within the football club. They know everything about the football club. We work with them very closely. We have a fantastic partnership. It's all about inclusion and it's all about building those bridges that have been broken by the previous administration — and we've done that extremely well. If it's one thing that I'm proud of, that would be what it is. We want success. We want to get up to the next level. Everyone knows that. But my god, we've come a long way, and I'm proud of the football club. I'm proud of the way everyone's come together.

Michael： Trust underpins any relationship, and not least with the football club and us. And that starts with openness and honesty and transparency. Day one mission was — the fan base felt a bit disenfranchised from the club. We've built that trust, as you say. We've built that engagement level with the community. We're at 50-year highs in attendances at the point we're at our lowest ever level in the pyramid. Which says something about the value of trust, right? And the value of a football club of its community asset.

On the commercial side, we've taken that to the bank where businesses have now seen — riding on the coat-tails of brand Torquay United and what the new values of that brand mean to the local community as a halo effect. They wanted to bask in the halo effect of that. And that's taken us from £200-something-thousand to over half a million in just stadium sponsorships, kit sponsorships, stuff like that — which is great.

It's a good base to build on. However, it's still a relatively small addressable market. We live in quite an economically depressed area. There are not oodles and oodles of businesses with big fat marketing budgets. So if we want to start tapping into regional budgets or national budgets, we need to progress on the field so we can get more media exposure, get on telly and all of that stuff.

We've covered a lot of yards quite quickly. We've added a million quid to the top line of the business in two seasons — which is going some, on the back of 50-year average home attendances. We haven't actually done anything on the pitch yet. We've come close twice. So progression is everything.

But because fans are behind us, there is the pressure. Obviously people want us to succeed, but they're also grateful that we've got a club, that the values of the club they recognise and are helping. And they've gone from being our fans — have gone from being hostages to apostles. And that has an incredible effect right through the community and everything that we do, whether it's the commercial side, or whether it's — and that's allowed us to bring youth development inside the club, rather than through the Community Sports Trust.

Which is why we've got now four, five, six-hundred kids running around wearing Torquay shirts from every age group from 7 to 18. And it's allowed us to form new partnerships to create a new under-19s elite academy. This is all new stuff that we've been allowed to create because the community's given us permission to do so.

第十一部分：学院制度的"不对称"——Ollie Watkins 的教训

主持人： Are expensive, though?

Michael： They are, you know. And they're a commitment. Listen — so what you have to do is partner with an education partner, right, which is what we've done. Because, as we all know, we can't be an EPPP-licensed academy. So we don't get any protection. We can nurture talent from the ages of 7 to 17, and then Chelsea can come and take them tomorrow. We get no compensation.

主持人： Probably be a bit younger than 17 if Chelsea…

Michael： Yeah, no — probably they'll probably get them at 11. But my point is: we have to look, where are we going to get return on our investment? So we do a lot of stuff with our college, which dual-register some young players so they get men's football. We've got a defined pathway into the first team now.

But this is a bigger governance piece of football, I think, needs addressing: when it comes to academy, your academy status shouldn't be determined by where your men's first team is in the pyramid. It should be around: how well-resourced are you? Where does the board of the football club put youth development? Where does it sit within the geography of the country? What is its commitment, financial and otherwise, to nurturing young talent, boys and girls? It shouldn't be tied to your men's first-team league position.

I think there's an asymmetry there that needs to be addressed structurally within football, because we would put proper money into the academy if we get protection from day one. Because it's needed. Otherwise — famously, Torquay shut their academy twice in the last 15 years. And famously, we sit there and look at Ollie Watkins, who's a Torquay boy, born in Torquay, could have been a Torquay — I wasn't a Torquay academy player, we shut the academy, went to Exeter, and Exeter benefited to the tune of five, six million pounds. And he should have been our player.

主持人： This is an institutional problem and there should be protections. Doesn't matter what league you're in, whether it's League Nine or the Premier League. If you're nurturing talent, if you have a catchment that gives you an opportunity to bring these kids in, and you are putting the work in to develop them — but whoever created these rules, it may well have worked 10, 15 years ago, but we all know the competition has got even bigger at the bottom level. We've seen all the clubs now and how many people want to get into the magic of the EFL. There's a lot more competition lower, a lot more opportunity, and therefore there should be considerations for that.

Why were these rules put in place? Because to me, I'm looking at it and what I hear more than anything else is — god, it's the lower leagues asking for more money again from a lot of people who are, should we say, in the higher leagues. Well, this seems like a very natural, business-like, fair way to provide opportunities for lower league clubs to make some — as you've said with an Ollie Watkins, Conacher — very good money.

Michael： Good question. I can't tell you. We've been in football for 24 months and we've had our head down trying to rescue and build the business. I don't feel qualified to answer that.

But all I do know is that to have a fully-licensed academy, which attracts match-funding from the Premier League, you have to be in the English Football League to do so. So whether that's the National League, who are our kind of parents, need to go and do a better job of negotiating deals with the Premier League where we can set up — where it's a meritocracy — that you can get EPPP status or match-funding based on the validity of your plan and your program that you're running, rather than based on where your men's first team is in the pyramid. Doesn't seem right.

There should be other factors — which I mentioned earlier — which is willing for funding, where it sits in the priority list, to what extent your addressable market, what else is around. In terms of down in the Southwest, you've got Plymouth and Exeter, and that's it, down in Dorset, Devon and Cornwall.

主持人： Also, player trading is one of the biggest opportunities to make money for any club — and that includes at the youth level. So you have 600 kids. That's part of that. Whether your first team is in the Premier League or not, the fact that you could receive nothing from that just seems — it seems crazy.

Mark： You would have thought there'd be some kind of fund that would come out of the Premier League, or something, over wages and things, where they could put it into lower leagues and feed some of the seeds through there to this type of academy — and maybe stretch it out, National League North, South, etc. Because the disillusionment of supporters is: one, not being able to see their clubs at the top end; and the second part is the way these players are paid and how much money they are paid. Isn't there a way of drip-feeding some of that — a percentage, maybe, that comes out of that — that could go down to the lower clubs to support academies, to support the hand that feeds you? I don't know. It just seems ridiculous to us.

I think maybe the rules were created a few years ago where maybe it's not so competitive. You know, you had a lot of players who were part-time and football was their hobby. But nowadays, as you know, and you'll know from your interviewing with different people, the lower leagues — now it's so competitive. The National League really is an extension of the EFL.

主持人： Just to highlight that, though: a couple of years ago when you didn't go up on the last day of the season — I think we were talking about this before we came — I said it was classed as the most competitive league because you had six teams that could have, fighting one goal between it to go up.

Mark： It was absolutely crazy. And to be fair to Truro, who went up — they had one of their lower budgets, and did actually go up.

It needs a realignment. There's an unfairness there. And here we are today — we're talking to you and we're doing everything possible to invest in our local football club to do the best that we can. But we realise that youth development is really important. We realise inclusion is really important. And surely the higher authorities should be thinking about this and drip-feeding that down. It just doesn't make any sense.

No one's asking for caps and things like that at this point. But for me, if you're a 20-year-old who's playing for Chelsea and you're on £300[,000] a week and you've signed a 5-year contract — what a better way to understand where you've come from, in football and lower leagues, than to drip-feed maybe some money out of that wage, whether it's £10,000 a week or whatever? A number of players who do that, and build that level of football and help to get those academies centralised — because it is an issue. It is an issue for us.

第十二部分：Neil Warnock——"火车车厢里的奇遇"

主持人： Okay, I'm going to say two words. Neil Warnock.

Mark： Yeah. What a legend. It's quite hard to accept with Neil Warnock, because he's one minute on Sky Sports and the next minute he's at Torquay United watching us on a Saturday afternoon.

But you know the story behind Neil: after we decided to put the proposal in to take out of administration, we were thinking about who could be the manager who could help us with that, and Neil Warnock came up. Michael was, I think, travelling to London, I was travelling back from London, walked in and he said, "Guess who's sitting in front of me" — and I said "I don't know" — "Neil Warnock." So I sent him a text, "I'll go and say hello to him." Next minute he's coming to the game on Saturday, and Warnock's coming in. Michael and Neil are very very close friends now. So we're very fortunate to have him there. Exceptional guy.

主持人： What's the role?

Mark： I like to think of him as a football consultant. Because as much as he's got all the experience of what, you know, as a manager and everything else — it can be quite a burden for a manager that you've got at the moment. So he doesn't — he's very clever, he doesn't get too involved — but he's always there if the manager wants some advice. He's been through everything. So he's there at the end of the phone, or go to training, or get involved with us about certain players, maybe open up some contacts for us for players and things like that.

He's also great from a marketing perspective. He supports us in the hospitality. He goes into the suites, talks to people. Having photos and things like that. He's a lovely fella, and we're very privileged to have him around the club.

主持人： Well, for you —

Michael： We often talk about football being a drug, and often describe that Torquay United is Neil Warnock's methadone to wean him off football. It's the next best thing.

Listen, he's become a really close friend actually, and I think he's really enjoying his relationship with us. In the early days — Mark's right — so we had this 10 days of crazy diligence in inverted commas, of trying to get the club out of administration against the deadline that we had. And then we realised: how many players we got? One. And even he ended up having to be terminated because he got done for betting. So we effectively had no players and no manager, and we were six weeks before the start of the season.

Mark told the story — this ridiculous sliding door serendipity moment. We spoke the night before, saying "Neil Warnock lives down our part of the world. He must be able to help us somehow find a manager that we need." And then it's like the boys upstairs were listening, and I sat up from my laptop and there was Neil Warnock sat in my carriage.

主持人： Go on. How did you do it?

Michael： First of all, I Googled his image just to make sure that — you didn't want to walk up — he just left Aberdeen, and I looked at my phone and go, "that is Neil Warnock." And then there was a lady sat next to him. I said, "who's Mrs. Warnock?" And that was Sharon — that's definitely her as well.

So I ran out to the back of the carriage and I rang him and said, "You're not going to believe this, but do you remember what we talked about last night? He's only on our bloody train." And he's like, "Hang up now and go and talk to him."

So we did, and we just got — 10 minutes into Paddington, down to the back to the West Country — and sat and talked to him all the way to Exeter. And he agreed that he'd come to the next game. There were only about two or three games left of the season. He came along, and we had lots of meetings with him and said, "we need a manager, can you help us?" And that's where he said, "I want to introduce you to Paul Wotton." And that was the start of that journey.

主持人： Amazing. Well, look — for you coming in, the best thing obviously that good leadership can do is figure out where they're best placed and where they need the support. And if you have someone like him who knows football — I mean, there's probably few people in this country that know football better than he does, have the networks that he does, particularly at the levels of EFL and below — that must have been an immense help, or at least just a level of comfort.

Mark： Reassuring comfort. Yeah. You got to get the balance right by not taking any of the management decisions that are made, but having him in the background for us as well. It's almost — I'm not saying a director of football or anything like that — but he's been very very good at grounding us. Some of the contact: like last season we had a problem, we needed to get a goalkeeper in very quickly. He got us the goalkeeper in. The goalkeeper played extremely well. Obviously we were very close to going up — unfortunately we didn't — but he's very good from that point of view.

He's a really really nice fellow, and he's got so many stories throughout his career. He goes around — I think he enjoys talking to all supporters. The last game of last season he went over the pop side and chatted with supporters over there as well. This is a guy who's done everything in the game. On a Tuesday night, he's commentating or in the studio on EFL football and championship football. Unbelievable. He's got football completely in the blood.

Michael： On a practical basis, he loves nothing more than being around the players. He loves going into the dressing room, and even with Jimmy [Ball] now on, our manager — he's got a relationship where Jimmy says, "Neil, come in the dressing room and talk to [them]."

主持人： I was going to say — nice, because that could be a bit of a challenge. If you're playing sixth tier of football for Torquay United and you've got one of the most decorated English football managers in history put his arm around his shoulder and say, "Come on, son, get it done for us today" — you know how he is. It's inspiring.

Michael： They walk 10 feet tall. He loves coming to training now and again. He'll drop into training because the manager will say, "Neil, can you come and have a look at this? Give us a second opinion." And this is all great stuff. As Mark said, he's a reassuring presence for the players. He's a sounding board for the manager.

For us, it's great to sound-check stuff with him — because being on the manager's side, as director of the football club: if you're in the manager's shoes, what would you be thinking now? So he can help us understand how we should resource and communicate and deal with the manager, because he's been on that side of the fence as well. He can tell us — he's been through 17, 18 different boards and chairmen. What did he like about the good ones? What did he not like about the bad ones, and why? For us to better understand — because everyone's important in the club, but the football manager is disproportionately important. And so to have Neil help us better understand the dynamics of that particular role, the better.

主持人： Have you tested that relationship yet? Have you guys had a moment where there's a disagreement? Because while this was working well it's great, right, and it sounds very nice — but to be able to have disagreements and come through them is really the test of a top function.

Mark： And I think that's why he's still there. This is a guy who can do whatever he likes. You're on about somebody who's got nine promotions and relegations — one of the most decorated and underestimated managers in domestic football. He is very forceful with his opinion, which you'd expect because he's been successful. For my communications with him, I respect his decision-making. Some of the ideas that I have, he'll sort of say, "Okay, son, let's just move this over here, let's let him do this, and then we'll do this." He's very clever at taking bits of information from directors, managers and other things, and then bringing it all together, and collectively then going through the right channels — maybe just turning up to a training session and going, "Have you tried…? What's his name here? Have you done this or have you done that?" He's been around, worked with different chairmen and everything else. He knows his way around a football world.

Michael： But we have tested that relationship with him. There's been twice that I can remember where Neil didn't like or agree with decisions we made. One was an internal disciplinary issue — he was pretty upset that he wasn't consulted. We felt that we needed to deal with a disciplinary issue in a certain way. And the fundamental one was: he didn't really agree with our decision to part company with Paul W[otton] when we did — which is interesting. And yet, to be fair, he took over from the next match — he looked after the team for three or four games. But he's still there, and he understands that.

Listen, I think ultimately we're super lucky to have him. He's a force for good. He brings a reassuring presence that brings experience to the table that is super helpful for us. Very lucky.

第十三部分：社区、父亲的骨灰与"多巴胺供应商"

主持人： I want to bring it around to the thing that underpins everything, and really is, I guess, the root of why you're doing it. Because we've talked around it. We know the importance of community. The relationship that you have with Torquay in particular — before, when we were speaking, you said you used to fly back from Hong Kong to see games. You talked about the family relationship previously. We can't underestimate how important these clubs are at every level. It almost seems too flippant to just say "that is a massive community asset" sometimes, because it does actually take away how much these things do mean.

You said something to me when we were on the phone yesterday, just having a quick chat beforehand — it stuck with me because it was just one of the points: "Look, it's about not selling heritage for promotion." Can you give — from the community piece and from your experience — a little bit of that link and the importance? Why you flew back? What it is about football that grabs you?

Michael： Well, I think, for me — for everyone who's football supporters — probably can all relate to this. But like many people, I was brought to Plainmoor age three, stuck on a vegetable box, peering over the railings. And it only takes you to about six or seven years old where then that is your team. As you get older, you walk, you go to different areas of the ground. And it just gets embedded within you all through your teen years. It's the one thing that gives you a bit of structure you can identify with. It's part of your rhythm of your life. It's where you celebrate together. You commune — we talk about the word "communing" with [your community].

As you grow up, a lot of these institutions that used to belong to — whether it was working men's clubs or going to church — those have kind of gradually eroded. Family structures have broken down. There isn't the extended families anymore. And so, football clubs — everyone's equal. You can stand shoulder-to-shoulder with people from every level of the economic scale, but you're all bound by one singular passion, and that's the love for your football club, because it's something for you to get behind.

I don't need to explain that. I think that's why football is the largest sport on the planet. I think that's stating the obvious. But for me, even that my career took me overseas for 16 years — the only result I ever cared about was: it wasn't Liverpool, it wasn't England, it was Torquay United. And when we got to a semi-final of a play-off or an FA Cup third round, I would jump on a plane and I would come home and watch the game, turn around, go back to Asia, and go back again — because I had to be there and be part of it.

For me, the football club is — you know, my dad was the stadium announcer, voluntarily, for 20 years. His ashes are under the home-end goal. So every time we score a goal at the home end, I have a look upstairs and go, "that was for you."

主持人： And that was emotional — the day we took over the club and they literally handed us a bunch of keys.

Michael： I went down to the goal and going…

主持人： Who would have thought this? That's incredible — to get the keys to the club. Your dad is that closely linked with the club.

Mark： And I wasn't as closely linked as Michael to the football club. I would go there 15 games a season. I would take my nephews there when my sister broke up from her husband — take them there, watch the football — and they were sending me texts when they went into administration. "Can you support it? Can you do something with it?"

You've heard Michael this afternoon talk about the football club and his passion. When I spoke to him and when he was telling me about his dad and everything — as well as in business being successful, you need to have that empathy to support the people that are around you and what's important in your life. And this is a traditional football club in the middle of a housing estate. Means so much to so many people. After talking to Michael, after talking to friends, my nephews, and everything — just couldn't walk away.

Now it's difficult. I mean, I'm involved in eight other businesses — but this one is like it's pulled me in beyond. It's like a girlfriend I can't get away from. It's a difficult one.

I said to you earlier: the day that we came out of administration, we did a presentation to the staff, and we were sat in our main bar that's there, the Gull's Nest, and I said to them, "I want Ian Wright in here. I want Mark Lawrenson here. I want Kelly Cates — whoever it is that matches today to be here — and doing the draw." Because we got through the FA Cup and we're going to pull somebody out. When I see some of the interviews that you've done with people who've been successful in sport, that's what we dream for: to bring those days back to the club. So, fingers crossed, that does happen. We're close.

第十四部分：被金字塔顶端吸干的 FA 杯

主持人： But I want to ask — all of this, right, is the key. But we are in danger now, we are in danger of losing this, because of the system that you're having to operate in.

Michael： Yeah. And we nearly lost — if you talk to a lot of football supporters, the one thing that connects the top end of football to the bottom end of football is the FA Cup. And we're very close to losing the coverage of that. You talk to people my age, they say to you: FA Cup day. You wake up at 11:00, you watch Football Focus, you watch it all. You see the coaches going to the stadium. What hotel they in? What shirts are they wearing in the FA Cup final? The whole pedigree of that. It's the whole institution of football, and we are losing it to money. We're losing it to money of — what, six clubs?

Leicester City probably the biggest shock in sport that I think we've seen in recent years, the fact that they won the Premier League. Apart from that, we pretty much know where the league is going, and we pretty much know where the Champions League is going. But that seems to be where all the revenue is. [I] worry about football — because how many people is that affecting, compared to those grassroots supporters who are there: Division One, Championship, Division Two, National League, lower leagues, Isthmian League and everything else?

It worries me about the fabric of community.

主持人： But you said something interesting again before we came in: about you seeing with a club, like, an increase in interest, fans coming more fans coming through the door — and you potentially have created a situation where they'd looked at it and gone, "maybe we're a bit disenfranchised with all of this, all of this money, all of this focus right at the top of the game. And actually, the community asset, the club that you can walk into with anyone, that you can stand shoulder-to-shoulder with anyone, that's affordable, that's still a great product — because the quality of players down in the tier are still really good players."

Mark： The product is there now. The product is there for your partner, the product is there for your family — if you're going on a stag, hen-do, we've got everything for everybody at the football club. That's what makes us proud: the fact that we have that offering to everybody.

I'm a massive Liverpool supporter. I used to go up to Anfield every other week — Devon Reds, get on the coach at 7:00. Now I'm almost not interested in what Liverpool are doing, because — it's important now: my community, my club.

Just imagine how this affects tourism and the whole of Torbay if Torquay get promoted. How does that work with hotels? How does that work with income around the whole of that vicinity? It's going to be massive. And to see — on Saturday afternoon from 1:00 through to 6, 7:00 now, because we got bands on and things like that — to see all the happiness around there. You can't buy that.

But I wonder how many owners of top-end football clubs see all that. I wonder how many of them do actually see those supporters and see how important they are in the fabric of the community. You saw a few years ago Bury go out of football. Now they're coming back and you see all the scenes of that — and they're getting like 10,000 fans going to watch Bury, whatever league they are, what, tier seven, something like that. Incredible.

Yeah, it's a really important part, and I think we underestimate how important it is in the community and how important football plays a part in people's lives. Like Michael said, it was the word we used quite a lot over the past few days — "communion." It's the way of getting their happiness for the week. We're happy to be part of that process.

Michael： It's quite interesting, isn't it, when for a few decades your average attendance has been 2.5 thousand and we're getting closer to four — albeit at our lowest ever level, as I said earlier.

So then we dug into the data, and our fastest-growing persona is young families. And they're not encumbered by 80 years in the football league. They're not moaning the "what are we doing at this level? Why are we still trolling along the bottom of the sixth tier of football? I remember the day where we were playing Brighton and Bournemouth in the league — it's only a generation ago that they were our peers, and look at them now and look how far we've fallen and how depressing is it?"

So there's that cohort — they tend to be the noisy ones, the ones on the forums and bemoaning the demise of this football club. And I look at it from a perspective like, "hang on a second: so we are at a 50-year high of attendances. We're suddenly a bright light in an otherwise quite depressed community. Suddenly families and businesses are rallying around this community asset. It's the largest, most visible place where people come together on a fortnightly basis, bar anything in the area. And businesses and brands are riding on the coat-tails of all these great values."

So we've created these new fans. And one of the most important parts of football is: it's where friendships become enduring. It's where you commune with your fellow Torquay supporters, where you make memories with friends and family that will stay with you forever. And that's an important part of the job. It has to mean something.

So I think that as we think about where we invest in the club, it's very much every bit as part of the experience as it is about making sure we've got the right money that gives the level of performance. Yes, of course, we all want to enjoy success, and that gets the endorphins going and that validates everything. Because football clubs — we are dopamine providers. That's the other part of what our job is. They come to us because, "you give me a dopamine hit on a Tuesday night or a Saturday. And I get pissed off with you if you don't win, because you're depriving me of my dopamine, in a life that otherwise is quite challenging and there's not a lot to be cheerful about. So if you don't give me my dopamine hit of the win, then I'm going to get my dopamine hit by bemoaning how crap I think the team is at the moment, by getting likes for that on social media."

It's a really interesting time. There are different cults — but I [am] very encouraged by the fact that we're now creating a value proposition that's appealing to families, and they're also super commercially interesting audiences for brands. But not forgetting that we've got this hardcore football cohort that have, and their families have, supported Torquay United through generations.

第十五部分：现在该把目光放回球场

主持人： Okay. So everything we've talked about is about improving the club as a whole because of where you picked it up from — and that, without doubt, was the most important thing that you had to do. We can sit and talk here about good business forever — it's about what happens on the pitch at the end of the day. You've now got the club on a positive trajectory. The numbers are going in the right direction. You seem to have the fans onside. Do you put pressure now on yourselves to go, "right, okay, it's time to look at the pitch now"?

Mark： It's our third year, really important year. If you look at the infrastructure of where we put the investment this season in the playing squad — obviously we've increased that dramatically from last season — but also in terms of a system: we've got Dan Way there, got a great pedigree in football, we've got an analyst now involved, we've got a strengthening coach involved, we've got the physios already there before, the goalkeeping coach, etc. So the background, the football side of things is very very professional. Apart from all the other aspects of nutrition, the training facilities — everything is very much first class.

So in answer to your question: we are doing absolutely [everything] — whether it be the preparation of staying overnight or what we're trying to do — we're doing everything possible to give that team the opportunity of getting promotion. I have learned over the past two years that is not necessarily an absolute trigger to us doing that, but we're giving ourselves every chance.

You need a little bit of luck. I think over 46 games, you're going to get a lot of peaks and troughs, etc. We've spoken about the number of teams that are in this league and the capability of it. So we've just got to be patient.

We've come very close. I look at other aspects of other clubs — I take on board, in a sport, other people who've lost out getting so close — and we have to learn from that, and just try to be focused on the fact that this season we are going to do it. This season, when it comes to that last 20 minutes when we're 2–1 up, we'll do it slightly differently to what we did before. When we're in the final stretch, perhaps we'll give a little bit more momentum to it by adding a few, maybe at the last minute, to try and get us over the line.

But we are doing everything possible on the playing side. And you've come up with a very good point about the investment that we've made, the foundations we've done in the football club — for this club to go to the next stage where we look at accelerating non-match-day income, accelerating the opportunity of academy, etc., success on the pitch is imperative.

So it's a key season for us, and I'm not a fool in terms of being the custodian of the football club. There'll be questions that are asked about change of management, change of players, change of circumstance, and they've got every right to question that — supporters. But we must, where possible, try to get promoted. Although, as you know, it's very very tough — one side up, one side through a play-off system that is so complicated, it's unbelievable. And this is why the "Free Up" campaign is so important, because it makes it so difficult for a club like us to get promoted.

Michael： Needs addressing. The amount of quality and the standard, both in the National League and even in the National League South and North at that sixth tier, is high. The budgets being spent on China — and this, what — only having one up, automatically is just accelerating this arms race for promotion. And this is a constant tension: is this not gambling for promotion? If we went back to the top of our conversation: is there a straight line between playing budget and league position? Yes there is. So against that backdrop, how do you square those two things?

The National League — of which we've got fully behind, by the way, this "three up" campaign — I just think that rather than a three… What's amazing about British football, why British football is probably the largest product in the world, is this pyramid, and it essentially is free-flowing, apart from the EFL to the National League, where it becomes an hourglass and a choke point.

I think that if you had three up, three down, and we thought about that in a different way, then I feel that that is more meritocratic. It allows clubs to be aspirational, and it also allows them to behave sensibly. I think it's in the best interest of trying — clubs that should be rewarded for trying to behave sustainably and with discipline and responsibly.

结束语

主持人： I think if you're looking for the best way to round it all out, that's not bad. Firstly, two people doing it together is not easy. I think you've done a great job. Well done. Secondly, I think it is a fascinating story that you are telling, and more importantly than anything else, I think it is great for the wider system to hear a little bit more about some of this — particularly at the levels with which you're operating in — because whether it is reducing some of those budgets and still pushing (right, even though you haven't quite achieved it yet, you've said you've got very close), that belief, that you can achieve and give yourself far better financial opportunity by being sensible, is great, and people need to hear it.

So on everything, I wish you the best of luck. I have lots of fingers crossed for you, and honestly, well done for doing it. I can only imagine what it was like going through that process, but to get it where you are now, two years in, is brilliant. So thank you for coming.

嘉宾： Come on down as well. Come and see us.

主持人： I will. Yeah.

嘉宾： You don't — I don't need to advise you to come to football.

主持人： Yeah. Thanks.

嘉宾： Thank you. That's very kind of you. Tell us. Brilliant.

## 一、最反直觉的发现：**"旅游衰退"才是这家百年俱乐部真正的病根**
表面上这是一个"烂摊子救援+财务翻盘"的故事，但真正惊人的是 Michael 轻描淡写地揭示的那条暗线——**托基（Torquay）作为英国"里维埃拉"小镇，过去 20–30 年因廉价欧洲航班而被掏空**。换句话说，这家足球俱乐部不是被老板搞垮的，而是被瑞安航空、被马洛卡的阳光、被全球化消费地理学慢慢杀死的。俱乐部进入管理清算只是最终的会计确认。
这就产生了一个让人意外的推论：**他们买下的其实不是一支球队，而是一个社区的"最后一盏灯"**。 Michael 原话——"如果足球俱乐部也没了，那还剩什么？"（what else is left?）这不是情感修辞，而是精准的宏观诊断。他们在做的，本质上是一场**地方性反熵工程**——用一个 125 年的符号，去对冲一个海滨经济体几十年的坍缩。
