item.title: [Sequoia Capital] David Silver and Lasse Espeholt of Ineffable Intelligence: A Superlearner for the Age of Experience
item.dc:creator: Sequoia Capital
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的洞见：Ineffable 其实在复制"寒武纪大爆发"，而不是复制"人类"

大多数人把 Silver 的路径理解为"不用人类数据的 AlphaZero 升级版"。但如果你仔细听他讲 crucible——"几百万相互作用的 agent + 简单奖励 + 涌现复杂性"——这其实是在用算力重演寒武纪生命演化，而不是重演人类文明。

区别极其关键：人类文明是一个单一物种内部的协作演化（有共享语言、共享生物基础）；而 Silver 要构建的是一个多智能体生态系统，让智能作为"物种间博弈"的副产品浮现。他引用围棋那一刻极其暴露底牌——"单智能体围棋无聊到死，第二个 agent 一进来复杂度爆炸"。这不是深度学习的隐喻，这是生物学的隐喻。

那个让人意外的推论是：如果他成功了，第一个 ineffable 产出的"超级智能"大概率不是一个超级智能，而是一个由多个相互博弈的智能构成的生态——因为他的 alignment 论述里反复出现"a balance of actors"、"society of super intelligences"。他已经悄悄放弃了"造一个 AGI"这个单数命题，转向"造一个 AGI 生态"。这是整个访谈最颠覆性的、却几乎没人注意的转变。

二、跨领域连接：Ineffable 的赌局 = 奥地利学派经济学 vs 凯恩斯学派

LLM 阵营的 RL（breadcrumb trailing、人在环上、每一步精心设计 reward）本质上是凯恩斯式的中央计划——"我们知道目标函数长什么样，我们一步步引导"。

Silver 的路径则是哈耶克的自发秩序（spontaneous order）：你给出极简规则（"survival"、"fitness"），让局部交互涌现出语言、贸易、科学、技术。他在访谈里几乎复刻了哈耶克 1945 年《知识在社会中的运用》的论证——你无法事先 specify 什么是"科学"或"有趣的数学"，因为知识是分布式涌现的。

跨领域连接的意外之处：这意味着 Ineffable 能否成功，赌的不是深度学习，而是赌哈耶克 vs 凯恩斯在计算基底上谁对。而历史上，这个争论从未在可控实验中解决过——人类社会只能跑一次。Ineffable 的 crucible 第一次为这场 80 年的经济学/政治哲学论战提供了实验台。

而且注意一个讽刺：OpenAI/Anthropic 这些"自由市场旗手"公司，在 RL 技术路径上其实是凯恩斯派；而 Ineffable 这个欧洲小团队，在技术上才是真正的奥派。

三、最该被追问的"系统性盲点"：ineffable 的名字本身暴露了一个认识论陷阱

Silver 讲 ineffable 的来由非常漂亮——"超级智能发现的知识会 profound 到人类语言无法表达"。但请注意一个几乎没人质疑的滑坡：

"人类语言无法表达" ≠ "更高级" ≠ "值得追求"。

生物演化产出了大量"ineffable"的东西——细菌的化学信号、章鱼皮肤的分布式认知、黏菌的网络计算。它们都比人类语言"更原生、更不依赖人类先验"。但没人认为它们是"super intelligence"。我们之所以识别一个东西为"智能"，恰恰是因为我们能和它建立某种可翻译的桥梁。

这里有一个 Silver 没有解决的悖论：如果 ineffable 真的 ineffable，我们如何验证它？ 他的回答是"wonderment（惊叹）"——像围棋手看 AlphaGo 的 move 37。但围棋的 wonderment 是事后可翻译的：人类棋手能复盘、能理解、能学习。真正 ineffable 的东西应该连 wonderment 都无法引发——因为我们连它在做什么都认不出。

这个盲点和他的 alignment 承诺之间存在深层张力：他说 "我们会在 simulation 里研究 super intelligence 如何 peacefully interact"——但如果它的推理是 ineffable 的，你连它是不是在欺骗你都无法判断。他想同时拥有"超越人类的深度"和"人类可监督的透明度"，这两者在信息论意义上可能是互斥的。

跨界联想：这正是神学里神正论（theodicy）的现代翻版——一个全知全能的存在如何让有限理性的生命"安心"？宗教花了两千年没解决这个问题；Silver 想三年内在 GPU 集群上解决它。

四、一个你可能没注意到的时间信号

Silver 把 timeline 从"3-5 年"压缩到"3 年"，理由是"coding agents 加速了研究"。这意味着 Ineffable 的赌局其实依赖于它所鄙视的 LLM 范式——它需要 LLM 把自己送到终点线，然后超越 LLM。这是一个漂亮的、几乎隐秘的寄生关系：反 LLM 的最前沿路线，由 LLM 作为研究加速器驱动。这个结构性讽刺，可能是整个 AI 产业最被低估的事实。

📝 转录文本

开场：集体发现的奇迹

Collectively, you know, we started with this kind of gray mush in our head. Um, we somehow started out knowing nothing at all and somehow discovered like everything that humans know today was like this process of collective discovery — like of languages and technology and science and mathematics and uh all the rest of it. You know, everything we learned, we discovered it for ourselves. And that's an incredible thing that no one has cracked yet in AI. And so to me, that is the essence of what it will take to get to super intelligence: like a system that can just keep learning and discovering knowledge forever.

[music]

嘉宾介绍

I'm thrilled to have Dave Silver and Lasse Espeholt with us — two of the co-founders of Ineffable Intelligence. Uh, great name, by the way.

Fun fact, Dave: you were the first person I cold emailed to come on Training Data when we started the show a hundred-ish episodes ago, and it feels like a full-circle moment to finally have you on the show. So thank you for joining us.

Dave: Um, thank you.

Dave 的研究信念：从 AlphaGo 到今天

Host: Dave, let's start with you. Your 2009 PhD was on reinforcement learning applied to the devilishly difficult game of Go. You demonstrated for the world, for the first time, that superhuman-in-one-domain machine intelligence was possible — and I think you were really the figure that inspired the entire current generation of reinforcement learning and deep learning researchers. So thank you for your contributions to where the field is.

I'm curious — thinking back to that point in time: what did you learn? What did you have conviction on? And what has remained the same and what has changed as AI has changed over the last 5 years or so?

Dave: Yeah, thank you — and pleasure to be here. I'm glad I finally made it after these hundred episodes.

So, I suppose I always had this conviction starting my PhD and going into the game of Go that the right approach to solve AI was through learning from experience — through systems that discovered things for themselves, that were learning through reinforcement learning to get better and better and better, and that that would be the thing which would lead to the emergence of intelligence and ultimately super intelligence.

We were able to show that in the game of Go, but it's a conviction that has held true throughout my career. And here we are now, applying that conviction at Ineffable — trying to show that indeed super intelligence can emerge all the way through systems that learn from experience.

In terms of things which are different: although we are not pursuing the human data path that the LLM world has pursued, I do think there's lots of interesting lessons to learn from that. In particular, it was definitely a surprise to me how a system that was trained on a massive amount of data could then be very quickly fine-tuned on a very small amount of data to completely change its behavior. That was something which changed my mindset — suggesting that if you get things at the right scale, a lot of things which seem incredibly hard or very slow — once you've experienced enough data, the things that were slow can become very fast. That's a lesson that wasn't obvious to me in advance until it happened.

为什么离开 DeepMind 创办 Ineffable

Host: Okay, we're going to come back to that later. You could have run this program inside DeepMind, where you could have probably had more access to compute than just about anybody. You decided the right thing to do was to start a new lab. Why'd you do that?

Dave: Yeah. So look, first of all, I had a fantastic time at DeepMind. I loved my years there and I have a huge amount of respect for the people there — still got on with them very well.

But at the end of the day, I have a really strong belief about how we can go beyond where we are today with AI and all the way to super intelligence. And the path that I believe in doesn't actually go through LLM-based products as an intermediate point. When I really thought about that — thought about it really hard — I realized that I felt that so passionately that this deserved to be more than just the corner of an organization that's focused on LLM-based products. It deserved to be represented by an elite AI lab that really just gives this approach its all and represents it 100%. Once I realized that, it felt very natural to create this company.

Another way to look at it: the world already has tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands, of really talented researchers all pursuing exactly the same approach — doubling down on LLMs with pre-training, post-training, coding, and that kind of LLM path. Am I going to be the hundred-thousand-and-first person pursuing that approach? Is that the most effective use of my time and energy?

In the end, I realized that there's this other lamppost that right now no one is looking under — and if I actually put my effort there, it has a much higher chance of really having a massive impact on the field, because if this works, it's going to change the whole of AI.

Host: Plus, you had a company name that couldn't go to waste.

Dave: That's right.

为什么叫 "Ineffable"

Host: You want to say where the name Ineffable came from?

Dave: Yeah. The name Ineffable came from this idea that knowledge could be so incredible — like the things which super intelligence will one day discover. This knowledge is going to be so unbelievable, incredible, something which is profoundly amazing, and perhaps so profound that we can't even express it in human language.

Really, it's in line with this other path that doesn't go through human-language-based approaches, but instead builds systems that discover things for themselves and have the possibility to discover knowledge that's unbelievably profound and ultimately ineffable.

I should say there was also a secret second reason: it's this idea that it really has to work. If you really just double down on learning from experience, it's an approach that just has to work — so you could say it can't possibly f up. So it's *in-eff-able. There you go — the secret reason as well.

Host: Amazing. Best lab name.

Lasse 的加入故事

Host: Lasse, what about you? You were at Google, you were in a different group than Dave — in the deep learning group at DeepMind — and you spent years scaling up reinforcement learning on GPUs. What made you decide to leave DeepMind, and what drew you to co-found Ineffable?

Lasse: Right. So I joined DeepMind in January '15, and I started working a bit with Dave around '16, where I was doing this work on scaling up reinforcement learning. As you said, I was part of the deep learning team and he was leading a reinforcement learning team, but we were working on an internal project together.

I actually left DeepMind twice. I left DeepMind in summer '18 and went to Google Brain. Then eventually Google Brain and DeepMind merged and I was back again. Then I left DeepMind again, a year before Dave left.

The first time I heard about Ineffable was actually through one of our eventual investors reaching out to me, asking what I thought about Dave. My first reaction was: "Damn, I missed out on an opportunity. I should have reached out to him." I recall Dave as more often than not being one of the smartest people in the room. Shortly after that sync with the investor, they actually reached out to me. So — I really love to work with Dave. I knew Wojtek and Chris from back in the day, and I thought the team was great. I also thought it's amazing to have an opportunity like this in Europe.

Dave: It should be said as well: we worked together on some of the early approaches to combining reinforcement learning with deep learning and trying to scale things up. Lasse — who, by the way, is very modest — actually worked on some of the original approaches that were the first attempts to actually scale up reinforcement learning and show that it could be done at large scale: ways to parallelize reinforcement learning, ways to build out architectures that were scalable. If you look today at the way the field's gone, all of the ideas that people use today kind of hail back to the original work that Lasse did back in the day. That's where all the roots come from of scaled-up RL. So he was the first to figure it out.

Host: Wonderful. We should have you guys introduce each other instead — you're both too humble to brag about yourselves.

什么是 Superlearner？什么是 First Contact？

Host: Okay, let's talk about Ineffable and what you're building. You have a beautiful mission statement as a company: you want to build a superlearner and make first contact with super intelligence. Can you define both of those things for us? What is a superlearner, and what does making first contact look like?

Dave: Yeah. So to me, a superlearner — it's got incredible capacity both in its depth of what it can learn and in its breadth.

Depth: It should be something that can start from not knowing anything at all and go all the way through to discovering things that go way beyond what humans know. An analogy: humans collectively started with this kind of gray mush in our head. We somehow started out knowing nothing at all and discovered everything that humans know today — this process of collective discovery of languages and technology and science and mathematics and all the rest of it. Everything we learned, we discovered it for ourselves. It wasn't that someone came down and gave us a blueprint of how this should work, and it wasn't that someone came down and gave us a trillion-element dataset of "this is what these things should look like." We actually figured it out for ourselves. That's an incredible thing that no one has cracked yet in AI, and to me that is the essence of what it will take to get to super intelligence — a system that can just keep learning and discovering knowledge forever.

Breadth: We want something which can do this incredible discovery, and it should be possible to drop it into any stream of experience. Whether it's a simulated world or a digital world or a physical world — whatever it's dropped into, it should be something that can just learn and learn and learn.

That's the dream. If we crack this, then to me it gives rise to a super intelligence that will be like encountering magic — something so profoundly amazing that it will be able to do wonderful things.

Host: What will it feel like when we first encounter it? Or is it one of these things where you can't predict ahead of time?

Dave: I think it will be amazing. We'll have an experience of wonderment. The only thing I can say from my own experience is what happened when we got to this point in — admittedly, much narrower fields. When we got there in board games — when we got to the point of superhuman play in the game of Go — it brought wonderment to the field. The Go players who saw AlphaGo playing were amazed. It was a joyful experience for them to witness this kind of Go playing. Same happened when we got to superhuman play in chess — the chess players were so excited.

Just imagine going far beyond that — but in things which are discovering incredible things: new fields of science, new types of technology that we've never even dreamed of. It will be incredible.

现有 LLM+RL 范式与 Superlearner 的区别

Host: So the current paradigm — these large language models with reinforcement learning — seem to be at least knocking out millennium problems and making some sorts of scientific discoveries. Does that count as a superlearner, or what's the difference between something that can make novel scientific discoveries versus a superlearner in your sense of the term?

Dave: Look, I think LLMs are doing a lot of great things and I have a lot of respect for what's being achieved. What I mean by a superlearner is something which, first of all, discovers completely autonomously. What we've seen so far with these approaches: there's a lot of human-in-the-loop effort required to make these breakthroughs. It's not fully autonomous yet.

And it's also something which should be applicable to real-world embodied domains — where the agent can learn from its physical experience. We're a long, long, long way off that. It's not at all clear that LLMs and language-based approaches are even the right vehicle to achieve that kind of knowledge. Thinking about these things in terms of language might not even be the right paradigm, and it might just be that all of this human data that's being used in LLMs is weighing things down.

So — a lot of respect for the progress that's made, but I don't think we're anywhere close to this true superlearner: something which can autonomously just discover everything for itself.

实际在建什么：Superlearner Stack 与 Crucibles

Host: What does building this look like in practice for you? We backed Ioannis, who was on your original AlphaGo team, and he told us that one of the things that's distinct about you is you can have these incredibly ambitious visions, but you also ground the team in very practical research milestones. I'd love to understand — big big big vision — what does this look like in the day-to-day, and what are you implementing? How do you spend your days right now?

Dave: Great question. Day-to-day, there's a lot of hard technical work by people like Lasse to build the whole stack — so we've got a state-of-the-art reinforcement learning stack that allows us to run things at massive scale, inhale data in the optimal way, be able to learn and have systems that keep learning and learning and learning.

On top of that — we've spoken about the superlearner — the other aspect we're building is: we're building out environments which are capable of superlearners discovering everything we mean by intelligence. Simulated environments in which a superlearner can discover everything that we mean by intelligence. We call those crucibles. They're environments in which it's possible for agents to make incredible discoveries, in which it's possible to express and learn everything that we think of as intelligence.

So it's a combination of: building out the superlearner, doing the research to make superlearners incredible and beat the state-of-the-art of what's possible with reinforcement learning — both in terms of engineering and research — and creating and placing the superlearners into these crucibles to see the emergence of incredible behaviors.

In terms of grounding — we ground it in milestones, and the milestones are analogous to what happens with the human journey, where we discovered incredible things. Those become natural milestones for our agents to rediscover the great moments that humans went through in our discovery of knowledge.

不走"面包屑"路线：涌现式发现

Host: What do you think the agents will rediscover first? That's going to be your first moment of "oh, this is working."

Dave: I imagine we're going to be surprised. One thing which is different about the way we take to doing reinforcement learning, versus a lot of the rest of the field: we're not breadcrumb-trailing the particular objective to be learned about.

A lot of the way people do RL with LLMs at the moment is to say, "Oh, the agent should be learning about this problem, and then this problem, and this problem" — and after following that trail, we're pulling the agent by its nose towards a particular desired outcome. We're not taking that approach. We're giving the agent some simple objectives and asking it to discover things that will surprise us and amaze us. The agent is in principle capable of discovering all kinds of things, and we don't necessarily know in advance what those discoveries will be. It's going to be exciting to witness that journey. So I hope to be surprised — that's the answer to your question.

Host: Interesting. So instead of explicitly giving the agent the goal to rediscover language, or build a calculator, or build a computer, you're going to give it other, more open-ended goals — and the agent may discover that the best way to accomplish that goal may be to build some of these tools that we as humans have already built. Is that one way of putting it?

Dave: That's one way of putting it. Another way to say it: people often think in RL, "Oh my god, how do I come up with a reward function that perfectly specifies this really complicated thing that I want to discover? How can I specify exactly what I mean by science, or exactly what I mean by interesting maths?" But there's an alternative — give the agent something really straightforward to optimize, but in a really complex environment where there's a lot to learn about.

It turns out that if you look at the way the world has worked in nature, the pursuit and optimization of very simply, easy-to-describe quantities can often give rise to incredibly hard-to-describe complexity and emergence.

Examples: evolution, which just optimizes survival of the fittest — some kind of fitness signal — and the pursuit of fitness gave rise to all of the complexity that we see in life. The human journey — the pursuit of relatively simple goals that we as humans have — gave rise to all of the complex behaviors that humans ultimately acquired, and all of the knowledge we eventually ended up with. The emergent complexity is much greater than the starting point. Evolution didn't say, "Hey, humans, here's this idea of science, and you need to get to the most complex science that's out there." It was something much simpler.

A way to describe this: perhaps humans, in the pursuit of our goals, started coordinating a bit more; in the process of coordinating, we discovered that it was helpful to start communicating; in the process of communicating, we started trading; in the process of trading, we discovered that basic arithmetic was useful; then we discovered that tools were useful; then some basic science was required to help understand how the tools would work; that gave rise to more complex technology; understanding the technology required more complex maths; and so forth, and so forth. All in the pursuit of relatively simple goals, this incredible complexity emerged.

If we can get that process right — things are going to take off and lead to unbelievable things.

关于奖励函数

Host: It's fascinating. Are the rewards for your agents kind of similar to human biology and evolution then — like, "try to make it to the next generation"? What does a reward function look like for you all?

Dave: We've been experimenting with quite a number of different rewards — so it's not like we have one answer to that question. But one thing we're not doing is crafting a reward that exactly describes what we mean by science, or exactly what we mean by technology, or exactly what we mean by language. We expect our agents to discover things. If we can't crack this problem as AI scientists, we're never going to have agents that discover whole new fields of knowledge that we don't even know about.

There are vast fields that will exist out there which we don't even know have the potential to exist at this point in time. Imagine you were back in the days of Newtonian physics and no one even knew that quantum physics was a thing, or that relativity was a thing. We should be in that process of open-minded discovery where our agents are free to figure things out for themselves. I think that's going to lead to much more exciting outcomes.

Crucibles 的样子

Host: What do these crucibles look like in practice? When people say "environments," oftentimes it's a set of tasks and you know what the agent should have done on the task. It sounds like your crucibles are very very different.

Dave: We are building crucibles which — without giving too many details away — have the capacity for a lot of emergent complexity. The key thing: it's not like we've handcrafted a whole load of puzzles for the agents to work with. There's just a huge amount of emergent complexity.

Some of that emergent complexity can come from different places: physics engines that give rise to complexity as you've got millions of interacting objects with a complex physics engine; millions of interacting agents, where the world becomes much more complex because it now includes the complexity of all of those other agents within the world that the agents are building.

There are ways to build worlds that are vastly more complex than the standard simulators — like Atari 57, whatever people have been working with in the past — and certainly more complex than the standard benchmark tasks people are using. If you get that right, you have a world in which there's the possibility for discovery by the agent — for the agents to discover everything from technology to science to mathematics to languages, in the same way humans — all the way through from more basic things like motor control or coordination — the whole spectrum is possible.

Lasse: Like if you look at a game like Go — which is very simple to represent, just a bitmap — the simulation is extremely simple. But you still see this emerging behavior of something complex, which is super interesting to us. Of course, Go is way simpler than we can imagine doing. But going all the way to 100%-realistic physics will be very computationally expensive. So we want to create this range of crucibles where we have simple ones that can execute quickly and we can iterate on, but where we can still see very complex behavior.

Host: Interesting. It's almost like what you choose to represent is tricky, right? For example, I can imagine a lot of economics arises from game theory, and most of that is completely unrelated to physics. So a crucible that represents physics is probably not that helpful. But if you have information theory represented — which agents know what — then you probably do end up rediscovering quite a bit of economics. Is that a fair way to put it? The primitives you choose to capture in the environment give rise to the type of learning that emerges.

Lasse: Yeah. The end goal is to have something that is grounded in the real world — but stepping stones.

为什么围棋是个好类比

Dave: I wanted to come back to the Go example — I really like this example. You'll be surprised to hear that I find Go to be a good example. What I find fascinating — which is what Lasse is talking to here — is that Go is just like a 19×19 grid where you're trying to maximize territory. If this was a single-agent game, it would be the most boring game you could imagine — you just place down stones on a grid until it fills up the whole grid, and there would be no strategy whatsoever.

The moment you put a second agent into the environment, you get this emergent complexity — because one agent has to reason about all the possible behaviors of the other agent. Suddenly it massively increases the complexity in the environment. And to the best of our knowledge — certainly all the compute which we sank into it when we were working on it — there was just this endless learning curve where, without end, you could continue to discover new things in this game.

None of this is to say that Go is the end point. Of course it's still just a board game and quite narrow in a certain sense — but it shows that very simple environment dynamics can lead to an infinite onion of layers of complexity that never stops. Infinite to the capacity of what our computers can do, of course.

智能体会重新发明语言吗？

Host: Do you think that the agents will end up rediscovering language, and will that language look like ours or will it look different?

Dave: My personal belief is that anyone who thinks that human language is the end point — or the best way to reason — that perspective is a little naive. It must be the case that there are far more sophisticated approaches to reasoning: maybe using parallelizable, rich, complex approaches — neural reasoning or whatever it is — these approaches will ultimately be far more expressive and far more capable than approaches based on human language.

I would also say that starting from human language as the approach for reasoning is somewhat problematic, because it pulls in all of our biases about how we think agents should think.

For example: imagine stepping back 500 years, or a thousand years, or 2,000 years, and only being able to use all of the language that humans used at that time. Maybe our agents would believe that the world was flat, or that diseases were caused by the four humors — all kinds of strange beliefs would be embedded there and very hard to remove because they're so fundamental to the language and the processes of thinking that humans have used. So going beyond this is a really important goal.

去除人类先验：从 AlphaGo 到 AlphaZero

Host: I'd love to talk more about this concept of removing human priors. Your experience with AlphaZero and AlphaGo Zero is maybe the best example that anyone can point to of what happens when you remove human priors. Maybe take us back to AlphaGo and then AlphaZero — was it surprising to you that removing human priors would result in even smarter intelligence?

Dave: I wasn't sure, honestly. I always like to do things in research where I think — you ask research questions which are on a knife-edge, where it's 50/50. It's not very interesting to do research where you already know the answer and you're 95% certain this thing's going to work — it's kind of boring, honestly. Good research is about asking questions where you're really not sure what the answer is in advance. In this case, I was about 50/50, and I thought maybe there was a good chance it might. But I wasn't confident, and it was very exciting to see it.

You asked about human priors. We are making a bet at Ineffable: that we can go further by giving up on the priors that everyone's relying on today — like human data, the whole internet of knowledge that everyone else is building their systems upon. That's an important choice, so we should probably talk about why we're doing that.

The reason for me: of course it's a short-term sacrifice. We give up a certain amount of performance in order to access something which is potentially far greater. It comes back to this — what does it mean to build a superlearner? Building a superlearner is about building something that has this potential for full depth and breadth.

Depth: We need to get to something which is capable of discovering things which go so far beyond human knowledge that it goes just far beyond the prior. The more we lean on human data, the less able we are to actually discover the algorithms that are really going to take us all the way to something that's going to — for example — discover a whole new field of knowledge.

Breadth: We need algorithms that can be placed down and discover things in environments for which language and human data that we've started with is just not a good fit. There are many areas — different kinds of sensors, for example — where human-like language data, or human data in general, is not a good fit for the description. By letting go of the human data, we put ourselves in a position where we can actually discover something which can go far, far beyond it.

Coming back to the AlphaGo example: what we found was that the moment we let go of the human data — which, by the way, we'd spent about two years building AlphaGo somewhat similar to the LLM approach, where we built every level of this, hand-put together the next level, put in a lot of human data, then were human-in-the-loop improving it, taking the previous generation and choosing how we were going to improve it to give the next generation. We were right in the loop of this process. It took us two years to get to AlphaGo and beat Lee Sedol.

When we got AlphaZero right — when we gave up on the human data and finally focused on what it would be like to build an algorithm that could discover for itself — once we got it right, that algorithm, it took just a few hours to outperform the two years of work which we'd done with human-in-the-loop. In the game of chess, it took four hours to beat the world champion — the best-ever AI that had ever been created. In the game of Go, it took, I think, a couple of days — but incredible progress.

You have to let go of the human data to allow yourself to discover these things that can then shoot past the competition and discover the things that just keep learning and learning and learning forever.

It has to be an active choice. If you don't make that active choice, what I see in a lot of the LLM companies today is they're basically building semi-autonomous human-in-the-loop learning algorithms with thousands of people in the loop of the learning progress — which works, and a lot of respect for how far it gets, but until we step back from that and really discover the process that's going to learn for itself, I don't believe we'll get all the way to something which is truly a superlearner and unleashes the potential we've talked about so far.

如何防止人类偏见"泄漏"

Host: That's very profound. There are humans at Ineffable, and some of you are creating environments or crucibles. What does it look like to actually try and make sure that human priors aren't leaking into what you're doing?

Lasse: When we design environments and reward functions and so on, obviously there's a human bias in there. But — as Dave was mentioning earlier — we don't want to bias it towards building a machine based on, say, the von Neumann architecture or something like this. If you're stating some problem where a machine would be useful, it would be very interesting to see what type of machine it comes up with — what computer-like machine it comes up with.

Dave: I totally agree. I would also say we're not religious about this. It's not a religion that you can't have any human prior anywhere. It's more of a pragmatic position that until we give up on relying on the trillion-item datasets of human knowledge, we're not going to make the progress that the field deserves to see.

In practice, there's going to be a certain amount of prior which — as Lasse says — applies to many different worlds, as opposed to trying to put in these very strong priors that exactly encode all the knowledge we know about this one particular problem or this one particular world. Weak, environment-agnostic priors seem perfectly reasonable, but these super-strong priors with trillion-item datasets — we're trying to avoid that because we think pragmatically it's going to lead to better outcomes.

对把握的判断与时机论

Host: Yeah, absolutely. You mentioned philosophically that you're drawn to research that's more on a knife's edge — 50/50. I'm curious what your confidence levels are for Ineffable, at the broadest level — will a superlearner emerge? — and then at the more pragmatic level in terms of the things you're trying to accomplish right now. Are you 50/50 on these as well?

Dave: First of all, I would say I strongly believe the approach will be feasible at some point. In fact, it's the only thing for which we have an example of — the example in our brains is the only existence proof of something which has discovered incredible intelligence that's very general and works in an embodied world and discovers how to do all kinds of different things. We have this incredible example of the human brain that we can look at.

Do I think we can achieve it? Well, like many great moments in science, it's about timing. Whether this succeeds or fails is about timing. When you create a startup, you want to be at the right time. You don't want to be too early or too late. If you're too late, everyone's done it — it's not interesting, a thousand other people have already done it. If you're too early, you might be banging on the door, but maybe the field isn't advanced enough, or there isn't enough compute to be able to succeed yet.

To me, it's all about timing. For example, with Computer Go, I made a prediction I think 10 years before Computer Go was solved and I got it right to the year. Got it right for StarCraft, which we also had a bet on and made a prediction. Same for AlphaProof — predicting when the IMO was going to fall.

Host: So you're a super-forecaster of sorts.

Dave: So far, so far I've done very well at this. I have a very strong sense that this is the right time for this to fall — that superlearners are possible. There's been enormous progress in the level of technology: the ability to accelerate research using LLM coding methods, or auto-research methods like we've produced in the past; the ability and understanding of scaling laws; the sophistication of technology and the stack. There are a lot of things that fall into place that make this the right time.

That's my bet — that this is the right timing. But yeah, of course — this is research. Research is never guaranteed, and that's what makes it exciting. If you get the timing right, you can be the first. You can be the ones to change the whole field of AI. That's what it means to take risks and do something exciting.

算力是关键驱动吗？

Host: For Ineffable — and also all the previous things that you correctly forecasted — is the biggest driver of timing compute?

Dave: I think it's a very big driver. An enormous driver. We're in a great position with the compute we've managed to get hold of, and I think it gives an opportunity to do things which are orders of magnitude more sophisticated than approaches that have tried to do self-discovered RL in the past.

If we compare to, I don't know, something like Hide-and-Seek from OpenAI — which was an early example where agents discovered some basic tool use — I think we could probably run experiments that use 100,000 times more compute. It's kind of amazing that people haven't come back and really pushed on these types of approaches given the availability of compute. Of course, Hide-and-Seek — I don't want to pretend that's the end goal. It's very basic. But it's suggestive of what could be done.

So compute is a huge driver — but it's not the only one.

Lasse: We're in a very fortunate situation that we have been able to secure a very large cluster. This is really an opportunity for us — we really have the cards in our hands to test this out. Very few other people are doing something similar. We can really test this out in a way that we couldn't do at DeepMind, for instance.

关于仿真的天花板

Host: It seems like one of the determinants of how far this can go is how far you can push simulation — because ultimately these crucibles are digital. Simulation has probably come quite far in the last handful of years, but it's not perfect. We recently had your friend Rich Sutton on the show and I asked him about simulation, and he was very dismissive of simulation. I'm curious how you guys think about this. Lasse — you've been on both sides of this. You did a lot in the digital world, but you also built MetNet, which touches real-world atmospheric data. How do you all think about where is the ceiling on simulation, and when is the right time to bring an agent into the real world?

Lasse: So MetNet was an example. This is a weather-forecasting model we did in the Google Brain Amsterdam office together with Google Research, where we were doing a machine learning model to predict short-term weather forecasts — and this was way better than the physics-based simulations. The physics simulations were accumulating errors over time. So there's a point to that — physics simulation is not perfect.

I do think there are a lot of relatively simple environments we can build where we can see this emerging behavior — let's say technology and so on — where we don't need exact physics. It's interesting to see how much we can build these days with a very small team in terms of these simulations. There's definitely a ceiling —

Host: Is there a ceiling, actually? I'm curious about this.

Lasse: Well, I guess quantum physics and whatnot. There's a ceiling somewhere. But we can do very interesting things without real physics, I would say.

Dave: I think the right question to ask is: can a super intelligence be built in simulation? If it is possible for it to be built in simulation, I believe it will happen 10 times or 100 times faster — just because simulation can be infinitely parallelized. You get perfect reproducibility. It has a lot of really nice properties. It's also the safest place for a super intelligence to be built.

Then we need to ask: is it possible? For the reasons we discussed earlier, there are very clear approaches that we can add into the simulation that allow it to be sufficiently complex to represent arbitrarily interesting things.

For example, let's say you wanted to build a computer in simulation — all you require is that your simulation is Turing-complete. If you have a Turing-complete simulation, suddenly everything we mean by computation — provably everything we mean by computation — can be expressed completely inside simulation. Indeed, humans have built incredibly complex computers inside simulated worlds.

Same for various other ideas. If you want to build an economy — money can be built out of coins, or paper, or bits — as long as you have some representation of money, everything we mean by economics can be expressed inside a simulation. Same for language: if you've got multiple agents and they've got some ability to express a channel of communication between the agents, suddenly everything we mean by language is expressible in simulation. Mathematics we know is expressible in any universe.

Science, in some sense, is the study of our world. Will a simulation be sufficient to study what we mean by science? There are some aspects of science which are expressible in many things — energy or entropy or evolution. It's also true that the agent will discover its own science: whatever the simulator is, if it's got this emergent complexity to its environment, the agent will discover its own science about whatever that world is.

It's provably possible to build environments in which it's possible to express and represent enormous complexity of all these things. I agree with Lasse — there might be some things which aren't well expressed. There will be things which can only be expressed in the real world — quantum computation is a good example.

The real point: if it's possible to get all the way to a super intelligence in simulation, it will happen faster, and it will happen safer — and for those reasons, it's something that we choose to put a lot of energy into.

I actually agree with Rich Sutton that you shouldn't expect that the things you learn in simulation will transfer "sim-to-real" into the real world, because the real world is vastly more complex and in very interesting ways that are hard to simulate. But what we can do is: we can do all of the science to discover the superlearner. Once we have that superlearner, we will have the answers, and we'll know how to build something — that same algorithm should be applicable to the real world. We can also make our simulations more and more high-fidelity towards the real world and check that they still work before putting them into the world.

Host: Great answer. Thank you.

对齐（Alignment）的科学

Host: I'd love to talk about alignment. I know this is a politically charged topic right now, and I'm less interested — I'm zero interested — in having the politics or policy discussion around alignment. But I am very interested in the scientific discussion around it.

It seems like so much of the misalignment that's emerged has arisen from scaling reinforcement learning to the extent that it's been scaled. Do you think that the superlearner you build will naturally be aligned to human interests and have human values? Is it important for it to have alignment with human values?

Dave: This is a big topic — let me start by saying a few things.

Where we are today with alignment: we are essentially relying very heavily on alignment approaches that are based on the language that the agents use, and priors based on human data. That has been very effective up to this point, but we're starting to see that approach is reaching its limits. By itself, I think it's going to be difficult to see a path where — as agents become inevitably more and more powerful (and we can already see this happening) — as agents are trained more and more, they're going to start to overwhelm their priors. They're going to start to learn to say one thing and act in a different way. It's going to be increasingly difficult to align them to the things that humans want them to do.

My belief is that we need something more. This by itself is not sufficient.

The most important single thing we can do as a company is to actually understand the science of super intelligence. If we can in simulation really build a super-intelligent agent and start to see these superlearners go all the way, we can start to actually understand what it takes for a super intelligence to interact peacefully. We can answer really important questions — fundamentally important questions — like: under what conditions, what are the structures, what are the leverages that we need to put into place to make sure that a society of super intelligences actually interacts peacefully — and in particular interacts peacefully with other lesser intelligences that are also going to be in their world.

If we get this right, we actually can get to some real science that will help us understand the right things to do in the real world — because we're hurtling towards that real-world outcome where there are going to be a whole load of different interacting super intelligences, and we don't quite know how that's going to play out. The faster we can actually get to these answers in simulation and publicly share that, the better situation we'll be in.

I also believe that we can use this to gate the actual decision-making of what we do in the real world. One of our commitments: we will gate anything we do in the real world on having sufficient evidence from this kind of science of super intelligence — that we are really confident that things are going to go well. We'll only push forward to the next level of what we do in the real world once we are absolutely confident that can lead to a good outcome.

These are two things that I believe we can do. We're in this world where a lot of things are happening very quickly. We're hurtling towards an outcome with lots of interacting super intelligences. I personally believe that this will lead to a good outcome for humanity — but it's happening very quickly. If we're able to actually understand this and run ahead in simulation, we'll be in a much better place to actually ensure that this goes really well.

监督超越语言的推理

Host: Fascinating. One of the primary things that current safety researchers rely on is being able to monitor the agents' chains of thought in English. So when they start speaking Rilean, that scares people — because we can no longer understand and monitor it. In your case, you have your agents going straight to rediscovering language. What do you think that means for monitoring? Or is the point that if you get the reward right, and if you get the environments right, then you shouldn't need to monitor?

Dave: Monitoring is still really helpful. Like it or not, the approach of monitoring the human language that these systems use is going to be increasingly difficult as agents get more powerful. We're already seeing that — agents are producing a tome of a million words of reasoning, or actively using subterfuge to think in one way and act in another. It's increasingly difficult to rely 100% on that.

I do think we need other elements in our armory anyway. It's really important that some people are looking at how to get this right. There are ways to monitor agents that don't use language. For example, you can use shadow actions — you start to have actions where you can look at what they would actually do if they were allowed to act in the world, but you don't actually let them take that action yet. You can start to have other super intelligences which are acting as the monitor — for example, you might have the idea of an incredible scientist agent that treads lightly upon the earth, and then another super intelligence that's monitoring the magnitude of its actions and regularizing it to make sure it can't do things which are affecting the world too much.

There are lots of ideas. There's a lot of research to be done here. I'm not claiming to have all the answers, but it's something that deserves a lot of investigation. If people aren't looking at this because they're only looking at the language-based approach, I think we're in trouble, because that language-based approach is not enough in itself to actually get to where we want.

Having said "in trouble" — I am optimistic about where the world is going. By "trouble," I mean we're not going to have agents that do the things we want them to do. I do think we're going to end up in a world with lots of complex interacting super-intelligent beings, and I'm optimistic that this will lead to a balance of actors — some supporting the flourishing of humanity, and some which may not. But the ones which do support the flourishing of humanity will end up supporting us and protecting us against the ones which aren't acting on our best interests. That's the world I think we can work towards.

Pacing the Frontier

Host: Well, given your super-forecasting abilities, I'm happy to hear that. What do you think about all the conversation around pacing the frontier?

Dave: I'm actually very much supportive of the idea that there should be pacing of what happens for the frontier of AI in the real world. At the same time, I think we should move as fast as possible in simulation.

The reason: in simulation we can develop a lot of things — like the science of super intelligence — that will actually help us find solutions that help things to go well in the real world. That kind of work should happen as fast as possible to make sure that, when things really happen in the real world, things have the best possible opportunity to go well and lead to human flourishing.

In general, I'm supportive of the suggestions — the direction that people like Demis and Dario and so forth are suggesting. I think it's generally a good idea. Part of that is: things are moving really quickly, and I do believe that when we accelerate AI and get to super intelligence, it will lead to a really great future for humanity. But I also think that the speed at which things are moving is not something that we are capable of adapting to that fast. By pacing a little bit, it gives us the opportunity for our governments and our organizations and our emotional responses to adapt to the changes that are coming — and also for this work to continue apace at really figuring out in simulation how to do this right.

Host: So — accelerate in simulation so we can understand what's happening and do science around it, and then careful in the real world.

Dave: Yeah, I think that would be my summary.

算力配置：集群、架构与挑战

Host: I'd love to transition to talking a little bit about compute. This is going to be an incredibly compute-expensive journey, and you are pushing the limits of what compute can do. Both Google and Nvidia have been great partners for you. Can you talk a little bit about your cluster? You're not simply renting spot compute from Neoclouds like many other NeoLabs — you're actually doing some really serious work on your cluster and the different other forms of compute you have.

Lasse: As I mentioned earlier, we are very fortunate with the compute we have. We are the first customers of the largest GB300 cluster on GCP by the end of the year — well, actually, in one month now. We're extremely fortunate in that. I actually feel quite bad about the startups that are getting compute now, because it's becoming harder and harder.

We have this very large GPU cluster — Nvidia GPUs — which is really fortunate for us because it means we can easily do simulation and training and inference. They are quite general chips, which is amazing. The GB300s specifically have this architecture where one rack can basically be considered one machine — there's very high bandwidth between the nodes in one rack, which is very important for reinforcement learning where you have really fast iteration cycles compared to LLMs, which are relatively speaking quite slow.

Some things we did 8–10 years ago at Google, where we basically had abundant CPUs at Google — that doesn't scale anymore. We really need to make sure that everything we do is on the GPUs, and we don't need millions of CPUs beyond these GPUs. So our simulations can run on the GPU — inference and training and so on. We have some good architectures for that.

The LLM companies now have kind of the problems that we had many years ago, where they need sandboxes running on CPUs — simulating computers and so on. We're trying to not put ourselves in that situation.

Host: All the compute — is it roughly fungible between the different things that you're doing? I imagine you're building crucibles and then doing these big rollouts where the agents are actually learning. Is that the rough bucket of what compute is being used for?

Lasse: You could split it up into training, inference, and simulation.

Host: Is the same compute equally good at training, inference, and simulation?

Lasse: No.

Host: Okay.

Lasse: It's pretty clear what has happened with GPUs over the last many years — since deep learning took off — they've been more and more tailored towards training, and maybe in the last few years also inference, but less about simulation. Similarly to the LLM companies, we also want to be in the case where scaling laws matter — we know that roughly, if you add this amount of compute and experiences, we get a certain amount of quality out of that.

Host: So if GPUs aren't great for scaling simulation, then what's the solution?

Lasse: There are many different solutions here. There's model-based reinforcement learning, where the model becomes much more expensive compared to the simulation. There's many different tricks you can do — various approaches for replay buffers, or reusing data many times. Other than that, we do spend quite some effort on just making the simulations as fast as possible and making them use the best use of the GPUs.

规模定律与 RL

Host: Are you seeing scaling laws yet, or is it too early to say?

Lasse: For reinforcement learning, scaling laws are slightly different. Scaling laws are the component of how much compute you put in, how much data you put in, and the model size. Reinforcement learning is a little bit different because the problem is non-stationary — as you progress in the problem the data changes, the data distribution changes. So they are a little bit different. It's a very interesting research direction.

Host: I understand they're different, but are you seeing some sort of scaling law where more compute in gets you closer to achieving the goals? Or is it hard to say right now?

Lasse: It's something we are actively pushing towards. Especially as we transition from a smaller cluster to the bigger cluster, we want to be ready for that.

基础工作：IMPALA 与 SEED RL

Host: Lasse, at the beginning, when David introduced you, he mentioned that you had done some very foundational work on compute and algorithms for reinforcement learning upon which the field really relies today. Maybe talk about some of that work — in particular your work around IMPALA and SEED. What are those and how do they relate to the work that you're doing at Ineffable?

Lasse: When I joined the deep learning team at DeepMind, most people were running single-machine, CPU-based reinforcement learning. The scale was quite small. So what I did together with colleagues was to make a reinforcement learning agent that really utilized GPUs. It could scale linearly with compute. Partially because it was very efficient — it was very good at scaling. And the third thing was: it was very easy to extend, modify, and do whatever you wanted with it. That contributed to it being the most popular reinforcement learning agent at the company. At one point, most RL teams used it or derivatives of it. That was quite successful and a nice project to work on.

Then later on, we got TPUs — racks of these TPUs — so we needed to scale beyond that. Some of my work at Google Brain, after I left DeepMind to found the Google Brain Amsterdam office, was to scale to racks of TPUs. That product was called SEED RL. It was really about utilizing the TPUs for both inference and training in the best possible way, while keeping the environments as flexible as you wanted them to be. It could be anything from Go to very expensive physics simulations.

Host: And how's that being used at Ineffable?

Lasse: We actually implemented a few of those algorithms — and derivatives of these algorithms. That is what we are using today. Depending on the environments we use, we have different algorithms — there are pros and cons between them. As we talked about, we have some very simple, fast-to-assemble environments and also some that are more expensive.

Dave: For those who are working on large-scale RL architectures today and haven't read those original papers, it's definitely worth a look — because many of the ideas currently in use trace back to that early work that Lasse did and figured out. Which was a little bit prescient, I would say.

Lasse: It's kind of fun to see the reinforcement learning space now versus 10 years ago — or let's say 8 years ago. The LLM community is also using reinforcement learning, in particular the last two years. A lot of the things they're using are rediscovered approaches that we used many years ago. That's interesting to see — with a lot of novelty as well on top of it.

团队与文化

Host: Can you talk a little bit about your team? How big is the team right now?

Dave: We have intentionally kept the team relatively small. We're not in a hurry to build a giant organization. You can do an awful lot nowadays with a small number of incredibly talented people. We have hired 20 people in total.

The people we've hired — it's about finding some of the exceptionally talented people. But it's not just about talent for us. It's also about bringing together people who are collaborative human beings. That's really important to the kind of culture we're trying to build. People who are really well-aligned with the mission that we're following. And people that fit the needs that we have — we try to build the team with the right set of skills as well. All four of those things are really important. We have very high standards and very high expectations of the people that come in. So we'll be very lucky to get amazing — really amazing — people.

Lasse: To tie it to the compute as well: this relatively small amount of people so far means that we have a lot of compute per person. These days you can do a lot of experiments as just one person. So it's really also to keep the compute-to-person ratio quite high. We're not fighting for resources from day one.

Host: Three of the co-founders worked together on AlphaStar. Many of you did work together. Are you assembling the Avengers — especially given the recent changes from DeepMind? Are you assembling the Avengers of folks that you've worked with in the past? Have you hired new people? And if so, what are the attributes that make somebody new to you likely to be a fit at Ineffable?

Dave: It's a mixture. AlphaStar was an exceptional team. It was intentionally assembled within DeepMind by choosing the best of the best to work on that project. So in some sense, it's not a surprise that four of our co-founders come from that team. But we are not exclusively drawing from that team, or indeed from DeepMind. The other three founders all came from very successful startups.

We hire people who are brilliant — but also kind and nice people to have around, who are going to work together well, who are aligned with the mission and fit the things that we need. We put a lot of effort into getting the right people. As uncomfortable as it is, I've had to say "no" to a lot of people I've worked with in the past, just because our bar is so super high. I've been fortunate to work with some amazing people, and I've been choosing amongst a very exceptional crop and bringing in what I consider to be a superstar team. It's not easy to get into Ineffable, but the people we have are wonderful human beings — and yeah, very proud of the people we've brought in.

Host: I can see why people are drawn to working at Ineffable. Especially at a time when the biggest clusters, the biggest labs, are locked in this prisoner's dilemma race, and there's a lot of dollars at stake, so decisions get made differently. I can imagine for a set of people that really, really deeply believes in the scientific mission of what you want to accomplish, this must feel like a breath of fresh air.

Dave: I think that's right. We've tried to establish a research-led culture. It's not a company that's led by building an incremental next product — V 17.1 on the thing that's come before. It's a company that's built on researchers pursuing their passion and trying to produce the breakthroughs they believe are possible. We center the company around that from the beginning and from the outset — to create a haven for research. We push back on product pressure, because we believe that if we make these breakthroughs, it will lead to far bigger products downstream and far bigger successes than if we started off from day one on "here's the product we're doing from the beginning."

So — it's research-led. We're creating, I think, a really special environment. People are loving it. I'm loving it.

预测：时间线

Host: Wonderful. I'd love to close with some predictions — especially since you're such a super-forecaster. What's your guess for when you'll have the first strong evidence that the approach is working? And then what's your forecast for when we'll achieve the mission that you've set out to achieve — this first contact with super intelligence?

Dave: These are fair questions. There are going to be some reasonable bars of uncertainty on this.

Host: Yeah, but you're being recorded, so we're going to hold you to it.

Dave: Exactly. [laughter]

I think we will see some extremely strong evidence that we're on the right track within a year. And I think we will achieve something which is a true super intelligence — according to the definition I gave earlier of something which discovers things far beyond what humans can achieve, across everything from science, mathematics, technology, languages, etc.

I originally thought within three to five years. My timelines have accelerated a little bit — so I'm going to say three years — because of what can be done with coding agents to accelerate things. Things are going to move fast.

Host: Buckle up — it's going to be a journey. Wonderful. Lasse, David, this is a wonderful, wonderful conversation. I'm so inspired by what you're building, and thank you for taking the time to sit down and share with our audience what you're building today.

Dave: Thank you, Sonya. Pleasure.

[music]

观看原视频 →

## 一、最反直觉的洞见：Ineffable 其实在复制"寒武纪大爆发"，而不是复制"人类"
大多数人把 Silver 的路径理解为"不用人类数据的 AlphaZero 升级版"。但如果你仔细听他讲 crucible——**"几百万相互作用的 agent + 简单奖励 + 涌现复杂性"**——这其实是在**用算力重演寒武纪生命演化**，而不是重演人类文明。
区别极其关键：人类文明是一个**单一物种内部的协作演化**（有共享语言、共享生物基础）；而 Silver 要构建的是一个**多智能体生态系统**，让智能作为"物种间博弈"的副产品浮现。他引用围棋那一刻极其暴露底牌——"单智能体围棋无聊到死，第二个 agent 一进来复杂度爆炸"。这不是深度学习的隐喻，这是**生物学的隐喻**。
**那个让人意外的推论是**：如果他成功了，第一个 ineffable 产出的"超级智能"大概率不是**一个**超级智能，而是**一个由多个相互博弈的智能构成的生态**——因为他的 alignment 论述里反复出现"a balance of actors"、"society of super inte

item.title: [Invest Like The Best] How He Built the World’s Largest Digital Bank with 140 Million Customers
item.dc:creator: Invest Like The Best
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、藏在"零利率存款"里的6000亿美元——一场看不见的全民财富税

David 顺口抛出一个数字，但它值得停下来凝视：美国零售存款约15万亿美元，银行平均只付40个基点利息，而无风险利率4.5%。差值×本金≈6000亿美元/年。

这是一个什么量级的概念？——它接近美国国防预算的 65%，相当于全体美国人每年自愿为"街角那座大理石分行建筑"交的一笔税。但没人把它记在T-账单上，因为它从未从你的账户划出去，它只是没有进来。

行为经济学家 Gabaix 和 Laibson 把这种现象叫做 "shrouded attributes"（遮蔽属性）——消费者看不见的成本。保险的隐性佣金、墨盒的后续更换费、酒店的 resort fee 都是同一个家族。David 的真正发现不是"分行贵"，而是：整个传统银行业的商业模式本质上是一座遮蔽属性工厂。Nubank 的攻击点不是技术，是让这笔税从黑暗中走出来。

二、Blockbuster 悖论：数据从来不是护城河，使用数据的文化才是

这是整段访谈最颠覆直觉的一句话——"Blockbuster 其实有海量数据"。每一张被租走的 VHS、每一次会员登录、每一笔晚归罚金，Blockbuster 都拿得到。它比 Netflix 早诞生 15 年，坐拥比 Netflix 多得多的消费行为样本。

然后它死了。

David 把这个事实拧到银行业头上：巴西几家百年老行有1亿客户、13年×30000个数据点的历史，却造不出基础模型。为什么？因为数据只是矿石，提炼它的组织代谢率才是价值。

这个洞察的跨领域回响极深： - 米其林餐厅并非赢在食材（Sysco 把同样的食材送到两家店），赢在组织化的"fire-pass-fire"规训； - 苏联拥有比美国更多的工程师和更多的工业数据，却跑输硅谷——因为没有把数据流翻译成行动流的回路； - 大语言模型的真正瓶颈从来不是参数或语料，而是训练文化的紧凑度。

Nubank 真正的护城河因此很诡异：它不是"我们有更多数据"，而是"我们有把数据变成决定的毛细血管密度"。这是组织生物学问题，不是数据科学问题。

三、AI 让办公室更重要——Jevons 悖论的倒影

几乎所有人都在预言 AI 杀死办公室。David 的直觉完全相反：个体在家做的事正在被 AI 商品化，所以在家工作的你不是在和同事竞争，而是在和一个免费的 Claude 竞争，你注定会输。能幸存的只剩协作、协调、在场的瞬时带宽——而这些只能在物理空间发生。

经济学里有个"Jevons 悖论"：蒸汽机效率提高后，煤的消耗量不降反升。David 揭示的是它的"组织学倒影"——AI 不消灭人类工作，它把工作重新分配到 AI 无法到达的物理层。这意味着未来 5 年，办公室地产的真正竞争不是"有没有"，而是"是否被设计成高带宽同步协作场"——会议密度、偶遇密度、白板密度，而不是工位密度。

四、塔可摊贩与"国家的凝视"——现金消亡的人类学意义

这是整段对话最被低估的瞬间。David 讲完"墨西哥城角落里的塔可摊贩无法获得信用"时，看似在讲 fintech，其实在讲人类学家 James Scott 的核心命题。

Scott 在《Seeing Like a State》里论证：19世纪现代国家做的第一件事是把人口、土地、树木、方言都变得可读（legible）。姓氏统一、度量衡统一、地籍图统一——不是因为统治者爱整洁，而是因为不可读的东西不能被征税、不能被动员、不能被治理。

现金的本质是不可读。塔可摊贩每天赚300比索，这条现金流对任何算法都是暗物质。Pix、UPI、稳定币做的事情，和腓特烈大帝做的是同构的：把非正式经济凝视进可见领域。

但这里有个漂亮的翻转——Scott 认为"被国家看见"对底层是危险的（更多的征税、征兵、强制搬迁）。而在数字金融时代，被看见反而是解锁资本的前提。塔可摊贩第一次因为"可读"而获得了资本权力。

这就是为什么 David 说"接下来的 10-20 年，几万亿美元信贷将被解锁"——不是因为算法变聪明，而是因为几十亿人第一次从暗物质里浮现出来。他做的不是银行业务，是可读性生产。

五、创始人作为"最后的护城河"——情感契约的不可稀释性

访谈结尾，David 丢出一个比任何战略都更尖锐的护城河论证：

"没有人在这个世界上比我更在乎这家公司，到了一种几乎可见的程度。"

这不是鸡汤。它是一个资产定价命题。

一家公司的所有护城河——专利可以被绕过、数据可以被追赶、品牌可以被侵蚀、规模可以被颠覆——但创始人与公司的情感契约不能被稀释、不能被收购、不能被 IPO。它是真正意义上的无法转让的资产。

把这个洞察和巴菲特50年的管理层评估拼起来：他从来不是在评估"CEO 聪明吗"，他是在评估"这个人是否在生物学意义上把自己绑在了这艘船上"。David 用"父亲对孩子"的比喻时，他其实在描述一种生物化学绑定——催产素级别的粘性。

有趣的推论：这解释了为什么 founder-led 公司在数十年尺度上系统性跑赢职业经理人公司。不是因为创始人更聪明，而是因为他们的决策函数里嵌入了一个非理性的情感权重，这个权重让他们在冬天不会卖出、不会裁员到骨头、不会为短期收益牺牲长期——不是因为他们算不出，而是因为他们算不动手。

这个洞察对投资者是个清单项：公司的生物化学紧度比资产负债表更难伪造。

📝 转录文本

Cold Open: The 10-Year Doubters

For 10 years, all we heard again and again and again was that it was impossible to compete with any bank, that we were going to get crushed, and that we had no shot at being successful.

Today, we have 140 million customers with 10,000 employees. Our competitors have 100 million customers with 100,000 employees and 6,000 branches. So our cost to serve a customer is about 3% of what a traditional incumbent bank is. That's pre-AI.

[music]

From 35M to 140M Customers

So the last time we did this, I think you had 35 million customers. Now you have 140 million customers. So well done. Well, well done. [laughter] Busy five years.

Yeah, busy five years.

One would be tempted to think that with that kind of growth, we've sort of saturated the potential of fintech as a category to create a new platform—digital, mobile-first—and that we're maybe in the later innings of the fintech technology transformation. I know that you think it's sort of the exact opposite, and I'd love you to detail exactly why and what you think we can expect in the next five years, not just for Nubank, but for digital financial services globally.

If you look at global consumer financial services, it's about a $10 trillion industry, and still something like 90% of that industry goes through banking branches. And it's owned by incumbent banks. So while there are a lot of neobanks and fintechs across the world in a number of different areas, we are—you are—all of those fintechs and all these new banks together, and we're less than 10% of that entire market.

So it's still—in financial services, it's still almost as if 90% of the world was going to Blockbuster to get VHS and DVDs, and Netflix-like services still had something like 10% of that industry. That transformation, that migration that you've seen in other industries—in media with Netflix, in retail with Amazon versus the Barnes & Nobles, in transportation with companies like Uber—that migration from incumbents to digitally native companies is still very, very early in financial services.

The Brazil Benchmark: Primary Bank for 65% of a Country

I think Nubank is very unique, specifically in Brazil and Latin America, because we are really the only neobank in the world where we've fully surpassed the biggest incumbent bank in terms of scale. We now have in Brazil close to 120 million customers. So upwards of 65% of the Brazilian adult population is a customer of us.

But even more than that, we've become the primary bank account of the entire country. About 60% of our customers use us as their primary bank account. We replace the incumbent bank. We're not a secondary wallet. We're not some money that you leave there. We are the primary institution where people are really banking day-to-day. And that is very unique to Nubank in Brazil, and increasingly we're doing that also in Mexico and Colombia.

We think that this is a little bit of seeing the future of what will happen around the world over the next 10 to 20 years—where you would expect a lot of shift of market share from the still-incumbent banks to the digital-native companies. And that is just migration of market share, but also you'll see a significant increase in market size as billions of people across the world enter the banking system. You still have three billion people that are completely outside the banking system, don't have access to credit.

Two Levers: Distribution and New Capability

I'd love to break this into two components. You could imagine if you froze the product today and just worked on getting it in more people's hands, that could be one dimension of expansion. But then of course, I'm sure you're thinking carefully about all the wonderful things that AI will allow you to do and technology will allow you to do for customers that you don't yet do today. Can you talk through each of those levers to achieve this Blockbuster-to-Netflix transition?

The first phase of transformation that enabled a lot of the migration in other industries was the smartphone. And this is sort of the same thesis you see repeating—the smartphone is the moment that we get to serve consumers without all that physical infrastructure. We have such a gigantic cost structure advantage that we could pass that efficiency to the end customer via lower fees and a better product.

Just to give you a data point: we have 140 million customers with 10,000 employees. Our competitors have 100 million customers with 100,000 employees and 6,000 branches. And you start thinking about what the cost of real estate of those branches is—it's gigantic. So our cost to serve a customer is about 3% of what a traditional incumbent bank is. That means we have so much margin to give back to the customer via no fees, better experience, better interest rates, and overall a better product.

That's pre-AI. We're still here in phase one of what a smartphone enabled. AI will be an additional multiplication on that efficiency. You get to choose: do you want to have much more efficiency and automate a lot of areas of the bank? You could imagine banks that have 500 million or a billion customers with 5,000 employees—that's totally within sight. Or you can just decide to increase your level of ambition. And for somebody like us, especially when we look at how early it is in the transformation, it's: why don't we go to 100 countries and try to accelerate this transformation by Nubank being one of the leading digital financial services firms in the world?

Three Buckets: Access, Cost, Intelligence

What are the craziest things you can imagine the product, or a bank like yours, doing for the customer in three or five years, because technology has made new things possible?

We like to categorize the problems we see in financial services in three buckets: one is access, one is cost, and the third is intelligence.

Access

On the access side, you still have three billion people in the world that don't have access to a credit product. It's crazy. Almost half of the world does not have access to credit. Even countries like Mexico or Colombia: 13% credit card penetration. Why hasn't that happened yet? Because you needed the creation of a lot of data, you needed sophistication in credit underwriting, you needed the digitalization of these systems to happen. And this is happening. Cash goes away, disappears. Enter a number of real-time payment systems, as you've seen in Brazil with Pix or India with UPI.

So there is a lot of transformation and catalysts that are accelerating the rails on which you increase access to consumer banking for the world, and this is going to be a massive, massive [snorts] opportunity. 10, 20 years from now, 100% of the population has access to banking services. 100% of the world population has access to credit. 100% of small business has access to credit. This is an insane push to global GDP. I don't think it's really understood how big of a motor this could be for every single economy, as you get half of your entire population in some areas access to banking.

Cost

Cost tends to be more hidden, especially in developed economies. The US is generally well-served in banking services, especially if you're a high-income consumer. But when you look at the cost of that banking system, it's pretty significant in ways that are not readily apparent.

For example, there's about $15 trillion of retail deposits in the US banking system, but banks pay on average about 40 basis points of yield a year, in a world where interest rates are four and a half, 5%. You look at the calculation on those $15 trillion—that's more or less $600 billion that are going to banks to pay for banking branches, that in a digital banking environment would actually stay in consumers' pockets.

This is a massive wealth tax. The fact that banks don't pay any yield—if you're high-income, you do; the lower-income you are, the less you get paid—that's a huge tax and a huge cost.

Then you look at remittances—for example, in the US, $100 billion go out of the US and people pay 5 to 10% per transaction. That will go to zero. Remittances—moving money is moving bits; that will trend towards zero in a more competitive environment.

Monthly accounts: people are paying $5, $10, $15 per month in the US banking system for a bank account. You look at Europe or developed economies, Japan, same thing. You see a huge amount of cost that consumers are paying that will eventually, with models such as ours that come to compete, also be competed away.

Intelligence

Finally, intelligence—I think this is also the one that is less understood and is beginning to be discussed with the advent of intelligence.

If you are in the top 1% of income, you have access to the best financial advice. You probably will have a private banker. That private banker is understanding all the bank accounts that you have, is optimizing your deposits, is thinking about what is the right tax-efficient structure. If you need a loan, they're going to go and compete a bunch of different banks with each other and get you the best yield.

But if you're in the other 99%, especially the more you go toward the bottom, you have access to nothing. Historically, there's been a lot of conversation about: "education is the answer. You just got to educate people." That never worked. People don't sit down to do classes. You're not going to solve this problem of intelligence through education. You can solve it through AI.

That's where I think AI will be really transformational in financial services—because it's almost providing every single person around the world super-intelligence to optimize their financial life on their behalf, and remove a lot of these profit pools that exist today in banking that, in an environment with intelligence, will be competed away.
