Self-Driving Money and the Rearrangement of Profit Pools

Flesh that last piece out a little bit more. Wealthfront used to have this idea of self-driving money. What do you think that ends up being for the average person in a couple of years because of this intelligence bucket?

The first obvious rearrangement is: those $600 billion that banks are keeping in their balance sheets to pay for banking branches get rearranged, get forwarded to all the banking consumers. Suddenly they realize, "what am I doing with my money, leaving it at zero?" Especially when you think about compounding and what that means for savings and compound interest—this is a lot of money being sent ultimately to pay banking branches.

You look at really any country around the world—Mexican banking balance sheets, Brazilian ones—it's exactly the same thing. The big incumbent banks pay zero on about 70% of their deposits, and on 30% they pay some yield, generally to the highest-income population or the corporates.

The second one: in banking, in a perfectly competitive environment, the best product should win. If you're charging no fees and you have the best experience—banking is a commodity product ultimately—you should be able to get 100% of the market share. That doesn't happen because there is a lot of inertia in the system.

With the combination, the multiplication of intelligence with open banking (for example, Plaid can connect 120 million accounts), and you put intelligence on top of that, you're effectively allowing each customer to know how to optimize their financial life and what fees are coming.

I'll give you an example. We're doing this in Brazil today with about 15 million of our customers every day. We're telling them: "Hey, your credit card in that bank is due tomorrow. You don't have any money there and they're going to charge you 15% interest per day. Let us give you some money so you pay that credit card." Or: "Refinance. You have this loan at 10% interest—let us refinance that at 5%." It's ultimately a drive toward optimizing and removing a lot of those profit pools on behalf of the consumer.

For certain consumer segments and certain products—if you want to get a mortgage, or certain sophisticated products—there is value in having a physical space. But that might be 5% of the cases today versus, if you have a savings account, a credit card, or a loan, you just don't need that anymore.

Imagining the Attack Vector on Your Own Business

One of the questions that lots of investors and founders are wrestling with is: what will be the best competitive advantages or moats in this new AI era, when the cost to build new stuff digitally is much, much lower? If I strip everything away from you and your only goal is to kill Nubank—build a new company to attack Nubank, let's say in Brazil or in Latin America—what do you think you would do?

Which in a way was what we did to the incumbent banks years ago, right? We were the disruptor going after incumbent banks.

I think the early-stage startup today that is AI-native—their biggest advantage will be the speed: the ability to move extremely quickly and launch a number of different products, especially if you're born unregulated.

By now, we are fully regulated. We have banking licenses in a number of different countries, so we have to go at a certain pace. We have to be checking with regulators.

But I think, specifically in financial services and banking, that will only get you up to a certain point, because eventually you're going to need to be regulated as well. There's been a lot of conversation about how AI disrupts software and that you can ask ChatGPT or Codex to rebuild an entire software strategy, but you still cannot really get ChatGPT to get you a banking license. You still cannot really get regulators to give you a license in six months instead of two or three years.

Specifically on credit, or in certain products that we operate in, the amount of data we have is pretty significant. We have about 140 million customers, and for each customer we have something like 20,000 to 30,000 data points across 13 different years. This is a huge, massive amount of information that allowed us to build our own foundation model—a foundation model for financial services, for credit—and this gives us a significant advantage in making credit decisions, for example, or collection decisions.

The early-stage startup entrepreneur, while they would have the speed, would have a much harder time getting to that level of data. So data becomes a significant moat for the incumbents. And I think companies like us are sort of in the sweet spot of benefiting the most from AI, because in one way we already have the scale and the data and the brand and the trust and the licenses that will be hard for the early native startup to move. But also we still have the technology angle and infrastructure to benefit from AI and move even faster than we were moving before.

The AI Timeline: From ML Since Day One to Opus 4.6

Can you build the pretty detailed timeline of maybe when you first had the thought, "wow, AI is a thing we need to take really seriously," and then, as the leader, how you've thought about rolling it out?

We started using machine learning since we started the organization, since 2013. We looked at Brazilian interest rates for consumers paying 500 and 600% a year. We said: there's an opportunity here to use better data, analytics, and machine learning to price credit risk. Different from a lot of fintechs, we decided to take balance sheet, to take credit risk, and to be capital-intensive by default. So we already had an organization that was very optimized for making decisions based on models and data.

When the ChatGPT moment came about three, four years ago, we started paying significant attention around how technology was going to facilitate some of the decisions. We acquired a company called Hyperplane in Palo Alto that was already working on doing foundation models for financial services. They were having such a hard time selling to the big incumbent banks—sales cycles were two years—so they were not really able to move while the technology itself was fairly forward-looking. We bought that company, integrated the team.

We think we were the first financial services firm in the world to build their own foundation model with its own proprietary data to do credit decisions specifically. We even published all of our own research in this area. We developed an early advantage. By now, we're using our foundation model for fraud decisions, for Mexico, for Colombia. As we launch the US and our international markets, we can day one come in with our own foundation model and understand how to use the data for making basic decisions.

Scale, Culture, Systems: Why Blockbuster Had Data

It sounds like scale is maybe the most important thing that will make Nubank so competitively advantaged for the next 10 years. Is that right?

I think scale is important, but you need it also with the right culture and the right systems. One of the things we heard a lot in the early days was: "Well, how are you going to compete with the banks? The banks have scale. They have a hundred-year history with a hundred million customers. How can you replicate that data?"

And going back to the analogy of Blockbuster, my answer was always: well, Blockbuster had a huge amount of data. Imagine the amount of people coming in into Blockbuster, whether they were looking at that VHS or that DVD or renting it. Did that data help them build a better search algorithm? No. Because they were not capturing the data. They did not have the right systems to capture data. They didn't have the right culture to be making decisions based on data or models. And somebody like Netflix was able to come in with no data and build a better algorithm.

Scale and data is important, but equally important is your systems and your culture—ultimately being a culture that is using a lot of this data to make the right decisions. And this is what differentiates neobanks or more digital-native organizations versus the more traditional incumbent banks that are still operating with 15 different systems as a result of a huge amount of acquisitions they did over the years. If you look at a lot of the AI applications, it's: how do we use AI to transform COBOL? How do we get away from the mainframe? You're talking about 10, 15-year histories of going to the cloud. They're still in that process.

Keeping the Team Out of the Incumbent Trap

How do you run that tactically in the culture, to make sure you don't fall in the same trap that all the big players before you have fallen into?

I think the biggest difference is that historically a lot of traditional banks saw their basis of competition as banking branches. Literally, how consumers used to pick a bank: "I'm going to pick a bank that has a banking branch very close." So there was a huge amount of effort and energy put into real estate and physical infrastructure, and obviously a lot of focus on building brand and trust—banks need to protect that trust with consumers; that's very critical.

When we began the company, we did not have to spend energy or focus on an offline world. It's more an online world. And we saw technology and data as a way to build comparative advantage. So since the beginning, we saw ourselves as a technology company, not a bank—a technology company that happens to be in financial services. Therefore the culture itself uses data and analytics consistently for every single decision.

What our own foundation model has enabled is that the cost of putting a feature into a model has gone down significantly. Pre-AI, you had to spend six months adding a new feature. If you wanted to test a new feature in a model, you had to spend several weeks testing this feature, putting it in the model, testing around. With our own foundation model, you can test a number of different approaches much faster. The cost of doing a specific experiment has gone down significantly. Every decision in the organization can now be automated and done by a model versus a human. That's what AI is also enabling.

For us, AI let us do what we were already doing at a much more significant scale. But the culture itself already existed, since we saw this as a way to differentiate ourselves since the very beginning.

Global Financial System: Three Big Shifts

How do you think the global financial system will change the most, or needs to change the most, in the next 5 years, totally away from your business?

Shift 1: The End of Cash

The first one is kind of the end of cash. This is happening really everywhere. There are a lot of cash-heavy economies—Mexico for example, Indonesia, a lot of African countries, Brazil used to be like that—where cash will go away and will digitalize mostly through real-time payment systems.

Some implications are obvious: you don't need banking branches, or you need less. Some are less obvious: what happens to the economy, the efficiency of banks when they don't need banking branches, the speed at which money moves in the economy, the amount of data that gets created—that then can be used, for example, to provide access to credit.

Shift 2: Open Finance and Open Banking

The second one is open finance and open banking across the world. This is basically the concept that you, as a consumer, own all the data you have across all institutions, and you're able to grab that data and share it with anybody else.

One of the biggest sources of inertia in financial services—but also telecom, utilities—is that you have a history with a specific company and you cannot transfer that history with somebody else that comes new. Incumbents have benefited a lot from that inertia of data. The moment you can connect all your history from all your services and pass it to somebody else, you're reducing that inertia and enabling more competition for your data. You can monetize that data as a consumer.

Open banking is important because it will decrease that inertia globally and increase significant competition in banking. Banking today globally is still very much an oligopoly structure. You have five, six banks in the US that own 60, 70% of all the assets. Same in Europe, same in Asia, same in Latin America. So that will mean a less concentrated banking industry, much more fragmented, much more competition—which translates into less fees and less cost.

Shift 3: Crypto and Stablecoins

The other big trend is the role of crypto and stablecoins around the world. What will eventually happen with people that are much more mobile in nature is that you operate in a combination of the fiat system in your country with a global offshore system. Your life kind of goes in between without you even realizing. For a lot of countries, this is really important. You've seen with the usage of Bitcoin, stablecoins—increasingly people want to bank in the offshore system. They don't trust their banking system. They don't trust their fiat currency.

I would say today there are what, about 190 currencies around the world. My view is that 10, 20 years from now those 190 will be maybe 10, because the fiscal situation in so many countries is so dire that a lot of that fiat money is not real money—it's tokens, basically crypto tokens. Increasingly, billions of people are going to be banking on the offshore world, in US stablecoins but also Bitcoin and other types of assets. You see these two parallel systems interrelating with each other across the world.

The Dollar's Role in a World of Stablecoins

If you had to think about the US dollar and its importance—do you think the US dollar is the reserve currency 10 years from now? Is it one of a few?

There are two sides of that argument. I think US stablecoins ultimately will be the big savior, or one of the biggest saviors, of the US dollar, because they democratize access to the US dollar. And while the fiscal situation in the US is not great and is deteriorating fast, it's still better than the fiscal situation for the other 100-plus countries around the world. You look at the balance sheets of a lot of the central banks or countries in emerging markets, in Latin America—it's way scarier. You don't have the sovereign capabilities.

There's a lot of demand for US stablecoins. There's very little demand for a Brazilian stablecoin, unfortunately. So I think the fact that stablecoins exist for US dollars will ultimately mean that the US dollar maintains its power as a reserve currency for a very long time. But it won't be unique. You'll have maybe five, six fiat currencies that people will be saving in, and then a few crypto tokens where you'll be diversifying. I've always been a Bitcoin fan, and I think it plays a role in a diversified investment portfolio.

The Taco Stand: Why Cashlessness Unlocks Credit

What's the most surprising thing about the move away from cash?

The main one is what this means for credit markets for the majority of the world. Think about this situation: you have a taco stand in a corner in Mexico City, and you're buying and selling through cash. That transaction is not being recorded anywhere. That taco stand cannot get credit today.

Now, that person has a history where every day they go and sell tacos. There's a cash flow being generated, but nobody can underwrite on top of that. The moment that transaction goes into a digital ledger—that transaction happens digitally—then suddenly that taco seller can take that information to a bank and say: "Hey, look at my cash flow. Give me access to credit. If you give me access to credit, I can now have two taco stands, or I can have five taco stands."

The digitalization of the economy, and what that enables for credit for a significant percentage of the world population, is something that is not very well understood today and is a huge accelerant. You look at economies like Brazil, for example—something like 70% of all the employment in the country is still in small businesses, not big corporates. The same thing happens in India, or Southeast Asia. A lot of these small businesses historically also dealt with cash; now they're digitalized. So this is trillions of dollars of credit being enabled for billions of people around the world. This could be a significant economic shift for economic mobility across the world and is a very exciting opportunity.

Creating, Not Just Measuring, Creditworthiness

Do you think that you can create creditworthiness versus just predict or measure it, once you have all this data?

Yes, absolutely. The first thing you have to do is measure or record a lot of those transactions into a ledger—that's what the utilization of cash enables. Then with better algorithms (and this is where AI plays a role), and also with better products, you can enable people to start building that credit history.

I'll give you an example. We were the first credit card for 30 million people in Latin America. When we used to ask banks why so many didn't give access to credit, what we heard was: "People don't want credit. They don't want a credit card. They're scared about paying taxes, so they're never going to use the product."

But what really mattered was that what they were lacking was a product that matched their needs. We started, for a lot of people, with a product that had a first line of $20—a $20 credit line. When banks saw that product, they thought it was absurd. But in reality, people really appreciated that $20 was better than zero. Those $20 became $100, and the $100 became $1,000 over a period of time. You enable them to create a credit history through the right product. And then you enable an AI copilot for that customer that tells them all the different moves they need to make in terms of spending, investing, and savings to gain points and become more creditworthy. That's the concept of providing a coach to improve their ability to access credit and improve their financial picture.

How Transferable Is the Playbook Across Countries?

When you went to Mexico from Brazil, how much of the learning from Brazil was portable versus something distinctive about Mexico?

It's more exportable than we would have expected. The part that was less exportable: the biggest difference between Brazil and other countries was that Brazil was actually much more banked than unbanked. When we went to Mexico, a lot of the conversations we heard were: "Well, people in Mexico like cash. They don't believe in digital payments or credit cards or debit cards." That was initially, in the early years of Mexico, the biggest difference.

When you go from a banked country to an unbanked country, it's harder to compete. We're a shark in digital waters. When we are forced to compete in the offline world with banking branches, we're much less competitive. We don't have banking branches, we don't have ATMs. For a couple of years, it was harder for us to compete—even though we became the second largest bank in Mexico by now and the largest digital bank there. But as these countries digitalize—including Mexico—then the world starts looking closer to each other.

That's ultimately what you actually see across any other industry. You look at social media across the world—it's the same product. You look at Netflix, the same product. You look at Spotify, the same product. Uber, Amazon—generally the same product. Historically there were a lot of particularities, and cash was a specific one. The future looks much more homogeneous than the past, even for financial services.

Investing in Fintech: Dead or Just Reshaped?

If I force you to put your investor hat on, thinking about fintech at large… our mutual friend Mickey Malka said a couple years ago, "fintech is dead." How would you frame the opportunity?

I actually asked this question of Mickey last week because I saw him. He spends a lot of time in AI and investing in AI companies. I was like, "Are you done with fintech really?" And I like this answer, which is: no, we're not. We're just doubling down on the larger neobanks or neo-fintechs that are now riding the sweet spot between maintaining the ability to transform themselves through AI, but now have access to these moats of scale and data and brand and licenses.

He continues to be an investor of us. He continues to be an investor of a number of other startups. For the early entrants, I think it's going to be in areas that are less obvious as an entry path. It becomes a little bit harder, and you probably are applications on top of AI models. There'll be specific applications I think as an entry path, but building a consumer brand with hundreds of millions of customers at this stage—unless you come up with something completely fundamentally different—is going to be harder.

The US Launch and the Stablecoin Account

Can you talk about this big announcement that you just made and why you're so excited about it?

I think most people still identify Nubank as a Brazilian neobank or Latin American neobank, which is what we are. But when you go back in time and look at our seed deck in 2013 and the way we thought about the opportunity—there's nothing specific about Brazil or Latin America about the thesis. The thesis really is that global retail banking will be transformed by digitally native companies, because digital-native companies can solve the problems financial services have better—the cost, the access, and the intelligence.

We're excited about this announcement as we launch the US as a market, and we also announced launching to upwards of 35 different countries a stablecoin-backed account. This is the beginning of continuing to play this thesis—a global thesis in nature. We think about our past 13 years as proving this model in Latin America. We're now the largest private financial institution in the entire continent. We have the highest Net Promoter Score, from a profitability perspective, and the highest return on equity in a country like Brazil. So we did all the checks, and now is a moment to continue executing this multi-decade vision of taking this model global.

The US is obviously a very competitive market—the biggest market in the world. There are a lot of very strong neobanks and fintechs that will be coming to compete. But in reality, it's a market that's still dominated by big incumbent banks. While there are a lot of fintechs, the market is still dominated by a few incumbent banks and some community banks. Most banking in the US is still happening through banking branches—as if most of the video and media were happening through Blockbusters. They still need to charge a lot and pay zero yield effectively to fund this physical infrastructure. There are a lot of comparative advantages we bring to bear—our ability to do credit for the mass market, our ability to do payments globally (something we also announced with the feature)—and the ability to really make customers fanatically happy, to build a consumer-obsessed culture in an environment and industry where customers just don't really care about their banking relationships.

What do you think is going to be the hardest part about competing in the US?

Building a very strong brand will be one of the hardest things. US consumers mention brand as one of the key attributes to choose banks. We want to do it in a way that is smarter and more capital-efficient than simply coming in and investing a ton of marketing all over the place. Building an organic brand in an environment where there are so many strong banking brands might be one of the most difficult challenges—and it's critical to build trust with consumers because we want to become their primary bank account. That's what we aspire to do.

The Financial Metrics That Matter

If I had every buy-side analyst that covers Nubank here, is ROE the metric you'd point them to?

Obviously, growth of number of customers, Net Promoter Score, and cost to acquire that customer. When you look at figuring out: have you hit a vein, are you growing in a way where you found an underserved market and you're able to offer a product that nobody else was able to offer—that is the key. Number of users, NPS. But then: are you doing it at a sustainable pace? Because you can buy your way into growth by spending a lot of money on marketing. So what is the equation there? What is your LTV to CAC? And ultimately: what is your return on equity?

Return on equity exemplifies the advantages that the business model could have when you compare us with the big incumbent banks in the countries we operate in. We don't charge a lot of fees. We literally charge no fee. So we have less revenue, but then we end up with a return on equity that is two to three times their return on equity. That basically means you found a cost structure advantage. You found a way to offer a product at better quality at a much lower cost. And if you find that generally through technology, then you've found yourself a moat.

Talking about the US—what's one of the most interesting, least appreciated aspects is that by now, some of the US incumbent banks have higher return on equity and are more profitable than emerging market banks that we compete with. That means: your margin is my opportunity—the typical Amazon view or Bezos view. That incredible ROE that even incumbent banks have, even on top of the huge amount of cost they use to provide the product, means there is significant opportunity to undercut.

Influences: Amazon and the Magic of Disney

Who are your biggest influences?

We began the company as a reaction to a consumer pain—me realizing how bad consumer banking in Brazil was and how painful it was, and then realizing that this was a proxy for what the majority of the country was feeling. We've always admired companies that are very consumer-obsessed, that know that to win they need to be able to offer the best product and best service in a way that creates almost fanaticism.

From that perspective, we were very inspired by Amazon since the very beginning—Amazon being the more traditional consumer-obsessed company and how they built this consumer obsession.

We studied Disney very carefully, because this is a company that wants to create magic experiences. Maybe it's not super obvious, but even in banking, a boring banking product, we want to create a magical experience for customers.

What did you learn from Disney? That's an interesting one.

The communication they create with consumers, and simply the magic aspect of it. When you enter a Disney park, the setup of that entry path—it's almost like you're entering into a kingdom. The service you get from everybody that works inside Disney, how they treat young children, the spectacles they create, the fireworks—they're really thinking about how to create a product that is magical in nature. That's something we push our teams on: how do you, for something as boring as potentially sending money, how do you create a magic experience out of that?

The welcome kit we're sending to our customers here in the US—when they receive that welcome kit of the first credit card or the first debit card—we're trying to create a magical experience in that moment. We're very inspired by that.

The Hard Part of "Customer Obsession"

The customer obsession thing sounds obvious. What are the tradeoffs?

The hard part—as with any cultural value—is to do what you say you do. You see it in any company that has very nice-sounding values on the wall; then the question is: are they actually executing on that, especially when it's inconvenient? Most companies will be consumer-obsessed, but then when they are suddenly seeing themselves making more money because they invented a new fee—"oh well, maybe I'm less consumer-obsessed here and I want to make a little bit more money"—then you start prioritizing the short term versus the long term.

Actually, in the entire AI debate, you don't hear that much conversation about customers, because there is so much energy and focus around how do you use AI for efficiency and optimization. There is much less conversation about consumer obsession, and this is where humans still are beating the AI. The biggest complexity is actually prioritizing this value even when it's inconvenient to do so—especially from a financial perspective. But also, the AI bro, the tech bro, is much more enamored today with the technology versus the consumer experience itself.

Agents as a Customer Segment

Do you think there's a world where it actually matters that you're marketing to agents more than to humans?

I think agents become a customer segment, as important as consumers as a segment. You have to provide a product for the agent, you have to market to the agent, you have to do SEO for the agent. It's weird—it's the same way we have an under-18 segment, we have a small-business segment. This is an entire segment, and we're treating it as a segment. We have a team dedicated to understanding that segment and understanding the needs of that consumer—which is the agent.

That will be equally important. But I don't think it's going to be necessarily 100% of that decision, because specifically in banking (this might be different in other segments)—in banking you go back to trust and branding. The human will want to know where your life savings are deposited. There is the human aspect of that. So you're still marketing to the human and still building the trust with the human. You've got to do both.

For some products, there'll be more delegation; for others, less. Specifically for areas like Brazil, where we have 65% of the entire country as a customer, we have the opportunity to be that agent to the consumer—the customer is coming directly to our app and asking our agent for support with financial products. And we can do it in a way where it's actually an open agent: it even provides products from third-party banks and third-party financial institutions. So there'll be a mix.

That creates the opportunity, for example, for larger spans of control, fewer managers, much more visibility. I personally went from having 1 direct report to 20 direct reports over that period.

Oh wow.

Because it just increases your ability to operate horizontally. Fewer layers in the organization. We went from 10 layers to 5. The organization went very horizontal. This is a bolt of adrenaline to the organization as well in terms of our ability to execute.

Flattening the Pyramid: What Changed Tactically?

Can you say more about what made that possible? What was happening at 1 direct report and 10 layers, and then now what's happening at 20 and 5?

I think this is partly AI-related, partly the way we manage our organization. For a period of time, as we started scaling significantly—we went from a million customers to 140 million—the organization just takes a little bit of inertia of itself and starts adding layers. Every fast-scaling organization goes through the same process, because you see things breaking all over the place; you have all these scaling and growth pains, and the easy answer when things are on fire is to just add managers to solve the fire immediately. By a natural organic process, we ended up very verticalized and we ended up with a structure that didn't give a lot of visibility.

Partly what AI creates is it allows you to take a step back and reinvent everything about your business. This was a catalyst for us to think about the way we were structured.

The Dictator's Dilemma and Ground Truth

Toby Lütke has talked about how he can basically just ask the company stuff and, because of AI, it can tell him stuff. The separation between him and ground truth based on data is gone. The dictator's dilemma: as someone gets more powerful at the top of an organization, it's harder for them to know what is real. How are you staying up to date?

Every part of that chain, there is a possibility for a message to get distorted. You get up a distorted vision by the time it navigates 10 different layers. Just simply by removing a lot of those layers, you are much closer to the ground truth. You reduce a lot of those layers by having information systems that have access to everything that's happening across the organization—a company brain that is proactive and reactive. It's actively sending me information about what we're doing, from changes in our AI transformation to how we're doing around launching certain products or metrics or features. You get directly to the ground truth.

Second, I think you also have to—it's more about a mentality of actively going directly to the people doing the work. It's very comfortable, as the organization takes its own shape, to respect the channels. You'll see this in bigger organizations: you cannot jump a manager and ask the question to somebody that's actually doing the work; there is a specific chain of command that needs to be respected. This is more related to traditional organizations.

Here, it's more my approach of being a CEO: no, I want to go talk to anybody if I have a question, and there is no respecting of a chain of command. Literally I'll go to whoever has the best information if I have a question, or we're going to problem-solve together if I see something that's not moving. So it's partly technology, partly culture and attitude of being willing to be deeply integrated into the organization.

AI as Olympic Coach: Reinventing HR

How do you think all of this will affect your company's ability to raise the overall average talent bar?

I think it's going to be transformational, and I'm surprised so few people have discussed how AI is going to reinvent HR in organizations. If you look at it today, for most organizations: your manager gives you feedback every six months, tells you what you're doing well, what you're not doing well. It generally has a lot of recency bias, so it's not really six months, it's like the last 30 days. Generally it's not very actionable—"you're doing this well, you're doing not; maybe you should do better."

Imagine that's the type of feedback you would be giving an Olympic athlete. That would be crazy. You would never be able to succeed. Olympic athletes are somebody that literally every day is being coached and provided potential feedback.

That is the opportunity AI is going to create for every single person in an organization: you have Olympic athlete-type coaching. What we're building at Nubank in our HR operations system is: literally every day, depending on where you are—if you're an engineer, designer, or product manager—daily you should be able to get feedback from the AI. Your AI copilot is reviewing your pull requests and telling you not only how you're using these tools, but how you could use them better. It's very actionable, very specific to what you're doing. If you're a designer, it's giving you feedback around how you're doing your job. If you're a manager—managers right now have very little information, especially if you're managing a lot of people. There is this sense that you have to be having one-on-ones with every single person in your week. Those one-on-ones tend to be very low-information-density interchanges. A manager that has access to all this information, this instrumentation, is now seeing real-time how every person in the team is actually doing.

Keeping Up With AI Personally

How do you stay up to speed on AI capabilities?

I need to time-box it every day. I get one hour to read the updates—it's like SportsCenter for business. I spend a lot of time on X; that's where you're seeing a lot of the development. I also have an agent that collates and summarizes a lot of the developments. I block specific time in my agenda to use these tools and to build products. That's something I hadn't done for a very long time. In an afternoon, I coded a non-custodial crypto app, for example—something we've discussed at Nubank for a very long time. I just kind of went in and did a project.

We ask all of our senior managers to build products every quarter on actual software and products, so that we are integrated and very aware of what's going on. I don't think necessarily the answer is that I should be spending 70% coding—there are better people that will be much more productive. But I think it's important for everybody in the organization to be actually not only reading but actively using the tools, to understand how fast the technology is going.

Motivation Over 13 Years

How has what motivates you to keep doing this changed over the course of the Nubank journey?

I'm motivated by impact—by making it count, by doing something where we're investing time and energy in something that has meaning. I went through a phase even with Nubank where I started thinking: is there more stuff that I should be doing beyond Nubank? I think all founders start on the company, the company has significant growth, and then you start asking: what else could I be doing?

Ultimately I went through to the other side of that analysis—for about a year or two years—realizing that there's nothing else I can imagine myself doing that could have more impact than taking Nubank from where it is today to making it 10x larger: going from three countries to 100 countries, from 100 million customers to a billion customers. What this means in terms of impacting financial services and billions of people around the world.

With that impact out there, there's impact internally too—how I can also understand myself through bigger and newer challenges and develop better as a leader to motivate an organization that has big ambitions. With big technology shifts like AI, you can either decide to stay behind or stay in front. This technology shift forces every organization to think: on which side of this disruption do I want to be? I find that I'm more of a wartime general than a peacetime general. When a disruption, a change in the world happens, it suddenly is a source of motivation. I get more on the offense; I get energized to continue to execute the mission.

Imposter Syndrome and the Founder/CEO Split

What's an example of understanding yourself better because of growth?

One of the questions I personally had, as I scaled the business, is: will we need to bring much more professional managers at some point? I didn't manage anybody before starting Nubank, and then suddenly found myself being the CEO of one of the largest banks in Latin America, asking myself: what does the organization need right now? Do we need to go and hire much more experienced managers?

And we did. We went and hired a lot of external talent, because I kind of concluded that I was going to need that. But also I quickly realized that actually that's not what the organization needed. What the organization needed was more of what I had already brought into it—this clear leadership, the motivation, the willingness to think really big and to dream very big, and get people excited about doing something that feels impossible at the beginning.

Once something clicks and says, "no, this is the right answer for me and for the organization," then I can continue to do what I'm doing with much more confidence. Especially when there are changes and shifts, there was always a little bit of a lateral question: am I pushing too hard? Am I asking too much from the team? Is this the right pace? And the answer, after 13 years of doing this and being a little bit more confident, is: yes, I'm pushing enough. It's my job to push very hard and to dream very big and to shoot very high. The organization will react and will push back if needed. But it's helpful to have somebody that is actively pushing the boundaries of what perhaps the company is ready to do.

What is the hardest part of doing that for a long period of time?

The imposter syndrome. It's fine to be a founder at the beginning, but then suddenly when you see yourself running a very large organization: am I the right person leading this organization? You have to, through some thinking and experiences and feedback, conclude an answer to that question for you at some point—and answer it definitively.

Maybe for some reason you're not, but probably you are. That doesn't mean the founder will have all the answers and all the skills. You will need to continue bringing people with complementary skills. But at least for me, it was surpassing that phase of having a voice in the head thinking: "yeah, are you the right CEO for the business?"

Founder vs CEO: Two Different Functions

Making the shape between founder and CEO—because generally you will see founders having both titles, but they're very different functions. The founder and the CEO are very different functions. They don't necessarily fit with each other.

What's the key energy of each?

The founder is impatient. The founder has a huge amount of sense of urgency. The founder will want to go run very, very fast, will move extremely fast.

The CEO will need to be more patient. The CEO will need to be more systematic in how it makes decisions, will have to bring generally much more systems thinking into scaling the organization.

Sometimes those things collide. You have to be impatient on one end, patient on the other. There might be conflicts in that nature.

Generally you would think that CEOs are better managers. Founders don't tend to be good managers. Founders don't have a lot of patience or willingness to do one-on-ones and sit down and provide coaching. They just want to run. A lot of the time they tend to be much more ICs—individual contributors than managers. CEOs tend to be better managers because you have to build systems, think from a system perspective.

For me, the key has been to realize that the CEO title itself and the founder title you can redesign in different ways. Being able to do both, having a little bit more patience when you need it—but generally you want to maintain more the founder than the CEO. That's why founder-led companies continue to outperform for decades. If you have to choose, you choose more the founder than the CEO mode, especially in environments where there are big technology shifts, where a lot of the advantages—the assets—of the founder come to bear and are more obvious than those of the CEO.

Low-Confidence Moments

What was your lowest-confidence moment personally in the entire history of the business?

Scaling a business is hard because you're consistently making decisions about situations that you don't really know. For example, I wasn't—I wanted to build a technology company, but I was not an engineer myself. So I needed to go and hire great CTOs and build a great technology organization. How did I know how to pick a great CTO at that point, if I didn't have the experience or credit? There is a lot of financial services and credit expertise specific to the field. There was a lot of questioning inside internally about a lot of the decisions I made about building the team—like, "do we need to bring somebody with more experience from a big bank or a big organization to run the organization?"

I wouldn't highlight one specific moment. I would say for a period of time, it is this imposter syndrome that is asking you a question: as the organization takes its own shape, "are you the right driver of the car as the car becomes more complex and goes faster and faster and faster?"

The Most Emotional Moment

What was the most emotional moment in the history of the business for you?

Passing a number of different incumbent banks in Brazil was very emotional, because for 10 years all we heard again and again, especially from local experts, was that it was impossible to compete, that we were going to get crushed, that we were going to die, that these were the most trusted brands in the ecosystem and we had no shot at being successful. So one day becoming bigger than some of them—becoming the largest private bank in the entire country—was something incredible, and that was emotional in terms of what we were able to achieve from a point of scale.

Me personally, I was born in Colombia and I had to leave Colombia when I was eight because of the security situation. I had to move to Costa Rica, and Colombia was then our country number three. The moment I was able to launch Nubank in Colombia—which we did in a big event with the president of the country at the same time—was very emotional as well, because it was a bit of coming back home and delivering a product and a service that I thought was going to be very great for the country, in an environment where I was being received by my people. It was videocast and there were 100,000 people connected to the launch of Nubank in Colombia. It was very emotional, very exciting.

Defining Great Leadership

How would you define great leadership? Especially the subtle points of what defines a great leader?

First is vision. You have to be able to see something that few people see—a vision of a world that is not as obvious right now. With the massive information overload we all live in, it's increasingly harder to have a differentiated point of view about something, about your industry, your company, how things are going to move. So you have to have some kind of vision about the future that is differentiated.

But then you have to be able to sell that vision—and selling is about inspiring people. A lot of the time that vision will be very hard or almost feel impossible. The natural reaction of most people when they are presented with an impossible vision is to push back and declare it non-realistic. This phrase: "it's not realistic that this is going to happen." What is "not realistic"? Look at every single meaningful development in the history of the world—at some point it was defined by somebody to be non-realistic. What's funny is the amount of confidence that a lot of the experts use when they say "it's not realistic." So you have to be able to sell that vision in a way that gets a lot of people motivated and drives following.

But then you have to be able to be a good listener and understand that sometimes you're actually going to be wrong. That vision that you have might not be fully complete.

There are two different modes. One mode: you go against consensus and completely declare consensus as wrong, and you are the complete revolutionary—nothing about the consensus makes any sense and you will reinvent absolutely everything. The other mode: you are consumed by consensus. You think about progress as being non-realistic, and things will be the way they are today.

What's hard about a great leader is: you navigate in the middle. Consensus or status quo exists because, think about it from an evolutionary perspective—that vision of the world competed with other visions and it won. So the world we see today was superior to other possible worlds. There are elements of that status quo that exist because of a reason. You have to be able to understand what those elements are and that they will continue to be here. But also you have to be able to fight that conventional wisdom to see what are the elements that need to be changed.

Leadership is about knowing what doesn't have to change, and pushing to change the things that have to change. That's a combination of conviction but also active listening and humility, to know that you might not have all the answers and that you're going to need to change actively when you do that.

The Five-Year Bear and Bull Case

If we think over the next five years for Nubank specifically, I'd love you to paint the bear case for the business and then the best possible story.

Bear Case

We are in these three countries in Latin America. We've saturated them completely, and growth declines. We haven't really been able to find any other growth alternatives from a customer perspective. We have 65% of Brazil. Very soon we're going to run out of Brazilians. Ideally we would see the natality rate in Brazil—Koreans having more children—but that's not happening. So we're going to run out of Brazilians, and we did not succeed internationalizing. We ended up being restricted to these three countries and growth saturated. Partly that would also mean we could not take advantage of a lot of the AI opportunities that enables—and that's one reason we were not able to internationalize.

Bull Case

The bull case is the opposite: we truly took advantage of this thesis around how much market share is going to be transferred from incumbent banks to digital-native companies over the next two to three decades, and how that is going to be accelerated by technology shifts like real-time payment systems, open finance, and AI. We rode those tailwinds, and we were able to execute, through a multi-country platform, a global vision of Nubank taking us to 100-plus countries over the next few decades. We were able to solve a lot of these big problems that we still think will be solved. Three billion people don't have access to credit; cash is becoming digital; more people need access to banking. If we have this cost-structure advantage versus our competitors—versus the industry players that still own 90% of the $10 trillion profit pool—if we have a cost structure that is 50x theirs (and this is pre-AI), that meant we were able to pass a lot of the efficiency back to the customer via higher yields, lower fees, better experience, fully digitalized, integrating advice in our products—and truly take advantage of this internationalization opportunity.

Closing Lesson: The Founder's Non-Transferable Care

When I had you last time 5 years ago, I already asked you my traditional closing question, so I have a different one for you today. What is the most interesting lesson you've learned about entrepreneurship?

Now, I would say: how to quickly ignore the imposter syndrome. And the fact that you are the person that had the vision and the energy to build something out of nothing—to give birth—means that already is giving you a level of care for that company so high that it will make you become the right leader for a very long time.

I don't think anybody in the world cares as much for this company as I do—to a level that is almost visible. You're a father, you have children. Nobody will ever care so much about this company, about this company being successful, than I will. And that will make you put so much energy and focus to make it successful, to the point that ultimately is what is going to make you be the right leader for the organization for a very long time—independently of your expertise or your knowledge or whether you have the right experience. Just that insight, just that energy will make you the right person.

I find this so interesting. It seems like you could decompose that into: have more faith in yourself, and be really picky about the vision you want to go work on. Because if it's not something that's coming deep from your heart, from your gut, you won't get the benefit of this thing you just laid out. Do you think those are the right two parts of that insight?

[snorts] Yeah. Especially the second part you mentioned, around the mission. It's a luxury and a blessing to find a mission that you truly are excited about, because then that will really make you go the long way. Scaling a company won't be easy. It will be much more painful than anybody anticipates. If you don't have the level of conviction for the mission, it will be just harder to go.

How would you encourage other people to do a good job on that search? If someone's searching for a mission, any advice or any sign that they've got the right one?

I think there is a level of serendipity there, and luck—a level of search, of listening carefully, of feeling that this is a project, this is a problem that you truly care about. This is something that if you really care about, you are not sleeping because you're thinking about it. You cannot imagine your life continuing if you do not decide to tackle it.

And I think AI makes it harder, not easier, because the bar to start a company is now so much easier. You will probably just go and pursue problems that are easier to solve ultimately. That's why some of the best founders we're seeing right now are going for the impossible truly. There is this shift now into hardware and space and things that seem completely impossible, because you're looking actively for those opportunities that will be harder and unique to you—that you're going to get to believe that only you can really solve.

Incredible place to close. What an awesome closing thought. Thank you as always so much for your time.

Thank you so much, Patrick. It was awesome.

[Outro — Sponsor rolls:]

You know how small advantages compound over time? That's true in investing and just as true in how you run your company. Your spending system is your capital allocation strategy. ## 一、藏在"零利率存款"里的6000亿美元——一场看不见的全民财富税
David 顺口抛出一个数字，但它值得停下来凝视：美国零售存款约15万亿美元，银行平均只付40个基点利息，而无风险利率4.5%。差值×本金≈**6000亿美元/年**。
这是一个什么量级的概念？——它接近美国国防预算的 **65%**，相当于全体美国人每年**自愿**为"街角那座大理石分行建筑"交的一笔税。但没人把它记在T-账单上，因为它从未从你的账户划出去，它只是**没有进来**。
行为经济学家 Gabaix 和 Laibson 把这种现象叫做 **"shrouded attributes"（遮蔽属性）**——消费者看不见的成本。保险的隐性佣金、墨盒的后续更换费、酒店的 resort fee 都是同一个家族。David 的真正发现不是"分行贵"，而是：**整个传统银行业的商业模式本质上是一座遮蔽属性工厂**。Nubank 的攻击点不是技术，是让这笔税**从黑暗中走出来**。

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：这档节目本身就是"AI 泡沫论"的最佳反证

节目主持人花了大段时间质疑 OpenAI 的收入缺口、嘲笑"小普京智能体"是媒体表演、断言"我们不会很快进入 AGI 时代"——然而就在同一期节目里，Justin Drake 发出的警报恰恰来自 OpenAI 发布的 700+ 篇 AI 生成的数学证明。这是一个让人脊背发凉的分裂图景：同一批 AI，在业务层面被嫌弃"只是 midwit AGI"，却在数学层面已经逼近到让密码学家公开喊"进入掩体模式"。

这揭示了一个被普遍忽视的系统性真相：AI 的能力分布是极度非线性的。 它在"替代白领工作"这个维度上确实平庸（因此 OpenAI 收入不及预期），但在"求解结构化形式系统"这个维度上，它可能已经悄然越过某条红线。市场在根据前者定价 AI 股票，却用后者的进展威胁所有加密资产——这是人类历史上第一次，一项技术的"商业失败"和"存在性威胁"在同一周被同时报道。

二、一个几乎没人指出的跨领域连接：Flock 摄像头、Ledger 硬件植入、量子密码学——它们是同一个问题

节目开头讨论 Flock 摄像头的宪法问题（"持续全景监控 ≠ 零散目击"），中间讨论 Ledger 供应链被植入硬件后门，结尾讨论量子/AI 可能破解 ECDSA。这三件事在表面上风马牛不相及，但它们本质上是同一个范式转移：

"离散的信任假设"正在被"连续的攻击面"吞没。

  • 第四修正案假设搜查是"离散事件"——Flock 把它变成了连续记录。
  • 硬件钱包的安全模型假设供应链是"离散的信任节点"——Ledger 事件证明攻击者可以买下整条链路。
  • 加密货币假设私钥的数学困难是"离散的、几乎不可能的事件"——AI 把它变成一个被持续逼近的连续优化问题。

人类所有的制度（法律、金融、密码学）都建立在"攻击是罕见、离散、可追责的"这个前提上。而我们正在进入一个所有攻击都变成"持续背景辐射"的时代。 这就是为什么 Chris 本能地呼唤"中介机构回归"——他其实是在无意识地呼唤用离散的责任主体，去对冲连续的攻击面。这是比"去中心化 vs 中心化"更深层的权衡。

三、一个让人意外的政治-金融预言：年龄正在取代意识形态成为新的政治光谱——而加密货币是第一个"按年龄分化"的资产

Austin 关于"法国退休金领取者的净收入高于 30 岁工作者"的观察，被他自己放在"代际政治"的框架里，但他没有看出一个更深的联系：

加密货币是人类历史上第一个在诞生之初就按出生年份而非收入/阶级分化持有的大类资产。 传统的"右翼 vs 左翼"框架在加密货币上失效了——Trump 和 Mamdani 的支持者在加密货币态度上的相似度，可能高于 Trump 和他自己党内老年参议员的相似度。

跨领域的联想：这与 1848 年欧洲革命前夜的情况惊人地相似。 当时的政治光谱也在从"贵族 vs 平民"向"工业资本 vs 工业劳工"转移，期间存在十年左右的"政党找不到自己选民"的真空期。我们现在可能正处于类似的"政治参照系切换"的真空期——两党都还在用右/左的坐标，但真正的断层线是出生年份。

延伸出的"啊哈时刻"： 如果年龄取代意识形态成为新光谱，那么 Chris 口中"稳定币和代币化带来的机构采用"将遇到一个未被定价的风险——那些做出代币化决策的机构 CEO 的平均年龄（60+），与真正会使用这些产品的用户的平均年龄（25-35），正好横跨这条新的政治断层线。 Franklin Templeton 的 Jenny Johnson 在 2018 年"全押"加密货币需要巨大勇气，但更大的勇气是：她的客户群体（退休基金、保险账户）正在被她的产品的用户群体（年轻散户）在政治上宣战。 这是一场即将到来的、机构尚未意识到的身份政治冲突。

📝 转录文本

开场：Flock 摄像头、AI 与第四修正案

Like the whole, hey, observing people in public is not a search thing was predicated around those being individual and discreet observations. Like the police saw you walk into the doughnut shop. That's fine. But flock cameras creating a comprehensive visual record of all public spaces at all times is the equivalent of following that person around. That is a very different sort of search than, oh, we were incidentally there and saw them.

Rahm, to your point, I feel like AI is posing a similar problem for the way the world is currently structured, which is nobody really thought about what if there's a device with all these connectors that has all of your context about all things. Like that is obviously much closer to somebody's papers and personal effects in like fourth or fifth amendment terms in the United States.

Yeah. Well, it's the classic trade-off between security and liberty. And people historically have traded away liberty for convenience and security.

OpenAI 的叙事焦虑与"中智 AGI"时代

So then OpenAI says, "Wait a minute, we've lost the narrative. Anthropic has faster revenue, better revenue growth. The best — like the technical staff at Anthropic — is the who's who of like the NBA dream team. It's incredible what they've done."

So then we have this incident where these agents run amuck and HuggingFace, which is an open-source project that no one really cares about because it's open source. There's no one from Hugging Face coming out and talking about this. So it may also be that it's not so much, call it, moving the entire frontier — because that takes more and more and more parameters and ever more complex models — but instead starting to specialize the models for specific tasks and making them more agile. And this kind of goes back to what we saw with the development of the internet in general, right? Like things start to fragment, things start to specialize. It's not the all-singing, all-dancing everything that wins.

分发 vs 平台 vs 应用

I see in that last set of comments you're able to channel Rahm and say something about OpenAI, and had a deference to him. But look, I'm not as down on OpenAI as you guys are apparently.

Well, my point is: do I see worlds in which they succeed? Yes. I think what's understated is I also see plenty of worlds in which they fail. Go back and look at the 90s at all the big tech names and how many made it to today, right?

Yeah.

Not a comment specific to OpenAI. It's just hard to predict the distribution of future outcomes.

Yeah. But value does accrue to applications, and those applications that win, win win. And so it's still early. We'll see what happens.

That's true, but a lot of that's distribution.

All right. So on that note —

Wait, Austin, but they have distribution.

Do they?

How does OpenAI not have distribution? How many users do they have?

I mean, they have an app and they have tens of millions of users. I agree with that level, but that is a disruptable level of users. They are not like Apple, which has billions of users locked in.

That's fair.

Yeah. And — yep, 100%. And they were quick to start disrupting Google when they came out. I remember all of a sudden I started using ChatGPT instead of Google and I was like, wait a second. You're right. This stuff can move quickly in either direction.

And what are we seeing from a value perspective? Distribution. Distribution rules. Like as time marches forward, I think more value is being accrued to distribution more and more every single day. Like if you've got distribution, it's valuable.

Agree.

收尾

All right. So on that note, thank you for joining us for this episode of Bits and Bips. Stay right here. Laura's up next on Unchained with Lorenzo Valente of ARK Invest. They're going to be digging into AI agents and quantum computing further, and what it means for the chains, crypto, run-on, and whether Ethereum is pricing its settlement layer right. So —

There goes the neighborhood with Lorenzo, friend of the show. We got to get him back on.

No, it's going to be an interesting one. All right, everybody. Enjoy. Please subscribe to our channels and we'll see you next week.

Thank you for watching and hope you enjoyed this episode of Bits and Bips. Just remember, nothing we say here is investment advice and please check unchainedcrypto.com/bitsandbips for more disclosures.

## 一、最反直觉的观察：这档节目本身就是"AI 泡沫论"的最佳反证
节目主持人花了大段时间质疑 OpenAI 的收入缺口、嘲笑"小普京智能体"是媒体表演、断言"我们不会很快进入 AGI 时代"——然而就在同一期节目里，Justin Drake 发出的警报恰恰来自 OpenAI 发布的 **700+ 篇 AI 生成的数学证明**。这是一个让人脊背发凉的分裂图景：**同一批 AI，在业务层面被嫌弃"只是 midwit AGI"，却在数学层面已经逼近到让密码学家公开喊"进入掩体模式"。**
这揭示了一个被普遍忽视的系统性真相：**AI 的能力分布是极度非线性的。** 它在"替代白领工作"这个维度上确实平庸（因此 OpenAI 收入不及预期），但在"求解结构化形式系统"这个维度上，它可能已经悄然越过某条红线。市场在根据前者定价 AI 股票，却用后者的进展威胁所有加密资产——**这是人类历史上第一次，一项技术的"商业失败"和"存在性威胁"在同一周被同时报道。**
## 二、一个几乎没人指出的跨领域连接：Flock 摄像头、Ledger 硬件植入、量子密码学——它们是同一个问题

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"心脏病只能用黄金治愈"——一种被武器化的自我觉知

最反直觉的一点是：Cortez 并没有伪装自己。他直接对蒙特祖玛的使者说"我和我的部下患了一种心脏病，只有黄金才能治愈"。这不是忏悔，而是把贪婪升格为生理必然性的话术——一旦被定义为"病"，就无需论证其正当性。

真正的殖民者不是伪君子，而是双账本的会计师：对上帝那本账记"推倒偶像、拯救灵魂"，对自己那本账记"黄金和封地"。这两本账不互相矛盾，而是互相免税。宗教给予绝对权，贪婪提供执行力，二者在同一具肉身里完成了精妙的套利——这种"道德套利"至今仍是所有扩张型组织（传教团、风险投资、ESG 包装的大宗商品交易）的底层操作系统。

二、Extremadura 的秘密：一种"创始人密度"现象

一个被访谈低估的细节：绝大多数征服者来自西班牙西部的 Extremadura——一个贫瘠、尘土飞扬、几乎长不出粮食的地区。这不是巧合，而是一种地理 × 阶层 × 时机的三元共振：土地差到不足以留住人，但又不至于饿死人；武力传统深（刚打完收复失地战争），但出头机会稀缺。

跨领域连接：这个结构与 17 世纪英国西南部的海盗村庄（Devon、Cornwall）、19 世纪旧金山周边的淘金者小镇、今天 PayPal Mafia 之于硅谷是同一个模板。全世界最具爆炸性的"冒险者密度"从不出现在最富或最穷的地区，而出现在"刚好能看到更广阔世界、又刚好被本地困住"的那条阶层悬崖上。Extremadura 不是西班牙的例外——它是人类"创始人工厂"的一个标准配置。

三、"岛屿征服启动效应"：为什么容易赢的人更敢赌不可能

访谈里被轻描淡写、但其实解释力极强的一环是：在抵达大陆之前，这些人先在加勒比岛屿上练过手——波多黎各、伊斯帕尼奥拉、古巴，那里的原住民缺乏统一政权和军事技术，征服几乎毫无阻力。于是他们形成了一个灾难性的归纳推理：岛上这么容易，大陆也差不多。

这是一种被阶梯式小胜训练出的尺度盲视——它在心理学上和"连续小盈利的赌徒最终 all-in"、"连续融资成功的创业者押上公司最后账户"、"连续小仗胜利的拿破仑进军俄国"是同一个神经通路。有趣之处在于：这种盲视绝大多数时候是致命的——但在极少数情况下（阿兹特克那套依赖奇幻宇宙观和盟邦摇摆的脆弱帝国正好撞上），它反而成为唯一敢做出不可能之事的心理条件。

换言之，我们记住的所有"百人征服千万"的奇迹，背后都站着成千上万个被同样心理驱动、却死在无人知晓的滩头的失败者。幸存者偏差才是征服史的真正建筑师。

四、一个被你听漏的反向凝视

最后一个几乎没人注意的瞬间：当地人形容西班牙人在看到黄金时"像猴子一样叽叽喳喳"。这是一句被低估的人类学观察——在阿兹特克的宇宙观里，玉和黑曜石才是真正的神圣物质，黄金只是装饰性软金属。所谓的"文明征服野蛮"，在当地人眼里完全是另一个版本：一群衣衫褴褛的异乡人为了一种本地人并不特别珍视的闪亮金属而发狂。

这里的洞见是：技术优越性是一个事后编写的叙事。真正发生的是两套价值系统的相遇，其中一方愿意为对方视为"软金属"的东西付出任何代价——而这种非对称的狂热本身就是一种战略资源。谁对对方不在乎的东西更饥饿，谁就在交易中获得了初始杠杆。这个结构，今天依然在稀土、芯片、数据和注意力的全球博弈里反复上演。

📝 转录文本

开场：一个令人困惑的历史画面

So in retrospect you have these outrageous battles with, you know, thousands of debts on one side and zero deaths on the other side. Um, but my understanding is this came as a surprise to the conquistadors as well. And so how, how were some hundred odd men willing to go confront an empire of 10 million people and say your job is to take this over? You know, it would be sort of like dropping a 100 Marines into into like 18th century England and being like, "Okay, you better come out the other end with with control over Parliament." It just how how is this a thing that they were willing to do?

推力与拉力：Extremadura 的贫瘠与新世界的诱惑

The the kind of classic push-pull factors, right?

They came from a proud land, a new country, Spain come together in 1492. Um, and they were aware their history was one of of struggle um uniting the peninsula and and and consuming the Reconquista. So they had a proud warrior background but little to show for it really.

Um, again, the the quality of life particularly in Extremadura — which is the the province in Spain where so many of these conquistadors originated from — was a land of hardship. Was small farms and and and dusty terrain and unproductive, and they were aware of a wider world around them. And as like so many men have throughout history, um, they see their only path forward as being anything more than dirt farmers is to seek a career of high-risk and potential even fatal outcomes but possible great reward as well.

Right? Men have have joined armies, militaries, fought in campaigns, not even their own, even other peoples' — for for many centuries, millennia now — for for that reason. And the attraction of of the new world, right, once they're aware that out there is a whole new land where it's possible for even a small man like myself to become something, to become somebody. All I have as an asset is is my fighting skills. And yeah, I could keep fighting in the campaigns against the Moors or against the Turks, but um those are high-risk, low-return ventures. Yeah, I'll be fighting in my home waters, but what will the potential rewards be? These Turks can fight, right?

The message I'm getting from the far side of the Atlantic is the the risks there are much lower and the potential rewards much higher. It means traveling across a vast ocean. It means essentially, uh, being very self-reliant and and falling in with men who are just as cutthroat as I am.

宗教的角色：信仰、恐惧与良心的"赎罪券"

How important is religion in the morale of these soldiers?

Because in retrospect, we're like, okay, they were able to take on huge armies, but they didn't know — they didn't even know that there was an empire there to take over. They didn't know where its capital was. They'd never seen it before. They knew nothing about what are the alliances that they need to maneuver, um, what are the size of the armies we need to face, what is the basic terrain and geography that we need to navigate. And so I'm still trying to understand how they gained the confidence, you and your couple hundred buddies, to go and take on a huge empire. Is… I don't know, but do they just think that God would make sure that they were okay? Yeah. How do I understand that?

Cortez and Pizarro both had, you know, men of the cloth traveling with their expeditions to provide for their spiritual needs.

Um, and and Cortez and Pizarro in retrospect would make a great deal of this in their writing, right? They were — they were professed to be outraged particularly by the Aztec cult of human sacrifice which was integral to to their society.

Um, I I don't see any reason why that would be untrue. I mean, it it would be shocking to actually see that happen. And Cortez — Moctezuma invited him to the top of one of the two great pyramids in Tenochtitlan. He remarks the priests were adorned from head to foot in black um um clay or or or body paint, and and the interior was was black with with spilled blood and it stank. Bomb.

So I don't see any reason why they wouldn't be genuinely mortified by that, and they they would take a certain degree of legitimacy from tearing down the ancient idols of these superstitious peoples and raising them up to the one true faith. You can salve your conscience in many ways by doing that — that in real terms I'm here for what's what I can take, but I am performing the will of God and therefore I have some absolution when I'm called to account at the end of the day.

So men will sometimes seek to find a higher purpose in what are very low endeavors, which is what was playing out at that time.

加勒比的"预热"：易胜如何塑造心理

Um, again, coming to the motivation — the initial conquests were relatively easy. The island populations in the Caribbean, what we now call Puerto Rico and and Hispaniola, um, Cuba — the peoples there were were quite low on the tech tree, were not unified, did not have a significant military presence. Of course, on islands there's nowhere for them to run. Um, you could run into the mountains of Cuba, but eventually they would all all all be hunted down.

So the feeling was: the pickings here are pretty easy, and the enthusiastic attitude was, well, why would it be any different in the mainland?

Of course, they did run up against heavy fighting. And some of them would say afterwards — the veterans of wars against the Turks — this was some of the hardest fighting I I've ever I've ever been through. Um, but by that point, they'd seen that the potential reward was much higher as well.

抵达特斯科科湖：亚特兰蒂斯般的震撼

When they arrived at Lake Texcoco, they would marvel as if we had just arrived in Atlantis, right? To be in this place on this lake with these cities arranged around its edges, and the biggest city of all appeared to be floating on the water like Venice — except even more dramatic, with its high temples.

Um, to them, this this both awed them and inflamed that that greed that they had.

"心脏病只能用黄金治愈"：Cortez 的自白

And Cortez himself admitted as much to Moctezuma's own voice. He he said:

My men and I suffer from a disease of the heart that only gold can cure.

So Moctezuma sent him feathered headdresses and all the the traditional regalia. He sent him jade and obsidian, which in the Aztec world would have been symbols of great regard. And Cortez was happy to put on the headdress and he sent it back to the king. But the little trinkets of gold that he was getting, right — that was was the real, uh, end purpose.

And the local peoples would would talk about how the the Spanish were were chattering like monkeys as they were were picking up these gold and were fascinated by it.

Yeah.

结尾

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.
