item.title: [All-In Podcast] Martin Shkreli: Big Pharma's Blind Spot, Betting Against Quantum & What Prison Taught Him
item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、Shkreli 其实在做同一笔生意——只是标的从分子换成了"量子叙事"

表面看，Shkreli 的人生有两条平行线：曾经在制药市场"低价扫货高价转卖"分子，如今在二级市场做空量子公司。但如果把两件事叠在一起看，你会发现这根本是同一个套利模型：他专门狙击"叙事资本 ≫ 数理资本"的错配。

  • 当年辉瑞把一个值十亿的分子按一百万美金卖出，是因为大药厂的内部估值模型里，这颗分子被归入"睡眠市场" ——他做的是把分子从错误的叙事抽屉里拿出来。
  • 今天 IBM/Google 的量子机器被塞进"下一代计算"的叙事抽屉里，但 Shor 算法只是一个 polynomial-time 的魔术，而不是通用加速器。他做的还是同一件事——把标的从错误的抽屉里拎出来。

出人意料的观察是：他本质上不是"做空者"也不是"涨价者"，而是一个叙事抽屉套利者。这解释了为什么他的名声和他的 P&L 看起来总是正交的。

二、Peter Shor 与 Shkreli 共享同一种"压缩"美学——这才是全场最隐秘的跨领域连接

Shor 算法真正惊人的地方不是"更快"，而是把一个指数时间问题压缩成多项式时间。这是一次量级的塌缩。

而 Shkreli 对 FDA 审批生态做的事情，是把一个20年、20亿美金的新药开发曲线，压缩成"买断-重新定位-再临床"的两三年价值释放路径（Sparsentan 从 Bristol 的"高血压睡眠药"被重新贴标成 FSGS 的孤儿药）。

两者都是在找一种"相位的改变"而非能量的改变——不是把事情做得更快，而是把事情放到一个让它天然变快的空间里（量子态 vs 孤儿药适应症）。这或许也解释了他对 Analog Optical Computing 的痴迷：光里的矩阵乘法"happen in instant time"，这是又一次介质替换。他真正着迷的，不是量子、不是光、不是药——是介质套利本身。

跨领域连接：介质套利 = Shor 算法 = 孤儿药再定位 = 光学 matmul。他的大脑运作的只是一个母题。

三、他把 Dario 的病症讲清楚了，却忘了自己蹲过同样的监狱

全场最黑色幽默的瞬间，是他近乎脱口说出："I had a hard time admitting I was not the best hedge fund manager in the world... That simple refusal to admit put me in prison."

然后几分钟后，他用近乎一模一样的框架攻击 Dario：fear-mongering 的本质是"nerd 不知道怎么面对聚光灯，于是把自己正在做的东西包装成末日级别"。

有意思的是，这其实是 Shkreli 对自己 2015 年那场定价事件的无意识注解——他当年把 Daraprim 涨价 5000%，官方理由是"研发再投入"，但他自己后来承认那是在扮演"最锋利的交易员"。他和 Dario 做的其实是同构的事： - Dario 用"AI 可能毁灭世界"来放大 Anthropic 的叙事权重； - 当年的 Shkreli 用"价格 5000%"来放大一个边缘药企的叙事权重。

两者都是用极端剂量换取公众注意力的仓位。他能看穿 Dario，是因为他已经付过这张账单。真正值钱的，不是他对量子的判断，而是他正在无意间演示的一条规律：金融市场、制药市场、AI 叙事市场，三者的"注意力贴现曲线"是同一条。

四、意外的身份谜题：他是全场唯一的"nerd × jock 双栖者"

他在节目里顺口说了一句"I was a little bit of both"（既是书呆子又是运动员），没人追问，但这可能是解释他全部定价能力的那把钥匙。

  • 纯 nerd 的量子批评家（如 Scott Aaronson）——有技术判断力，没有叙事杀伤力；
  • 纯 jock 的做空者（典型华尔街人格）——有叙事杀伤力，没有技术判断力；
  • 双栖者 Shkreli——既能和 Chelsea 讨论 ECDLP 问题，又能在推特上把一家公司打到跌停。

这是一个在当代极其罕见的组合，因为教育系统倾向于单栖分化。你偶尔会在物理学家兼期权交易员、医生兼风投合伙人身上看到类似的现象，但他们通常温和得多。Shkreli 把这种双栖性调到了反社会档位——这既是他赚钱的护城河，也是他进监狱的原因。

一句令人意外的推论：监狱并没有驯化他，只是让他第一次意识到自己的双栖身份本身是资产。这就是为什么他出来之后不再做对冲基金（jock 游戏），而是直接做个人账户 + 短量子 + 投光学计算（nerd 游戏加 jock 执行）——他终于把自己放到了对的介质里。又一次介质套利，这次标的是他自己。

📝 转录文本

Martin Shkreli on All-In Podcast — Formatted Transcript

Cold Open: The Reputation

"He's been called the most hated man in America because he jacked up the cost of a life-saving drug — raised the price of a life-saving drug 5,000%. He became the poster child for capitalistic greed."

Martin Shkreli (archival): "Seven years in prison. We definitely plan on raising the price, that's for sure. You can be prosecuted for not maximizing profit, and you have to do everything in your power to make as much money as possible. And if I'm the enemy for you — good. I'm happy, man. I'm fulfilling some need in your life."

"...purchased the only copy of a legendary Wu-Tang Clan album with no immediate plans to play it."

Shkreli: "It's not a good record. Ego is the fountainhead of all progress."

Host: "Please welcome Martin Shkreli."

Welcome & Framing

Host: Welcome, Martin. Thanks for coming out. Shkreli: Nice to meet you. Host: You wore Brad's outfit today. Shkreli: Exactly.

Host: All right, welcome, Martin. We've got so many topics to go into with you, but I want to start with one. You've basically taken down quantum computing. You said you think this is a fraud — that people might be going to jail. So, two-part question:

  1. Give us your thesis on why this is a fraud, or a fugazi — a fugazi, whatever it is. Discredited? A discard.
  2. Your best advice for those CEOs when they do go to jail. You've got a little experience.

You don't seem to be the kind of guy who would thrive in prison, but from what I understand, Martin — you shot, you turned into Lex Luthor, and you were running the yard, I understand. So break us through the quantum trade, and best practices when you go to the hoosegow.

Chelsea, Scott Aaronson, and a Family Gene-Pool Swap

Shkreli: Yeah. So I have to shout out my wife, Chelsea. Chelsea — very few people know her, but she's, I think, a big deal in technology. She was one of the first people at OpenAI, and her father, believe it or not, was one of the first people at NVIDIA. In my family, I was one of the first people in prison. So I thought I'd switch the gene pool, you know — shift it over a little bit.

Chelsea studied at MIT and taught quantum computing with Scott Aaronson, the preeminent guy in quantum. Over many hours she penetrated my thick head on what exactly quantum computing even is.

What Quantum Computing Actually Is

Shkreli: A lot of people synonymize it with faster computing, which sounds great. That's really not what it is at all.

The whole field was invented because of Peter Shor's thought experiment. Peter considered this idea that there are kinds of algorithms you can run faster in different media. That was a revolutionary idea in computing — but it's not really a revolutionary idea for business, because (and this is my thesis) there's one algorithm that runs faster in a quantum computer.

So if you ask somebody which computer can sort a deck of cards — if anybody knows the famous algorithms book CLRS, the first five pages are about sorting algorithms like bubble sort and merge sort — I asked quantum fans, "Well, which one can sort it faster?" And they said, "Well, of course, the quantum computer." And I said, "Of course not — that's not the case."

Modern quantum computers run at a clock speed of hundreds of hertz, or thousands of hertz — not at the gigahertz we're used to. They're single-core, and they're single-threaded when it comes to doing a job like a merge sort.

The only thing it's really good at — which indeed is a magic trick — is going from an exponential-time algorithm, which is integer factorization or the elliptic-curve discrete-log problem (shout out to the ECDLP problem), and running them in polynomial time. That's remarkable. To a nerd, that's the greatest, coolest magic trick ever. But to a business person — unless you're in the business of factoring numbers — there's not a whole lot to be excited about.

The other algorithms quantum could do aren't much faster. They'll never beat an NVIDIA machine. They'll never beat a million NVIDIA machines. And quantum doesn't have storage — there's no such thing as quantum RAM. So you have to design a problem that has a really, really small input. You cannot put the world's compute into it. Every time somebody pitches OpenAI, from what I've heard, on a quantum computer, they say, "No, we're not interested."

Steel-Manning the Other Side

Host: I'm closer to you in my perspectives on quantum. But let me take the other side. The other side would say: look, we're in a very early primordial phase of actually constructing the transistor. And from the transistor, we're going to put a bunch of these things together, figure out gates, figure out logic, build some reasonable operating system on top of it, have reasonable mechanisms to write software — and none of that really exists. Do you buy that we're just at an early phase, and that's why we're frustrated that there's a computational limitation except for a very narrow use case?

Shkreli: Yeah — no, of course. The issue, though, is: would you go long punch cards and vacuum tubes? Mercury delay lines, core memory — these are all things that disappeared and went bankrupt. Those were stocks at one point. CTR, Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company, got incorporated into IBM.

Host: But is your critique business-model and timing, or is it technological?

Shkreli: I think it's both. When you talk to Google, IBM, or Microsoft and ask them, "Why are you spending hundreds of millions a year on this?" they say, "Well, someday there might be something that comes out of it." That's not a great business to me.

Host: It's actually very shocking — how many machines does IBM or Google actually have?

Shkreli: Very few. Google has a few prototypes. IBM has a little cloud. Chelsea and I have tried every single quantum computer in the world. We cannot multiply 300 by 200 on any of these.

Host: And you're shorting them?

Shkreli: Yeah, I've been short them. Unfortunately, we lost millions of dollars shorting quantum computing companies — but I told my wife that we gained billions in insight.

Host: Right. It's not easy to time the markets.

Encryption, Matmul, and Analog Optical Computing

Host: Where is the natural computational edge? Some people would say it's going to be towards encryption — defeating encryption — because now we can use what quantum is actually good at to brute-force solutions to things we can't solve today.

Shkreli: I think it's crazy to even think about it, because we have a computational problem we're trying to solve. Every time somebody uses the word "AI," I actually think of the word matmul. These are matmul machines.

Host: Matrix multiplication is what he's referring to — multiplying two lists of numbers is what a GPU spends 99.9% of its time doing.

Shkreli: Right. But it does it in n-cubed time. I think things like complexity-log algorithms are going to be parlance in the next 5 to 10 years. N-cubed means: if you want to multiply a thousand-element square matrix versus another thousand-element square matrix on an NVIDIA machine, it takes a billion operations. That's a lot.

I was flipping through a paper from Microsoft called AOC — Analog Optical Computing. In New York, "AOC" means something different… but in this case: what I saw out of the corner of my eye was that matmuls in light are free. They happen in instant time, which is a really remarkable thing.

So we're investigating — maybe we'll start a company. There are a couple of startups — Neurophos, Opticore, Lumi — that want to make these photonic matmul cores, which would run circles around what NVIDIA does. Of course, that's not the whole story. There's a lot of details — nonlinearity, storage.

From Jim Cramer's Desk to Drug Arbitrage

Host: Beyond the hatred for quantum and your raging short that may or may not be winning — you were a hedge fund manager, correct? The famous episode, just to catch everybody up, was: you bought a drug and then you inflated the price of the drug. Is that what happened? Can you just give us the history?

Shkreli: Yes. I started at 16 at Jim Cramer's hedge fund. Cramer was actually a tremendously effective and skilled trader. Cramer's idea of investing was to buy and sell all day, every day, everything — and he somehow squeezed profits out of it. That was the way you did it in the '80s and '90s. He made 23% a year, net of fees.

Host: And you worked for him as a 16-year-old. How did you get that job?

Shkreli: Just being in Manhattan, having a big mouth — it's a great city. Loving stocks, loving investing. Bill Gates was my hero. I found a way to get into that. Cramer one day pointed at me and said, "Genomics — you're going to look at genomics." I said, "Okay." It was a lot of fun. I went to a Tiger Cub, started my own fund.

I realized I was a much better entrepreneur and private-equity guy than a trader. We found that the marketplace for molecules had huge amounts of alpha — whereas the marketplace of public companies… I bought a drug from Bristol-Myers for 2 million. That same company is public today — it's worth 6 billion. That was my first startup.

It was a really inefficient market. Pfizer would sell you a drug for a million bucks that was worth a billion dollars. They didn't care.

Host: Sell you the rights to the drugs — you could productize it, price it. I'm sorry — what do you mean? You just knock on Pfizer's door, they're like, "Take what you'd like for a million dollars?"

Shkreli: We saw this and we built two very similar companies. Our biggest constraint was finding people to vet these assets — reading papers, reading patents, going to universities and small drug companies and big drug companies, making relationships. It's called business development in our field. Our biggest bandwidth problem was reading these papers.

So I started a small NLP company on the side in 2015. We had Watson — it was great. (It wasn't great.) We tried to read every paper published in medicine. It was 40 million papers. Having humans do that is a really tough thing.

The Sparsentan Playbook

Host: How do you take a molecule and flip it from 25 million to 6 billion? What are you doing in that 6 or 9 months that you own it?

Shkreli: What I did with Sparsentan — a drug that I named, and that is now FDA-approved, now a blockbuster — Bristol discovered and developed it for hypertension, which is a dead, sleepy market that nobody really needs.

Host: Hypertension — high blood pressure.

Shkreli: Yeah. We moved it into a disease called FSGS, a disease that never had a drug approved for it. So you try to angle it in a way that makes sense. In that case, the drug got FDA-approved. Thirty thousand people who have focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, and never had a drug before, now have a drug. I can be a good guy too. That's the art of that field. It's a great way to make a billion dollars.

Host: Is this what Royalty Pharma does?

Shkreli: Royalty is a bit of a different player. Genius guys — obviously, their big claim to fame was going to NYU, which was getting a big royalty from Remicade, and buying it for like one-times earnings. That royalty 20x'd.

Host: They buy the cash flows at a bigger discount than how they're being modeled.

The AI Capex Cycle — Boogeymen and Bets

Brad: Martin, take this framework — you know the big levers in the market today, what's expected in terms of compute, in terms of this capex buildout. Are you spending much time looking at that? Do you see any boogeyman there? What are you worried about? What would you be shorting? What would you be long in that complex?

Shkreli: Yeah — I mentioned photonic computing before, because I do think in 20 years these H100s are in the scrap heap. B100s in the scrap heap. B200s in the scrap heap. We're going to find ways to do this better.

I think it's insane that we're thinking about space. I think it's insane we're thinking about nuclear. Sam Altman finally said publicly that he thinks photonic computing is on a rival podcast — that photonic computing could be the future. So I'm wondering why we think it's a sane idea to cover the earth with computers when we can make a faster one.

That doesn't mean NVIDIA is not a long — I'm long semis right now. Jevons always wins in the end. Alex Wang told me Jevons is going to take care of all this — it'll be a million-x computer improvement. There are guys in the Valley talking about better transformers that are a thousand times better. If there's a thousand-times-more-efficient transformer, that's bad for NVIDIA. There's no doubt about that.

We're not going to have a million-x demand. We might, in another way — but there aren't a million-x more people. Whether we have a million-x more compute needs, we'll have to see. For now, my guess, like anybody else's, is long — but I probably would have guessed in 2000 that Yahoo and Cisco belonged long too. So it's a tricky place.

Portfolio Allocation Today

Host: Do you run a hedge fund still?

Shkreli: I don't.

Host: So you're managing your own money. When you think about portfolio allocation, are you thinking about it the way you did when you ran your fund, or are you looking for specific high-alpha events — startups, disruption — and really going long behind those, not really thinking about competing with the market?

Shkreli: I'm sort of nimble. The Dario trade was a great reason to go long. I sort of piled in — onto the sphere.

Host: You're saying the selloff yesterday was sort of a head-fake?

Shkreli: Yeah, I think it was ridiculous.

On Dario Amodei

Host: What did you think about his essay?

Shkreli: I want to pay deference to him creating a trillion-dollar company — but I kind of hate the guy. He's a fear-mongerer.

Imagine you and I started a business, and I said, "I'm going to show you Pandora's box. Here it is." And you say, "Wow, that's amazing." And then you said, "Thanks a lot, Martin — I'm going down the street. I'm going to start Pandora's Box 2." What are you doing? I would probably sue you for trade secrets or something. This is exactly what happened.

Host: So you're saying — because he was at OpenAI, and then he and his five or six co-founders leave — you're saying…

Shkreli: Would you be friends with that guy? Would you like that?

Host: I mean, the thing with Silicon Valley is that it kind of happens a lot. It's sort of hard to pinpoint what is a patent versus what is retained knowledge. I'm not excusing it and I'm not saying I know anything that happened, but —

Shkreli: The Waymo guy went to jail for it.

Host: Well, I think that was because he was found to have actually stolen physical documents.

Shkreli: You have an issue with sort of the origin story of —

Host: The fear-mongering, the ridiculous hyperbole, right? He says the AI is going to help drug development — will kill —

Effective Altruism vs. Effective Accelerationism

Host: Let me ask you — what about effective altruism?

Shkreli: Yeah — even worse.

Host: Why? What do you find so bothersome about this group of people? Let's unpack it.

Shkreli: So I helped popularize — and I think I would say start — the EAC movement, which was this counter-insurgency.

Host: Sorry — there's EA, and then there's EAC —

Shkreli: Which was intentionally named.

Host: EA is effective altruism. EAC is —

Shkreli: Effective accelerationism.

Host: Which means —

Shkreli: Which means — that's a great question. It does mean sort of "move fast and break things." It's no secret that Zuckerberg came out the other day and said we should move fast in AI.

The fear-mongering is a little ridiculous. There'll be time to panic — it's just not now. Physical AI presents those opportunities. For now, you can turn off the computer. It's not that big of a deal.

Nerds get carried away. If you ever were a nerd or a jock — I was, believe it or not, a little bit of both. The jocks know what to do when the spotlight's on them. The nerds don't — they clam up, and some of them, instead of saying "everything's fine," want to draw attention to themselves. They want to say, "Well, the thing I'm working on is really amazing."

The reality is that this is just software. It's the most important kind of software ever made, as you said earlier — but it's not going to kill us all.

Dario also said we'd be fully unemployed within one to five years, about two years ago. He's got three years left. He also said we'd cure all diseases. I don't think there'll be a single AI-relevant drug in the next 10 years. AI does not help drug discovery. If you've ever built drugs — raise your hand if you've made a drug, gotten FDA approval for a drug. Okay, I'm pretty sure that's it.

It's pretty hard to do. We've had computers for a long time. I built a Cray cluster to analyze drugs. Now I can use GPUs — it's great — but there isn't much AI can help us with in drug discovery.

Valuation, TAM, and the "McDonald's $10B Sandwich"

Host: What is the revenue cycle that's driving valuation? Just unpack it from a hedge-funder. You're sitting there — you see these run-rates. Jensen mentioned it yesterday: $400 billion have gone into venture that has been redirected into AI. Do you interpret that as VCs funneling LP money to buy tokens, effectively? Is there a valuation trap?

Shkreli: I don't think so. What you mentioned earlier with productivity — there is infinite demand for intelligence and infinite demand for work. When you said "the workforce," I thought Brad was making a mistake — if you take the TAM and limit it to knowledge workers, you're really undercutting the TAM.

Brad: Trying to be conservative.

Shkreli: There's no limit toward intelligence. My buddy left OpenAI, started a company called Core Automation, which we're really excited about — I think I mentioned the other night — he invented the reasoning model at OpenAI, and he's got a somewhat under-the-radar startup.

You're going to have AI starting businesses. Part of his plan is to have, within OpenAI: OpenAI Pharma, OpenAI Motors, OpenAI Aviation, OpenAI, etc. He'll have his versions of those. You're going to have a whole S&P 500 within OpenAI or Anthropic or wherever. The opportunities are boundless.

And one last thing: McDonald's can afford to spend $10 billion and say, "OpenAI, give me 10 million GPUs — I want to know what the best next sandwich we should launch is." That's an NPV-positive. If the intelligence is worth it — if it's not asymptotic (at some point, more tokens doesn't get you a better answer) — but when that day comes where you say, instead of hiring McKinsey or a focus group, "I need 10 million GPU-minds to think about what McDonald's should do right now"…

A Mental Model for the AI Market

Host: What is a good analog for the AI marketplace? You see a handful of providers of a critical resource; you see incredible valuations that obviously attract a lot of incremental capital; it breeds a lot of competition; there are various solutions. Jensen made the analogy yesterday that it's kind of like water — you still have $8 water, but you still have the free water. There's a world in which all flowers bloom. What's your mental model? How do you equate this to previous markets we would understand — oil, or other?

Shkreli: It has to be like the internet — at least part of it. The only winners are going to be consumers and businesses. They get this tax-free kind of internet. Cisco and some other guys will get a little bit out of it, but the main highway that we're all going to benefit from — which we already are — is free intelligence in our pocket.

Host: So, I would interpret what you're saying as: right now we have to be guessing around (a) who's going to over-earn, and (b) the duration of that over-earning.

Shkreli: Sure. And I think it's Meta.

Host: Timing?

Shkreli: I think it's Meta.

Host: The company Meta.

Shkreli: They have the distribution with Muse. They showed they still have product chops. We're still in day one of AI. I actually think the chatbots are something we're going to look back and laugh at — "these are the early…"

Host: Would you go out today and buy OpenAI and Anthropic?

Shkreli: Yeah. We have OpenAI, obviously, through a few different ways. Sam's hedge with hardware is really brilliant — he'll always have the best model, I think, but being able to deliver that model is probably more valuable. That's where we saw with Muse — this really creative product work that Alex did — a new avenue for them.

Elon, Nick Bostrom, and "It's Just Computer Science"

Host: What did you think about Elon's suggestion of competitor peer review, as kind of this third-way, middle-ground pragmatic solution to balancing safety and speed?

Shkreli: They said that if Warren Buffett could go back in time, he'd go back and shoot the Wright brothers and stop the aviation industry from ruining capitalism. I think Nick Bostrom wrote this book, Superintelligence, that scared the hell out of Elon. I'm not advocating for violence — but it would have been better if some of the EA kind of folks never had this narcissistic self-importance that is driving some of this fear-mongering.

OpenAI doesn't believe it. They're in this as wanting to not be too different from Anthropic. Thankfully, some other guys have the spine. Meta has the spine to call it out and say this is nonsense. The president has the spine to do the same. Jensen has the spine to do the same. It's just computer science. It's not that big of a deal.

Sam Bankman-Fried, Elizabeth Holmes, and the "Albatross of Giftedness"

Host: Some of these EA guys are pretty brilliant. Dario's no dummy. Dustin Moskovitz. Sam Bankman-Fried.

Shkreli: Sometimes you can be really smart at one thing and really dumb at another.

Host: Let me ask you this question — and actually, yeah, I'm a good example.

Host: So this is actually my point. Some of the smartest people are unconventional thinkers, and you're clearly a brilliant person. People that are brilliant are generally brilliant because they're not conventional — they're heterodox in some way. But in the same vein, if you have that brilliance, perhaps it's also hard for you to be conventional in the ways that are, perhaps, call it, law-abiding. Hold on one sec — I want to ask your opinion on Sam Bankman-Fried. You've met the guy — right?

Shkreli: I gave him advice. Gave him advice on how to tough it out.

Host: Can you give us your sense on the guy? He was early in Anthropic at the beginning. You look at the portfolio of investments he made across the board — it was crazy. In 2021, 2022, it looked like genius.

Shkreli: Genius.

Host: Can you just tell us a little bit about what got that guy off track? Is it that he was so out of the bounds as a thinker — that's what got him all the alpha, but in the same way also got him in trouble? Or was it speed?

Shkreli: I think it's both. One of the problems: if you grow up as an intellectually gifted person, you have this big albatross. I think this happened as well to Elizabeth Holmes. Raj Rajaratnam was another example — a hedge fund manager that was a decent investor.

To keep it short: you have this self-consciousness — you have to live up to something. And sometimes wanting to live up to that big thing can be very detrimental. Just failing and admitting that you are not that great at that is not that bad. I had a hard time admitting I was not the best hedge-fund manager in the world — but I was a wonderful entrepreneur. That simple refusal to admit, put me in prison.

What Prison Changed

Host: Have you changed your views, or behavior? What has changed about you from prison?

Shkreli: Psychology is a really powerful force. All of our actions are motivated by innate drives that we don't always understand. I didn't realize how petrified I was of not being seen as a great trader. What a stupid thing. You can be a great long-term investor, value investor, entrepreneur, startup guy, whatever.

Child (off-mic): Dad — what's up, Dad?

Shkreli: Yeah — a great guy, a great scientist, whatever. But if you really fixate your own mind on "I have to be this," then that can be really detrimental.

Host: Putting aside your case — valid or not — if you were targeted for whatever reasons: what did you learn during your time in the big house, and how did it change you as a person? Because you're very different. You seem to have gotten a lot sharper, and a little bit more methodical in your approach to life. Take us through what you learned in that time.

Shkreli: Oh, thanks a lot. One of the interesting things about prison is that no matter where anybody's from, or what they did — everyone sort of has a lot of these same real common features that bind us as humans. Everyone's upset that their friend didn't stay in touch, or longing for that person they miss, whatever the case is. It's refreshing to remember that no matter what heights we achieve, at bottom, like you said earlier — we all want to be the best dad we can, or whatever the case is.

Close

Host: Martin, you're a very independent thinker, and you're willing to say the things and communicate in a way that other people don't. That's why we wanted to have you here. I think obviously this was a great showcase of that. We really appreciate you taking the time to be with us. Thank you.

Shkreli: Thank you so much. That's great.

Host: Thanks. Nice to meet you. Nice to meet you. Hey man — come back anytime.

Shkreli: Thank you.

item.description:
## 一、Shkreli 其实在做同一笔生意——只是标的从分子换成了"量子叙事"
表面看，Shkreli 的人生有两条平行线：曾经在制药市场"低价扫货高价转卖"分子，如今在二级市场做空量子公司。但如果把两件事叠在一起看，你会发现这根本是**同一个套利模型**：他专门狙击"叙事资本 ≫ 数理资本"的错配。
- 当年辉瑞把一个值十亿的分子按一百万美金卖出，是因为大药厂的内部估值模型里，这颗分子被归入"睡眠市场" ——他做的是把分子**从错误的叙事抽屉里拿出来**。 - 今天 IBM/Google 的量子机器被塞进"下一代计算"的叙事抽屉里，但 Shor 算法只是**一个** polynomial-time 的魔术，而不是通用加速器。他做的还是同一件事——**把标的从错误的抽屉里拎出来**。
出人意料的观察是：他本质上不是"做空者"也不是"涨价者"，而是一个**叙事抽屉套利者**。这解释了为什么他的名声和他的 P&L 看起来总是正交的。
## 二、Peter Shor 与 Shkreli 共享同一种"压缩"美学——这才是全场最隐秘的跨领域连接
Shor 算法真正惊人的地方不是"更快

item.title: [a16z] Recursive Self-Improvement and the Future of AI
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

RSI 的三个反直觉洞察

一、分母才是真正的战场——"流血榜"颠覆了整个硅谷游戏

大多数人盯着分子（性能、能力、benchmark 分数）看，但这家公司的核心哲学藏在一个黑色幽默里：他们有一个 bleederboard（流血榜），公开追踪谁烧钱最凶。这是对硅谷"leaderboard 文化"的一次釜底抽薪——当所有人都在卷性能的数字时，他们在卷"每单位改进消耗的卡路里"。

跨领域的意外联系：这与进化生物学中的"代谢经济"原理惊人一致。在寒武纪大爆发中，真正胜出的物种并不是"更大更强"的，而是降低了代谢成本的——比如昆虫的外骨骼之所以统治地球数亿年，不是因为更坚固，而是因为用更少的材料实现了相同的强度/重量比。RSI 真正的护城河，可能不在"模型多聪明"，而在"每瓦特能产出多少聪明"——这更像是在造蒸汽机效率，而不是造火箭。

二、"威斯康星州花园水管公司"——RSI 的真正试金石在最不性感的地方

全场最惊人的一句话："RSI 的秘密藏在威斯康星州某家花园水管公司里"。这不是玩笑，这是一个深刻的方法论断言：当所有人都盯着"推理加速"、"代码生成"这些本身就是 AI 问题的 AI 问题（自指捷径）时，真正能验证通用 RSI 的，恰恰是那些没有被 AI 污染过的庞杂工作流。

让我意外的洞察：这其实暴露了当前 AI 领域一个隐形的 selection bias——"RSI 看起来有效，是因为我们只在 RSI 容易生效的领域测试它"。这就像用物理学家最熟悉的理想气体验证理想气体定律。GPT 之父用 Einstein-GPS 的类比说得很狠：如果没有相对论，GPS 工程师也会凑出一个修正公式，但他们永远不会知道那是时空收缩。今天很多 RSI 的 "glimmers"，可能只是在无意识地凑经验公式，而真正的"相对论"藏在水管公司的订单流程里——那里没有基准，只有真实复杂性。

三、"人类是多智能体系统中的一种特殊智能体"——边界的消融

这句话被轻飘飘地说出来，但它是整场对话里最具颠覆性的本体论断言。他们并不是在"让 AI 取代人类"，而是把人类研究员数学化地归入了同一个 agent class。公司架构不是"人 + AI"，而是"异质 agent 协同系统"。

跨领域连接：这与现代生物学中的 holobiont（共生功能体） 概念几乎同构——我们现在知道人类不是"独立个体加肠道菌群"，而是一个共进化的功能系统，大脑决策受微生物影响。RSI 的真正突破可能也不是"数字优化器取代生物优化器"，而是系统学会不区分它们，让瓶颈自然浮现（阿姆达尔定律）。更深一层：如果人类是 agent 的一种特例，那么"对齐问题"就从外部伦理问题变成了内部拓扑问题——不是"AI 要听谁的话"，而是"这个异质网络中哪个节点的梯度主导了整个系统的收敛方向"。

一个额外的"啊哈"时刻：他们对 take-off 的真正定义不是"性能爆炸"，而是分母保持不变甚至下降时，分子仍在指数增长。这把整个 AGI 讨论从"能力竞赛"重新框定成热力学问题——最终的上限是宇宙的 10^80 个粒子 × 光速。换句话说，奇点不是哲学问题，是普朗克常数问题。

📝 转录文本

Recursive Self-Improvement and the Future of AI

a16z — 对话录

开场金句集锦

"The fundamental idea here is to build AI that improves itself. And I think we're getting there."

"For the first time, we could swap the optimizer as the optimizee. And this leads to a reinvestment of cognitive improvement into itself."

"You can think of RSI at many different levels of the stack — prompts, harness, weights, and you can go all the way to basically chips. Our goal here is to optimize all the levels of the stack."

"Our approach to RSI is that we have a multi-agent system working together that's been recursively improved."

"I'm so impressed by your belief that like this idea of a model improving itself—" "But it's not a belief."

"It is a dramatic statement, which is I think it's the first time I've heard you say it."

"Because we have been so thorough, we have not released things until we're super sure it's correct."

"Do you envision a system where the amount of energy that goes into it somehow decreases over time relative to the improvement?"

"We can't share too much, but one of the very important things that we've tried to do…"

一、自我介绍

Host: Welcome both of you for joining. We're going to be talking about everybody's favorite topic, which is RSI — recursive self-improvement. Maybe to start, it'd be great to just introduce yourselves and your backgrounds. Then we'll talk a little bit about what you're working on now, and then we'll dig into the content.

Guest 1: Yeah, I think of myself as like a physicist of some kind. I studied that. Then I did the PhD in reinforcement learning at the MIT Media Lab. I really like building things and I'm very excited to be building a cool startup — a maker — with Owen and Grace.

Owen: My name is Owen. I was first studying math, and then one day I realized that all mathematicians are proving theorems. I was taking a class called Formal Language and Logic, and they were showing how you can build a theorem prover. And I was like, "Oh, that would be cool — I can just build a machine that proves theorems for me." That's how I got into AI.

Host: Amazing.

Owen: And then for my PhD I worked on continual learning and meta-learning, then worked for a few years at DeepMind as a research scientist. Now I'm working on RSI.

二、什么才算真正的 RSI？—— 自催化 vs. 递归自我改进

Host: I see a lot of pitches come in and a lot of them use the term RSI, and I'll be like, "Oh, so what do you do?" And they'll say, "We use AI to create AI." That sounds very interesting — so what do you do? "We use AI to create GPU kernels." Which, to me, kind of doesn't match the definition of what I would consider to be RSI. So maybe can we start by you defining what you think, or what you would include in RSI, definitionally?

Guest 1: Yeah, I think RSI is definitely an overloaded term today. Many people when they say RSI, they mean different things. So I think the important thing when you are differentiating them is to ask the question: what is the optimizer and what is the optimizee — like when you're self-improving, who is improving?

There are people saying, "Okay, we're doing RSI, we have humans using AI to develop better AI." But that to us is just autocatalysis — in the sense that the improver is still human with tools, even though these tools are getting better and better. But the idea and the improvement come from human brains.

Host: And just — I don't mean to interrupt, but to be clear, most technical epochs have had autocatalytic effects, right? Like there's no way you can create a computer chip without a computer. You could argue that the internet's development was sped up by the fact that people that weren't geographically located could coordinate. I mean, the steam engine — you could build better steam engines because you could get coal faster, etc. So this notion of like "using the thing to build the thing faster" is not new. And so you're saying something different.

Guest 1: Yes. I think for us, in the history over civilization, we have this autocatalysis — computers using computers to build better computers — but the idea for this change, for this improvement, come from human brains. The human brain was never the optimizee, never the thing being optimized. Whereas now, for the first time, we could swap the optimizer as the optimizee. The brain of the agents, which is the LLM — the model — can be the thing that you're optimizing. And this leads to a compound, this reinvestment of cognitive improvement into itself.

三、为什么选最难的问题？—— 闭环 vs. 开环

Host: But there has to be a reason that you decided to take on this hard problem, as opposed to what anybody else would do, which is like chew off pieces of the problem.

Guest 1: Yeah. I mean, before I answer your more important question — the reason I did this is I think it's a hard problem, and it's fun working on the hardest problem.

Host: But do you have an intuition that this is the actual right answer, as opposed to something more pragmatic?

Guest 1: Yeah. I think a pragmatic thing would be — just from a control theory perspective — if you have a gap in the system, you can't have a closed loop. And autocatalytic has no closed loop. Whatever you improve, there's still a gap. Humans have to come in. You have to pour in other resources to make it work. But if you have a closed loop, you still have to pour in resources, but the marginal gains ideally get either constant or larger over time. And that's the fundamental difference.

四、分子与分母 —— RSI 的数学框架

Guest 1: What's really different here can be explained pretty easily. If you think of capability, what we're trying to do here is we're trying to improve the rate of improvement of capability. The first derivative of capability with respect to time is the thing that everybody is trying to improve.

And now you can put that to be equal, driven by two things: the numerator and the denominator.

  • Numerator = performance — which is what everybody is trying to improve.
  • Denominator = cost — let's say capital, or difficulty. And this one is pretty set, because the higher the capability, the higher the difficulty of the next step.

Now the numerator is the interesting part. For things like steam engines and whatnot, that was fixed. So then you end up with a very simple differential equation where you basically plateau.

Now, if you have a system where the thing being improved is also the thing that's doing the improvement, you now have a new way to think about it. The simplest case: the numerator is also correlated with capability — which makes sense, because the better you are, the better you are at also improving. If you do that, the math cancels out and you basically get constant improvement over time. That could be one level of RSI.

And then there's one more case: the numerator could be correlated with a higher power of capability. And then you get exponential takeoff.

五、闭环 ≠ 收敛 —— 为什么 RSI 本质是经验问题

Host: Can we dig in a little bit more between RSI's having closed the loop and actual convergence properties? For some reason, when people see a graph where there's a circle with an arrow to another circle, and it goes back, and they look at that closed control system, then they say "takeoff." Which — I mean, if this is a nonlinear control system, it's very difficult to know what the hell happens, by the way. Most people don't seem to understand this distinction, because we very quickly go to "takeoff" and "FOOM" and all that stuff when we talk about these things.

Guest 1: Well, as a network guy, you know that it depends on the exponent of your function that's self-referencing. And what we've found is that it's almost not useful to speculate on what we think could happen, because this is really an empirical problem. The real way to know what's happening is to test things. And testing things is really, really hard — reward hacking is one of many problems that we have to deal with. But the question you're asking is very empirical.

Host: Interesting. As a networker, that's how I would have answered. I would have thought math people would have been like, "We've got this differential equation, I took out my pencil and I wrote down the answer."

Guest 1: I mean, it is possible to write down the differential equation, but you still have to empirically measure the variable — the exponent.

Host: So there's no analytical solution.

Guest 1: I mean, honestly, we don't even have a learning theory of deep learning. We don't know fundamentally why it works. And then now you're five, six layers on top of deep learning. So we don't have a good theory. I think the closest things we have are scaling laws — and these are empirical laws.

六、多智能体 RSI —— 人类作为一种特殊 agent

Owen: I think one misunderstanding people have about our approach to RSI is that they think the entire system has to be fully automatic and digital. But actually, if you look at our mathematical foundation, we have a multi-agent system, not just one digital agent. And in this multi-agent system, human researchers and engineers are actually a special case of these agents. It's this hybrid system of multiple agents working together that's been recursively improved.

Guest 1: And we don't want to leave out any component. If it's possible to optimize in the model, why wouldn't we do that? You will have more gains if you do include those. Anything that you don't optimize will later become your bottleneck.

七、不要被资金堆积欺骗 —— 真实分母的计量

Guest 1: One observation that we have made here: there are claims of "speed is improving," which is actually the case, right? If you look at the model release time, it is reducing. So on one hand you can be like, "Okay, so clearly we're in some sort of rapidly improving phase." But if you divide by the actual amount of capital raised by these companies, that's no longer the case. And so you're like, well, maybe they just raise a whole bunch of money, and then AI allows you to apply that money.

Host: So how would you encourage people that are either evaluating claims about this, or even working on them, to think about not fooling yourself by throwing more money at the problem — like you're actually showing that you're making an improvement here that's meaningful with the denominator?

Guest 1: For us it's pretty straightforward. If you get improvement and they just come at more and more resources being poured in, it's not RSI. You have to be able to back your claim of how much improvement you're getting.

Host: But do include like all the man-hours and experimentation that went into that. Because I feel like at some level, they'll talk about the actual flops that go in and money that go in, but the reality is this is like the 23rd experiment, and it's actually a human burning a lot of mental capital to get to that final configuration. Do you actually include that in the denominator?

Guest 1: We do, and I think it's good company discipline to do that. We've tried, very intentionally from the beginning, to have a culture of tracking where things go — cost, time, all that kind of stuff.

Bleederboard —— 反向排行榜

I share a funny thing internally. People talk about leaderboards — you know, score. We have something called a bleederboard, where we keep track of the cost of experiments of everybody who's running experiments.

Host: That's awesome.

Guest 1: You know, everybody — any day — can look at who's high up on the bleederboard.

nanoGPT 作为对照组

Owen: I can also give an example from AI. I don't know if you know this nanoGPT benchmark they are running. It's basically asking you to retrain GPT-2, which when it just came out is a very expensive model to train — takes weeks, I think, on multiple GPUs. And right now people can train on a single GPU within hours, and that number has been shrinking constantly.

Host: But that's also totally separate, right? Like that's just like Moore's law —

Owen: No, no, it's the same GPU. It's the same hardware.

Host: Using the same hardware, and then you improve the techniques of pre-training.

Owen: Yeah. What has improved is algorithmic techniques, data techniques, kernels, all of that kind of stuff.

Host: Do you know how much it costs to train GPT-2?

Owen: I think it's a few hundred.

Host: $100? Wow. So the same GPU, same data, and this is just algorithmic. And do those come from humans or do those come from agents?

Owen: A lot of them are auto-research results.

Host: But that's definitely the denominator, that's not the numerator. Like what you want to see is like you can do that with GPT-5 — which we're not seeing. The cost to these things is going up dramatically.

Guest 1: I think one of the most closely guarded secrets in the industry is exactly this thing — which is how much compute you can get out of this. Because in some sense, even if all you were improving was your denominator, you could get faster training because now you can get more rollouts. And that means you can sample the manifold of the space of language more extensively, and then you can get better trajectories, which means you can get smarter models when you use that to train. For sure improving the denominator is good. For sure improving the numerator is good. I've yet to see — which is great that you have glimmers — where you can improve both the numerator and the denominator. I mean, that's a pretty meaningful statement, which is awesome.

八、简单的闭环胜过复杂的点子

Guest 1: What we found is that a lot of the papers that claim to do RSI, when we test it in our internal infra, we find that they don't work. And a lot of it is because they're cool ideas that humans try to introspect and say, "Oh, this is what I think should happen." They're complicated. They sound cool, they get you a good paper. But then when we test it at scale on benchmarks, on real economic problems, they don't scale. And what we found is that the simpler thing that closes the loop is the thing that scales.

第一性原理与统一数学框架

I would say one thing that we do that's probably unique is that we always start with a very grounded mathematical framework that basically lays out the map of the whole space. And the reason is because this space is so large that if you don't do that, and you don't have this very principled way of doing it, you get lost very quickly in this complexity.

The other reason: often when you have this really complex system, there's two extremes of how you can build it. You can take an approach where you basically build like 200 different systems and you hope that this Rube Goldberg machine will kind of work out. Or you take the other way — you spend some time thinking about these 200 things, and maybe you realize they're actually just 12 abstractions that generalize to these 200 things. And so what we have tried to create: a culture of "let's really think from first principles, let's look at the math, and then we realize what are the assumptions we make to be practical" — because you have to do both. And then we see what works. When you do that, you can see that, oh, multiple papers or ideas are actually subclasses of the same general framework. And if you do that well, you can scale.

Feynman —— 物理 vs. 集邮

Owen: I think Richard Feynman said once that there are two kinds of sciences — there are stamp collections, and then there is physics. So without a unified math framework, all these research are sort of just stamp collections. A lot of these papers we're reading, they're just ideas inspired by some human behavior, and then they try to mimic that and say, "Oh look, we have RSI." But then if you don't put into a unified system, you don't know if the overall system is actually improving, or you're just locally applying an idea that's getting better.

So what we have is: we're putting all these components that you could possibly recursively improve into a unified framework, and look at it from a holistic view, so that improving one part does not negatively impact the other part.

九、全栈 RSI —— 从 prompt 到芯片

Owen: For example, there are people who are doing recursive improvement just on harness, and then there are people who are only doing weights. But weights and harnesses are not isolated components. They have impact on each other.

Guest 1: You can think of RSI at many different levels of the stack: prompts, harness, weights — and you can go all the way to basically chips. Our goal here is to optimize all the levels of the stack. We started with harness. We've tried to be always very capital-efficient because we care so much about the denominator. Then we started doing weights, weight updates. And what we found is that you get more gains, but you still have to do harness stuff. And you can keep going down the stack. My guess is that you probably will need to do a lot of the co-optimization of many different parts of the system to make it work.

十、问题域选择 —— 为什么是推理

Host: Can you talk a little bit about the problem domain that you're going after, just to prove that this works?

Guest 1: We are trying very hard to pick areas of the AI space that are as close as possible to AI itself. Again, we try to be recursive. And if you think about it, there's not that many problems that are super close to AI and gives you improvement on both the numerator and denominator. One of those is the inference problem. Because the more you can get improvements and efficiency out of inference, the more everything kind of unlocks. And it's not just for technical reasons but also the most promise of both the numerator and the denominator being improved.

Host: It kind of breaks the mind. Just for everybody that's listening to this: there's two improvements going on here. One of them is the ability of the model to make inference faster. And then the second one is: now that the inference is faster, it can do that faster.

Guest 1: And again, that does not necessarily mean takeoff — that can still, at some point… But it's just wild to think of this kind of compounding impact. We're a startup, we're not a research lab. One of the reasons we chose it is because everybody in the world right now wants to serve their own model. Everybody wants to use the latest — for example open-weight model, Kimi K3 or whatever just coming out — and they want to be able to serve it as efficiently as possible. So it's an economically extremely important problem right now.

用 Kimi K3 自己给自己加速？

Host: Just for the sake of discussion — if I wanted to make the inference for Kimi K3 faster, would I use Kimi K3 in a recursive way, or would I use a separate model and system to do that for Kimi K3? To improve the serving stack of Kimi K3?

Guest 1: Our system is not just using one LLM — you have many different LLMs that are doing many different things. We pick whichever is the most effective, because it's being used the most time. But the interesting thing is: the choice of which LLM to use for which thing is also not always up to us. We let the model choose. To be honest, today it's not really us who are deciding what to optimize. It's our agent — because it's recursively self-improvement, and what we're trying to do is not to limit itself to only one component. So it chooses whether to —

Owen: Yeah, we try to be as hands-off as possible. Let it do its thing.

Host: Do you have like a single master prompt? Is it like "improve yourself"?

Guest 1: Even that master prompt has been improving. [laughter]

Host: Really? It improves the master prompt.

Guest 1: Yeah. And it's not one RSI system, because you can think of it as there's the thing that does the improvement, but then you also have to have the thing that knows what to improve. And those are both dynamic problems and they are very coupled.

十一、通用性 vs. 物理极限

Host: How general do you think this ends up being? Right now you're focused on speeding up inference in a specific domain. Do you think that whatever approaches you're coming up with here generalize, or do you think there'll be a different one per target solution space?

Guest 1: Mathematically we have defined it so that it's one system that generalizes to everything.

Host: And by "everything" mean any problem domain that you can point AI to.

Guest 1: Correct. But then there are physical limits. One big limit is the human element. A lot of AI companies are thinking: let us use AI to replace humans. But what we found is that there's so much that if you have good researchers and good engineers, that they can bring to the table that's going to be very hard to replace by agents. And so that's why from the very beginning we've tried to think of our basically entire company as a multi-agent system where humans are a kind of agent that's cohabitating with other AI agents.

能耗递减与普朗克极限

Host: Can we at least reduce bounds? For example — do you envision a system where the amount of energy that goes into it somehow decreases over time relative to the improvement?

Guest 1: We can't share too much, but one of the very important things that we've tried to do in our company is not just work on the numerator (performance), but to work on the denominator — how much you can get out of the same amount of physics, money, whatever you want to call it.

Host: But do you think it's possible to have a system where the numerator continues to increase at the same way with the denominator being fixed or decreasing?

Guest 1: It's not just possible. I think it's happening.

Host: Really?

Guest 1: Yeah.

Host: So it takes less energy to get better results over time.

Guest 1: Yeah.

Host: Do you think there's a universe in which that continues without asymptoting? Because if that was the case, then you actually have takeoff.

Guest 1: I mean, but it just seems to disobey information theory and the laws of physics. Yeah. I think at some point you're going to reach Planck constant, Planck length, Planck energy, Planck time. So it will asymptote at some point.

Host: Oh, I see. And so you think that asymptote is basically like the computation of the universe.

Guest 1: At least. I mean, how many particles are there? 10^80. Like we know speed of light. You multiply those two and you basically get an upper bound of computation. And so given this fixed amount of computation, you can do every — we know we have a limit.

十二、不是信念，是实证测量

Host: I'm so impressed by your belief that this idea of a model improving itself —

Guest 1: But it's not a belief.

Host: No, you got to tackle that. That's amazing.

Owen: Also, it's a question of what metric you use to view the progress. If you use benchmark accuracy, it's upper-bounded by 100%. You're never going to see exponential improvement on that because eventually bottleneck 100%. So for a long time we had this question: how do we even know if something has taken off if we don't have the right metric?

Guest 1: It's not a belief that this is happening. I think we're already seeing glimmers of that happening.

Host: But it is a dramatic statement, which is I think it's the first time I've heard you say it. Is this a continuous result, or is it relatively recent that you're starting to see glimmers of this?

Guest 1: No, we've been seeing these results kind of grow and grow and grow over the last few months.

Host: That's amazing. How do you have confidence in the results, given it's not working yet and you don't know?

Guest 1: No, it's not belief. It's empirical measurement.

为什么还没发布 —— Viceroy of Variance

But also, as a company, there's a very funny thing that is happening: because we have been so thorough, we have not released things until we're super sure it's correct. Every few months there's an announcement of something RSI-related, we look at it, we're like, "We should have released our results." And then we look at it, we try to replicate it, and we realize — oh, it's noise, it's cherry picking. And so it's very, very hard to know in this sea of AI — I don't know what you want to call it — like everybody's trying to do AI, RSI stuff, to know what's legit or not.

The technical answer is: you have to be really, really good at measuring things. For example, we have one of our engineers that we named him the Viceroy of Variance. That's a real thing. His job is to go and destroy the results we have and find what's wrong. We even have little Slack emojis — there's one where there's red laser stuff coming out of his eyes when he finds that there's bad variance in stuff.

Quality Time —— 没有替代品的东西

One of the things that we found: when you're dealing with a new benchmark or a new problem of economic value that you want to apply this to, so far we have not found a replacement for what we call "quality time" — literally running hundreds of experiments, looking at it, developing an intuition, trying to figure out what is wrong, what is not wrong, what is just variance, what is this weird thing that actually shows that there's some kind of reward hacking like two levels down — the agent that built the agent that built the agent did hack something, and now you have this weird results.

十三、非线性控制系统的"退化行为"

Host: When I have dealt with nonlinear control systems — there's a bunch of degenerate behavior you have to deal with. It's not just convergence and divergence; you have things like oscillations. This is a very multi-dimensional problem. So do you have to deal with all of that stuff — like potential oscillations?

Guest 1: Absolutely. And then on top of that you have noise — are fundamentally super stochastic. What we find is that specific agent on a specific benchmark — there's levels of noise that's sometimes unpredictable. And some of them are extremely weird — like you even have some weird noise that comes from this GPU and this other GPU. They're both B200, but they have slightly different behaviors on the physics, and you can see some of that being replicated at the high level. So that's why it has to be an empirical thing.

智能是多维向量，不是标量

Owen: From that you could already see that intelligence is not a single scalar — it's more like a multi-dimension vector. There will be domains and fields where this RSI will give you takeoff, and there will be dimensions where you might plateau, or you will have relatively slow improvement. The defining factor is: what is the slowest component in it?

So you're an optimization person. You know that there's this Amdahl's law where the speed-up you can get by optimizing a component — you just take it to zero, nothing else dominates. Exactly. So the digital part we could optimize and accelerate. You could get like a thousand times faster or a million times faster. But if it's only 20% of your overall time, you're only going to get 20% speed-up.

So for domains where you still need to move atoms that interact with the physical world, that's really slow — you're still going to be bottlenecked by that. Let's say every evaluation you need to do — drug discovery — you still need to do wet lab experiments and then clinical trials. That takes months. Then every new idea has to go through months or multiple months of evaluation. So those fields probably won't be accelerated as fast as coding or mathematics where you have very fast and cheap evaluations.

十四、威斯康星州的花园水管公司

Host: What I've yet to see is anybody put a bound on that. Like to say, "In order for me to improve this by X to solve this problem, I need this much net new energy to do it." If you had that, you could actually predict — "How big of a warehouse do I need to solve a drug discovery problem? How many different robots would I need?" So do you think that we're getting any closer to actually having bounds? Because I think this is such a critical question for all of us to answer.

Guest 1: One of the internal jokes we have in the company is that the secret to RSI is somewhere in a garden hose company in Wisconsin. And the joke here is this: if Einstein hadn't discovered relativity, he would not have these laws that tell you how speed and the contraction of time works. And if some unfortunate engineer had to design the GPS system, they would have had to find a correction of time, and they probably would have said, "No, no, it's clearly not the fabric of spacetime that's contracting — I don't know why, but this is the formula I've devised empirically." Some fudge. Exactly. And then people later would have been like, "Holy —, this is spacetime contracting."

We have this theory that RSI right now is being thought of as "let's solve all these super hard, fashionable problems." But what we think is that the complexity of the world is such that the real challenges probably exist in spaces that are not being applied to. And so that's the joke — that there is some workflow somewhere in a garden hose company in Wisconsin that, if we solve it, we get —

Host: I love that.

十五、总结

Host: I just want to quickly summarize. So you're going after RSI — in your case, this is not autocatalytic effects, this is actual RSI where the system improves the full system. And for you, it's an actual system which includes the harness and the weights. If you think about the problem, you've got a numerator and a denominator. The numerator is like how good the system gets, and the denominator is how much energy goes into it. You believe you're seeing glimmers of the sign where both improve at the same time using this type of approach. Is that correct?

Guest 1: Yes.

Host: When can we expect to hear more from you?

Guest 1: Very soon.

Host: Amazing. Thanks so much, both of you, for joining.

Guests: Yeah. Thank you.

观看原视频 →

# RSI 的三个反直觉洞察
## 一、分母才是真正的战场——"流血榜"颠覆了整个硅谷游戏
大多数人盯着分子（性能、能力、benchmark 分数）看，但这家公司的核心哲学藏在一个黑色幽默里：他们有一个 **bleederboard（流血榜）**，公开追踪谁烧钱最凶。这是对硅谷"leaderboard 文化"的一次釜底抽薪——当所有人都在卷性能的数字时，他们在卷"每单位改进消耗的卡路里"。
**跨领域的意外联系**：这与进化生物学中的"代谢经济"原理惊人一致。在寒武纪大爆发中，真正胜出的物种并不是"更大更强"的，而是**降低了代谢成本**的——比如昆虫的外骨骼之所以统治地球数亿年，不是因为更坚固，而是因为用更少的材料实现了相同的强度/重量比。RSI 真正的护城河，可能不在"模型多聪明"，而在"每瓦特能产出多少聪明"——这更像是在造蒸汽机效率，而不是造火箭。
## 二、"威斯康星州花园水管公司"——RSI 的真正试金石在最不性感的地方
全场最惊人的一句话："RSI 的秘密藏在威斯康星州某家花园水管公司里"。这不是玩笑，这是一个深刻的方法论断言：当所有人都盯着"推理加速"、"代码

item.dc:creator: 投资TALK君
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、体感与数据的"认知错位"：市场参与者正在经历一场集体幻觉

本期最值得玩味的一点，不是高通CEO的采访，而是小陶一笔带过的那个反直觉发现——软件板块和半导体板块在10日滚动相关性上并不显著负相关，但几乎所有人的"体感"都坚信两者此消彼长。

这是典型的"显著性偏误"（Salience Bias）在金融市场的投射：人类大脑会放大那些发生在同一天、同一屏幕、同一新闻周期的反向波动，而忽略大量"同涨同跌"的沉默样本。这与行为经济学里卡尼曼讲的"可得性启发"是同一机制——我们记住的是戏剧化瞬间，不是平均状态。

跨领域连接：这个现象与神经科学中的"情绪记忆巩固"高度同构——杏仁核会优先存储情绪强度高的事件（恐慌日的负相关），而默认模式网络会主动忽略平淡的正相关日。换言之，散户不是在交易市场，而是在交易自己杏仁核的放电模式。真正的Alpha可能就藏在"体感和数据冲突"的那个夹缝里——当所有人都确信两者对立时，往往是均值回归的最佳时点。

二、"50日均线参与度低于20日均线"：一个被忽视的"基座空心化"信号

小陶提到三大指数的50日均线参与度全部低于20日均线参与度，他解读为"短期强势尚未传导到中期"。这个解读是对的，但不够狠。

真正的隐藏结构是：指数接近新高 + 中期广度低迷 = 由少数巨头抬轿的"倒金字塔市场"。这种结构在物理学里有个精确对应物——倒立摆系统：顶端质量越大，底部支撑越细，看起来越壮观，但对任何微小扰动的敏感度呈指数级上升。

出人意料的观察：这种结构其实和生态学里的"关键物种崩溃模型"（Keystone Species Collapse）是同一数学——亚马逊雨林里90%的生物多样性依附于不到5%的关键树种，一旦这几棵树倒下，整个生态会在数月内塌缩。当下美股的"七巨头依赖症"在数学结构上和这个模型完全对偶。CPI、PPI、财报季真正的风险不在数据本身，而在它是否会成为那个"扰动倒立摆的手指"。

三、高通CEO那句"28年底手机上要跑100个本地模型"：被低估的产业重构信号

这句话被小陶轻轻带过，但其战略含义远比它表面严重。注意："100个本地模型，24/7全天候运行"——这不是"手机变聪明"，这是手机架构的根本性颠覆。

一部24/7跑100个模型的手机，意味着： - 能耗曲线彻底重写：电池不再是"白天用、晚上充"，而是像心脏一样持续放电 - 散热成为核心设计约束：手机会从"娱乐终端"向"微型数据中心"演化 - 隐私边界模型倒置：不是数据上传给云，而是云把能力下沉给硬件

跨领域连接：这个趋势和19世纪末的"电力分布式革命"几乎完全镜像。1880年代，爱迪生推直流（本地发电），特斯拉推交流（远程集中），当时的主流认为"集中式必胜"。但真正的终局是——集中式电网 + 本地化电器共存，没有一方消灭另一方。小陶敏锐指出"不是零和游戏"是对的，但更精准的说法是：AI的未来是"交流电模型"——云做发电厂，端做家用电器，中间站（AI RAN）做变电站。

真正值得警觉的产业暗线：当手机变成"微型AI工厂"，手机厂商的护城河将从"品牌/摄像头/屏幕"转移到"NPU架构 + 散热工程 + 模型调度OS"——这意味着苹果过去十年积累的拍照护城河正在失效，而它尚未宣布的Siri智能体，决定了它是否能守住下一个十年。小陶说愿意把隐私数据交给苹果——这个"信任溢价"可能是苹果在AI时代最后、也是最重要的一张牌。

四、一个藏得很深的交易暗示

小陶聊UNH时说"上个季度管理层暗示margin改善会在后两个季度体现"——这句话配合"过去三个月股价一路回调到360-370"，构成了一个经典的"管理层指引 vs 市场情绪的时差套利"。如果管理层诚实，这就是预期差最大的时刻。但他没明说的是：市场之所以不信，是因为医疗板块整体在PBM改革阴影下，个股基本面被宏观叙事压制——这和2020年油气板块的"价值陷阱 vs 困境反转"剧本有70%相似度。

📝 转录文本

开场与本期背景

各位观众大家好，欢迎来到一个不单只聊新闻的专业美股频道，我是市场分析师小陶。

今天因为时间的关系已经比较晚了，所以我会把这期视频稍微压缩一些。但是因为还是有些东西想和大家分享，那正好在周一市场开盘之前，先来为大家录这期视频。因为周一我们加拿大这边是放假的，是一个国定的假日，但是周一美股市场是开市的，所以我个人认为大家还是希望看到这期内容的，对吗？

好吗，那就废话不多说。在开始之前大家记得留言、点赞、加转发。

我先回顾一下上周资产价格的走势，我们可以去看一下当下市场的参与度，然后我就对于本周的市场做一个展望。那最重要的是，在上周三四天之前，高通的CEO接受了一段采访，在这段采访里面，他非常清晰地表达了自己对于未来AI手机市场在端侧AI这一块的一些展望。我认为对于未来AI的发展，在端侧这一块的发展，包括高通这家公司，是一个比较完整的描述。

一、上周资产价格回顾

那我们就非常快速地先回顾一下过去一周资产价格的走势。

美债与黄金：美债市场的收益率出现了小幅下跌，TLT反弹了0.6%。随着TLT的反弹，黄金在上一周也出现了1.3%的反弹。

美股主要指数：总体来说，上周的美股市场是OK的，标普500上涨了1.2%，三大指数基本上都出现了上涨。

软件 vs 半导体——一个反直觉的现象：这边有一点是我想指出的，可能和我们本身的感受是有一点点反逻辑的。比如说，IGV（软件板块）在上一周上涨了3.4%，涨幅非常好。其中一些软件板块，包括Palantir破了一个新高，上周的微软我记得也走得不错。同时，芯片板块在上一周下跌了5%。

我们体感上非常明显的感受是，软件板块和硬件（或者半导体）之间出现了一个非常明显的负相关。但其实从结果或从相关性去看的话，其实我并得不出这个结论。

前七大科技股上涨了1.4%，等权指数上涨1.6%。所以上一周是一个市场比较完整的反弹。

软硬件相关性的真相

从这张图我们就可以看到半导体板块和软件板块的相关性：白色这条线是IGV，蓝色这条线是SOX（半导体板块），下面是一个相关性。当下面这条线在红色区间的时候，代表这两者之间是负相关；绿色区间代表是正相关。而我这边看的是滚动10个交易日的相关性。

基本上看到一段时间是负相关，一段时间是正相关。那如果要从交易这个角度去看的话，因为它是一个10天的滚动相关性，当这两者之间出现了比较明显负相关的时候，那接下去我们可以期待这两者之间有可能会出现正相关，反过来这个逻辑也是一样的。

但是这条线基本上告诉我们，从今年的6月份到现在为止，这两者之间（软件和硬件之间）的相关性没有那么明显。这就是我说的，我们从体感上，从有些时候当日的走势、日内的走势或者一周的走势感觉非常明显，好像当软件板块上涨的时候，半导体就一定会下跌。但其实从相关性这个角度并得不出这个结论。

很多时候体感和客观数据是可能矛盾的。那当这两者之间出现矛盾的时候，我个人认为我们更加应该去尊重比较客观的数据。

二、三大指数的市场参与度

那聊到数据这块，我们去更新一下上周收盘完之后三大指数的市场参与度。

  • 纳指：20均线和50均线分别在31%和28%，还是处在悲观的位置。
  • 罗素2000：36%和27%，同样也是相对悲观的位置。
  • 标普500：情绪面就好很多了，20均线和50均线分别在54%和35%。

有一点我们需要注意的是什么？我们看到这三大指数50日均线的参与度都低于20日均线的参与度。说明什么情况？说明短期之内市场的走势是比较强的，但是并没有把50日均线给拉上来。

所以接下去我们可以有一个期待：如果当20日均线这个参与度持续反弹的话，50日均线这个参与度也会被慢慢地拉上来。但是总体来说，如果我们去看这三大指数的50均线的话，现在仍然是在一个悲观的位置。你都不敢相信，三大指数的参与度是在一个悲观的位置，但是指数本身非常接近于新高。

三、本周数据与财报展望

对于本周的一些数据做一个展望。首先是CPI和PPI数据，其次是财报——我们马上就要打开财报季度了。那正好也是我在过去几天给自己稍微放了一个假，稍微休息一下，更好地去迎接第三季度这个财报。进入财报之后就会非常忙了，每天要看很多的财报，然后还要来和大家分享。

CPI 与 PPI 预期

首先是本周将要公布的CPI数据和PPI数据，也相当重要。但我认为重要的可能是市场会有一些波动，但是对于月底的时候美联储加息的决定，我不认为会有非常大的影响。

CPI数据（周三公布）：我们主要是看核心CPI。广义的话非常高，环比增速0.6%，因为油价和能源价格的上涨。核心的话，环比增速0.2%，彭博他们的预期是在0.23%。所以如果彭博他们的预期是正确的，那最终环比增速核心如果停留在0.2%的话，完全是美联储可以接受的。上一个月的数据是环比增速0.3%，即使退一步去讲，这一组的数据在0.3%，我个人认为也不会影响到10月份加息这个决定。

10月份大概率的情况下是不会有加息，按兵不动。因为11月份会有一个中期选举，如果要去加的话，完全可以在12月份继续加息。

PPI数据（周五公布）：PPI数据相对会高一点，市场的预期是在环比增速0.4%。

第三季度财报季开启

除了本周的CPI和PPI数据之外，我们将要迎来财报季度了，正式打开第三季度的财报记录。

周二盘前：UNH、Johnson & Johnson、JP Morgan

首先将要迎来的是周二盘前公布的UNH。那么医药医疗板块的个股，当然周二的盘前还会有Johnson & Johnson。UNH是我持仓之一，占比没有那么大，那我对于这个季度财报可能没有那么担心。

我清晰地还记得上一个季度财报发布完之后，股价破了短期内的新高，最高应该去到了450。去到450之后，接下去到现在已经要三个月了，三个月的时间基本上是在一路回调，现在是在360、370吧，我都忘了。

很多时候一个标的是这样——上个季度财报本身是没有问题的，所以发布完财报之后股价出现了上涨。但是管理层有聊到，其实不如他们的预期——他们在margin（利润率）这一块可以做到更好。所以有一部分他们在上半年所做的基本面改善，没有完全在上一个季度财报里反映出来。所以他们的期待是在接下去的两个季度，margin这一块会有更大的改善空间。

所以如果管理层在当时上一个季度财报聊的是正确的，或者能够有一个比较好的把握的话，我的期待是这个季度财报将会继续比市场预期要高。再加上从上一个季度到这个季度之间的这段时间，股价的走势不是那么强势，所以这个季度财报无论从股价也好、从基本面上也好，其实我倒没有非常担心。

不要赌财报：当然我再强调一遍，我每次在和大家聊财报展望的时候，我不希望大家去赌财报，没有意义，在背后就是55%这个概率。当然很多时候，如果进入这个财报季度之前，我们可以从市场的价格去判断——这个概率本身，如果一定要去赌的话，那么这个概率本身是不是站在我们这边。如果（股价走势）相对会弱一些的话，很多时候这个概率可能就站在我们这边。

银行板块：JP Morgan 领衔

周二的盘前还会有JP Morgan，正是打开了银行板块的财报。银行板块在过去一个多月表现相对弱势，但是这个季度财报你觉得会非常差吗？不可能差。因为当下的IPO市场又是那么的好，所以银行板块的财报也绝对不会非常差。那交易（sales）又比较好，所以在进入财报季度之前，市场相对是比较悲观的。

周二的盘前还会有高盛、Wells Fargo，这些相对来说就没有那么重要。我基本上会挑JP Morgan的财报仔细地去看一下，因为JP Morgan的财报既能够看到企业，也能够看到个人。

周三、周四重点：ASML、美国银行、台积电

周三盘前会有阿斯麦（ASML），还有美国银行——从消费者的健康状况这个角度去看，最重要的财报没有之一。

周四盘前会有台积电。这一周会有台积电和阿斯麦的财报。台积电财报是明牌了，几乎每一个季度出来之后都会比预期要高。但是因为他们每一个月都会公布上一个月的数据，所以每一次台积电的财报出来之后，市场的反馈或者影响都不会太大。

四、重点深度：高通CEO谈端侧AI的未来

最后我想和大家聊一下高通CEO在三四天前接受的一段采访。在采访里面，他聊了未来对于AI端侧这一块的看法。

主持人的挑战：既然有云，为何需要端侧？

首先主持人问了一个问题："我要挑战一下你的理论——前段时间Meta公布的Muse个人智能体，多数的行动是在云上进行的，然后把答案传回到你的手机。那这样的情况下，人们为什么需要手机？"

这个问题背后的思考是：已经有云在那边了，那为什么还需要端侧？

CEO 的回答：这不是零和游戏

CEO回答："我必须要小心，不能披露这个名字。但是已经有一家AI的前沿公司告诉我们，在28年底之前，他们需要在手机上能够跑100个本地模型，并且24/7都在进行跑。"

他继续说道："你会发现有很多的任务的确是需要在云上进行的，但是必须有很多的任务只能在设备上完成——我只能在端侧这一块完成。所以现在很多讨论云或者设备端这一块的争论是没有意义的，这并不是一个零和游戏。"

我的看法：AI 市场的三层架构

我个人也是这么看的，我并不认为这是一个零和游戏。整个市场对于云端这一块的需求只会越来越大，但是不代表端侧这一块的需求就完全没有。

而我个人对于未来AI整个市场，特别是在Agent市场这一块的预测，我个人的期待是：

  1. 端侧（On-Device）：首先在端侧的On-Device这一块，就不需要跑任何的云，对云没有任何需求。这一块的AI一定会有市场在那边，就类似于你手机上装一个AI智能体，其实就是类似于Siri的一个智能版本，一个智商更高的Siri，我觉得完全是有市场在那边的。

  2. AI RAN（基站层）：然后对于一些比较高需求的任务或者请求，可以去到类似于AI RAN——类似于现在是一个信息的基站。比如说我们现在手机的基站，可以去到这边。

  3. 云（Cloud）：然后对于那些需求更高的，可以跑到云。

英伟达的佐证：40%营收来自新兴渠道

他们CEO继续聊到："如果你有听上一个季度英伟达财报的时候，他们在上一个季度财报里面有聊到40个百分点的营收是来自于新云、端侧和主权AI。" 这边聊的端侧是on premise。

那如果当你在接受端侧AI的时候，你就必须要考虑未来这个端侧到底是在手机还是电脑端。

什么是 AI 手机？

那么到底什么是AI手机？高通CEO的回答是："当OpenAI面世的时候，AI手机的未来就比较清晰了。"

这个观点我是完全认同的。我一直在和大家最近这段时间聊AI智能体，我说AI智能体的第一代就是ChatGPT，然后我们在前段时间所看到的Meta下面的Muse算是智能体的第二代。

但是在C端、在消费者端这一块的AI智能体，绝对不会停在Muse。未来苹果一定会有自己的智能体，我个人也比较看好苹果未来这个智能体，主要是从安全这个角度去出发——我个人未来可能愿意把自己的一些比较隐私的数据和苹果去进行分享，包括谷歌也会有自己的智能体。

智能体起来后，硬件必须跟上

而当C端这一块的智能体在慢慢起来的时候，这时候人们就会考虑到对于硬件这一块的更新。当你有了智能体，当你有了应用场景之后，硬件端——无论是在手机端这一块，还是在电脑端这一块——这个硬件都必须要跟上。

而其实AI PC这一块，我们已经聊了起码两三年了。AI PC的概念，我记得苏妈在两三年之前就已经开始在聊AI PC了，只是当时很多人都认为AI PC没有任何的意义，没有任何的应用场景。但是现在你会发现AI PC——现在去聊AI PC你会发现非常合理了。包括英伟达自己，他们也有一个类似于AI PC这样的产品，我记得六七千美金吧。

当我们有了端侧AI之后，对于手机端和电脑端这一块硬件上的更新，几乎是一个必然的趋势。

那我在前两天发了一条推，我说：以前我们在买手机的时候，关注的是这个手机品牌本身、它的拍照功能到底如何；未来我们在挑选手机的时候，我们会挑选的是这个手机的硬件本身到底能够跑多强的AI。

五、合作活动：Seeking Alpha

最后，今天的活动来自于Seeking Alpha，这边是他们Alpha Picks量化的选股策略。

  • 业绩：YTD到现在为止，标普14%，这个策略本身是28%。
  • 近期选股：他们从9月1日到10月1日以来挑选了三只个股，这三个标的走的还是不错的。我在前段时间就和大家聊过，其中有两个标的其实是我最大的两个持仓之二。
  • 优惠：现在有一个优惠活动，是免费试用期，同时首年订阅可以立即节省50美金。另外大家知道他们一直有Premium的这档订阅，所以现在Premium加上Alpha Picks加在一起的话，有一个combo的价格，原本是798美金，现在是629美金。

大家对于Seeking Alpha的产品感兴趣的话，可以在置顶的留言里面找到订阅的链接。

好吗，那今天这期内容就到这边，下期见。
