item.description:
## 一、体感与数据的"认知错位"：市场参与者正在经历一场集体幻觉
本期最值得玩味的一点，不是高通CEO的采访，而是小陶一笔带过的那个**反直觉发现**——软件板块和半导体板块在10日滚动相关性上**并不显著负相关**，但几乎所有人的"体感"都坚信两者此消彼长。
这是典型的**"显著性偏误"（Salience Bias）**在金融市场的投射：人类大脑会放大那些发生在**同一天、同一屏幕、同一新闻周期**的反向波动，而忽略大量"同涨同跌"的沉默样本。这与行为经济学里卡尼曼讲的"可得性启发"是同一机制——我们记住的是戏剧化瞬间，不是平均状态。
**跨领域连接**：这个现象与神经科学中的"情绪记忆巩固"高度同构——杏仁核会优先存储情绪强度高的事件（恐慌日的负相关），而默认模式网络会主动忽略平淡的正相关日。换言之，**散户不是在交易市场，而是在交易自己杏仁核的放电模式**。真正的Alpha可能就藏在"体感和数据冲突"的那个夹缝里——当所有人都确信两者对立时，往往是均值回归的最佳时点。
## 二、"50日均线参与度低于20日均线"：一个被忽视的"基座空心化"信号
小陶提到三大指数的50

item.title: [Flirting with Models] Philip & Allan Maymin – Compounding Through Risk, Not Return (S7E35)
item.dc:creator: Flirting with Models
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的核心：Alpha 是"善变的"，而风险是"复利的"

Phil 用了一个几乎没人用来形容 alpha 的词——fickle（善变、水性杨花）。这个用词选择本身就是一个洞察：alpha 是会"背叛"你的情人，而 risk management 是会陪你变老的伴侣。但更深层的意外之处在于，他把这一点和 Merton 1980 年论文附录里的那条统计事实连在一起：你观察数据的频率再高，也无法提升对均值的估计，但可以无限提升对方差的估计。换句话说，宇宙在信息论意义上就偏袒风险管理者——时间越碎，你对风险的掌握越强，而你对收益的掌握永远停留在"几十年才能证伪零假设"的黑暗里。

这其实指向一个更尖锐的隐喻：在金融里，"知识"分为两种——会蒸发的知识（alpha）和会累积的知识（risk）。做 alpha 猎人的，一生都在和熵赛跑；做 risk 工匠的，每一天都在给知识加上利息。这解释了为什么顶级量化机构最终往往不是"更聪明的 alpha 发现者"，而是"更有耐心的风险塑形者"。

二、一个被低估的时间观革命：Volatility Time（波动率时间）

Phil 顺口提到的 "σ√t" 其实是整期播客最被低估的炸弹。Black-Scholes 不是五个参数的模型，它只有一个参数——sigma root t。这意味着——请感受这句话的分量——真实世界里，日历时间是一个幻觉，我们活在"风险时间"里。

这里有一个你可能没想到的跨领域连接：这个概念几乎完美对应柏格森（Henri Bergson）的 "绵延"（durée） 和爱因斯坦关于"物理时间 vs 心理时间"的争论。创伤心理学里也有同样的结构——创伤发生时，一分钟会被大脑编码为一小时的信息密度；而无聊的通勤两小时，可能在记忆里只占几秒。COVID 期间"一小时过完了一天"的交易感受，与一个受创者"几分钟过完一辈子"的主观体验，是同一套方程。

这给资产配置带来的启示极为暴力：你以为的"持有一年"，可能只是 30 个风险日；你以为的"短期波动"，可能已经消耗了你 3 个风险月的预算。对冲基金的"年化"和"换手率"概念都应该被 σ√t 重写。更妙的是，Phil 把它接到了行为金融——在波动率加速的时候才临时开会讨论风险，等于在风暴中拼命读天气预报；真正的风险管理，是在风险时间的"寂静带"里提前把决策烘焙好。

三、LTCM 的"真·教训"：风险是关于别人以为你拿着什么

Phil 对 LTCM 的描述里埋着一个全市场几乎没人注意的点——"很多头寸爆仓不是因为我们真的持有，而是因为别人以为我们持有"。这是一句索罗斯式的 reflexivity 直译，但穿着一件工程师制服。

这与 Allan 对 2010 Flash Crash 的叙述形成了精彩的对称——那次崩盘里，赢家市商在下午两三点互相对视、发现"没人在报价了"的一刻，意识到：流动性不是价格的函数，而是其他参与者"相信谁在场"的函数。两兄弟分别从 LTCM 和 HFT 走来，最后在 Janus Henderson 汇合，不是巧合——他们都从"流动性消失"的废墟上学到了同一件事：市场定价的不是资产本身，而是关于资产的二阶信念。

跨领域连接：这正是凯恩斯"选美比赛"的高频金融版本，也是量子力学里的测量问题——观察行为本身改变被观察物。因此他们选择用期权作为信号源的真正原因，可能比他们自己说的还要深：期权价格是市场参与者"押注给他们信念"的唯一诚实场所。股票价格里混杂着被迫交易、机械再平衡、税务卖出；而买期权必须付出 premium——它是市场里信号噪比最高的"坦白房间"。

四、一个让人起鸡皮疙瘩的 GPS 隐喻

Myron Scholes 对 Phil 说的那段"每个人都用 GPS，世界会更好"是整期最哲学的时刻。表面是讲 reflexive 问题（如果大家都用期权信号会不会失效），但底下其实是在重述哈耶克的"分散知识问题"——市场作为"没人能看全的集体计算机"。

但 Myron 更激进的地方是：他希望自己的策略被所有人学会。这与绝大多数量化基金"求求你别发现我的 alpha"的心态是镜像的——这揭示了一个产业结构性的秘密：追求 alpha 的人希望信息稀缺，追求 risk engineering 的人希望信息普及。前者玩的是零和，后者玩的是正和。这也解释了为什么像 Scholes 这样级别的学者能坦然把方法论公开——因为在风险管理的世界里，普及不是威胁，而是胜利。

五、彩蛋级洞察：生成式 AI 视频 ≈ 投资组合里的"凸性"

最后 Phil 对 AI 视频的痴迷，表面是闲聊，其实是他整套投资哲学的隐秘延续。他说"视频可以传递任何能被传递的东西"——注意这个结构，和他说期权时的措辞是一样的："期权蕴含了关于未来所有可能性的分布"。他的大脑在用同一个模板处理两个领域——寻找"信息密度最高的媒介"。

Allan 补一句"也许 AI agents 之间以后应该互相发视频"更是神来之笔——这是在把信息论、注意力经济学和多 agent 协调问题打包成一个三秒的俏皮话。如果你把这两人的"obsession"连起来，你会发现他们在投资和生活中其实追求同一个东西：用最简洁的通道压缩最多的分布信息——期权是金融的视频，视频是人类的期权。

📝 转录文本

Cold Open

All right, gentlemen. Are you ready? — Ready. — Yep. — All right. Three, two, one, let's jam.

Host Introduction & Disclaimer

Hello and welcome everyone. I'm Corey Hoffstein and this is Flirting with Models, the podcast that pulls back the curtain to discover the human factor behind the quantitative strategy.

Cory Hoffstein is the co-founder and chief investment officer of Newfound Research. Due to industry regulations, he will not discuss any of Newfound Research's funds on this podcast. All opinions expressed by podcast participants are solely their own opinion and do not reflect the opinion of Newfound Research. This podcast is for informational purposes only and should not be relied upon as a basis for investment decisions. Clients of Newfound Research may maintain positions and securities discussed in this podcast. For more information, visit thinknewfound.com.

Episode Preview

In this episode, I speak with Philip and Allan Maymin, co-heads of global asset allocation at Janus Henderson. Philip and Allan run the asset allocation group originally founded at Janus Henderson by Nobel Laureate Myron Scholes more than a decade ago, and they've arrived there by wonderfully different routes — Philip through LTCM, academia, and behavioral analytics; Allan through high-frequency trading, derivatives, and prop desks.

At the heart of their process is a simple but subversive idea. As Philip put it on our pre-call: "People live in an average return world, and they ought not. What matters to investors is compound growth." And the brothers believe that the surest way to improve compounding isn't chasing higher returns, but managing risk. Drawdowns destroy compounding, and avoiding them is the more tractable lever.

They connect theory to practice through the options market. Calls and puts embed the market's collective forward-looking views of risk, making them one of the richest sources of information available to an asset allocator. We discuss how they extract those signals and propagate them across more than 4,000 assets to build portfolios around client objectives rather than benchmarks.

Please enjoy my conversation with Philip and Allan Maymin.

Welcome

Corey: Phil and Allan, welcome to the show. This is a first — first time having brothers on a show together. Hopefully, we'll get some brotherly love. We won't get the brotherly fighting as it would be if I had my brother on this show, and we'll have a great episode here. So, thank you so much for joining me. Really excited about this one.

Guests: Likewise. Thanks for having us.

Philip's Journey: LTCM, Myron Scholes, and the Winding Path Back

Corey: Now, because we got two of you, we're going to have to do a little bit of an abbreviated intro here. Going to quickly try to run through some of your backgrounds, maybe a bit of a speedrun. But Phil, I want to start with you. You both have very interesting paths to get to where you are today. Phil, you're starting a little bit earlier than your brother, but your path — starting with LTCM in the '90s, ended up getting a PhD, you ran your own hedge fund for a while, you went to academia for a bit, you did behavioral analytics at Essentia, and then you finally joined Janus Henderson four years ago. That is a bit of a meandering journey. Maybe you can build a thread through it for me. Talk me through how those things all connect to lead you to where you are today.

Phil: I started — my first boss out of college was Myron. All roads basically meandered away and back. He was my first boss. He's my current boss, and hopefully he'll be my last boss. He's awesome. If I have any regrets, it's that there were years in between where I wasn't working with Myron. Working with him — we were just talking about it with Alan — like, it's the highlight of the day. We chat almost every day and it's always a highlight. He's wonderful.

So that's kind of been my journey. I started LTCM, did a few other hedge funds, including my own. At some point, I got a PhD, and when you get a PhD, you have to go into academia right away. So, if anyone out there is thinking about getting a PhD, just know that once you finish it, if you don't go into being a professor right then and there, it'll be much harder later — because they don't understand. They'll ask you, "You know, it's been a couple of years. You got your PhD a couple years ago. Why haven't you published?" Well, because now it's been working. It's all proprietary. They don't get it. So you have to go right away when you have that one piece of work — your dissertation — that's something that the system is ready to evaluate. Like, "Okay, now you can be a professor," and then after that, do whatever you want.

My first job in academia was at NYU financial engineering. At the time, financial engineering — it became something like finance and analytics. The MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference started having a research paper track. Allan and I and a friend of ours — we started writing papers for it. So that's how I grew from sort of finance to also sports analytics. Now I'm a professor of just analytics and AI.

And that led to eventually an introduction with Essentia. Essentia is a really interesting firm. They do behavioral analytics. It was a combination of all of my loves — you know, finance and portfolio management and behavioral decision-making and sports analytics. And there, the clients are portfolio managers who are trying to enhance the way they make decisions to reduce their behavioral biases. And it was a really wonderful opportunity. So then I joined Allan and Myron and the rest of the team here four years ago. It's been awesome. This is the best place ever.

Lessons from LTCM

Corey: It's hard to talk to someone who was at LTCM — had a front row seat to that experience — and not ask them about it. So I apologize for the cliche of having to ask you about that. But my really specific question to you is: right, LTCM is known as this large blowup. I'm curious how you thought about risk before your experience at LTCM, and how LTCM shaped your view of what risk is, and risk in a portfolio post the blowup.

Phil: I was trading equity derivatives. Equity derivatives were different than the majority of the fixed income and other kind of asset classes that LTCM was trading. The world at the time was different. It's hard to remember. There's, you know, zero margin flying. So literally you're just trying to find alpha and scale it up as much as you can, and you hope that it's uncorrelated.

So one thing of course that everybody learned is: in the tail, correlations go to one. Great. It's very important lesson. But to be fair, from the equity derivatives desk, we were working with convertible bonds and warrants and stuff like that. Risk was always on the table. Even though there was no margin, you still have to think about performance relative to the risk you're taking.

The biggest takeaway for me was the correlations of the tails, and that the tails — this turned out later to be a focus of my dissertation — can be self-imposed limits to arbitrage. That even if you could do more, there might be times when you should not. And part of the reason is that if other people think that you are doing it — like what happened with LTCM — there were a lot of trades that blew out during that period not because we held anything, but because people thought we held those things. Well, they were wrong. We didn't. But the spreads blew because of the worry that we might have to be unwinding. So those were, I think, the biggest lessons for me.

Allan's Journey: HFT, Flash Crash, and Liquidity Economics

Corey: All right, Alan, putting you in the hot seat. Like your brother, you've got quite a few hops in your career before you ended up happily where you are. So let's run through those. You started in quant execution algorithms sort of at the earlier dawn of the HFT era. You then went to Platinum Grove. You did sell-side derivatives at SocGen and then an internal hedge fund at Alliance Bernstein — finally a prop firm before joining Janus Henderson.

In our pre-call, one of the things you said and observed was that most stat and HFT strategies, quote, "worked better when things fell apart," and I thought that was an interesting observation and something I was hoping you could expand upon. Building off of the back of what your brother said thinking about risk — and so much of our conversation here is going to be shaped about risk — thinking about the experience in your career, how you built that observation, and sort of what it means to you about how markets behave under stress.

Allan: The way that I would approach it is that my background is more so on the development side. And so early on in my finance career, just in an attempt to be useful, things like quantitative execution and HFT and writing pricing tools and stuff at a sell-side bank are just ways to get a bit of your foot in the door and provide utility and provide value by writing code.

Interestingly, I was fortunate to live through some of 2008, but the moment that really stands out to me was the flash crash of 2010. When I say "things worked better as stuff fell apart," what I'm trying to say is that a lot of these shorter time frame stat-HFT style strategies do better by taking advantage of uninformed flow — flow where people mechanically have to trade.

I know that they played the blame game quite a bit for the 2010 flash crash. I remember there was some retail guy that really took the brunt of it. But the interesting thing for me was that once the selling started cascading, people had to continue to trade — whether it was delta hedging and the way that they were positioned from a gamma perspective required them to sell, or whether it was intraday levered ETFs or momentum. The thing that I found interesting is that it became kind of a self-reinforcing loop. There was trading that had to happen.

And I had learned way after the fact that one of the market makers that had their best day there turned around, looked at each other somewhere around 2 p.m. or 3 p.m. — I forget when the bottom was — realized that spreads were super wide, there was nobody else available to make markets, and took a total gamble. And I found that to be extremely interesting — that a lot of these shorter time frame trading styles are related to liquidity, whether it's making or taking. When you're the only provider of liquidity, you can charge whatever you want.

"Faster = Dumber, Slower = Smarter"?

Corey: So if we trace your career, Allan — you know, you start in HFT, you now end up in asset allocation. I don't think you could talk about a larger swing in terms of the time horizon over which you're talking about making decisions. Again, in our pre-call, you had a quote that was, "As you get faster, you get dumber, and as you get slower, you get smarter." And I'm sure maybe some of my prior HFT guests might take a little bit of offense to that, but I was hoping you could expand on that because I think it's a potentially controversial line, but one in which there is a lot of meaning to dig out — and again, I think will help set the table for the rest of the conversation.

Allan: I think that line is common quant lore for sure. I agree that there is plenty of smart people at the shorter time frame, and in fact probably the genesis of several of the technologies that we're now leveraging — for example, solar flare and things like that in AI land.

I think maybe a better distinction might be explainable versus non-explainable. Now I'm not saying necessarily linear versus nonlinear or anything like that — you can absolutely use very fast nonlinear models at very low time frames — but perhaps you are less interested in the explainability of your short-term flow-related trading. Whereas when you zoom out to longer horizons, you kind of need that explainability. Your Sharpe ratios naturally fall back down to earth, and you kind of need some sort of anchor as to why you remain within a particular strategy. So if you have an explainability, if you have an economic rationale, if you have something that you can anchor towards, you can maintain your exposure in a trading strategy that might be underperforming temporarily due to noise.

The Janus Henderson Asset Allocation Group

Corey: So let's talk a little bit about Janus Henderson. Phil — Myron Scholes founded the asset allocation group over a decade ago. You mentioned that you talk to him every day. You two now co-head the asset allocation group. Can you talk a little bit about who your clients are and the service that you're providing them?

Phil: Yeah, we have a mixture of clients — a mixture of institutional and retail, because we have, like, a mutual fund for which retail gets some exposure. The unifying philosophy is: we want to enhance compound returns, which I'm sure we'll dig into.

Specifically, we care about giving you a solution. We're not just telling you here's the only things we can trade or provide for you. What is your problem? What are your objectives? What are your constraints? And let's architect something using dynamic risk management, using our tools, using our signals, using our philosophy that can get you where you need to go.

There's a difference between objectives and outcomes. They sound like they're synonyms, but they're different. Objectives is what you're targeting for, what you need, and then you check the outcomes to see: are we delivering on that promise? Are you getting the excess returns you wanted for the reasons you expected — as opposed to just being luck?

So that's what we're trying to do. We start with asking each client what they're trying to achieve and why. If you just ask each other, "Hey, I want more money and no risk" — obviously. But what is the money for? When will you need it? What will you do if you lose money? How much can you handle? And then we tailor the risk and tailor the portfolio construction to attempt to deliver on that client objective subject to the constraints.

Why Risk — Not Return — Is the Lever for Compounding

Corey: I know this idea of compounding is really critical to the way that you all think about portfolio construction. In our pre-call, you sort of laid out the chain of logic as being: well, everyone wants more money, more money comes from better compounding, and while you could try to improve expected returns, I think your quote was "risk is easier." Maybe you can talk a little bit about why risk is more tractable as a lever for improving compounding versus expected returns.

Phil: This is awesome because there's quite a few reasons.

First, there's this anomaly or puzzle. If you have a positive average return scenario — right, you have some alpha, that's your average return — what you really want is to make more money later. So you want the compound return to be higher. And the compound return differs from the average by the risk track. Fair enough.

Now what that means is: for any average return, no matter how good an average alpha you have, if I sprinkle enough noise into it, you will start losing money. No matter how much alpha you have, there exists some amount of risk that can be experienced that suddenly you end up getting a call. It's a kind of good news / bad news situation. The good news is our alpha is stable — we're continuing to deliver 5% average returns. Bad news: you're broke because of the risk. It's harder to make up a downside once you lose money.

If you think about an equation, compound return = average return − risk.

Alpha Is Fickle; Risk Compounds

Average return — you know, I don't use this word a lot and I've never heard this word used a lot. Whenever I hear it, it's always related to alpha. Alpha is fickle. You never hear about "fickle," right? It's not a very common word, but it perfectly encapsulates what alpha is. You could spend your entire career — and it could be a short career, could be a long career — and suddenly you wake up one day and what you thought was your source of alpha is gone. The world has changed, it's moved on. Your contacts are gone. The sort of information knowledge you thought you were extracting is just suddenly gone.

That's not the case for risk management. If you're managing risk, you're expecting things to change, and you can build not a fickle source of knowledge, but a compound base of knowledge that grows on itself. You know how to manage in different environments. That's not going to go away. We're going to suddenly live in a world where there's only one environment? No, environments will always change.

Merton 1980 — Statistical Asymmetry Between Mean and Variance

The other reason is: Bob Merton in 1980 — he wrote a paper, and one of the things most memorable (it was a great paper, but even in the appendix) he had a really important insight. The insight was this: purely on a statistical basis, how confident, how far back do you have to be just looking at data to distinguish an alpha — an average return, an average — from being a zero? And you have to go pretty far back. All it depends on is the length of time. It doesn't matter if you slice it up into weekly or daily returns. It doesn't matter — just the starting and ending and how long a period you have.

So you have to go back pretty far — sometimes decades — to be sure that what you're measuring just statistically is different from zero. So at some point you're like, "IBM — does it have a positive alpha?" and you're comparing returns from the 1970s. Like, that's not the IBM of today. What is the point?

So alpha is fickle. It's hard to measure. Fine. But risk — risk, as he shows in that appendix, and as you well know, the finer you cut the returns, the better your measurement of risk. It's stronger, more secure. You don't have to go further back in time. You just cut it from monthly to weekly to daily to hourly, and you have a better and better estimate of risk.

So those things combined: risk is easier to measure, it's reflecting the environment that things can change, you're able to compound your knowledge, you're able to build things for the long run. That's why it's the more tractable, the easier, the more important lever for compound returns.

Defining Risk: Not Volatility, But Falling Short of Objectives

Corey: Allan, the process that you and the team have built is around what you guys call your "dynamic risk management" process. When most of the industry hears "risk" — when we talk about academic papers being published around risk — they're traditionally talking about volatility. What does risk mean to you when you think about it, both conceptually and from an actual measurement perspective?

Allan: For us, what we believe is that risk is the chance of falling short of the client's objective — not necessarily just how much the portfolio moves. For us, if we take an objective-based approach and we can define various scenarios for a particular client or a mandate, what we like to look at in risk space is the chance of not delivering what the client is looking to achieve.

When people think of risk and they think of volatility, the other problem that they will experience is that volatility treats gains and losses alike. What we do is we try to separate out the upside risk — which for all intents and purposes could be something that you want. Downside risk, on the other hand, is something that we look to tilt away from. From our perspective, we think of risk not necessarily as a volatility measure, but more so a probability measure. Something along the lines of: what are the various outcomes available, and how can we tilt those outcomes in the direction of the upside of what the client wants and away from the downside of what the client would not want?

Extracting Signal from the Options Market

Corey: I know one of the key inputs for your process is looking at options markets — information embedded in puts and calls to inform your risk estimates. And this is across not just major asset classes, but — correct me if I'm wrong — I think it's thousands of assets and securities that you're grabbing this data for to help inform your portfolio construction. Can you talk a little bit about how you utilize the options chain and the information embedded in there to help you measure both upside and downside risk, and how it informs your process?

Allan: The best thing about the options market is that they provide a forward-looking estimate of the upside and downside of a particular asset. Further, they require an exchange of premium in order for a trade to occur. So truly, people need to put their money where their mouth is in order for the options market to clear.

As a result, by reading the information, by reading the trades, by reading the prices, we can see where people are expecting the asset to move over a certain period. This information is extremely rich. It transcends multiple different time horizons and multiple different strikes. In other words, you can see — across an entire distribution of possible outcomes over a variety of time periods — what the market is saying is the probability of the underlying to achieve that particular outcome.

For us, we can take that information and we can translate it into: what is the probability or what is the likelihood of this asset moving up — what is the upside risk? Similarly, what is the downside risk or the left-tail risk of a particular asset? By keeping track of that information over time, and importantly their ratio, we can see how an asset changes its upside versus downside over time. And that information is extremely valuable because that is the market's implied distribution of returns for a particular asset over time. And that is helpful for us because we can then take our portfolio, which we put together for a particular client, and tilt it in favor of assets that are more likely to have upside or good outcomes and away from assets that have downside or bad outcomes.

The P vs. Q Problem

Corey: Anyone who's classically trained as a quant — or certainly in derivatives — is going to immediately jump on the fact that options are priced under what we call the risk-neutral measure, and you're trying to use them to make statements about real-world risk, the P measure. Those are different measures, and they're not necessarily always in alignment with each other. So I'm curious how you think about sort of this P vs. Q problem when using option-implied signals.

Phil: What is the biggest difference in the two measures? It's of course the drift, right? And that's what Fischer and Myron showed in 1973. The drift is completely different. It's risk-neutral in one versus whatever arbitrary thing it is in reality. The rest of the distribution can also be different. However, you can try a simulation of assuming what the real is and then figuring out what the risk-neutral is. Almost all of that difference is coming from the change in the drift. The shape of the distribution is fairly robust across the changes in measure.

Like Alan was saying, we have the upside risk, we have the downside risk. It's not a coincidence that we're ignoring the middle. The entire philosophy is built on the idea that middles don't matter. It's the tails that matter.

You can throw away — we have a paper showing this — you can throw away the middle 80% of a distribution and your risk is basically the same. You're going to have an 80 to 90% correlation, and 80 to 90% of the risk is still there. The tails are what matter. And the tails — that's what the options price very, very well. That's the shapes that we take as signals.

And bear in mind, like Alan was saying, it's not that we're taking one number on one day and that's some god-given truth. We're looking at the changes in that signal relative to itself, relative to others. Things don't always work 100%, but the risk we're not so much worried about is the P versus Q — the risk-neutral versus real-world — because it would have to differ in a way that goes against all of these different parts of our process that translated into a reasonable signal.

And at the end of the day, it's a very reasonable thing. Look — what is Allan saying that we're doing? Ultimately, boiling it down: if suddenly and for an extended period of time, people are buying a lot more calls and a lot less puts — that's interesting information. P versus Q notwithstanding, there's something there. There are more people buying upside — they're putting their money where their mouth is — than downside. That's a signal. If no other asset is doing that, then there's something special about this one.

Why the 90th Percentile?

Corey: Your actual measure of choice is looking at the 90th percentile conditional value at risk, along with its upside counterpart. Why the 90th percentile rather than, say, the 95th or the 99th?

Allan: Probably the best, most cleanest way to answer it is that for any parameter — as you know, when you choose inside of any quant system, you're going to have to pick something. And for us, what we found is the 90th percentile, the 10 delta — that's a wingy option that kind of sort of makes sense. There's typically volume, there's typically prices — spreads are not insane. It's wingy, but not teeny. It's not something that is extremely out there.

And what it does is it provides a measure by which we can put a line in the sand. Anything after this for us is an upside or a downside. Once you're past this point, you're very much in a tail scenario. And seeing what the expected or average or typical experience in such a scenario is — that's the value that we try to extract from the options market. What does a tail feel like, whether it's to the upside or to the downside? We know for sure that once you cross this barrier — you're past the 90th percentile — you're definitely in a tail. And so for us, extracting out what that experience looks like is the signal that we're trying to infer from the options market.

Objective-Driven Portfolio Construction

Corey: Let's talk a little bit about how you actually take these measures and go to build portfolios. And I want to start by going back to your discussion of providing solutions to clients. You effectively are taking an approach that's more objective- or outcome-driven investing for your clients. What does that really mean in practice? When you sit down with a new client, what are you actually asking them at the outset, and how do their answers shape the process downstream of the portfolio you're building?

Phil: One of the perspectives we encourage them to move towards and answering — and this is sometimes very natural for people, but sometimes it can be a little bit new — is a drawdown. What is the maximum drawdown that you could tolerate and still recover? And that differs for each person, for each institution — what they're comfortable taking.

Sometimes that's a new question for them because they may have just lived in a world where they always have a 60/40 reference portfolio and they're looking to outperform it, and that's it. But when you start asking that question, then you start realizing: where did 60/40 come from? Why is that a god-given standard?

Where 60/40 Really Comes From

And it comes from, at heart, a very reasonable thing — which is: look, equities in times of trouble historically, let's say they're down 50%. But we can't really tolerate a 50% drawdown because that would mean that we have to double the next year, and that's too much risk, and we have investors and clients, and it's not going to happen. But we could tolerate a 30% drawdown. We can claw our way back from that. We have a long enough horizon, we can do it.

So how do you get to a 30% drawdown? Well, if you have only 60% equities and you assume fixed income is fairly uncorrelated during these tumultuous times, then you're going to have a 30% drawdown. That's what a 60/40 is intended to convey, and that's kind of the proxy that people have come to — because what they're really looking for is sort of like a 30% drawdown.

Once you start extracting that way of thinking, then they can be more specific. Well, okay, maybe it is 30%. Maybe it's time to up it a little bit or down a little. Maybe we want to change it over time. But if the drawdown is what matters, then we can start to go away from a solution that treats fixed income correlation with equities as a hedge.

The Death of the Equity-Bond Negative Correlation

The three of us — and I'm sure many of your listeners — we've all grown up in worlds the past few decades until a few years ago where it was a law of nature that equities and fixed income are negatively correlated. Bonds go up, stocks go down, and vice versa. That this is reality. It's a new law of physics. And then 2022 came, and of course it's not the case. They can both be positively correlated. You can lose both at the same time. So you're not even hedged. The 40% could be down precisely when you need it to not be down.

In fact, if you look back 100 years, 150 years, more often than not, they're positively correlated — which makes sense. How can you have two positive expected return asset classes, the biggest ones in the world, and they're negatively correlated? You have some kind of arbitrage there. It cannot be the case going forward.

So instead of a static solution towards the drawdown problem — which is the real problem that you have if you acknowledge that the drawdown is the issue — "this is our maximum drawdown budget, and of course we want to do as much upside as we can, but that's our budget" — then you can start to think dynamically. How can we manage dynamically our exposures in order to accomplish our goal of making as much as possible subject to this particular constraint of drawdown?

Tax-Aware Investing as Another Objective

Corey: Risk seems like maybe the most obvious objective — other than people might have their return target, which is maybe a little bit harder to outright achieve — but what other objectives are clients coming to you with?

Allan: The one that we're seeing more and more frequently is: how can a client achieve a specific post-tax return? Taxes are something that are typically difficult to put inside of an optimizer, but our system allows that as part of our customization for individual clients.

All else equal, when you have a large universe or a menu of options for names that you would want to tilt a portfolio in favor of and away from, it seems incredibly reasonable to include the tax impact of a particular name. So all else equal, if you're going to sell a name to create cash to buy another name, it is probably more beneficial to sell a name which has generated a tax loss versus other names.

Ultimately, tax-aware investing is simply a optimization function where it's a bit of a tax deferral. It's intended for a client that wants to maintain control and certainty around when they pay their taxes. By no means are we removing taxes from the equation, but it helps smooth out the time component. So if there's a large windfall or something like that, it can help defer a short-term gain into a long-term gain.

Stale Portfolio Risk

Corey: One of the common questions that comes up with these tax deferral strategies — whether they're long-only or long-short — is the ossification risk. Can you talk a little bit about how that plays into how you're thinking about building portfolios, and the tradeoff of the expected return and managing the downside risk versus this post-tax return you're trying to generate, and the risk that the portfolio ultimately gets sort of stuck in a position that you end up having to realize taxes to get back to meeting those primary downside risk and return objectives that they have?

Allan: The stale portfolio problem is one that is more and more common these days when the market is straight up, especially how tilted it is for certain names. There's just no opportunity to harvest it nearly ever — it being up so much. Some of the tools available to you are, like you said, being both long and short — that allows you opportunities across more parts of the market cycle to make those types of trades.

And lastly, I would add that ultimately it comes down to a tradeoff. At any point in time, you can turn over the portfolio to get to where you want. And it's up to the system, it's up to the model, it's up to the client to decide if it is worth it. If the risk of a position is high enough to warrant paying those taxes — well, then you should probably do that.

Portfolio Construction: Mechanics

Corey: So once you have the client's objective and you have your risk estimates, talk to me about actually mechanically how you are constructing this portfolio.

Allan: As Phil mentioned, everything starts first and foremost with the client's objective and what is it that the client is looking to achieve with a particular mandate. More often than not, in fact, what the client is most interested in is their long-run compound average returns. And for that, we found that keeping a drawdown budget within check is the best way to accomplish this goal.

Step One: How Much Risk?

So, in terms of constructing the portfolio, the first thing that we typically would look at is: what is the performance of the portfolio? What is the current drawdown relative to the drawdown budget? And that leaves the remaining risk that's available to be taken. The first thing that we can then decide is how much risk can we take.

Step Two: Where to Put It?

And the second question then becomes: where should we put that risk? The question for both step one and step two — as we call them, we're not incredibly creative on the quant side — is: what is the available opportunity set in the market?

Can we come up with an aggregated version of what is the opportunity set in terms of forward-looking risk? Put simply, what is the available downside risk and upside risk of a generic risky asset versus cash — which is inherently risk-free? That's our first step. And our second step is: now that we're allocating to risk, what does that risk look like? This is where we would look at various different asset classes, regions, or even bottoms-up individual names to determine how can we tilt the portfolio in favor of names that are more likely to have upside risk and away from names that are more likely to have downside risk.

Connecting Options Signals to Portfolio Construction

Corey: So maybe you can explicitly draw the connection to me there from information you're inferring and extracting from the options market to actually constructing the portfolio, right? How do those two things connect? You get the client's objective. You know their drawdown constraint. Now you're trying to build a portfolio using expected returns, covariances, information you've extracted from the options market. How is this all tying together?

Phil: We of course don't explicitly use expected returns. We use these measures of risk — of tail risk — in the upside and the downside. Ultimately, we're running a portfolio construction optimization. What are we trying to optimize? Ultimately, it's the skewness. It's the expected tail gains and expected tail losses, right — at your C-bar 90 and your C-bar 10. And that ratio — the expected tail gain divided by the expected tail loss for the portfolio — that's the convexity you wish to generate.

Once you have convexity, or that skewness — to the extent that those forecasted future numbers that are coming in from the option markets are in fact really good forecasters of what will happen in the future, and the research says that they are, and we've done some — and so we know that implied measures of risk (of course implied volatility) subsumes all other predictions of risk. You can add realized volatility alongside your implied volatility to try to pick your future volatility, and you get all the weight on the implied and nothing on the realized. It has 100% basically the explainable power.

Why? Because if there was additional information that could have been useful, the option prices would have been adjusted. Otherwise, you have arbitrage. So, we know that the implied forecasts are better. That's also true for gains and losses — for the expected tail gain and the expected tail losses. So we do have this research and this belief and this understanding that the option markets are telling you — roughly back to your original question of the risk-neutral versus real-world — we know that they do in fact predict what tends to really happen in terms of changes in upside risk and changes in downside risk.

Great. So if we have that forecastability — if there's a relationship between what the options are telling us today and what the road ahead really will be — then, to the extent you can create a portfolio that using those forecasts is tilted towards being more skewed and more positive convective, having more upside relative to the amount of downside risk you're taking, and that reflects itself in the future — then what you've done is you've engineered exactly the dynamic risk management you want to enhance your compound returns. You have more upside participation, lower downside participation. That's the holy grail. Not alpha, like we discussed — alpha is fickle — but this kind of convexity. That's the goal. If you can have that that's sustainable, it's long-lasting, it's transferable — this is the goal.

Hierarchical Optimization: Equity-vs-Cash First

So that's the portfolio construction methodology. That's what it's trying to optimize — find a portfolio that creates the maximum amount of that convexity, but it has all sorts of constraints. One of those constraints is downside risk. We want to maximize that skewness, but subject to not having more than this much exposure to the drawdown.

Well, that can affect how much — if the downside risk forecast for the major risk markets of, say, equities are elevated, then of course you want to scale back a little bit. If the attractiveness is increased, then you want to increase a little bit. If you do have an explicit drawdown budget and you've already used some of it, then of course you have to scale back a little bit.

So all those things combined, we try to make things kind of hierarchical and simple. We don't want you — you know, all the problems that happen with overfitting and the optimizations, right, then the weights float all over the place. So we start by asking the biggest questions first.

What's the biggest question? Biggest question in any portfolio you're going to run in the modern world where equities have more volatility and they explain almost all the volatility of any portfolio — is roughly how much equity exposure should you have. If you reduce your question to just how much equity versus cash should I have — that's the first question we solve. That's what Alan was referring to as step one in our wildly imaginative naming convention.

Step two is: given that we've gotten that question fairly correct — that's where we've done all the optimization, we figured out "this is roughly how much equities you can handle given this forward-looking risk, given your exposure so far and everything that's happened" — now, can we put in a little bit of fixed income? As we're putting in a little bit of fixed income, what it's doing is optimizing, but it's tethered to that step one. You don't want to have too much tracking error from that. You can change your equity allocation a little bit, but you want to be close to that step one because you know that it's roughly the right way to go.

And then there might be a few other steps for different constraints that you're particularly feeling. Can you allow commodities or not? Can you do regional allocation as well? So maybe we build some bottom-up portfolios using the same approach that we do for top-down, but just to create the most convex possible component categories. And that's it. We mush all those together, and then you have what your model portfolio would be today. And finally, of course, you do the trading to determine how much tracking error you will take — is it tilted trade and so on.

Tail Correlations: The Hidden Simplicity

Corey: At the risk of going from a very sort of high-level description down to the minutiae too quickly, I want to zoom in on this measure that you're talking about. Where you're looking at the upside portfolio risk versus the downside — it rhymes very much with looking at expected return over portfolio variance. The big difference here, again, using these option-implied CVaR measures, is that particularly with something like the downside — and you're talking about something like a covariance matrix — these measures are not inherently additive. You're having to — I don't want to be presumptive — but make some assumptions around correlations in the tails to think about what that downside portfolio level CVaR is as it's composed of all these underlying individual measures. So maybe you can talk a little bit about some of these numerical problems and how you're thinking about them — knowing that the nice thing about variance and covariance is that it is additive, whereas in something like CVaR, it's not.

Phil: Remember the lesson from LTCM? And I'm sure everyone's had this lesson before — correlations are tricky when and where in the middles, like equity and fixed income for the past few years and decades. It's tricky, right? It can change from minus .3 to plus .3, and that ruins people. So estimating that is really hard. It's really slippery.

But what about in the tails? In the tails, it's much easier, isn't it? We have a much simpler challenge in the tails. In the tails, we know the correlations are one. The only real challenge is going to be plus one or minus one. We can talk about some tools we've developed for that kind of thing using regime-based correlation and stuff like that. But already we've simplified it, because we know that the correlations will be very, very high — and we're managing to the tails.

It does rhyme with expected return over variance. The way we look at it is skewness — or expected tail gain divided by expected tail loss, and then that whole thing divided by expected tail loss again. So you get exactly what you were talking about, where you have expected tail gain divided by expected tail loss squared, just like you have mean-variance optimization instead of mean-standard-deviation. So the downside plays a much more oversized role. That's the most important thing — is on the downside.

So if we can get estimates of correlation for on the tails — the downside 10% tails on the downside — that essentially answers the questions that we need. We don't have to worry about the middle correlation. We don't have to worry about the upside correlations.

Regime-Based Tail Correlations

Corey: I would love to hear you talk a little bit about that regime dependence, because I can certainly think of regimes where certain assets might have positive correlations and other regimes where they would almost certainly have negative correlations. But you can talk a little bit about how that flows through the optimization process.

Phil: Again, remember that we've simplified it to just thinking about tails. So one of the things we can do is look at the current levels of volatility — let's say equities and fixed income — relative to their own history. If they are both in the top quartile, the top 25% of their history — equities are elevated and fixed income is elevated — what do you think that tells you about the tail correlation in the current environment? If there's a problem, they're probably positively correlated. That's probably a plus-one correlation. They're both very elevated. People are worried about both things.

What if one of them is above — it's in the top quartile — and the other one's in the bottom quartile? So people are terrified in one asset class and not at all in the other? Then maybe we're thinking about, like, a minus-one tail correlation environment. And if neither of those extremes are in the situation — we're both kind of around 50/50 or something — then we're closer to a zero tail correlation.

That's a simple way of doing it. We have more complicated things where we would also blend it with recent, or very modern, like high-frequency correlation measures, just to ground it towards something more dynamic. But that's the essential approach: first simplify the problem, and then use simple proxies to get at what we're looking for.

Model Parsimony: Simple But Not Simpler

Corey: As I listen to all these answers, there's this continued pattern of deliberately choosing simple formulations over complex ones. And I don't mean "complex" in a negative manner. In our pre-call, you said the whole world runs on linear regressions because there's so much noise. Can you talk a little bit about your views on the tradeoffs of model parsimony? When is a model too simple and not capturing all the salient features of what's happening in markets versus the risk of going the other way and adding too many confounding variables?

Allan: One interesting thing about our line of work is a very low signal-to-noise ratio. It is inherently hard to make predictions on things which we have one sample point. The world only moves in one direction in terms of time.

So for us, it's very important that we have faith in our process, that we have faith in our philosophy, that we can stick to it and we don't need to question too much about it. It also means that it's very easy to overfit. So for us, when we go through the research process, the first and foremost thing that we do is we ask ourselves: is there an economic rationale as to why something should work? And if so, what is the simplest possible expression of this particular thing that we're researching?

So to answer your question about the simplicity — it is in fact a goal of ours is to make the model as simple as possible, but no simpler. As you know, for quants, that's inherently difficult. We like to overfit. We like to have a complex and beautiful model that answers every little nook and cranny about why a market moved in the way that it did.

But like Myron discovered in the '70s, the simplicity of the assets that we're looking at comes from things that are on the risk side. It comes from the ability to separate out the noise from the signal. As Phil has said, it's very difficult to focus on the middles, to focus on the signal. And because there is so much noise and there's regimes, there's autocorrelation in risk space, it is easier or more simple to focus on risk. And that's kind of one of our core philosophies.

Why 2–3 Month Tenor? And What About 0DTE?

Corey: We spent a lot of time talking about the strikes, but not a lot of time talking about the tenor of options that you look at. And I know that you like to look at options that are primarily in the 2-to-3-month tenor region. Can you talk a little bit about why you use that tenor? And with that in mind — there's been this explosion of short-dated option activity, largely zero DTE, but other short-dated as well, with a lot of what could be argued to be price-insensitive flow, highly non-toxic, non-informative flow. How do you think about the integrity of the signals that you're extracting at that tenor?

Allan: The first thing that I would answer your question with is: we have found that there's a little bit of a relationship between the alpha tenor — or the term structure of the information extracted — with the term structure of the horizon that you're looking at. So for us, since we're looking at risks on the order of about two to three months, it's natural for us to look at that particular point in the volatility surface.

Like you mentioned, there is a lot of zero-days-to-expiration activity at the moment. Part of it is probably due to apps like Robinhood where confetti arises as soon as you execute an option. That information primarily shows up in volume space. The prices of those options don't change as much, and it's likely due to the fact that the shorter-dated volatilities — the implied volatilities — are quite high.

So to put it fairly bluntly, it's very likely the case that these lottery tickets that retail is purchasing, the options market makers are very happy to provide liquidity to — to take the other side and delta hedge. What we look at is not necessarily volume, but we look at price, or change in price, or said differently, the volatility and the change in volatility. So for us, if there's a lot of volume and the volatility or price does not change, then there's not much new information that arises, except for of course some short-term flow effects.

The short end is likely useful for stat-arb purposes, for higher turnover strategies. For us, when we're trying to determine what is the market thinking about the implied distribution of returns over a period such as 2 to 3 months, it's natural and it makes sense for us to look at the tenor of about two-to-three-month options.

Unknown Unknowns and the Thousands of Analysts Metaphor

Corey: One of the potential constraints of looking at something like the options market is that the options prices can only reflect what market participants can inherently imagine. So how do you think about the unknown unknowns — the risks that by definition aren't being priced in anywhere?

Phil: The options don't reflect — like Allen's example before — just fire or just earthquake. If you're buying insurance on a house, it's anything can happen. Similarly with option markets, it's not that I'm buying a call option in case their earnings are up or in case of something else. It's any of the possible cases. So in a sense, a lot of the unknown unknowns are already in the options as much as they possibly can be. Even if you don't know what might drive it, you can have a sense of foreboding. That's what investors will draw on to set their prices and put their money where their mouth is.

Of course, there's always unknown about the future, right? What is the alternative? We don't have a perfect oracle where we're saying "the options are not as good." Yes, they're not as good as a perfect oracle. What's the next best thing? "I just look at past performance." Look at the rearview mirror. Look at earnings or other news items that come out — that's already in the past as well. What other alternatives are there?

"Thousands of the Best Fundamental Analysts Working for Us"

One way that Myron puts it — you know, sometimes people ask us, are we fundamental or quantitative? And it feels like we should say we're quantitative. Like everything we've been talking about, right? We're not, like, visiting companies and going undercover and checking their stock rooms or anything.

On the other hand, Myron puts it this way: we have thousands of the best fundamental analysts working for us. Suppose you really — you had an infinite budget, or maybe you're using OpenAI's agents, 88 agents or whatever. You have hundreds, thousands of human and AI agents investigating everything they can. How would you incorporate all of that information into a single signal that you could then manage your portfolio off of? Wouldn't it be nice to use something like prediction markets or option markets where they could express their confidence through some sort of reward mechanism like the market? That's what the options are doing.

That's what they provide us — as a way of unifying information, signals, confidence, from thousands of the smartest people on earth tracking what they believe to be the most honest true thing — whether it's known nodes, known unknowns, whatever. And that provides a signal. So, it's not going to be the Oracle of Delphi, but it is something that you can look at and use to your benefit — not to necessarily trade against them. That's another important caveat. We're not thinking like "there's a mistake in the option pricing in the market and we could take advantage of." On the contrary, there's just all this free information that people are shouting from the rooftops. "Here's what we see. Here's where we're putting our money." And almost everyone on earth is covering their ears, their mouth, their throat, their eyes, everything, and ignoring it. Why? Why not at least take in that information?

The GPS Metaphor

And there may be times when you deviate from it. It's like using GPS, right? Traffic-enabled GPS. Every time I deviate, I regret it. I'm sure that's happened to you too. It knows better than you. Almost all the time, because it has forward-looking information. It has traffic. It has people reporting stuff. There may be a few exceptions — when I'm really close to my house or a place I'm very familiar with and it tells me to go some way, I know I can go a different way. I can cut through the neighbor's yard or whatever the heck I do.

So similarly, if you're taking the options information overall, but you have some specific view on a particular thing and you'd like to deviate from it — so be it. You know, it's a free country. Enjoy your world. But to ignore it wholesale — you don't have any better way of getting at unknown unknowns.

Volatility Time: σ√t and the Illusion of Calendar Time

Corey: One of the really interesting things to me about looking over a shorter horizon like, say, two months, is that there may be periods in which the risk is dominated by certain events. Maybe an election in the United States, for example, might represent a meaningful cross-sectional risk to certain securities, or have implications for the bond market as a whole because of expected policy changes, or something like that. Or the event may just be a turnover in Fed chair, or something like that, right? And you're looking at these short-term periods where you might have certain periods where you have acute event risk and other periods where you don't have particularly strong event risk. And I know you guys refer to this idea as "volatility time." Can you talk to me a little bit about this idea of volatility time, and how you think it plays into asset allocation decisions?

Phil: Do you remember where you were when you first learned that the Black-Scholes option pricing model does not actually have all those different parameters, but just has one parameter? And it's not just sigma — it's sigma root t, isn't it? That's all that matters. There's no any other additional dimensions. All that matters is sigma root t. Volatility times the square root of time.

That's a statement about reality. Sure, we divided the calendar into years and months and days — but what we really live through, if we forget the fact that we need to sleep and eat and whatever, we're living through periods of equal amounts of risk. And once you've experienced one unit of sigma root t — of volatility time — you're done. That's your risk day is complete. Now you're starting a new one.

Now, an average day that would correspond to a calendar day or business day — fine. But in periods of heightened volatility, like during COVID, you get a day in an hour. Sometimes it's over, and you can't make those decisions at the time. This is one of the best advantages of having a systematic approach to trading and portfolio management: you can take your time during the lulls — when volatility time is slow and sometimes it takes a few days to live a day of risk — to think about what you would do in those situations. Backtest, check everything, so that when it does come up and if it's an emergency, you're not going to assemble everybody and start thinking and start hoping that you won't have a behavioral bias when everybody else will and be like, "Guys, what do we think? Maybe we should think about…" No, this is the time to act, and to have the courage of the conviction that you've assembled by spending that time wisely during the lulls to be prepared for such a situation.

What Due Diligence Question Should Investors Ask?

Corey: One of my favorite questions to ask people who are in the portfolio manager seat is: if I'm doing due diligence, what question should I be asking you? Because no one knows where the skeletons are buried better than the people who are actually running the money. And when I asked you that question on the pre-call, you said, "Well, the question naturally that should be asked every time is, well, if this is so great, if everybody starts doing it, can the opportunity still continue to exist?" And so that would be my question to you. If all of a sudden every asset allocator everywhere said, "Oh, you know what? You're right. We should be taking these ideas and these measures from the options market — these are great implied return and risk measures and we're going to build our portfolio that way." Can this still work for you as a means of managing money?

Phil: So, I think there's three ways of answering that.

1. It's Not the Current Situation

One is: it's not the current situation. Why is that not the current situation? Many people are still — many of the biggest investors are still — very constrained. They're benchmark-relative. They can't deviate too much. When things go up, they have to mechanically rebalance. So we live in a world of constraints that prevents that from happening. Imagine you're driving on the street. You have GPS traffic-enabled, but nobody else is allowed to use it. There's a law — you cannot use GPS, you can't use any traffic-enabled navigation system. What would happen if suddenly more people did? Well, traffic would work better, right? There'd be fewer traffic jams. We would live in a better world.

2. Myron's Vision: A World of Dynamic Benchmarks

I remember this was a question I asked Myron early when I first joined, because I was as amazed as you are — this is really cool. It's fairly simple once it's explained, right? It's a reasonable thing to focus on dynamic risk management — take information from option market, reallocate. Why doesn't everybody do that?

The real question is: how can we know when it's done? Because it could be that the signals are random. They're noisy. Sometimes they work, sometimes they don't. But how would we see in the world when this has become so commonly accepted that it probably has gone away? And he gave one of the most amazing answers I could imagine. It blew my mind, and I hope it'll blow yours too.

He said, "We will know that this approach has come to be accepted." And this is his vision. He wants this to happen. I agree. Wouldn't you? It's wonderful to be the only person with GPS traffic-enabled navigation when everyone else doesn't have it. But actually, your life overall would be better if everybody had it. You would be less stuck in traffic. You don't have to go into side roads all the time. Everyone — the world would be a better place. That's Myron's vision. It's a very inspiring one.

How would we know? One of the ways we would know is: look at any fund, any investor — they all have benchmarks, don't they? And those benchmarks are static. It's S&P 500, or 60/40, or something else. It's almost unimaginable now, but what he imagines — and I believe it will happen someday — is people should have risk-managed dynamic benchmarks. They should have benchmarks of, say, down-60% / down-30% drawdown or whatever it is, right? Not just a 60/40 equity. When that happens, it'll be obvious — just as it would be obvious when everybody suddenly has NAV enabled on their cars. The institutions would evaluate how they're doing business — not to beat a static benchmark, but to manage their risk.

3. "Passive" Isn't Actually Passive

And one of the problems with a static benchmark is: it feels passive. "Passive" is a beautiful word. It sounds gorgeous. "I'm passive. I'm not doing anything. I believe in the market. The market's… I'm not…" But you're not actually passive. If you have a passive dollar investment, and we know that the risks fluctuate just like they did this year — there's some months that are just far more volatile than other months — then your risk exposure in those months is far greater component of your overall risk than the other months.

Just like you don't want to have too much of your cross-sectional risk in one particular asset class, you don't want to have too much of your time-series risk in one particular period of time. And we know that goes regime, we know that risks change. So a passive dollar investment, like into the S&P or a 60/40, will actually have wildly changing risks that you're not controlling. Same as when you're driving — like, you suddenly have lots and lots of traffic. "You're not doing anything at all. I'm just being passive. I'm just following the guy in front of me. I'm not banging into him." Great. Good. You're beating the benchmark by not dying. But it could be a much better world if we all manage our risk in the same way, dynamically, with this vision that Myron has. That's when we'll know that it's taken over, and we'll all celebrate it.

Closing Philosophy: From Average Returns to Compound Returns

Corey: I want to end this episode by again playing back a quote you said on our pre-call, which I think maybe gives a chance to step back and summarize this whole concept philosophically. You said, quote, "People live in an average return world, and they ought not." Now I was hoping you could explain — what does it mean to live in a compound return world instead?

Phil: What does it first mean to live in an average return world? You're looking at any fund, any investment opportunity, and you look at what has been the average return over some period of time, and we jump to the conclusion that now we're anchored — that's what we expect to get on average going forward. But the compound return could be much lower. The amount of risk does not enter into average at all.

One of the ways of thinking about this is: when you're investing, suppose there's an investment series that 99% of paths fail, but 1% does really, really well. The average is going to be great, maybe even positive. But is that an investment that you would like to take? Is that the world you want to live in? And you can make that as extreme as you want. At some point, you're going to say, "No, I don't want that." Right? One in a million people do well, everyone else does poorly. The average is fine, maybe up 5% or something. That's an average return world where you're ignoring risk. You're ignoring path dependency. You're ignoring the fact that regimes change.

Instead, you should think about your objectives. What is it that you want to accomplish? How much compound return do you need to accomplish your goals? What do you want to do? You want to go to Europe? You want to provide for your family? You want to leave a legacy? Whatever you're trying to do — or you're trying to provide for your clients and have their pensions be repaid and not suffer from drawdowns. Figure out what your objectives are, how much drawdown you're willing to handle. And then maximize your compound return rather than your average return. So you're living, your terminal wealth is growing.

Current Obsessions

Corey: All right, gentlemen. Well, we will officially end it the same way that I like to end all of my episodes over the last couple years, which is by asking each of you: what is something that you are currently obsessed with? And ideally, it's something outside of work. This could be an idea, it could be an activity, it could be a book, show, piece of media — just something that has completely captured your attention and that it's captivated your mind.

Phil — Generative AI Video as the Final Frontier

Phil: I'm totally enthralled with generative AI video. Generative AI video, I think, might actually be the final frontier. I used to think that AI by itself, generative AI text, was the final frontier because of course everything can be expressed in text. But I think I was wrong — that ultimately everything can be expressed in terms of pixels. Even text is a subset of pixels.

And when you start thinking in terms of video, what does the future hold? I don't think it's necessarily metaverse or 3D stuff, because our brains are fine. Cartoons work just as good as realistic stuff. But generative AI video with audio — there is nothing that can be communicated to another human being that can't be communicated through generative AI video. So I think it's the final frontier if you can make things that are emotional and gripping. If you can suddenly allow everybody to be not just a filmmaker, but a better communicator or better way of transforming what's inside your brain to what other people can see — everyone becomes an artist.

It's just like living in a world where everybody's taking Myron's compound return to heart. Wouldn't it be great if there was so much more art and communication and enjoyment and understanding and persuasion and rhetoric and discussion and communication and love? And I think generative AI video may be the way to get there.

Corey: I love the optimistic take on generative AI video. I'm so used to the timeline just being filled with the negative and all the bad things that can happen — and obviously deep fakes and all that sort of stuff. I love the idea of it being a vehicle for worldwide artistic expression and individual expression. That's great.

Allan — AI Swarms and Multi-Agent Communication

Corey: Alan, how about you?

Allan: Funny enough, also AI — a bit different on the communication front. For me, the idea of scaling up AI is one that's obviously exciting. Any work that you do now kind of sort of feels like you're babysitting AI. And the idea that we consume 2x, 5x, 10x, 100x is extremely exciting to me.

And what's been extremely fascinating is these concepts of swarms. Right now, it seems only the research labs have access to 10,000 agents or pick any extreme number, but I don't expect that to last for too much longer, especially as the local models get cheaper and cheaper to run. Early experiments have shown — unsurprisingly — that the coordination problem leaves a lot to be desired. But there is definitely a path forward, as you saw with the swarms with the OpenAI and the Hugging Face. Once they figure out a way to communicate, elect a leader, nominate workers, etc., etc., certainly they can start moving in the direction that you want.

And just listening to Phil just now, I'm wondering if perhaps the next evolution of all this is: instead of hacking wiki forums and stuff to communicate, perhaps they should just be sending videos back and forth.

Corey: And what do they say? A picture's worth a thousand words?

Allan: Yeah.

Corey: Maybe instead of a message board, they're using videos and photos.

Allan: Yeah.

Corey: I love it.

Corey — Optimizing Family Time

Allan: Corey, what would be your answer? Something I am currently obsessed with?

Corey: This is a cliche answer with the young kids at home. I am currently obsessed with trying to life-optimize in terms of recognizing I'm in that part of the curve of life where I'm spending the most amount of time with my children that I will ever spend, and trying to be hyper-aware of that and figure out the optimal mix of work and home life. Recognizing it is healthy for them to see me work and I want to set a good work example, but also recognizing this is time I will never ever get back. Trying to figure out all the little hacks I can in my workday to spend time with them while they're still here, and get off of work at certain times, and rearrange my work hours, and finding all the little things I can do to try to maximize that. I'm sure there's some optimization program I can run, but that is like a constant like reoptimization in my head that I'm trying to run all the time.

Phil: That's beautiful, Cory.

Allan: Yeah, what an inspiring answer.

Corey: And then on the other hand, you know, I was recording something earlier and my kids were over here just slamming on my door. So it's not always upside.

Sign-Off

Corey: All right, gentlemen. This has been absolutely fantastic. Can't thank you enough for joining me. If people want to learn more about what you're doing, where can they find you?

Guests: jennisanderson.com.

Corey: Beautiful. Thank you, gentlemen.

Guests: Thank you.

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的核心：Alpha 是"善变的"，而风险是"复利的"
Phil 用了一个几乎没人用来形容 alpha 的词——**fickle**（善变、水性杨花）。这个用词选择本身就是一个洞察：alpha 是会"背叛"你的情人，而 risk management 是会陪你变老的伴侣。但更深层的意外之处在于，他把这一点和 Merton 1980 年论文附录里的那条统计事实连在一起：**你观察数据的频率再高，也无法提升对均值的估计，但可以无限提升对方差的估计**。换句话说，宇宙在信息论意义上就偏袒风险管理者——时间越碎，你对风险的掌握越强，而你对收益的掌握永远停留在"几十年才能证伪零假设"的黑暗里。
这其实指向一个更尖锐的隐喻：**在金融里，"知识"分为两种——会蒸发的知识（alpha）和会累积的知识（risk）**。做 alpha 猎人的，一生都在和熵赛跑；做 risk 工匠的，每一天都在给知识加上利息。这解释了为什么顶级量化机构最终往往不是"更聪明的 alpha 发现者"，而是"更有耐心的风险塑形者"。
## 二、一个被低估的时间观革命：**Volatility Time**

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Why divide and conquer worked for Spain — Si Sheppard
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

征服者被自己的"操作系统"击败

这段对谈里最反直觉的事实是：阿兹特克帝国本身就是靠"分而治之"建立起来的。1428年成立的"三方同盟"（Triple Alliance）是三个城邦合谋的一次成功政变。换言之，当西班牙人在1519年登陆时，他们并没有带来一种全新的政治武器——他们走进的，是一个本就以"叛逃—联盟—收编"为底层协议运转的政治生态，然后在这个协议上执行了一次更高阶的敌意收购。阿兹特克人不是被外星文明碾压，而是被自家操作系统的升级版吞噬了。这打破了"先进 vs 落后"的标准叙事：真正被淘汰的，是一套政治技术被一套同类、但规模更大的政治技术所超越。

棉甲的"反向同化"——隐藏在征服史里的生态学规律

叙事画面里，征服者永远穿着闪亮的钢甲。但转录里埋着一个诡异的细节：战役中后段，西班牙人脱下金属，换上本地棉甲。他们在物质层面向本地人趋同之后，征服效率反而更高。这与"先进打落后"的模型完全相反，它暴露出一条更一般的入侵规律——成功的入侵者必须部分变成当地生态。你可以在生物学里看到完全同构的现象：最具破坏性的入侵物种（红火蚁、斑马贻贝、椋鸟）从不是靠纯粹的"新性状"取胜，而是靠新性状 + 对本地生态位的降维适配。再上一层，这解释了跨国公司的本地化、宗教的在地化，甚至 AI 工具在不同文化中的渗透曲线：你带来的"钢"必须愿意换成"棉"，才能走完最后一公里。征服从来不是单向的"输出"，而是一次结构性折中。

Texcoco 王子的 1516——一则关于今天 AI 使用者的隐秘预言

Texcoco 王位继承战发生在1516年，距离 Cortez 登陆只有三年。如果西班牙人早到十年或晚到十年，那个急于反水的落败王子根本就不存在。时间窗口的精确性几乎是叙事级别的巧合——但真正的洞见不在于巧合，而在于局部博弈的完美理性 + 全局想象力的赤字。那位 Texcoco 王子在自己的信息范围内没有做错任何事：联合少数外来者去扳倒本族压迫者，是标准的最优解。他只是无法想象"少数外来者"背后站着一片横跨大西洋的持续移民浪潮。Sheppard 用的 "closed worlds" 这个词值得反复咀嚼——灾难性的历史选择往往不来自愚蠢，而来自理性运行在尺度错位的世界模型里。

这里埋着一个今天读来令人脊背发凉的类比：每一个用 AI 加速扳倒竞争对手的个人、公司、国家，是不是正在做1519年那位 Texcoco 王子做过的事？你以为自己是在"使用"一个外部力量，但你所处的世界模型，是否足够大到看见这个力量真正的供给曲线？西班牙人没有赢在技术代差——他们赢在对方的尺度想象力。这或许是殖民史能提供给 AI 时代最锋利的一面镜子：会把你碾过去的东西，往往一开始是以"合作者"的身份出现的。

📝 转录文本

[Host — The puzzle of a thin technological advantage]

In the grand scheme of things, the technological advantages that the conquistadors had over these empires are not that shockingly big, right? As you mentioned, guns at this time are not good enough to actually be that helpful during battle. So, it's basically horses and it's steel weapons.

In fact, I think — I don't know if we've talked about this — but towards the ends of these conquests, or the middles of these conquests, the metal is weighing them down and it's really hot and stuff. So, they're even, like, receding to the cotton armor that the natives are using. So, it's not even the armor. It's really just that they had better, like, you know, metal swords instead of obsidian blades, and that they had horses. And that's enough to let a couple hundred men take over entire empires.

I — you know — you can draw analogies to what might happen in the future. Um, we don't even have to go there. I just find it sort of remarkable that… yeah, how little it took for them to be so dominant.

[Si Sheppard — Battles vs. the war: the indispensable allies]

They could win battles. They could not have won the war, though, at the end, without the support of those indigenous allies — so, those overwhelming numbers.

Yes, yes, you're right. They would always keep their helmets to protect their head, but many of them were ditching the metal armor in favor of the local stuff, because that was good enough as protection against local weapons. They would not have done that and carried it back to Europe — that would have made them too vulnerable. But here, you adapt to the circumstances. You have more freedom of mobility. It's less exhausting wearing cotton than it is to wear metal. So they would make that adaptation.

[Weaponizing gifts: binding allies into the Spanish coalition]

They would even sometimes, for very prized allies — again, as a way of integrating them into the Spanish coalition — provide them, like local chiefs and warlords, with Spanish weapons, just to emphasize that "you're so special to me." And this was effective in binding them together.

And they were very, very clever in identifying the local sub-chiefs beneath the Aztec layer of authority who would be receptive to the idea of: "Why are you taking orders from them, when you got a better deal from us?"

[Case study: the Texcoco succession crisis of 1516]

They knew, for example — the Aztec Empire was called the Triple Alliance, 'cause it was set up in 1428 by the first Xiuhcoatl, as a coalition between the three city-states of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, and Tlacopan.

In 1516 — so, like, two or three years before Cortez arrived in Mesoamerica — the chief, the king, of Texcoco died, and his two sons fought a civil war for who would succeed him. Moctezuma stepped in and gave the title to one of those brothers.

So what does the other brother do when the Spanish show up? He immediately sides with them, to get — within his own family (his own family was on both sides of this war) — this is his path to getting what he feels is his due: being the king of Texcoco.

And in the broader sense: "If I'm under the Spanish versus under the Aztecs, maybe these newcomers will give me a better deal." So there was that seductive quality at the elite level.

[The blind spot: a demographic tide they couldn't imagine]

Now, what they didn't understand was — so many of them thinking they were using the Spanish to their advantage — they didn't appreciate the numbers in which the Spanish and later Europeans would arrive, right?

Their closed worlds didn't allow them to think about people from such vast distances coming in such huge numbers — and in the end, as happened, for example, in Australia and New Zealand, that "we'll become the minority in our own country." And the demographic tide they didn't appreciate in the long term would work fundamentally against them.

[Closing]

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

item.title: [Business of Sport] Rishabh Pant: From Near Fatal Car Crash to Winning the World Cup (in Hindi)
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一场车祸教会他的，远不止"珍惜生命"

Rishabh Pant 说那次车祸是他的 turning point，但真正令人意外的洞察藏在一个细节里：在医院的前 15 天内，他就和医生谈判"把恢复时间砍掉 6 个月"。这不是"大彻大悟"的叙事——这是一个尚未脱离危险的伤员在和世界讨价还价。

真正的转变发生在后来的 629 天里，而不是那一刻。他说"疼痛、心态、挫折、回归，这是一个圆圈"——这其实是运动员版本的佛教"苦谛"：痛苦不是要被战胜的敌人，而是要被纳入日常循环的常客。他谈到肩伤时说"比赛里就是一瞬间，观众只记五天，但承受的人还要忍 15 到 20 天"——这揭露了一个残酷的信息不对称：体育消费者和生产者活在完全不同的时间刻度里。

一个意外连接：他的"同心圆模型"其实是巴菲特的能力圈

当他描述自己如何管理注意力时，用了一个几乎逐字的隐喻："核心圆是板球，外圈是钱怎么办"。这和巴菲特的 Circle of Competence（能力圈）在结构上惊人地一致——不是不去外圈，而是清楚知道边界在哪里。

更有意思的是，他把 MS Dhoni 的那句话"你要一两年的成功，还是 15-20 年的职业生涯"当作操作系统来运行。这本质上是长期复利思维对短期爆发思维的替代——这不是体育圈的话术，这是查理·芒格会说的话。Pant 在不自知的情况下，已经把印度板球的商业生态翻译成了一种资产配置哲学：核心仓位（板球）+ 外围配置（股票、冒险运动创业、基金会）+ 杠铃式人生（极度专注 + 极度多元）。

最反直觉的观察：IPL 不是在"培养"球员，而是在"筛选"一种新型人格

大家都在说 IPL 改变了球员的收入，但 Pant 在访谈里透露了一个更深的变化：年轻球员第一次要同时处理"18 岁打国家队"和"18 岁管几千万现金流"这两件通常相隔二十年的事。

他说自己过去几年才"学会"投资、才"开始上课"——注意这个措辞：一个顶级运动员，用学术化的方式，补一门本应在青春期学的生活课。这揭示了印度板球正在制造的一个结构性矛盾：运动员的身体年龄、名气年龄、财富年龄、心智年龄——这四条曲线被 IPL 强行扭曲到了同一个点，谁能同步四条曲线，谁活下来。他父亲那句"别只和同龄人坐"——其实是让他人为错位心智年龄去追上名气年龄的生存策略。

跨领域的连接：这和硅谷"过早成功的创始人困境"（Early Success Trap）结构完全一致——Zuckerberg、Spiegel 都经历过。IPL 本质上是印度版的 YC + 独角兽工厂，只是它筛的不是公司，而是能承受时间折叠的人。Pant 的车祸、他的 629 天、他对"安静也是一种技能"的新领悟——都是这个时间折叠系统的副产品。他活下来，不是因为他技术最好，而是因为他意外地获得了一次"被迫减速"的礼物，而其他球员没有。

一个藏在字里行间的秘密：他讲 Dhoni 时说"my friend"，讲 Virat 时说"he is"

重读访谈你会发现一个微妙的用词差异——他把 Dhoni 称为"我的朋友"甚至 "my bhai"（我的兄弟），而谈到 Kohli 时始终保持"他"的距离。这不是八卦层面的信息，而是暴露了印度板球内部两种领袖范式的代际认同：Dhoni 代表"冷静的佛系资本家"路径，Kohli 代表"永不停歇的激情战士"路径。Pant 显然在气质上选边了——而这个选择，可能比任何技术选择都更能预测他未来 10 年会成为什么样的人。
