欢迎来到 Business of Sport

主持人： ऋषभ पंत, वेलकम टू द बिज़नेस ऑफ स्पोर्ट। लंदन में भी आपका स्वागत है। मैं काफी एक्साइटेड हूं।

Pant： हां, मैं भी। मुझे यहां बुलाने के लिए थैंक यू।

主持人： थैंक यू। सच में यह बहुत अच्छा है। हमें यह साथ में करना पसंद है। हमारे लिए टाइम निकालने के लिए थैंक यू।

अगर क्रिकेट के हिसाब से देखें तो आप एक इंटरेस्टिंग टाइम पर यहां आए हैं क्योंकि वन डे टीम की अनाउंसमेंट कल हुई थी और उसमें आपको इंडिया के लिए सेलेक्ट नहीं किया गया। तो अभी आपके क्रिकेटिंग माइंडसेट में यह बात कैसे बैठ रही है? और इस समय आप अपना ज्यादातर टाइम किस चीज पर लगा रहे हैं?

Pant： तो डेफिनेटली जब ऐसा कुछ होता है तो बहुत ही ज्यादा बुरा लगता है। लेकिन अगर हम इसे एथलीट के माइंडसेट से देखें तो हम हमेशा कहते हैं कि जब कोई सेटबैक आता है तो कमबैक भी जरूर आता है। और फिर यह तो ऐसी चीजें हैं जिनसे एक एथलीट को अपनी रोज की लाइफ में डील करना ही पड़ता है।

जब लोग कहते हैं "मेरे साथ यह हुआ, वह हुआ" — मुझे लगता है एक एथलीट के लिए यह गेम का हिस्सा है। लेकिन उसी वक्त एक इंसान के तौर पर आप खुद ही जानते हैं कि आप कितनी मेहनत कर रहे हैं, अपने गोल को लेकर कितने क्लियर हैं और कभी-कभी इस लेवल पर खुद को बनाए रखना आसान नहीं होता।

लेकिन इसी के साथ जैसा मैंने कहा, अगर आपके दिमाग में क्लेरिटी है तो आपको सबसे पहले इसे अपने दिमाग में देखना होगा। बहुत से लोग यह कहते हैं, लेकिन इसे हर दिन करने के लिए आपके दिमाग में एक आवाज होती है जो लगातार बनी रहती है। एक बहुत डिसिप्लिन तरीके से आपको वक्त के साथ उसे ट्रेन करना होता है कि चाहे जो हो जाए, आपको आगे बढ़ते रहना है, आपको बेहतर होते रहना है।

बस मैं इसके बारे में अब यही कहूंगा कि हर समय ओपिनियंस बनाना आसान होता है। लेकिन इसके साथ ही लोगों को चीजों के होने का इंतजार करना पड़ता है।

关于肩伤：一个无人知晓的时间差

अब मैं आपको एक बात बताता हूं। जैसे कुछ दिन पहले हम एक टेस्ट मैच खेल रहे थे और मेरे कंधे पर चोट लग गई और उसकी वजह से मुझे सच में बहुत दर्द हो रहा था। लेकिन साथ ही अब उसे 15 से 20 दिन हो चुके हैं। लेकिन वो मोमेंट गेम में शायद सिर्फ तीन-चार दिनों के लिए ही था।

लेकिन मेरे लिए तो मेरे कंधे में अब तक भी बहुत दर्द हो रहा है और इसमें वक्त लगता है। है ना? गेम में तो वह बस एक मोमेंट ही था और लोग भी शायद उसे सिर्फ पांच दिनों तक ही याद रखते हैं। लेकिन जो इंसान उस दौर से गुजर रहा होता है वो अगले कम से कम 15 से 20 दिनों तक उसे झेलेगा।

हां, यह मुझे कोई भी काम करने से तो नहीं रोक रहा है। लेकिन जब मैं अपने कंधे पर सोता हूं तो हर वक्त मुझे उस चोट पर दर्द होता रहता है।

主持人： क्या डॉक्टर्स चाहते हैं कि आप आराम करो?

焦点、训诫、以及重返球队的信念

主持人： क्रिकेट में फोकस आपके लिए कितना जरूरी है? आपने अलग-अलग तरीकों से क्रिकेट खेला है। तो वहां आपका फोकस करना किस तरह काम आता है? जहां आपको डिसाइड करना पड़ता है — जैसे कि "यहां मुझे अपना बेस्ट देना है, यहां मुझे थोड़ा कॉम्प्रोमाइज करना पड़ सकता है। मैं इसे खेलने के लिए फिट हूं, लेकिन यह करने के लिए मैं फिट नहीं हूं।" आप इस सिचुएशन को कैसे अप्रोच करते हो?

Pant： हर चीज को अच्छी तरह से समझ कर देखना चाहिए। हर चीज पर उंगली उठाना बहुत मुश्किल है। जब मैं क्रिकेट खेल रहा होता हूं तो मेरे लिए डिसिप्लिंड रहना बहुत आसान होता है। यह मेरे लिए एक बिजनेस जैसा है। मुझे पता है कि यह मेरे लिए कैसे काम करता है। यह एक पूरे सेटअप जैसा है। आपको पता है कि ऐसे तैयारी करनी है।

यह मेरा माइंडसेट है। यह वो एरिया है जहां मैं लगातार काम कर रहा हूं। क्योंकि एक एथलीट के तौर पर आप हर दिन खुद को बेहतर बनाना चाहते हैं। लेकिन उसी वक्त दिमाग में वह क्लेरिटी होना — इसमें वक्त लगता है क्योंकि आपको बहुत सी चीजों को पीछे छोड़ना पड़ता है और फिर भी हर दिन फोकस करना होता है, क्योंकि जैसा आपने पूछा, वो सेटबैक तो रहता ही है।

हम खासकर मुश्किल वक्त में ऐसा लगता है "अरे अब बस मुझे यह और नहीं करना" — लेकिन एक माइंडसेट होता है, वह डिसिप्लिन होता है जो आपसे इसे पूरा करवाता है।

主持人： तो इस सिचुएशन में आपका माइंडसेट यही है — "मैं टीम में वापस आकर रहूंगा।"

Pant： हां। ओके। मैं सोचता हूं कि इसमें कोई शक नहीं कि मुझे यह करना ही है। क्योंकि मुझे अंदर से ही ऐसा लगता है कि मुझे अभी तक अपना बेस्ट देने की अपॉर्चुनिटी मिली नहीं है। लेकिन इसके साथ ही इंटरनेशनल क्रिकेट और बाकी गेम्स भी हर वक्त बदलते रहते हैं। लेकिन कई बार आपको सिर्फ अपने लिए सही मौके का इंतजार करना पड़ता है और अपने टैलेंट को बड़े लेवल पर साबित करना होता है।

2022 的那场车祸

主持人： मैं आपकी लाइफ की एक बड़ी घटना के बारे में पूछना चाहता हूं। जिसका असर शायद आपके सोचने और अपनी लाइफ के बारे में बात करने के तरीके पर पड़ा होगा। 2022 में आपका एक लाइफ थ्रेटनिंग कार एक्सीडेंट हुआ था।

आपने सेटबैक्स के बारे में बात की। ऐसी सिचुएशन से गुजरते हुए आप गेम के बारे में सोचते हो और फिर अचानक आपको रियलाइज होता है कि गेम तो बस एक जॉब है। यह मेरी लाइफ का सिर्फ एक छोटा सा हिस्सा है। तो क्या उस क्रैश से पहले और उसके बाद ऋषभ पंत में कोई बदलाव आया?

Pant： मैं कहूंगा हां, बिल्कुल। मेरे लिए तो यह सच में एक लाइफ चेंजिंग एक्सपीरियंस जैसा था। मैं इसे सेटबैक नहीं कहूंगा क्योंकि मैं अपनी जिंदगी को बहुत पॉजिटिव तरीके से देखना पसंद करता हूं।

आपको बस आगे बढ़ते रहना होता है। बातें तो वहीं होंगी, सिचुएशन जैसी है वैसी ही रहेगी। लेकिन आप उस सिचुएशन को कैसे लेते हैं और अपने फायदे के लिए कैसे इस्तेमाल करते हैं यह आपके ऊपर है, क्योंकि एक ऐसा इंसान है जो हमेशा आपके साथ बात कर रहा होता है, वो आप खुद हैं। आपको अपने दिमाग से भी ज्यादा स्ट्रांग होना पड़ता है क्योंकि यह कहीं भी जा सकता है।

मुझे लगता है कि उस एक्सीडेंट ने जैसा आपने कहा, उसने मुझे लाइफ के बारे में और भी बहुत कुछ सिखाया। और अगर सच कहूं तो मैं लाइफ के बारे में या दूसरी किसी चीज के बारे में सोच भी नहीं रहा था। मेरा मतलब, जब आप किसी चीज में इतना डूब जाते हैं तो आपको यह भी नहीं पता होता कि आपके आसपास क्या हो रहा है। आप बस अपना बेस्ट वर्जन बनने की कोशिश कर रहे होते हो।

क्योंकि देखिए, जब आप एक्सपीरियंस्ड लोगों से बात करते हैं, तो आप हर वक्त हवा में नहीं उड़ते। लेकिन अगर आप हवा में उड़ रहे हो, तो आपको पता चल जाएगा कि "भाई, यह सही नहीं है।" वैसा माइंडसेट है ना?

तो मुझे सही लोगों के बीच रहने से सच में बहुत मदद मिली क्योंकि इसी वजह से मैं अपनी रोजमर्रा की जिंदगी पर फोकस कर पाया हूं। फिर आप सर्कल बनाते हो। जैसे यह मेरा कोर सर्कल है। मैं क्रिकेट एंजॉय करना चाहता हूं, जी भरकर खेलना चाहता हूं। फिर दूसरा सर्कल बनाते हो — जो पैसा आ रहा है उसे सही तरीके से इन्वेस्ट करना चाहता हूं।

क्योंकि जब आपका फोकस कहीं और होता है तो लोग उस वक्त आपको ढक भी लेते हैं। और ऐसा हुआ भी है, क्योंकि आपका ध्यान नहीं होता। आप सोचते हो "अरे, यह तो अपना ही आदमी है। वह भी अपना ही है।" लेकिन कभी-कभी क्रिकेट पर फोकस करते हुए बाकी चीजों से आपका ध्यान हट जाता है। लेकिन फिर आप सोचने लगते हो कि "नहीं, मुझे जिंदगी के बाकी पहलुओं पर भी थोड़ा ध्यान देना चाहिए।" और फिर आप इन सब चीजों को बेहतर तरीके से मैनेज करने लगते हो।

मैं अभी भी सब कुछ करना चाहता हूं। देखिए, मैं अपनी टीम से हर वक्त यही कहता हूं कि "मैं चाहता हूं कि आप मेरी सोच को और बड़े लेवल पर ले जाओ। मैं नहीं चाहता कि इसका उल्टा हो" — क्योंकि आजकल आपके आसपास इतने लोग होते हैं।

主持人： सही कहा।

媒体、沉默与"真实"的代价

Pant： देखिए, मेरे लिए तो मैं बहुत — वैसे ऐसा लग रहा है कि आप थोड़ा शर्मा रहे हो।

主持人： हां।

Pant： मतलब मेरे लिए यह काफी मजेदार है क्योंकि एक बात — मेरे एक मेंटर हैं, मैंने उनसे बहुत कुछ सीखा है। और एक बात यह है कि मैं मीडिया वगैरह से ज्यादा बात नहीं करता। है ना? यहां-वहां जो भी सामने आ जाता है वह ठीक है। लेकिन मैं बहुत लो प्रोफाइल रहने की कोशिश करता हूं।

समझ रहे हैं ना? हर वक्त मीडिया में नहीं आता। जब यह करना जरूरी होता है, तब मैं करता हूं। लेकिन ज्यादातर समय मैं खुद को बहुत ज्यादा सामने लाने से बचता हूं क्योंकि कभी-कभी आप मतलब डरते हो।

शायद आप सबकी भलाई सोचकर कुछ कह रहे हो, लेकिन जरूरी नहीं कि लोग उसे उसी तरह से लें। लेकिन साथ ही थोड़ी झिझक भी होती है कि पता नहीं इसे किस तरह पेश किया जाएगा। शायद मैं आपका भला सोच रहा हूं, लेकिन अगर आपका माइंडसेट अलग है तो आप उसे पॉजिटिव तरीके से नहीं लोगे।

तो वह बैलेंस ढूंढना बहुत मुश्किल है, खासकर मेरे लिए। और जब मुझे लगता है कि वह बैलेंस नहीं है, तो ज्यादातर मैं दूर रहने की कोशिश करता हूं। और उन्होंने मुझे सिखाया कि चुप रहना भी अच्छा होता है।

तो मैं उस पर काम कर रहा हूं क्योंकि मैं खुलकर जीना चाहता हूं। लेकिन खुलकर जीने की भी काफी कीमत चुकानी पड़ती है। आप सिर्फ अपने घर पर ही खुलकर रह सकते हो। लेकिन बाहर हर चीज मायने रखती है। मेरा मतलब, अच्छा-बुरा, आपकी हर हरकत, हर चीज पर नजर होती है।

तो आप फिर भी खुलकर जीना चाहते हो हर वक्त इन सबके बारे में सोचे बिना। लेकिन मैंने एक बात समझी है कि आपको यह साफ पता होना चाहिए कि आप आखिर में क्या करना चाहते हो।

旅程，而非终点

जिंदगी में सोच-समझ कर कदम बढ़ाने होते हैं और बस उसके साथ रास्ते में जो भी आए उसे एंजॉय करना होता है। क्योंकि जो कुछ भी हम आज कर रहे हैं वह मंजिल नहीं है। यह एक सफर है जिस पर हम चल रहे हैं। हर इंसान का अपना एक अलग सफर होता है।

इसीलिए मैंने एक बात कही थी — इंटरनेशनल क्रिकेट कोई मंजिल नहीं है, यह एक सफर है। क्योंकि बचपन में मेरा सिर्फ एक ही सपना था — "मुझे इंडिया के लिए खेलना है, बस और कुछ नहीं।" उस वक्त दिमाग में कोई और ख्याल ही नहीं था।

लेकिन मैं 19 साल की उम्र में इंडिया के लिए खेल लिया। अब आगे क्या? फिर मैं तीनों फॉर्मेट खेलना चाहता था और मुझे सबसे बेस्ट बनना था। यह माइंडसेट वाली बात है। लेकिन आपको एक-एक करके अपने टारगेट पूरे करते रहना है।

हमेशा कोई बड़ा गोल होता है और आपको एक इंसान के तौर पर खुद को बिजी रखना है और अपने लिए बेहतर गोल, बड़े गोल तय करते रहना है। और मतलब, जो आप सोच भी नहीं सकते, जिंदगी आपके लिए वो कर देगी।

मैं हमेशा कहता हूं — आप कितना भी बड़ा सोच लो वो कम ही है। आप उतना बड़ा सोच ही नहीं सकते।

मतलब अगर 10-11 साल पहले बचपन में आपने मुझसे पूछा होता कि आगे मैं क्या करना चाहता हूं या मैं खुद को कहां देखता हूं? क्या मैं यहां बैठा होगा? तो मैं कहता "मुझे कोई आईडिया नहीं है।" मैं कुछ बहुत बड़ा करना चाहता था। लेकिन बचपन में मैं बस $1 लाख डॉलर कमाना चाहता था। उस वक्त मेरी सोच बस उतनी ही थी क्योंकि मैं उत्तराखंड के एक बहुत छोटे से शहर से आता हूं। वहां रुड़की नाम का एक शहर है।

तो उस वक्त हमारी सोच कुछ ऐसी ही थी कि "मैं थोड़े पैसे की एफडी करा लूंगा और उससे हर महीने ब्याज आता रहेगा।" उस समय हमारी सोच इतनी ही थी क्योंकि हमें बाहर की दुनिया का ज्यादा एक्सपोज़र नहीं मिला था।

मैंने कभी इस बारे में अलग तरीके से सोचा ही नहीं था। लेकिन मैं अपना दिमाग ठंडा भी रखता हूं और चीजों को ज्यादा सिर पर हावी नहीं होने देता।

Pant： अमेरिका में, न्यूयॉर्क में। और यही कहता हूं कि हमें यह फायदा है कि हम कहीं भी जाएं इतनी बड़ी कम्युनिटी मिलती है। स्टेडियम भरे हुए थे। और यूएस में क्रिकेट खेलना — क्रिकेट के लिए भी एक अलग एक्सपोज़र है।

और जैसा मैंने कहा, यह लगातार बड़ा होता जा रहा है। मतलब जहां कुछ भी नहीं था, वहां उन्होंने सिर्फ वर्ल्ड कप के लिए एक नया स्टेडियम बना दिया। और फिर आप देखते हो कि "अरे, चीजें सही डायरेक्शन में जा रही हैं।" इसका मतलब खेल बढ़ रहा है, एक्सपोज़र बढ़ रहा है।

है ना? लोग उन अलग-अलग मार्केट्स में भी इंटरेस्ट लेने लगे हैं जहां क्रिकेट को पहले उस लेवल का एक्सपोज़र नहीं मिला था। लेकिन आप लोगों के अंदर मैच देखने आने का वह जुनून महसूस कर सकते हैं। वह प्यार देख सकते हैं जब वह हमें या दूसरी टीमों को सपोर्ट करने आते हैं।

ऐसा नहीं है कि लोग सिर्फ भारत को ही सपोर्ट करने आ रहे हैं। वो सभी टीमों को सपोर्ट कर रहे हैं — चाहे पाकिस्तान हो या इंग्लैंड जैसी टीम हो। इस देश को क्रिकेट से बहुत प्यार है। एक बात तो बिल्कुल तय है।

主持人： और आपको यहां वो फील होता है?

Pant： देश से बाहर जब आप खेलने जाते हैं तो आपको वह लव और रिस्पेक्ट साफ फील होती है। जब आप वहां जाते हैं तो यहां लोग क्रिकेट से इतना प्यार करते हैं यह आपको पता होता है। और खासतौर पर जब आप यहां परफॉर्म करते हो तो वह रिस्पेक्ट ग्राउंड पर भी फील होती है।

आप कहीं भी लोगों से मिले वह वाइब मिल ही जाती है। यह बात सच है कि विदेश में वह आपका सबसे हार्ड टेस्ट लेते हैं। लेकिन एक बार जब आप उनका दिल जीत लेते हैं तो यह लोग बहुत लव और रिस्पेक्ट देते हैं।

基金会：没有期望的回馈

主持人： हां, आपकी फाउंडेशन के बारे में बताओ।

Pant： सच कहूं तो मेरे लिए यह पर्सनली बहुत ही इंटरेस्टिंग और दिल के करीब वाला प्रोजेक्ट रहा है, क्योंकि बचपन से ही मैं सोसाइटी को कुछ वापस देना चाहता था और मैं वह करता आ रहा हूं। मतलब मैं करता तो हूं ही, अभी भी करता हूं और बिना लालच, सालों से कर रहा हूं।

लेकिन अब मैं इसे एक बड़े लेवल पर सही स्ट्रक्चर देना चाहता था। क्योंकि जब आप पर्सनल लेवल पर कुछ करते हैं तो उसे बहुत बड़ा बनाना मुश्किल होता है। अगर मैं किसी की लाइफ बेहतर बना सकता हूं तो क्यों नहीं बनाऊं।

और खासतौर पर मेरे होमटाउन और मेरे राज्य उत्तराखंड के लिए मुझे लगता है कि वह एक ऐसी जगह है जिसके लिए मेरे दिल में बहुत कुछ है और मैं समाज को लौटाने की शुरुआत वहीं से करना चाहता हूं। जितने ज्यादा लोगों की लाइफ में हम पॉजिटिव इंपैक्ट डाल सकें उतना ही बेहतर है।

主持人： आपकी फाउंडेशन का मुख्य काम क्या है?

Pant： देखिए, अभी तक मैंने कोई एक चीज फिक्स नहीं की थी। जैसे कि कभी अस्पताल में किसी को जरूरत हुई तो मदद कर दी, या कभी पढ़ाई के लिए मदद कर दी। अब तक सब कुछ थोड़ा रैंडम चल रहा था।

लेकिन अब मैं इसे एक प्रॉपर स्ट्रक्चर देना चाहता हूं ताकि बड़े लेवल पर ज्यादा से ज्यादा लोगों की मदद हो सके। और यह सब करके मुझे अंदर से बहुत खुशी मिलती है। खासतौर पर मेरे एक्सीडेंट के बाद जब मैं बिना किसी उम्मीद के किसी की मदद करता हूं तो एक अलग ही सुकून मिलता है।

तो जब आप ऐसा कोई भी काम करते हो, तो अपने मन में और दूसरों से कोई एक्सपेक्टेशन मत रखो। बस जो सही काम है वह करते रहो। चाहे उसका रिजल्ट आए या ना आए। बस सही काम करते रहो।

球员之间的联结与遗产观

主持人： हां, तो एक बात बताओ कि जब हम आप खिलाड़ियों की बात करते हैं — चाहे टेस्ट टीम हो, वन डे हो या टी20 — क्या आप लोग आपस में काफी क्लोज हैं? क्या मैदान के बाहर भी वैसा ही बॉन्ड रहता है? क्या आप एक दूसरे के इनिशिएटिव्स या फाउंडेशन में मदद करते हैं? जैसे आपका कोई टीममेट आपके फाउंडेशन के लिए साथ आ जाए। Like इंडिया में स्पोर्ट्स एनवायरमेंट एक दूसरे को लेकर कितना सपोर्टिव है?

Pant： अगर सच कहूं तो मुझे लगता है कि अब तक ऐसा कोई बहुत बेहतरीन इकोसिस्टम नहीं रहा जहां खिलाड़ी एक दूसरे के साथ मिलकर कोलैब कर सकें। लेकिन जैसे अब चीजें बदल रही हैं और शायद बड़े लेवल पर बदल रही हैं, लोग एक दूसरे के साथ बेहतर तरीके से जुड़ना चाहते हैं। स्पेशली फाउंडेशन जैसी चीजें जो बहुत लोगों की मदद कर सकती हैं। और मेरा मानना है कि यह एक ग्रेट आईडिया है।

अब, जैसा आपने कहा, बहुत सारे क्रॉसओवर होंगे। खिलाड़ी एक दूसरे की मदद करेंगे, खासकर इस तरह की चीजों में। मुझे लगता है कि यह सच में बहुत दिलचस्प कांसेप्ट है।

主持人： बिल्कुल। जब पूरी टीम एक साथ मिलकर अपने से बढ़कर किसी बड़े मकसद के लिए खड़ी होती है तो उसकी ताकत ही अलग होती है।

关于 Legacy

मैं आपकी लेगसी के बारे में बात करने वाला था। क्या लेगसी आपके लिए अहमियत रखती है? अगर आप आज की बातचीत पर सही से काम करते हैं तो आपकी अपनी एक लेगसी बनेगी।

Pant： आप सही कह रहे हो। मैं आपके कहने का मतलब समझ सकता हूं। आप बिल्कुल सही कह रहे हैं। एक कहावत है कि हर दिन यह डिफाइन करना मुश्किल है कि आप चीजें कैसे करना चाहते हो। आप अपनी लेगसी कैसे बनाएंगे? क्योंकि जिंदगी हमेशा आपकी प्लानिंग के हिसाब से नहीं चलती।

लेकिन साथ ही अगर आप सही दिशा में, स्टेप बाय स्टेप सही चीजें कर रहे हो — फिर चाहे वह बिजनेस करना, क्रिकेट में फोकस्ड रहना, अपने फैमिली का ख्याल रखना — छोटे-छोटे स्टेप्स सही डायरेक्शन में।

हां, आखिर में रही बात लेगसी बनाने की — वो दिमाग के किसी कोने में जरूर रहती है। लेकिन आप हर दिन सिर्फ उसी के बारे में नहीं सोच सकते। आपको बस सही डायरेक्शन में छोटी-छोटी चीजें सही तरीके से करते रहना है और सही डायरेक्शन में आगे बढ़ना है। लेगसी अपने आप आपको फॉलो करती चली जाएगी।

场外学习：课堂、酒店房间与股票市场

主持人： ठीक है? तो जैसा आपने कहा, आप क्रिकेट में लगातार बेहतर होना चाहते हैं जो कि एक शानदार विचार है। लेकिन बिजनेस के बारे में क्या? जब हम उस खेल से दूर वाले काम की बात करते हैं। आपने लर्निंग की बात की, आपने कहा कि आप खुद को समय देते हो।

जब आप पिच से दूर यह काम करते हो तो आप खुद के साथ कितने पेशेंट हो और आप इसे अच्छे के लिए कैसे harness करना सीख रहे हो?

Pant： शुरुआत में यह डेफिनेटली काफी मुश्किल था क्योंकि यह एक नई स्किल थी जिसे मैं सीखना चाहता था। क्योंकि जब आप एक ही डायरेक्शन में फोकस्ड होते हो तो आपका दिमाग उतना एक्सप्लोर नहीं कर पाता।

तो इसलिए मैंने इन्वेस्टिंग और बाकी की चीजों के बारे में सीखना शुरू किया, क्योंकि फैमिली में मुझे ही यह सब संभालना है, तो मुझे अपने फाइनेंस की समझ होनी चाहिए।

मुझे सीखना पड़ा कि मतलब जैसे अपना दिमाग शांत कैसे रखूं। मेरी मां और फैमिली ने मुझे पूरी छूट दी है। उनका कहना है "हमें तुम पर भरोसा है कि तुम सही फैसला लोगे।" और फैमिली की यही बात सबसे खास होती है। चाहे वक्त अच्छा हो, बुरा हो या कैसा भी — वे चट्टान की तरह आपके पीछे खड़े रहते हैं।

जब आपको ऐसा सपोर्ट मिलता है तो आपका कॉन्फिडेंस एक अलग ही लेवल पर होता है। जब पता हो कि परिवार पीछे खड़ा है, तो फिर आपको कौन तोड़ सकता है। और फिर आप अपना काम पूरी फ्रीडम और क्लेरिटी के साथ कर सकते हो। और यही चीज है जिसका मैं हर दिन इंतजार करता हूं।

股市与课堂

主持人： इन्वेस्टिंग की बात करें तो आपने अभी स्टॉक मार्केट का जिक्र किया। हमने कई एथलीटों से बात की है। ज्यादातर लोग स्टार्टअप इन्वेस्टिंग की बात करते हैं। स्टॉक मार्केट पर कम ही लोग ध्यान देते हैं। तो बिजनेस के इस साइड में आपको क्या इंटरेस्टिंग लगता है? इसमें आप आगे क्या करना चाहते हैं?

Pant： मुझे लगता है कि मेरे लिए दोनों ही एस्पेक्ट बहुत इंपॉर्टेंट है। मुझे लगता है कि स्टॉक मार्केट को समझना मेरे लिए थोड़ा आसान रहा है। हालांकि किसी कंपनी में पैसा लगाने से पहले काफी स्टडी करनी पड़ती है।

बट मैं कुछ सालों से यह स्टडी कर रहा हूं। जैसे करीब 5-6 साल से मैं क्लासेस ले रहा हूं। यह सीख रहा हूं कि कैसे इन्वेस्ट करना है। क्योंकि जब आप अपनी मेहनत की कमाई कहीं लगाते हो तो आपको अंदर से पूरा कॉन्फिडेंस होना चाहिए।

हां, तो यही कारण है कि मेरे लिए इसे सीखना जरूरी था। मैं स्टॉक मार्केट में काफी इन्वेस्टिंग कर रहा हूं।

主持人： आप क्लासेस लेते हैं?

Pant： हां, प्रॉपर क्लासेस।

主持人： सच में?

主持人： ओके। यानी अपने फ्री टाइम में।

Pant： हां, मेरे फ्री टाइम में।

主持人： स्पोर्ट्स के साथ यही बात है। लोग अक्सर सोचते हैं कि एथलीट्स हमेशा बिजी रहते हैं। और आप रहते भी हैं। मैं इससे इंकार नहीं कर रहा। लेकिन बहुत सारा टाइम ऐसा भी होता है जब आप होटल के कमरों में सिर्फ बैठे होते हैं।

Pant： हां, आपने बिल्कुल सही कहा। जब भी मुझे फ्री टाइम मिलता है तो कोशिश करता हूं उसका पूरा इस्तेमाल सही जगह करूं और बेहतर तरीके से इस्तेमाल करूं।

जैसा मैंने पहले भी कहा — मैं एक ऐसे माइंडसेट में रहना पसंद करता हूं जहां मैं हर दिन कुछ नया सीख सकूं और खुद को बेहतर बना सकूं। मेरा माइंडसेट यही रहता है।

और जब आप कुछ सीखना शुरू करते हैं तो आपको उसे करने का कॉन्फिडेंस आता है। चाहे फिर वह बिजनेस ही क्यों ना हो।

冒险运动与故乡

जैसे मैं कुछ खास सेक्टर्स को एक्सप्लोर करना चाहता हूं। खासकर एडवेंचर स्पोर्ट्स जैसी चीजों को — वो भी इंडिया में।

主持人： एडवेंचर स्पोर्ट्स?

Pant： हां, मुझे लगता है यह एक ऐसी चीज है जिसका मुझे इंतजार है। खासकर मेरे होमटाउन उत्तराखंड में।

主持人： अच्छा। एडवेंचर स्पोर्ट्स के लिए उत्तराखंड एक बहुत शानदार डेस्टिनेशन है।

Pant： तो वहां काम करने के काफी स्कोप हैं। अभी यह आईडिया मेरे दिमाग में अर्ली स्टेज पर ही है। लेकिन सच में मुझे इसके आसपास बहुत सी चीजें करने का इंतजार है। फिर वह चाहे बिजनेस के नजरिए से हो या मेरे फाउंडेशन के नजरिए से।

主持人： ऐसा करना बढ़िया है, और आपको इस तरह बात करते हुए सुनना बहुत अच्छा लगता है। क्योंकि मुझे यह बहुत पसंद है और हम बार-बार इसी पर वापस आते हैं — जब आपने सचमुच बैठकर कहा "मैंने अभी तक अपनी पूरी क्षमता हासिल नहीं की है। मैं और बेहतर होना चाहता हूं।"

यह वाकई कमाल है, क्योंकि देखने को बहुत कुछ है — चाहे वो निराशा हो, मुश्किल दौर से उभरना हो, या खेल के अलावा दूसरी चीजें करना, जहां आप सोच सकते हैं — "ओके, क्या अब सब कुछ सिर्फ क्रिकेट के बारे में है?"

हां, लेकिन इसे अपनी जड़ों से जोड़े रखना और साथ ही आगे बढ़कर कई अलग-अलग चीजें करने की चाहत रखना — यह सुनकर बहुत अच्छा लगता है।

हमें टॉप लेवल की ऐसी insight कभी नहीं मिलती। यह बहुत जबरदस्त है क्योंकि हम क्रिकेट के context में इसके बारे में बहुत बात करते हैं। लेकिन आपसे यह सुनना, सीधे अनुभव जानना और यह समझना कि असल में चीजें कैसी होती हैं — वाकई कमाल का है।

इसलिए मैं आपका बहुत आभारी हूं। आपने कहा कि आपने ज्यादा मीडिया इंटरव्यू नहीं दिए हैं। मैं सभी से वादा करता हूं कि मैंने जबरदस्ती नहीं की है। उन्हें टेबल से हथकड़ी लगाकर नहीं रखा गया है।

तो आपके साथ यह सब करके बहुत मजा आया। लेकिन मैं सच में बहुत आभारी हूं कि आप यहां आए और बातचीत की और मुझे लगता है कि सभी को आपसे यह सुनना बहुत पसंद आएगा।

Pant： उम्मीद है लोगों को पसंद आएगा। मुझे यहां बुलाने के लिए शुक्रिया। थैंक यू भाई, सच में बहुत अच्छा लगा।

主持人： ये बहुत शानदार रहा।

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一场车祸教会他的，远不止"珍惜生命"
Rishabh Pant 说那次车祸是他的 turning point，但真正令人意外的洞察藏在一个细节里：**在医院的前 15 天内，他就和医生谈判"把恢复时间砍掉 6 个月"**。这不是"大彻大悟"的叙事——这是一个尚未脱离危险的伤员在和世界讨价还价。
真正的转变发生在后来的 **629 天**里，而不是那一刻。他说"疼痛、心态、挫折、回归，这是一个圆圈"——这其实是运动员版本的佛教"苦谛"：**痛苦不是要被战胜的敌人，而是要被纳入日常循环的常客**。他谈到肩伤时说"比赛里就是一瞬间，观众只记五天，但承受的人还要忍 15 到 20 天"——这揭露了一个残酷的信息不对称：**体育消费者和生产者活在完全不同的时间刻度里**。
## 一个意外连接：他的"同心圆模型"其实是巴菲特的能力圈
当他描述自己如何管理注意力时，用了一个几乎逐字的隐喻：**"核心圆是板球，外圈是钱怎么办"**。这和巴菲特的 Circle of Competence（能力圈）在结构上惊人地一致——**不是不去外圈，而是清楚知道边界在哪里**。

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Why the conquistadors thought they could win — Si Sheppard
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、真正的"军事优势"藏在人事部门里

视频中最被低估的洞见是 Dwarkesh 的那句话：我们总谈技术优势，却从不谈治理技术的优势。东印度公司能做的事，莫卧儿和马拉塔都做不到——不是因为火枪更精良，而是因为它能"开除 CEO"。

这里有一个让人脊背发凉的数学直觉：世袭君主制本质上是在基因彩票上押注国运。假设任何一个王朝每代有 20% 概率出现无能或精神失常的君主，那么三代之内出现一个"玻璃国王"（法王查理六世坚信自己是玻璃做的）或"疯王亨利"（亨利六世连续数月精神关机）几乎是必然的。英国人赢百年战争是因为法王疯了，输百年战争是因为自家国王疯了——这不是运气，这是制度的信号/噪声比。

而东印度公司只需要一个董事会会议就能换掉罗伯特·克莱夫的继任者。它用人事可替换性，把君主制几百年来积累下来的"坏国王债务"，一笔勾销。英国人不是打败了印度，而是用一个更不容易自毁的操作系统，等待印度自毁。

二、"康帕尼奥斯"——被遗忘的词源学暴击

这是全集最震撼的一处细节，Sheppard 几乎是顺口说出来的：征服者们自称 compañeros——"同伴/股东"，不自称士兵。

这个词源学事实瞬间重写了我们对殖民史的叙事。皮萨罗、科尔特斯手下那群人不是"军队"，他们是合伙制公司。每个人入股（自备武器、马匹），按份额分战利品，签合同、留账本、告状打官司。换句话说：征服墨西哥和秘鲁的，不是西班牙王国，而是一家家 LLC。

跨领域连接——这意味着现代硅谷的叙事其实是倒着走的：我们常说"创业像征服未知大陆"。错了。是征服大陆像创业。先有了合伙制的金融技术（追溯到维京人集资造船抢修道院），才有了"远征"这个商业模式。资本主义的组织形式比民族国家更古老，征服者文化本身就是风险资本的中世纪原型。

硅谷式的 cap table、员工期权、董事会罢免 CEO——这些结构的真正鼻祖，不在华尔街，而在 16 世纪 Castile 一群破落贵族（hidalgos）签下的合伙协议里。

三、印度不是被征服的——它是被"外包"了

真正令人不适的事实：英国征服印度的军队里，绝大多数士兵是印度人（sepoys）。这意味着什么？

英国人没有征服印度，印度自己征服了自己——只不过是在英国人的组织表上运行。

这是殖民史里最被回避的一层结构：当地的放贷人、兵源供应商、小邦国的权贵们看着现任纳瓦布是个"精神病王子"（孟加拉的 Siraj ud-Daulah 继承 Alivardi Khan 之后），然后做了一个纯粹理性的商业决策——把钱和兵借给看起来更能稳定分红的那一方。英国人不是外来者，他们是本地权贵资产组合里风险调整后收益最高的那只股票。

跨领域连接——这与今天的平台经济惊人相似。Uber 不拥有汽车，Airbnb 不拥有房屋，东印度公司不拥有士兵。它只拥有一样东西：协调结构。平台把分散的、本来内耗的资源重新组织，收取"协调租金"。18 世纪的东印度公司和 21 世纪的 Uber 共享同一套底层数学。

四、一个让人睡不着的推论

如果王朝周期律的根源真的是选择机制而非文化、地理或道德——那么它对今天的含义是：

任何依赖单一不可替换决策者的系统（独裁国家、家族企业、以创始人为宗教的创业公司），在足够长的时间尺度上，必然败给可以用低成本更换决策者的系统。不是因为后者更聪明，而是因为前者会在基因彩票 × 时间的函数下，不可避免地抽到一张"玻璃国王"的牌。

这不是政治哲学。这是可靠性工程。

📝 转录文本

莫卧儿帝国的"异族困境"

Q: 在印度，比如我们确实有许多不同的欧洲势力。为什么莫卧儿不能一直玩弄它们相互制衡，以维持对印度的控制？

The Mughal — I mean, it peaked under Aurangzeb at the beginning of the 18th century. Subsequently his successors didn't have — whatever you call it, the authority, the charisma, the rizz — [laughter] — to maintain that hegemony which he established by almost taking over all of India.

And the Mughals, at root, had the same problem that the Manchu did when they conquered the Ming in the 17th century and they built the Qing dynasty — China the greatest physical extent it ever had, but they were always outsiders. They were not indigenous to the population in the background. There was always that vague resentment that we're being ruled here by foreigners. And that was okay while they were going from success to success. But when the momentum halts and it begins to roll backwards, that's when the local power brokers begin to feel to themselves: maybe we have more to gain from breaking away from the empire than we do from remaining within it.

So both Mughal India and Manchu China had that kind of fatal defect, as it were, coded into the ultimate basis for their authority. So even without the Europeans, I think the Mughal Empire would have peaked and it would have disintegrated. Now what would have happened next would be more like a patchwork quilt of different authorities, some larger, some smaller. The Maratha Confederacy I think would have been a major player, but not one that could incorporate the entire subcontinent within its authority.

And of course we look at Chinese history — it's the constant cycle of the rise of a dynasty, its peak, its decline into anarchy, and then the rise of a new imperial hegemon in the region. So that cycle would play out, I think, regardless of whether the Europeans intervened.

皇家海军与投射能力

Specifically in terms of why the British took over at the end — well, in its bluntest terms, the Royal Navy rules the waves. And in terms of projecting power, the Brits were able to force the French out of Canada and out of India because they controlled the sea lanes. And although the French had, in terms of population and military, a larger force, if you can't project that force it's really of no value to you.

治理优势：被低估的"公司性"

Q: 这很有趣，因为它解释了为什么英国人能成为印度的主要势力之一。但在马拉塔、莫卧儿残余和其他众多派系之中，为什么偏偏是这个英国前哨站能完成整合，而别人不能？

I think one hypothesis here is that we often talk about advantages in technology, but we don't talk about advantages in governance or in organization. And the East India Company was like a company. It had a board that could fire and hire CEOs and lieutenants and whatever — it wasn't called the CEO obviously. And so it wasn't necessarily the most competent people who were in charge of the East India Company; it were pretty competent people. Robert Clive and his underlings.

坏国王问题

And you would have instances — for example, I think the Nawab of Bengal, right before the British are able to gain control of Bengal, which is the initial attack base that they set up in order to further their conquest — Alivardi Khan is considered to be a pretty good ruler who was able to hold the British at bay and stuff. And then he dies, and his prince is this kind of crazy psychopathic guy who doesn't listen to advice and so forth.

Because there's this monarchical tradition across all these principalities in India, there's just going to be sooner or later a bad king, and that king will not be able to stop the British incursion. There's also all these forces around these principalities who are like: okay, who are we going to lend money to? Who are we going to lend our troops to? And they realize there's a bad king right now; the British seem pretty competent. I'm going to make an alliance with the British instead.

And similarly with the case of the sepoys — maybe even more so — the overwhelming majority of the troops/forces that the British are using are Indians, right? Yeah. Sepoys.

So I think this is an underrated thing: being able to delegate competent people, and then being able to replace them one after another if they get killed or if they resign or something. There's not going to be some crazy succession crisis that creates this anarchy that then somebody else can swoop in and take control.

两位疯王的历史侧证

Absolutely. Just to give one example: the British were winning the Hundred Years War because the king of France, Charles VI, was insane — he was convinced he was made out of glass, for example. And then the English lost the Hundred Years War because their king Henry VI was insane — he would just shut down months at a time, mental, just couldn't function.

公司作为超越王朝的组织形式

In non-democratic environments, yes, the corporations — for the reasons you outlined — profit-driven, and therefore not loyal to bloodlines or any other kind of extraneous circumstances, but just looking for the most competent leadership and a capacity to exchange and replace people — are much more flexible than those kind of hierarchical states. Even in many ways you could argue in democratic societies the corporations can still maneuver them, because they're untied to particular loyalties and it's just their brand awareness that they're trying to push.

The British and Dutch were late to the game of imperialism, and you wouldn't give them much a chance given the differentials. But they unleashed the power of the free market. As you say, the East India Company, the English and Dutch equivalents, the British Hudson's Bay Company — which is really what made Canada as we understand it today — those corporations, driven by those motives, acting with almost plenipotentiary powers at vast distances, had the flexibility on the ground to take advantage of local circumstances, to insert themselves into diplomatic arrangements which have persisted for centuries with all the accumulated grievances.

Here — we're the fresh newcomers, we have obviously skills at what we do, as you say taken control of the tax revenue of Bengal, effectively took control of the entire political orbit. What can you do without taxation? Reorient that towards the shareholders, force the local people to stop producing these crops even if it means millions starved to death in order to produce opium to take advantage of that. It was devastating in its impact on political structures that had no real environment where that was part of their established traditions.

从维京人到征服者：资本主义的深层谱系

And even the conquistadors, even the Vikings — if we go back far enough, these were business operations. The Vikings would be men who would assemble with what weapons they had, enough capital up front to pay for boats to go raiding, to make this profitable by looting churches and monasteries.

That's what the conquistadors were. They were freebooters operating within a capitalist system. These were not desperadoes of the lowest of the low. Many of them had some education. A lot of them were hidalgos, which is the lowest rung of the petty nobility in Castile, who inherited titles and attitudes but not much assets beyond what they could put up as soldiers of fortunes. They called themselves compañeros — which is colleagues or companions, not soldiers.

So this whole operation was, if you like, the most raw unbridled capitalism at its finest — pulling assets to derive enormous profits from very risky ventures.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

item.title: [邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain] 銀行拿你的錢豪賭只給0.1%？美債狂發，比特幣將成為全球避風港？ Mike Belshe【邦妮區塊鏈】
item.dc:creator: 邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三个让人意外的系统性观察

一、"系统性风险"的话术，实质是对银行寄生模式的辩护

Belshe 讲了一个很多人没注意到的细节：SVB 收到了那么多存款，但他们"找不到足够靠谱的人去贷款"，于是把钱塞进了 10 年期美债——然后爆炸了。

把这个故事和"美国人在支票账户上拿 0.1%，而无风险利率是 4%"连起来看，一个惊人的真相浮现：今天美国的商业银行很大程度上已经不再是"把储蓄转化为生产性信贷"的金融中介，而是一个纯粹的利差提取机器——它们从散户那里以 0.1% 收钱，自己转手买 4% 的国债，把 3.9% 的利差装进口袋。然后 ABA 游说这种模式"关乎系统稳定"。

这是一个监管套利伪装成金融服务的典型案例。稳定币真正威胁的不是"经济的信贷流动"，而是这个寄生层。所以才打得这么凶。

二、历史在押着同一个韵脚：1970 年代的 Regulation Q 就是今天的 Genius Act 收益禁令

这是整段访谈最隐秘的洞察，Belshe 一笔带过但分量极重：1970 年代，美国有一个叫 "Regulation Q" 的规定，禁止银行给储户支付超过某个上限的利息。然后通胀抬头，货币市场基金（以 T-bills 为抵押、锚定 1 美元）出现，收益率比银行高——银行当年也喊"会挤兑！金融崩塌！"。

结局：没有挤兑，Regulation Q 被废除，货币市场基金成了金融系统的正常组成部分。

今天的 Genius Act 禁止稳定币向零售持有者付息，和当年的 Regulation Q 是同一套逻辑的转世。监管周期有一种近乎潮汐的节律——每当技术提供了比旧式银行更高效的"T-bill 包装器"，监管就先设防，再被现实打破。看懂这个节律的人就知道：稳定币付息不是会不会发生，而是什么时候。

三、量子威胁的真正性质，不是密码学问题而是博弈论问题——与核不扩散同构

主流叙事认为"量子计算机能破解比特币"是技术威胁。Belshe 的回答揭示了一个美得出奇的结构：

"The first quantum computer would be a white hat hacker... if you try to steal Satoshi's coins, you'd be left trying to launder the money of a diminishing currency."

换句话说：真正能偷中本聪 100 万枚币的那个攻击者，其攻击行为本身会摧毁被偷之物的价值。 这不是加密强度问题，这是一个反身性毁灭（reflexive destruction）——攻击成功即是攻击失败。

这个结构你在哪里见过？核武器的"相互确保毁灭"（MAD）。核武器最大的"安全性"不来自技术防御，而来自"使用它的收益为负"这个博弈均衡。中本聪的沉睡币是比特币协议的"核威慑"——它们的存在证明了一件事：在一个足够大的去中心化网络里，经济攻击的成本会超过攻击收益。

一个跨领域的加挂连接：加密货币的"大区块之争"和城市规划里的"最优城市规模"

Belshe 最后关于区块大小的讨论值得深挖。小区块意味着更多节点、更高去中心化；大区块意味着更多交易吞吐、但传播延迟增加、运行门槛提高。

这个权衡在物理学和城市经济学里都有同构： - 中子星有一个钱德拉塞卡极限——超过某个质量就坍缩成黑洞； - 城市人口超过某个阈值，就从"规模经济"滑向"拥堵不经济"； - 蚁群规模超过一定数量，必须分裂成子群落。

所有去中心化系统都有一个"最优尺度窗口"，不是越大越好也不是越小越好。中本聪设计的 1MB 区块是一个赌注——他赌的是"维持家用电脑级别的参与门槛"比"交易吞吐量"更重要。十几年后看，矿池集中化证明这个赌注部分输掉了——门槛没能挡住中心化，只是把中心化从"交易层"赶到了"算力层"。

这给稳定币监管留下一个隐喻：当你在系统某处设防，中心化压力只是迁移，不是消失。Genius Act 禁止零售收益——这个压力会在 DeFi、海外、衍生工具里重新冒出来。规则不是在"阻止"什么，它只是在决定权力下一个寄居之处。

1970 年代的历史回声：货币市场基金 vs Regulation Q

By the way, we've seen this movie before. Back in the early 1970s was when we first introduced money markets completely backed by T-bills. Again, they're pegged to a dollar and they're backed by T-bills. They get you a T-bill rate.

The reason this was interesting is because inflation was ticking up. So suddenly T-bills were getting to interesting rates. And back at that time, banks had a limit — there was a thing called Regulation Q on banks, which prevented them from having interest rates for their clients above a certain level. So the T-bill interest was higher, and they said "there's going to be a run on the bank."

There was no run on the bank. There's no longer Regulation Q either. Everybody's happy. The banking system works. These are a valid part of our financial system products today, and everything's good.

Really, what's happening is just people trying to preserve their existing business model because it's easier. But at the end of the day, it's your money. You should get an interest. You should be able to get risk-free rate on it.

And this has happened historically many times.

Eventually, we came up with this concept of FDIC, which is insurance for the banks because sometimes they screw up. So the insured bank is insured because you take risks that need to be insured.

They can't do it, because they don't actually have the assets. And of course, this is exactly what caught up SVB.

So, look, I understand his concern about crypto. There's a lot of stuff going on in crypto that you can point out that looks fishy, but that's different than taking risk. So the bank keeps safety for one set of groups — the depositors — and lends it out to others. You get a small business loan. The banker knows who you are. There's a lot of community around it.

These days, banks don't really have the ability to mention lending anymore. They don't have a really good ability to do risk assessment. And on top of that, we have computers which make it global.

A great example of this is mortgages. It used to be you would go to your local branch in San Francisco, you would get a mortgage, it would be with your bank. Today, you go into your bank, he still underwrites it, he takes the paperwork, he checks your ID and all that, but by the time the door closes, he has sold it off to Wall Street. That thing has been securitized and packaged and is now liquid on the capital markets. It's a better way to do mortgages. And of course, ultimately, those all land at Freddie and Fannie.

So banks aren't really doing mortgages anymore. What else do they do? Well, they do commercial lending and small business loans. Small business loans is often cited as a problem — if you didn't have depository banks, who would do the small business loans? I think there's some legitimacy to that, but it's a small cry from what they used to be providing in terms of service.

Then on the commercial loans — let's move that to private equity. Let's put that on a blockchain. Let's make that open, allow everyone to participate. Some countries have had this so repeatedly that they've already moved to dollar-backed or dollar-denominated as their currency. Panama uses dollars directly. 什么情况下会让美元遭遇抛售？

Well, like you already answered your own question. The reason the dollar will decline is erosion in trust. That comes from a couple of different things:

(a) Are you printing it unreasonably so that you're devaluing it on your own? Which, you know, is happening and is very visible.

(b) Can I trust that if I hold it, I'll be able to have it tomorrow? Russia and Iran obviously don't feel like they can trust it. Other countries also will worry if there's ever a political climate in America that dislikes them — will America just come and yank the dollars?

So look, when you are the reserve currency, you have a responsibility to maintain trust, which comes on both of those axes. I need to know, no matter how much you disagree with me, you're not going to just steal my money. You violate that premise, I can't use you as a reserve currency. Number two, of course, you can't devalue my currency.

机构投资者反复问同一个问题：量子计算

— During your IPO road show, you said a lot of institutional investors kept on asking you about quantum computing. — Yes. — What are they asking? What is your answer?

Look, quantum computing is a concern. Some people are afraid that we could, in the not too distant future, have a quantum computer that cracks your Bitcoin or your other digital assets.

Quantum computing is advancing quickly. AI helps things advance quickly. Personally, I think it's pretty far away. When you really talk to the cryptographers, there is no evidence of any near-term quantum attack against Bitcoin or other assets. However, it's a fear, right?

And what are we talking about? We were just talking about trust in the US dollar. At some level, people have to be able to trust Bitcoin. You have to be able to trust digital assets as well. So this is going to continue to be a concern. Will there be a computer that can crack this cryptography? Maybe some period there is, maybe there won't be.

Good news: we have — in fact, we have them — quantum resistant algorithms today that could be used for signing. We can put that into the Bitcoin protocol. We could put that into others. And then also, even better news: I think really the emphasis on this in the last 12 months has really grown. The Bitcoin teams are working on it hard. The Ethereum teams are working on it hard.

So I think in another year this is not going to be an issue — not because we're going to have quantum computers, but because we're going to put in defensive mechanisms for it. I don't think it's something people need to worry about much, but the next wave of entrants — they want to come in with billions of dollars, they need to know absolutely that there's not a risk for their money.

— Will BitGo take measures to make the custodian side of the business quantum resistant?

So we, as a custodian, we will do everything that we can to make sure that we're quantum resistant. By the way, at BitGo, even without having everything solved at the Bitcoin protocol layer, there's a bunch of things that we already do. We never reuse addresses. We make sure that when you're spending an unspent that's been exposed on this public key, that we can construct your wallet in the safest way so that you have minimal exposure. But as new protocol developments come in, we'll incorporate those too for sure.

中本聪的沉睡币：量子攻击的靶子？

— Last year when we were talking, I think you said the biggest concern is Satoshi's wallet. Is it still a concern?

It is. So, for those that haven't understood, haven't studied this: Satoshi, who has about a million bitcoins — and there's only 21 million that will ever exist — his coins were done at a time when the way we encoded them on the blockchain exposes its public key. And that public key makes it potentially exploitable by a quantum computer.

So even though we will solve a problem so that everyone can move their funds to safe wallets, Satoshi might not be alive. We don't know why he hasn't moved his coins. He won't be able to move his coins. So Bitcoin has to deal with this debate of how to deal with that.

What if a quantum attacker does get those coins? Look, I don't think this is a very realistic problem, either, for another reason — which is that if you were to try to steal his coins, it's very noticeable very quickly, and the price of Bitcoin would tank most likely.

It would be a white hat hacker which would build the first quantum computer. They would use this as an example to claim quantum supremacy. But I think they're unlikely to try to steal it. Remember, if you try to steal somebody else's coins — even if you don't know who that person's — Satoshi may be — it is still theft. So you will be left with the problem of trying to launder the money of a diminishing currency. I don't think it's really a big practical problem, but I realize some people are worried about it.

TradFi 会大规模采用区块链吗？

— Final question. What is the future of TradFi going to look like in relation to Bitcoin and blockchain? Is TradFi going to start adopting blockchain on mass? Are we going to see BitGo within JP Morgan, for example?

They're right over there. JP Morgan's right over there with a big display booth about their settlement on chain.

— So what did you get right about the industry that maybe Wall Street hasn't adopted early on?

Look, to say we got something right — I would never use that wording. I think what it is is: you know, sometimes you see a technology, and as a technologist, I think I saw some value in it, and it's turned out to be right. But I think somewhat it's speculative.

The reason I was able to see it earlier is really just a higher tolerance for risk. Any technology when it's new is higher risk. And then over time, you mitigate those risks — you change things, you go get regulatory licenses, you get insurance, you get backing, you do all of these things.

What's happened is it's had enough time where people are like, "Hm, this actually does work. It does provide transparency. It can be done with cryptography which protects us in a better way." And then now we've overlaid some of these other controls. So as we keep moving, the more and more conservative companies can participate in the asset class.

如果能问中本聪一个问题

— If you could ask Satoshi one question, what would it be?

That's a great question. Look, I'll first answer with a non-answer, which is: I don't really care who Satoshi is. It's like a curiosity, and other than that, it really doesn't matter.

Maybe — you know, since I personally was fighting for larger blocks as a technologist perspective (I've never tried to take over Bitcoin despite what some people might say) — I would ask Satoshi what he thinks about the size of a block.

— Could you elaborate a little more on that?

So, look — Bitcoin doesn't scale very well. It's got relatively small blocks. There's a trade-off. As the block size gets larger, the propagation around the world takes a little bit more time. So some people really want to have really small blocks so you can always run it on very small machines, which allows people to run it at home. So as we increase the block size so that we can have more transactions in it, does it impair the ability to have it be as decentralized as it might otherwise be?

So another question I might ask him is whether he had really anticipated that mining pools would be as big as they are. I think he might not have anticipated mining pools. I'd be curious to hear his answer.

— But why does that matter?

Well, mining pools allow one party to aggregate a bit more power than we'd really like. As you know, you've heard of a 51% attack — you don't want anyone to have 51% because then they can control what goes in the blocks. With the mining pools, you have some of that possibility as well.

Mining pools — they take all of the miners together. They make a nice steady stream of income. So it's actually a good thing for the miners and stabilization and steadiness. But on the other hand, the pool itself, if it ever gets over, even though it may have many miners inside of it — if it ever got over 51%, then it has control. So I think maybe he didn't anticipate this, but I'm not entirely sure.

— That was very interesting. — Well, thank you. I hope he can answer those questions to you alive one day. — Yes. — I'm not sure I care. — All right. Great way to —. Thank you. — Thank you. Thank you, Mike. Thank you, Bonnie.

item.description:
# 三个让人意外的系统性观察
## 一、"系统性风险"的话术，实质是对银行寄生模式的辩护
Belshe 讲了一个很多人没注意到的细节：SVB 收到了那么多存款，但他们"找不到足够靠谱的人去贷款"，于是把钱塞进了 10 年期美债——然后爆炸了。
把这个故事和"美国人在支票账户上拿 0.1%，而无风险利率是 4%"连起来看，一个惊人的真相浮现：**今天美国的商业银行很大程度上已经不再是"把储蓄转化为生产性信贷"的金融中介，而是一个纯粹的利差提取机器**——它们从散户那里以 0.1% 收钱，自己转手买 4% 的国债，把 3.9% 的利差装进口袋。然后 ABA 游说这种模式"关乎系统稳定"。
这是一个**监管套利伪装成金融服务**的典型案例。稳定币真正威胁的不是"经济的信贷流动"，而是这个寄生层。所以才打得这么凶。
## 二、历史在押着同一个韵脚：1970 年代的 Regulation Q 就是今天的 Genius Act 收益禁令
这是整段访谈最隐秘的洞察，Belshe 一笔带过但分量极重：**1970 年代**，美国有一个叫 "Regulation Q" 的规定，禁止银行给储户

item.title: [Business of Sport] Man City & LA Clippers: How To Deal With Naughty Owners
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反常识的观察：Ballmer 的"投降"不是失败，而是精算后的理性选择

表面上看，Ballmer 从"誓将抗争到底"到"深表遗憾"的 180 度转弯是一次公关崩塌。但如果用俱乐部会员经济学的框架重新看，这其实是一次极其冷静的止损：

  • NBA 本质上不是竞赛联盟，而是一个封闭的亿万富翁俱乐部（billionaire's club）。入场资格比赛场胜负更稀缺。
  • Ballmer 身价 1550 亿美元，30M 罚款相当于他净资产的 0.019%——这不是惩罚，是停车费。
  • 真正不可替代的是"会员席位"本身。所以当他走到悬崖边往下看，他看到的不是财务损失，而是社会资本的归零。
  • 他"认怂"的那一刻，恰恰是他作为前微软 CEO 的理性决策能力在起作用：在一个你比对手更需要留下的游戏里，不要玩鸡博弈。

这里有个让人意外的推论：惩罚的威慑力不来自金额，而来自"驱逐权"的隐性存在。NBA 从未真的说"我们要赶你走"，但 Ballmer 听见了。曼城的问题恰恰在于——阿布扎比皇室可能根本不在意是否被这个俱乐部除名。

二、跨领域连接：这是一场"微软反垄断案"的镜像重演，只是 Ballmer 换了身份

一个几乎无人提及的历史回响——Ballmer 本人恰恰是从微软反垄断诉讼的硝烟里走出来的。1998–2001 年，Ballmer 作为微软高管亲历了美国司法部对微软的拆分威胁；他目睹过"傲慢对抗监管"的代价。

  • 当年微软最初也是"奋战到底"派，几乎被判拆分；
  • 后来换帅、认错、和解，才换来后来的 Azure 帝国。
  • 25 年后，Ballmer 作为被监管方又站到了同样位置，只是这次他是"owner"而不是"CEO"。
  • 他之所以能在 24 小时内从"witch hunt"切换到"severe regrets"，不是因为他软，而是因为他见过结局。

与此对照，曼城的决策者从未经历过类似的监管羞辱史。没有历史伤疤的人，往往会把悬崖当作传说。这就是为什么同样的指控，两家俱乐部给出完全不同的反应曲线。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：谎言的"时间折叠"效应——Etihad 正在被自己 10 年前的证词反杀

视频里一笔带过但极具系统性意义的点：Etihad 在 2015 年美国商务部反垄断调查中、2021 年 CAS 上诉中、以及2012–13 年 Etisalat 支付事件中给出的叙述，正在和曼城今天的辩护策略互相爆破。

这是一个被低估的现代监管规律：

当一个主体必须在多个独立司法/监管场域都保持"自洽"时，谎言的维护成本随着时间呈指数增长，而不是线性增长。

因为每一次新的辩护都必须兼容： - 过去所有的公开证词 - 过去所有的内部文件 - 过去所有的交易对手记录 - 媒体可检索的所有历史报道

跨领域连接：这其实和加密学中的"零知识证明"问题结构同构——你每多说一句话，就多暴露一个可被反推的约束条件。情报界有一个古老的说法："间谍不是被敌人抓住的，是被自己过去的某一份档案抓住的。" Etihad 现在面临的，正是这个困境。

而更深一层的洞察是：体育监管正在从"证据驱动"进化到"叙事一致性驱动"。曼城案的真正杀伤力不在于某一笔付款，而在于它迫使被告在多个历史时点的叙述之间做出不可能的选择——认哪一个都伤。这是一种全新的"叙事型反欺诈"框架，未来会从体育扩散到企业合规、ESG 审计、乃至主权财富基金的透明度要求。

四、彩蛋式观察：Richard Masters 的"二号位逆袭"遵循了一个被低估的权力模式

Masters 的轨迹——第四备选、副手上位、无光环、被各方轻视，但连续解决 5–6 场危机——其实复现了一个在历史上反复出现的权力积累模型：

"扫地僧式 CEO" = 继承者悖论的解法

伟大前任（Scudamore）必然留下三类遗产： 1. 被神化的方法论（不能批评） 2. 被掩盖的烂摊子（必须收拾） 3. 对继任者的隐性比较（无法挣脱）

Masters 的赢法不是"做得比 Scudamore 更闪耀"，而是让每一次危机本身替他说话。这与丘吉尔、与库克接乔布斯班、与阿兰·穆拉利重整福特，是同一个套路：不要在前任的强项上竞争，去赢前任没打过的那些仗。

而这里埋着一个让人意外的推论：曼城案越拖、越激烈、越公开——Masters 的权威就越被加固。所以从博弈角度看，曼城上诉对他个人反而是权力资产的增值事件。你不觉得这个结构，有点阴险的美感吗？

📝 转录文本

开场：不是曼城，是 LA Clippers

I wanted to start off this week with the story of a major sports club that has been found guilty of contravening cost control regulations, and which has engendered an explosive response from the owners of that organization — and indeed threats of massive sanctions and punishments. Not even threats. It's actually, in this case, actually happened. Because we're not talking about Man City. We are talking about the LA Clippers.

The naughty LA Clippers.

The naughty LA Clippers, a naughty Steve Ballmer — their owner, who has been caught really on a quite personal level here. He's been absolutely pinged himself by the NBA for being at the heart of this.

背景：Ballmer 是谁

I'll read it out. I've written a nice little chronology of it, because it's going to ring true to a few of you based on what we talked about last week.

Just to give a bit of context to anyone that doesn't know: Steve Ballmer is a former chief executive of Microsoft. He's the biggest single shareholder in Microsoft actually — I think he owns about 4%. He's worth 155-ish billion dollars. Which, if you're looking at individuals who own sports assets, firmly places him right at the top of that.

And yes, him and the team have been being a bit naughty.

他们到底做了什么：绕过工资帽

So to break down what they've done: every NBA team has a salary cap, and there's also a cap on how much a single star can earn — they call that a maximum contract. Now, a team can't get around those limits by finding a player extra money on the side. That would be called circumvention, and it's banned under the deal between the league and the players union — these collective bargaining agreements. We've talked about where it's a split between the revenue of the leagues that goes to the players and then back into the system.

Now, a player called Kawhi Leonard, one of the biggest stars in the NBA, who joined the Clippers in 2019 — there's been found that payments have gone beyond that salary cap, manufactured, created, come to him through means that do not fit within the existing regulations.

The Clippers went to four companies that were already doing business with the club. That includes Aspiration, Boeing Go Wireless, Daktronics, and Locked in Insurance. They got those companies to give Leonard endorsement deals. The companies were persuaded by being offered more business from the team. So in effect: "sponsor our player and then you'll get more from us." The club also paid the personal expenses for Leonard and his people.

So they failed to report the improper solicitations for the off-court income opportunities made on Leonard's behalf through the business manager that he had, a guy called Dennis Robertson. Leonard, through the conduct of Robertson, violated those circumvention rules by pressuring the Clippers to assist him in obtaining the off-court income opportunities. And when he successfully did get those opportunities, he failed to reimburse the payments that the Clippers had paid for the personal expenses.

The NBA calls this a pattern of misconduct and notes that the Clippers are a prior offender on these rules. Interestingly, in the statement, they didn't actually develop what they meant by that.

调查速度：对比曼城的 8 年

The investigation was run by an independent law firm called Wachtell Lipton.

How long did it take?

Uh, I don't actually know.

Not long is the answer.

How did you know?

It was not long.

Wow. So they were clean and effective, were they?

So it was definitely not 8 years from original discovery through until final verdict. I'd have to go back and check exactly how long it was, but it was obviously much swifter.

处罚清单：史上最重的选秀权剥夺

Punishments. Well, they've been pretty severe, haven't they?

Quite chunky. Yeah, quite — lay them out.

I've got them in front of me here:

  • $30 million fine — you can park that as being not particularly relevant.
  • Loss of five future first round draft picks. Now, this is an absolute killer within American sport, because they don't have the academy system that we have, or indeed to a significant degree the same transfer system that we have in European football.

Their main way of attracting talent is through the draft system. The top young players come out of college sport, they get ranked, and effectively the teams get to choose in turn from this pool of players who have been laid out in front of them. Your first round pick is your opportunity to select one of the top ranked players, and this is absolutely treasured. There are many instances where teams who are going along in a middling way in a particular season will deliberately tank the rest of their season just to make sure that they get a better first round draft pick — because the lower you finish, the further up the pick list you get. That's their attempt to balance out the entire system.

So they have lost their first round draft picks for every season from 2029 until 2033. That is going to be a colossal amount of value lost during those 5 years. So forget the $30 million fine — that is not just going to affect their performance on the court, but it's also going to affect the value of their rosters.

It's been described as the harshest draft-related punishment in league history.

So, bringing it back to football — the harshest transfer market punishment that could be handed down.

  • Ballmer himself has been banned for a year from active involvement. Again, that's a very, very heavy and humiliating punishment.

Ballmer 的"开打再认怂"

Now, quite amusingly, when this verdict was originally reached, Ballmer did come out fighting, came out punching. He said: "We are going to challenge the NBA through every avenue available to us." Ring any bells?

Ballmer's lawyer, in a letter to Adam Silver — the commissioner of the NBA — described the findings as a "witch hunt" and said it was "a gross injustice."

My god, this is mad, isn't it?

It really is quite extraordinary. It's just so similar to the City situation.

But I'll tell you one thing which did amuse me about all this. In the end, Ballmer caved. He just caved in, and said that he had severe regrets about what had happened. And then in a fit — moment of genius — he pulled a Kirsty.

He pulled a Kirsty! Oh, it's back. We haven't had a Kirsty in a while.

So imagine this. You're Ballmer. You're running this big sports organization. All the stuff that Charlie laid out happens. You then decide to come up punching. You get humiliated. You get handed all these massive punishments. And actually, you decide at the end of it, "What I'm going to do is I'm going to fire my lawyer."

插话解释：什么叫 "pulling a Kirsty"

Sorry — to anyone, we may have some new people since we last pulled a Kirsty. Do you want to remind everyone what pulling a Kirsty actually means?

So quite early on when we started doing this podcast back at the start of the year, the relatively new head of the IOC, the International Olympic Committee, Kirsty Coventry, the former Zimbabwe swimmer — she was doing a press conference. She was asked a question to which she didn't know the answer.

And which she should have known the answer to. It was an obvious type of question.

Her answer to this was to say that she was probably going to have to fire her press officer for not having briefed her properly beforehand.

So we described this punching-down / dumping-the-staff thing as "pulling a Kirsty" — where you basically say "I've got no responsibility with this whatsoever, I fire a junior member of staff as a sacrificial lamb." It's called pulling a Kirsty, and Ballmer has pulled a Kirsty. He's decided that amidst all of this wrongdoing at his own club, he's just going to fire his lawyer. Brilliant. I absolutely love it.

其他被处罚的人：高管连坐

Do you know what? Alongside some of the other punishments — because they do link into City, and it is something that we did and have drilled in as the thing that must happen within the City case — it wasn't just Ballmer that got punished:

  • Gillian Zucker, the president of business operations — a one-year suspension without pay. She was named as primarily responsible and found to have given false and misleading statements to investigators.
  • Lawrence Frank, president of basketball operations — a six-month suspension without pay, including for approving improper expenses for Leonard and his family.
  • Kawhi Leonard — must pay the league $700,000.
  • Dennis Robertson, his representative — banned for 5 years from doing business with NBA teams.

Adam Silver 的声明

Now, we mentioned the strength of statement that had come out of the Premier League. I just wanted to quickly read out NBA Commissioner Adam Silver's statement, which said the following:

"The NBA's collectively bargained system for determining player compensation is a fundamental component of the basketball competition that the league oversees for the benefit of the teams and players, and ultimately the fans. I am deeply disappointed by the flagrant violations of our rules and by the Clippers' institutional and leadership failures that led to this misconduct. The severity of the penalties reflects the seriousness of the violations."

And don't forget — this is one case. I know they sort of referred in general terms to a prior offense which we don't know about, but this was one case. Not 114. One case, in one signing, etc.

So it's just interesting to see how another major sport can cope with this, deal with it, and exercise its authority. And I think it lays out that, whatever people say about "oh, this is going to very much damage the Premier League" or "it's going to damage the NBA" — the thing that damages competitions most of all is if they're seen to be unable to deal with stuff.

严肃职业联赛的处理范式

Right, and we're going to come on to Man City in a moment, but it's just worth bearing in mind that that is how a serious professional competition deals with misdoing. It deals with it swiftly, effectively, efficiently, and harshly. Because the message you then send out to all the other NBA owners is: don't cross the line. Don't even think about it. Make sure you're well the right side of the line.

But this feeds into Man City — because even though we have this decision now, this verdict, we are still now entering the beginning of the appeals process. We are still listening to conversations that suggest this could run on and on depending on how they decide to fight it. So the swift action here is one thing. The line in the sand that is drawn is another. It is not just their speed at coming to a verdict. It is how clinical and final that actually is. Because everything that we worry about now is not what's been handed down to City. It's what happens next. Because the longer this goes on, the less we talk about the product.

关键差异：Ballmer 想留在俱乐部，阿布扎比呢？

I think a critical thing here, and one potential difference between the two cases, is that Ballmer very much still wants to remain part of the club. Those US sports franchise leagues are like a club — and they are ultimately the billionaire's club. And they can just throw you out. They can just say "no, we don't fancy you as an owner, you're out the club."

So ultimately Ballmer's taken it right the way down the line, and then he's taken a look over the cliff and gone: "I still want to be part of the club. I don't want to risk that. Who knows what might happen if I take this all the way down all the avenues, as he said earlier — maybe. But ultimately if that risks me being out the club, I don't want to be out the club."

Now, the challenge that we have with City and the Abu Dhabi royal family is that it's open to question how determined they are to be a member of the club, if you were to put the EPL membership like that — and that being played off against any sense of national pride, any sense of national shame, all these types of things that play into that decision about "are we going to risk it all for trying to maintain our pride and try not to feel ashamed?"

If the answer to that is they would rather take it all the way down the line than risk feeling that shame — then that's something which they may well feel more emboldened to do than Ballmer did.

曼城上诉的理据

I think it's worth talking about this prospective appeal.

Yeah — there have been a couple of things that have come out in the last week which are historic incidents which would seem not to help City's grounds for appeal.

Right now. Is it worth, Charlie, going back and just quickly discussing what it is popularly supposed City's grounds for appeal are going to be?

Very simply: that the money which has been claimed to have come from their owners — i.e. Sheikh Mansour and his business holdings, which would be the owner inflating the value of the sponsorships — it has come from the Abu Dhabi government. Basically.

And of which he is deputy head.

I mean — yes, I mean — but we can't go down the…

It is a category, but let's not go down that rabbit hole.

In theory, if it comes from — let's say the government subsidizing a national carrier, an airline for example — then that does happen and would fall within the terms, I think. I mean, again, it just seems crazy anyway.

Regardless, City are basically claiming that it doesn't come from Mansour — it comes from elsewhere. Elsewhere being more legitimate reasons, and therefore they're not in breach of a lot of these charges.

Now, reportedly this was raised throughout the process, and it was dismissed by the panel as not being a sufficient explanation and not changing the way the panel viewed the breaches. They also said that it was an explanation that had been made at quite a late date — it was not part of the original pushback. This was something that was raised later in the day.

妈妈教的道理：别撒谎，会忘记

Now there are a couple of incidents. This reminds me — I remember being told when I was young by my mother: "don't lie." And one of the reasons given for not lying is: if you keep on lying, sometimes you can forget which lies you've told.

That was just brought to mind by a couple of things that have been dragged up by the media as to this defense — this central defense that says "it's totally normal for a state entity like Etihad, for instance, to have its sponsorship payments topped up by the sovereign government."

Etihad 的历史证词：2015 年美国反垄断调查

Now, I wouldn't even say ironically, but unfortunately for the City case — Etihad were being investigated along with other state-owned airlines by the US Department of Commerce 10 years ago.

Basically this is antitrust legislation. The US government saying: it wouldn't be fair for independent American airlines to have to compete in that market against airlines that were being massively subsidized by sovereign governments. Because the American government doesn't do it, so if other sovereign governments do, then our airlines are basically competing in a false market. That's the basis of that federal investigation.

So Etihad were — not formally charged, but it was alleged during that investigation — that Etihad, when they make sponsorships, were having those topped up by the Abu Dhabi government, and that this was a specific example of state aid, as it's called.

Which is their defense here.

And said: "no no no, when we make a sponsorship, it all comes from us." So they specifically denied that the Abu Dhabi government, the Emirati government, was topping up their sponsorships. That was quite specific in 2015.

I think this is why Etihad is now threatening to sue the Premier League. I think Etihad is now crapping itself that this whole case by the US federal government is going to get reopened now that they're claiming that their sponsorships were topped up by the Abu Dhabi government.

2021 年 CAS 听证会：James Hogan 的证词

And that same argument was given by James Hogan, the CEO, in 2021 to CAS — to overturn the punishment that UEFA had given them, the 2-year ban from European football.

The specifics of it here: he swore to CAS that Etihad's sponsorship of Manchester City was not government-backed, and did not involve disguised equity funding from club owner Sheikh Mansour or his vehicle ADUG. He testified that the sponsorship obligations were paid exclusively out of Etihad's own liquidity and funds.

Right. And now we know, based on this case, that that isn't the case. And the defense, as we've said, has been: "no no, it's come partially from the government."

And that's fine, that's okay.

As you say, Charlie, there's a whole other question which I think most people in this country would go — well, even if it was being paid by the government, that's not fine. The reason why that wouldn't be fine is because it would mean that certain football clubs — i.e. Man City and Newcastle — would be able to totally circumvent all the regulations that do apply to all the other clubs, because effectively they would have the benefit of being owned by either a sovereign, or somebody so close to sovereign as to be indistinguishable, who are able to access government money to totally change the nature of their sponsorship arrangements.

2012–13 年 Etisalat 支付：第三份互相矛盾的叙述

But there was another problem for them, which actually goes back to 2012–2013, and this regards Etisalat payments. Again, these are all historic investigations. This is why you've got to be so careful about what lies you tell — because forget "what do we say now, how do we push back on this or that?"

These were payments that were made by a guy called Jaber Mohamed on behalf of Etisalat to City. And City had informed UEFA, I think it was at the time, that these were in fact being made on behalf of Sheikh Mansour's entity, ADUG. Right?

But now apparently — no it never was. It was actually the Crown Prince Court payment, i.e. CPC payments, i.e. sovereign payments.

So it just feels to me like, even in as much as this appeal and the grounds of appeal were ever really going to fly — when people start going back and saying, "well hang on a second, but you said this in 2015, you said this in 2021, you said this in 2012–13… which of these stories is true?" Because each of these stories is going to cause you a problem somewhere. So you're now going to need to choose which one of these is actually a lie, and which one of these you're sticking by as being your true version of events.

It's not a great grounds for appeal.

保留一分可能：也许上诉还有底牌

We should say, Charlie, that it is possible that there are grounds for appeal which have not been leaked into the public domain, which nobody knows about, which have been kept underneath the table by the City lawyers — who are suddenly behind closed doors going to whip them out and put them on the table, and the appeal lawyers are going to go "oh wow, okay, that's something totally different." So we have to recognize that is logically a possibility.

It just feels that, given that we're talking also about the course of public opinion and reputation, it feels a bit unlikely that City wouldn't have let some of that be known. Why wouldn't you? You'd want that to start leaking out — that they actually do have genuine grounds — so that there's enough doubt being sown in the minds of enough of the public. Which is a huge amount. This is all being played out in the court of public opinion.

And again, let's not forget — when they walk out at Anfield at 4:30 on Sunday — you know, make no mistake of it, this is going to be an absolute bloodbath. This is going to be brutal.

Whether the people it's directed at are directly involved or not is irrelevant. Anyone associated with that badge, with that club, is going to cop the full extent of it.

I meant cop. Sorry, that was a — [laughter] — very good, Charlie.

Oh guys, you're actually… anyway, you get the point.

为 Richard Masters 说句公道话

Charlie, there was one point I just wanted to ask you on. We touched on it on Substack, but I haven't really heard other people talk about it. And I did think it was something that we should mention — a little bit of the congratulatory side, should we say, to Richard Masters and the team, and the importance of the work that has gone on.

Look, the time frames are not ideal. The reporting, the communications has annoyed a lot of people. We fully accept that. But can we just give the credit maybe where it's due — for pursuing this the way that he has done. The foundations from which he came into the job, the tough time he's had, the things he's had to work through, to the time to now get to this moment. I think it's quite a momentous thing, and I do think it's worth just a few minutes.

保密与证据工作的胜利

Yeah, it's true. I mean, I think there are a lot of people questioning what this means for the Premier League next, but I haven't seen anyone question that the Premier League haven't done the right thing. And I have noted in a few places people applauding the Premier League for the fact this has all been kept totally confidential. Because one of the grounds for a retrial would have been if there had been stuff leaking out. There has been absolutely — it's been watertight. Nothing has leaked out.

And from the verdict, it seems as if three independent lawyers have decided that the Premier League has prepared its case immaculately. Now let's not forget that that was not the case with UEFA. UEFA lost at CAS because they'd actually screwed up. The Premier League have not screwed up, and they've delivered the evidence in such a way as to win this comprehensively, hands down. Absolutely full square.

Masters 的背景与压力

That's a big win for Richard Masters, the chief executive of the Premier League. And that's a guy who's been under a lot of pressure.

To give the background: Richard Masters took over from the legendary Richard Scudamore, who had been the chief executive of the Premier League for 20 years and had overseen a period of immense growth in revenues during that time. Now, how much of that was actually down to Scudamore is open to question — because the fact is, the Premier League was gaining in global popularity for reasons which were beyond just what the chief exec of the Premier League might do or say in his negotiations with TV companies. But broadly speaking, he was given a lot of credit for the growth of the Premier League from the late 1990s until, I think it was 2016, 2017.

When he was retiring, there were various other candidates who were recruited effectively to try and do that job, and they all turned it down. So in the end, the Premier League end up going to Scudamore's number two, his commercial guy, Richard Masters. And Masters wandered into that job basically in a bad place — because all the club bosses and owners looking saying "well, you were our fourth choice, our fallback option."

You don't have the natural authority of Scudamore —

Of course he doesn't. He hasn't been running it for 20 years. Much younger. And has, until now, been doing the commercial deals, sponsorship deals, etc. So why would he have that natural authority?

一连串硬仗

He then — he got the job in 2019, just for context people — walks into:

  • COVID happening two years into his watch — a massive issue for football.
  • The Super League — again, a massive issue for the Premier League.
  • All the problems with the football league to deal with.

Obviously it wasn't Scudamore's fault that COVID didn't happen on his watch. But all these other things were basically left in the in-tray by Scudamore. These were all things that had not been properly comprehensively sorted out.

And don't forget — all the offences that City allegedly, well not even allegedly, have been proven to have committed, happened on Scudamore's watch. So Masters has been mopping up the mess from what happened back then.

He then also had to get the associated party transaction rules through, which he did. And then he's had to mop up this case as well. And he looks like he's almost got all his clubs to agree to a kind of comprehensive deal with the football league that the football league might agree to.

一个连赢的 CEO

So you've got to look at it and say — that's five or six issues that Masters has won every single one, despite in every single case there being significant moments in time where people were like "well, that could be a real problem." But in each case, he's won.

I don't know him. I've never met Richard Masters. But I will give him great kudos for — despite continual criticism and frankly downplaying him — he's kept his cool, he's kept his dignity, and he's kept winning.

And I think he's now getting to the place which you see with people like Adam Silver and the other Leviathans of the American Leagues, where he's now got so many wins under his belt that he's got the authority now to actually run that league properly.

Well, it demands respect now, doesn't it?

Yeah. Previously, I think — it has been dismissive, been patronizing to an extent. Tap on the — "oh, our little Richard" type thing. "There's our lad Richard, but he isn't quite as good as the other Richard" type thing.

But he's dealt with all these issues, and I think he's now earned the right to be the authoritative Premier League CEO that the game needs. It needs to have somebody in that seat who can knock the heads together of the various different clubs, and I think he's now got to that state where he should be able to do it.

## 一、最反常识的观察：Ballmer 的"投降"不是失败，而是精算后的理性选择
表面上看，Ballmer 从"誓将抗争到底"到"深表遗憾"的 180 度转弯是一次公关崩塌。但如果用**俱乐部会员经济学**的框架重新看，这其实是一次极其冷静的止损：
- NBA 本质上不是竞赛联盟，而是一个**封闭的亿万富翁俱乐部**（billionaire's club）。入场资格比赛场胜负更稀缺。 - Ballmer 身价 1550 亿美元，30M 罚款相当于他净资产的 0.019%——这不是惩罚，是**停车费**。 - 真正不可替代的是"会员席位"本身。所以当他走到悬崖边往下看，他看到的不是财务损失，而是**社会资本的归零**。 - 他"认怂"的那一刻，恰恰是他作为前微软 CEO 的理性决策能力在起作用：**在一个你比对手更需要留下的游戏里，不要玩鸡博弈**。
这里有个让人意外的推论：**惩罚的威慑力不来自金额，而来自"驱逐权"的隐性存在**。NBA 从未真的说"我们要赶你走"，但 Ballmer 听见了。曼城的问题恰恰在于——阿布扎比皇室可能根本不在意是否被这个俱乐部除名。
