item.description:
## 一、英伟达"独自掉队"背后的结构性信号——这不是技术面问题
视频里反复追问"为什么 Nvidia 没跟上回弹"，但真正值得警惕的洞察是：**它不是被 OpenAI 流言拖累，而是市场正在悄悄完成一次"从卖铲人到淘金者"的坐标系切换**。
你看节目中一组反常的组合——Oracle 跌 5% 后反弹、Palantir 创历史新高、Snowflake 持续走强、Palo Alto 把前一天的下杀全部吃回；而 Nvidia 却停在 242 附近、"假突破"。这不是巧合。软件股的 re-rating 从六七月 capitulation 开始，意味着市场终于愿意为"**AI 落地的现金流**"付溢价，但同时在悄悄降低对"**AI 基础设施的无限扩张叙事**"的估值乘数。Nvidia 的 PE 和下游应用的 PE 第一次出现了"剪刀差"——这才是 Nvidia 独自走弱的根因，OpenAI 流言只是导火索。
**跨领域连接**：这幕像极了 1849 年加州淘金潮的后半段。Levi Strauss（卖铲人）的股票初期一骑绝尘，但真正的大牛股是那些建立起稳定销售网络、把矿工收入变成重复消费的

item.title: [Latent Space] Why AlphaFold Didn't Solve Protein Folding — Pushmeet Kohli, Google DeepMind & Sal Candido, Biohub
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个被广泛忽略的真相：AlphaFold 解的不是"折叠"，而是"复刻"

Pushmeet 在闲聊语气里丢下的那句话值得被单独拎出来反复读——"We are trying to replicate and get the same structure. That's what we did." 这是整个 AI-for-science 叙事里最具颠覆性的一次自我祛魅。公众以为 AlphaFold 回答了"蛋白质为什么会折成这个样子"，但它其实只回答了"PDB 里的那个晶体快照长什么样"。我们从未知道蛋白质的真实基态是什么，也不知道它们的构象分布是什么——我们只是在高精度地模仿一张静态照片。这几乎等同于：用 100 万张恒星的照片训练出一个"宇宙模型"，然后宣布我们理解了恒星演化。更吊诡的是——它居然 真的有用。这揭示了一个几乎没人敢说出口的科学现实：复刻能力 (replication) 和理解能力 (understanding) 的脱钩，正在成为 AI 科学的默认范式。这与计量经济学里"预测准不等于因果对"是同一个幽灵，只是换上了生物学的外壳。

跨领域连接：从元基因组"垃圾数据"到互联网预训练——所有大模型都在偷偷吃"腐殖质"

Sal 说他们训蛋白质语言模型用的是 metagenomic sequences——"much of that data I can guarantee you isn't even a real whole protein"，但模型效果反而更好。这与 LLM 领域一个被反复验证却很少被哲学化的现象形成惊人同构：Common Crawl 里的垃圾、拼写错误、机翻、半截代码，恰恰是让语言模型获得泛化能力的养分。生物学家花一百年把蛋白质分类成"正确的"，机器学习告诉我们"错误的"才是信号。这呼应了生态学里的一个古老洞见：森林的生产力不来自大树，而来自腐殖质层。真正支撑 AlphaFold 这类"干净模型"的，是地球四十亿年演化留下的、我们曾经视为噪音的基因垃圾堆。另一个几乎没被注意到的隐喻跳跃是 Pushmeet 对 cryo-EM 微片的渴望——他想绕过 PDB 这个"策划过的博物馆"，直接从原始感光底片学习。这其实是计算机视觉 2012 年之后同一场革命的回放：从 SIFT/HOG 的手工特征到端到端像素学习。生物学正在经历它自己的 ImageNet 时刻，只是慢了十年。

最反直觉的一击：可解释性 (interpretability) 根本不是模型的属性，而是观察者的属性

Pushmeet 轻描淡写地抛出的那句"Interpretable by whom?"把整个 XAI 领域的根基抽掉了。他的逻辑是：AlphaFold 对人类认知带宽不可解释，但对未来一个更大的前沿模型也许完全可解释——"maybe they will come up with a theory of how AlphaFold was interpreting."这把可解释性从本体论问题（模型本身是否可解）变成了认识论问题（谁在解）。这几乎是把 Nagel 的"做一只蝙蝠是什么感觉"直接搬进了生物信息学：不是模型不可解释，而是我们不够复杂。令人更不安的推论是——人类正在成为 AI 科学里的"解释瓶颈"。未来真正的科学突破可能发生在"大模型给大模型解释小模型"的循环里，而我们只能通过第三手翻译去理解自己工具的决定。

额外一个藏得很深的洞见：Pushmeet 真正在意的不是"准不准"而是"校准 (calibration)"——"PLDDT 要是没校准，哪怕模型 95 GDT，也会毁掉一个博士生的一年"。这是整场对话里最像风险工程而不是机器学习的时刻。它暗示生物 AI 的下一个范式转移，可能不来自更大的模型，而来自把不确定性量化当作一等公民——这与 Gigerenzer 几十年来对医学概率素养的呼吁、与金融领域从"预测"转向"VaR"是同一场迁徙。谁先把"诚实的不确定性"做成产品化能力，谁就能把 AlphaFold 的"好玩的玩具"变成临床医生敢签字的工具。

📝 转录文本

开场：protein folding 真的被解决了吗？

So when people sort of say the protein folding problem has been solved like at a conceptual level yes there might be sort of yes there has been there have been some advances — we don't know what is the actual true ground state that proteins take and what is the actual distribution of structure that proteins take. What we are trying to do is basically someone got a structure, deposited it in the PDB and we are trying to replicate and get the same structure. That's what we did, right? And it just so happens that it's useful. But that does not mean that we have understood all of protein dynamics.

建模者的开场：数据有没有自己的 bitter lesson？

Yeah. So, um, great to be here. Uh, what an exciting morning. So many cool announcements. I think the future of bio science is being like announced right here. Um, so this is the modeling session. Uh, we are all modelers. So of course it's natural for us to talk about data.

So to start out with, I think one of the things that I like to think about when it comes to data is — or is like — is there a scaling, like how do you scale data properly? And uh, this has brought me to this question about the bitter lesson but recast in the frame of data.

So the bitter lesson, for those of you who are not AI people, is the statement that methods that scale win eventually. If you can just scale enough, it wins. And so my question — I'll start with Sal here — is: is there a bitter lesson for data?

Sal：找到 scaling law 本身就是功夫

Yeah, I mean for sure. I think that you obviously need the right data, right? Like in order for it to work. So I think one misconception of scaling laws is that scaling laws are everywhere and they always exist. I think a lot of the work is actually finding that scaling law, right?

Like so a lot of what we really do is trying to figure out what's a situation where if you put more compute into it, if you put more data into it, you actually get a better result out. And the reason — that's a great situation is then, you know, once that happens, you can kind of just turn the crank, right? Like it becomes an engineering problem, which is something I like.

But that has to do with architecture, but it also very much has to do with data. So if you don't have the data with the right information statistics to solve the problem that you want — which is, you know, I think probably pretty obvious — like if you think about it for a second, you're not going to get a model that has the capabilities and the understanding of you want. So you can only really pull the information from the data that you have and then use that to generalize beyond, right?

数据模态与"懒惰建模者"的两面性

Q: So when it comes to data collection, how do you think about what types of data modalities are best? And maybe a kind of related question is: do you think that modelers have a tendency to work on problems where the data is available, rather than maybe the data that solves your goal most, or has the most impact for translational medicine?

Sal: Oh for sure. So I think that — uh, I won't speak for all modelers but like I'm lazy, so I'm going to work with what's available. And you know, I think there is actually a good side and a bad side to this.

The good side is that when you're doing like machine learning, or like conventional machine learning, you're really looking for the most pristine high-quality data examples that you can find. But when you actually, if you're like me, you're actually someone who goes and you're kind of like rooting around in the back room, looking through people's junk, like what's there.

So a concrete example of this is when we train a protein language model. We train on metagenomic sequences which are not the highest quality data. In fact, much of that data I can guarantee you isn't even a real whole protein. And yet that makes the performance of the model go up for designing real proteins that work, for understanding proteins that we know are things.

And so that's the positive side of it. But that can lead you to a negative place where you say, "well, let's just scale up the data that we can generate easily." And I think that's not necessarily the way to do it.

社区共建：谁决定"该生成什么数据"？

I think that's one of the things that's really exciting to me about what we're talking about here today with the BBI. You know, it's really going out and saying: what is the data that we need to solve the problem? It's the right resources but also the right community.

Like I think one thing that we try and do at Biohub anyway is to work in the open, work with the community and move the whole community forward. And I think that's a really critical piece — because if you just have people who are building models, we're going to lean towards the data that exists. If you just have people who generate the data, they're going to lean towards the things that can be generated. But if you can work together as a community every step of the way in an open fashion, then you can actually figure out what is the data that we need, and then you can find that scaling law.

Pushmeet：Rich Sutton 讲 bitter lesson 时真正讲的是什么

Cool. What do you think — the bitter lesson for data?

Yeah. So I was at DeepMind when Rich was with us and working and thinking about this idea of the bitter lesson. When Rich and I took — the thing that I took from Rich's original lecture that he actually gave at DeepMind was not about the actual notion of whether data is useful or how should we think about machine learning.

I think my take was that he was talking about something more conceptual. And the conceptual thing that he was talking about is: sometimes when we are looking at problems, we think about solutions in a very religious way. "I'm a modeler" or "I'm a data generation person." And I think that is the bitter lesson — that if you approach the problem with that mindset, you might not succeed.

The problem comes first and you should be flexible in terms of your solution space. You should try both things. You should try to understand what is the problem that you're trying to solve, and if it requires modeling effort, do the modeling effort; and if it requires collecting more data, then collect data.

But the thing that happened in machine learning in those times is people said, "we are machine learning researchers. The data set is there. Here's some training data, here's some test data, and we will just optimize the model." And that is broken, right? In the sense that if your eventual goal is to solve the problem, then you have to be able to look at both aspects of what goes into the process. And what goes into the process is not just data or modeling — it's also about expertise.

两种策略：AlphaFold vs 细胞基因组学

So the example that I have is — with AlphaFold, we looked at what was possible with current existing data sets, because we did not have the core expertise of now going to — or even the resources, by the way, to say "let's augment the PDB by a significant order of magnitude." The amount of investment that organizations and scientists across the world had put in to construct that data was invaluable. So there you have to focus on getting the biggest bang out of your buck by investing it in modeling.

But in other areas — when if you're approaching, say, cell genomics — then we took the same approach and said, "well, what can you do with CZ CELLxGENE if you're looking at cell genomics?" And there it was very clear, after a bunch of work, that the data was not there yet to be able to build — to go after that grand ambition of building the virtual cell.

And so it just brings people together to focus on what are the actual challenges, if you want to advance science, rather than being religiously following advances on data generation or in modeling.

给年轻研究者的建议：先成为多学科的人

Q: Cool. I really like that answer. So what do you think is the actionable takeaway from this? Like always define the problem first and then figure out what solution space to search over. But more broadly, how should the community be thinking about this as we go forward for the next generation of basically trying to solve translational medicine?

Pushmeet: Yeah, I think the advice that I give to anyone who is starting in the area is: think of yourself as a multi-disciplinary person. Understand the problem first. Why are you working on this problem? What are we trying to achieve? And then think about what is it that will be needed — whether it's modeling, whether it will be compute scaling, whether it will be data generation.

So understanding of that problem is extremely important, and of course then you have to build your expertise in the house. But it's not as if you don't have constraints. Maybe there are constraints — like there is only a specific amount of data that you can generate, or there is a specific model size that you can afford to train. Understand those constraints and try to fail fast, and look at what are the approaches that are going to be feasible in the long term in getting you to that intercept — the impact level that you're going after.

下一个问题：工艺美术品 vs 可扩展通用方案

Okay. Cool. So this actually leads me right into my next question, which was: when I look at the evolution of modeling — let's say AlphaFold 2 was essentially a work of art, like a bunch of very carefully handcrafted features, there was a lot of thought, very intentional thought done to every part of the solution — and then, I think, some of Google or Alphabet's work has been kind of still stays in that space, but seems like the general consensus is to move to more scalable, more general strategies.

Do you think that there's still a lot of artisanal craft solutions or problems that need that? Or is our resources better spent, generally speaking — fixed resources, fixed money — can go to compute, it can go to talent, it can go to data: should we be focusing on scale first?

Pushmeet：归纳偏置 (inductive bias) 不是意外，而是用科学直觉给模型"开挂"

So my — again, let's approach it from first principles — and think about: when you think about the arts and crafts of how do you construct a model to be better, it was not an accidental thing. We did a lot of experimentation, but there was a vision behind it — all this scientific intuition that came from biophysics and biochemistry — that those interactions, that amino acid residues are not just doing their own thing, they are being influenced by other residues. So let's bake that in.

Like, if you have learned something from the scientific community, use that information and try to encourage the model and give it that unfair advantage. And it does basically make the model much more data-efficient, because it doesn't have to replicate everything.

I also have to mention that curating good data is an art in itself, right? It's not as if you will say "well, put more data" — if you replicate the same amount of data, you're not going anywhere. So it's not just about big data, it's about good data, and actually understanding the coverage of what data is necessary for making progress in the problem is, in fact, I would say a much more interesting and much more challenging problem in itself.

Sal：扩展本身也是一门工艺

Yeah, I think, I mean I very much agree. I think, as you — it really depends on, as you're saying, the problem to be solved. So if you have kind of a smaller amount of data, then certainly having more inductive bias in the model is going to help you, right? Like you actually need that to get the results on smaller scales of data.

As you get more and more data, you see that sometimes the model can find things that you didn't necessarily know about. And sometimes that inductive bias, if it wasn't exactly correct, can hold you back, right? So there is definitely that tipping point as things get better.

But I guess I kind of object to your question too, because I think there actually is a lot of — I think there's a lot of craft actually to the scaling part of things as well. So you need very — there's a lot of algorithmic work that actually goes into taking these models and training them on more data, putting more computing in, and making them bigger, right?

And we see that not only is that from an infrastructure perspective and making the models run inference faster, but we're actually seeing that things are going beyond transformers to more bespoke architectures that can — well, I mean, I don't think we're in a post-transformer world in any way, shape or form, but we're modifying those architectures in order to make them more fit for purpose, and actually work better even at internet scale data.

So I think that's kind of the project. As more and more data comes in, it's not only helping to curate that data and select what is the next batch of information that we actually need — you know, it's more information than data. How do you get that next batch of information that the models need? But then also at every step of the way, at every scale, what is the right architectures then to get the most out of that data?

五年之后：蛋白质结构预测真的"解决"了吗？

Cool. So if you think about the state of protein structure prediction right now, the news will say protein structure prediction has been solved. But then if you talk to my friends, they will all say we have so much left to do here. So many things — like function, dynamics, and then design — are still just wide open problems.

It's been five-ish years since AlphaFold 2 was announced. Progress has been made. But I'm curious — Pushmeet, what do you think? Is there another big leap being made here? Are there blockers in solving these problems? Do we not have the right data yet? Do we not have the right algorithms or ideas? Or is this something that we can see evolving in the future, and it's just a matter of time?

Pushmeet：蛋白质不是积木

Yeah, I think science, how it operates, is basically by isolating something and then making progress step by step. So when people say the protein folding problem has been solved — like at a conceptual level, yes there might be, yes there have been some advances. But I think it's also, when you think about that narrative of proteins being the building blocks — proteins are not blocks, and they don't act as blocks, right? I say proteins are the building blocks all the time, but actually, I don't believe in it, right? Proteins are extremely complex. They are disordered. Their shape might change depending on the context.

And like what AlphaFold did — and in fact, John Jumper and I used to discuss this — like, what are we trying to solve? We don't know what is the actual true ground state that proteins take, and what is the actual distribution of structure that proteins take. What we are trying to do is basically: someone got a structure, deposited it in the PDB, and we are trying to replicate and get the same structure. That's what we did. And it just so happens that it's useful. But that does not mean that we have understood all of protein dynamics.

So at the top level, it's easier to communicate that we have made progress. But the scientists among us — and in this crowd — we know, right? And I think that's the really important thing for us to understand, and have that common ground: that a lot of work needs to be done, and we have made progress, and there's a lot to celebrate. But let's not stop the funding of protein structure prediction and protein dynamics, because we are just getting started.

魔杖问题：如果能召唤一样东西，是什么？

Q: So what do you think the biggest blocker — if there's one thing you could wave a magic wand and say "we have more of blank" that would accelerate one of those things, function, dynamics or design, what would the magic wand be? What would you wave into existence?

Pushmeet: Oh, I have — basically — when you asked me that question, like, I'm a machine learning — my background is quite eclectic. I started as a security researcher, then went into computer vision, Bayesian theory, and finally got into discriminative machine learning and deep learning, and so on. And then AI for coding, and then finally science.

So when you asked me that question, the computer vision researcher in me was super excited about cryo-EM micrographs. I was like, what is this PDB data? I should be working at the source, right? I should be looking at the cryo-EM micrographs. I don't want those structures — they must be missing out all the data. I should just directly operate at cryo-EM micrographs.

Now getting models that can scale at that level with the right amount of data and can extract all the dynamics and distributional information that is captured there — would be an amazing thing. I tried, I did, but it requires more work, right?

Q: Still work on it, but you believe that this is a route — this can give you —

Pushmeet: Yeah, I think at some point of time, maybe people better than me would take a stab at it, and we'll get somewhere.

Sal：我们建的是辐条，但人们想要自行车

Q: What do you think, Sal?

Sal: Yeah, I think it's really interesting because I think these models are quite useful, but they're not exactly the problem that most people want to solve. Like they serve a very specific purpose, and then you can also use them to do other things — like you can use them to design new proteins, for example, which is not the thing that you would kind of start with.

So they're very useful, but I kind of think of the models that we build right now as — you know, you've got someone who's trying to understand how a bicycle works, and you're modeling like a spoke on it, right? And you kind of have to — those models can get better and better over time, but a lot of what you really need to do is you need to move from models of spokes to wheels to maybe whole bicycles, because that's actually what people want to understand.

Actually, I think, to continue the analogy, it seems like people want to use the model of the bicycle to design this part for a pickup truck or something like that, right? But I think that as we put these models more into the particular context which they're in — then we'll actually be able to learn more about these interactions on a broader sense. And that's really where things are going to be going. But I agree with you — I think we should keep trying to work on folding models, because I think they're going to keep getting better and better.

Feynman 的反转：不理解也能创造的时代

So with regards to design — there's this famous Feynman quote, "that which I cannot create, I do not understand." Now we're in a world where it's really easy to create things without understanding them at all. So I'm curious — what are your thoughts about how important it is to actually have models which can help humans understand things, versus magical black boxes which can effectively, you know, one-shot a picomolar binder or something like that?

Sal：从模型里"把知识挤出来"

I mean I think that we were designing things with magical black boxes long before AI came around, right? So in some sense I think that's still useful. But I think that the understanding is really important, and I think that's actually one of the big things I think about a lot with AI — because there's so much for these models to learn, and as intelligence is getting cheaper and cheaper and more available, you can deploy it to learn more and more things about what's going on in the world. But then how do you actually pull that knowledge out of the machine, so to speak?

And so it's something that — I can understand, maybe that's just like my esoteric curiosity — like, I think there's so many things to learn.

Q: I think lots of scientists really want to understand things, and the end points are maybe not as important. But then, you know, we are here to solve translational medicine as a problem, right?

Sal: Or — I mean I think it's — I think you do have to, the more you dig into things, the more that you can find the right way to keep pushing them forward.

So one thing that's really salient to me about this is: I think the models actually have a lot more information in them than we know. We've worked a lot on interpretability for our models, and you find a lot of information in there which — I think people know that protein language models learn some notion of structure within their representations, but we find information about some functions, we find information about motions, right? So I think there's a lot in there still to be unlocked, even from the models that we have now.

And I think that's important for us to understand — how do these models work as we move up, as we raise the capability. At the end of the day, you expect a world model to come out of trying to compress all this information into the model, right? How does the model do its job? How does it design a protein? Well, it's compressed all the information from evolution into this model. So in addition to it being able to spit out something which is useful to us, there's certainly something to learn just by looking at what's inside.

Pushmeet：可解释性是"由谁来解释"的问题

Yeah. What do you think, Pushmeet? Design versus understand?

So I have a different take on this, in the sense that I think when we think about models, some level of understanding is necessary. So I'll say what level of understanding is necessary.

So AlphaFold actually is not perfect, right? It's not perfect. It's 90 GDT — AlphaFold 2 was 90 GDT at that time on that set. But even if it was 95 GDT — if the pLDDT score was completely uncalibrated, who would trust it? It would just magically give good answers, but suddenly tell you "here's very very confident," and you will be working on it for the next one year and finding out it was completely wrong.

The calibration of the uncertainty measure was extremely important. So in that sense we do understand, and we actually made a lot of progress in understanding how does AlphaFold 2 behave.

Now that's different from "how did it work and find the solution." And there, I agree with Sal, that there's a notion of interpretability. Why did it work? Why did it give this answer?

And I think if you think about it, AlphaFold 2 was at the highest level interpretable — because if you look at its ability to generalize (and we did not discover it before launching), when we launched AlphaFold 2 and made the weights available, people found out that it was a great disordered protein predictor. It could figure out which elements of the protein are disordered. So it just shows that it generalizes.

Now, interpretability asks the question: interpretable by whom? If you're saying interpretable by a human rational system — with the cognitive and computational limitations of the human brain — then no, AlphaFold 2 is not interpretable. But if you are asking: is AlphaFold 2 interpretable to a much larger and more sophisticated model as to how it works? Maybe it is. We just don't get it, right?

But I think, as users of AlphaFold 2, we do need to understand what it is able to do and what it is not able to do. So understanding the behavioral characterization and the strengths and limitations of the model — I think that is extremely important. And we can't just be using these models without having that behavioral characterization, because otherwise it will, rather than help, being helpful — harm us, right?

Q: So your take is that interpretability strictly speaking isn't necessary, but a way of ensuring the model is trustworthy so humans can make actionable decisions is the thing that people should be focusing on?

Pushmeet: Exactly. And I also think that interpretability is also in the eyes of the beholder — like, who is interpreting it? If it is a human scientist who is trying to interpret how the model is going about and how will it make this prediction — that's a different question from another much larger LLM. If you give some of these large frontier models of the future access to the activation layers and say "okay, tell me, can you predict what AlphaFold will do?" — maybe they will be able to predict, and they will come up with a theory of how actually AlphaFold 2 was interpreting and producing these results.

终场：AI 什么时候真正改变临床？

Cool. Okay. That's the two-minute warning. So I am — one last question for both of you. Quick one.

So there's a real chance that AI will make dramatic improvements in human health in the near, immediate future. I like quantitative predictions — best guess, how long until we start seeing AI results in the clinic? Pushmeet, you want to start?

Pushmeet：问题提错了——AI 已经在那里了

Uh, I mean the point is — AI results in the — I think it's ill-posed. It's not a — AI is being used today already in every part of the drug discovery process. So from that perspective, it's already there, right?

But if you're asking me the question "when will we see that 10x acceleration or 100x acceleration in the timelines?" — then the other question is, what are we accelerating? Is it doing lead optimization? Is it the target discovery? Is it the pre-clinical or the tox work?

I think over the next few years — and this is why this effort that we announced today is extremely important — we need to tackle some of these hard challenges of biology, and only then will we be able to get these true unlocks of acceleration that dramatically transform how drug discovery will happen.

So AI will be there in the clinic, and will be impacting things that go into the clinic all the time. But the actual larger acceleration that will be unlocked only with a better understanding of the biological models that this effort is trying to create.

Sal：10x 思维 vs 10% 思维

Right, thanks. So real quick question, if we're almost out of time — but you?

Yeah. I mean I'm tempted to literally put on my bio hat to answer this question. But you know, I think it's really important to think about this, as you were saying, like what does it mean to push the field forward?

Like the thing that we really want to see is those outcomes. And so when will it be that a drug that was made entirely by AI, by an AI or something — I don't know. It's hard to know that. But I do think we're going to see rapid progress here very very quickly, because all these tools are being used.

And you know, going back to your point about the basic — you know, we need basic research, we need basic understanding — one thing I learned a long time ago in my career actually back at Google is like: sometimes it's easier to approach a problem by looking at what is it going to take to make a 10x improvement rather than a 10% improvement, right? And that's not because that's necessarily an easier path. It's because it allows you to take a broader view and see some solutions that you haven't been approaching, right? Like, and what is actually the path to do it? And you would go back and look from first principles — like, how are we going to do this? How are we going to really push this?

So I think both approaches — the 10% and the 10x — are valuable, and we should do both. I'm just very happy that at Biohub, like, we have a very beautiful and lofty mission statement to cure all disease, right? And if you want to do that, you really need to go and figure out: what is the 10x approach? And so I think it's a really great opportunity to be able to go do that.

Awesome. Thank you both. Thank you for being in the literal hot seat. Yeah, very interesting.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一个被广泛忽略的真相：AlphaFold 解的不是"折叠"，而是"复刻"
Pushmeet 在闲聊语气里丢下的那句话值得被单独拎出来反复读——"We are trying to replicate and get the same structure. That's what we did." 这是整个 AI-for-science 叙事里最具颠覆性的一次自我祛魅。公众以为 AlphaFold 回答了"蛋白质为什么会折成这个样子"，但它其实只回答了"PDB 里的那个晶体快照长什么样"。我们从未知道蛋白质的真实基态是什么，也不知道它们的构象分布是什么——我们只是在高精度地**模仿一张静态照片**。这几乎等同于：用 100 万张恒星的照片训练出一个"宇宙模型"，然后宣布我们理解了恒星演化。更吊诡的是——它居然 **真的有用**。这揭示了一个几乎没人敢说出口的科学现实：**复刻能力 (replication) 和理解能力 (understanding) 的脱钩，正在成为 AI 科学的默认范式**。这与计量经济学里"预测准不等于因果对"是同一个幽灵，只是换上了生物学的外壳。
## 跨

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Could the Aztecs and Inca have beaten the Spanish? - Si Sheppard
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、空心帝国的"特洛伊木马"结构：被低估的脚注，才是真正的核心

讲者几乎顺口提到了一个被埋没的关键数据——10万印加人统治着1000万人的帝国，纳瓦特尔语和克丘亚语都只被极少数精英使用。这不是"统治"，这是一层极薄的油漆覆盖在火山上。所以西班牙人根本没有"征服"帝国，他们继承了一场早已蓄势待发的内部叛乱。库斯科围城期间最反直觉的细节正是明证：战斗持续数月，加入西班牙一方的当地部落 不是减少、而是增加——他们不是在押注谁会赢，而是在围城的每一天都"看见"了印加的脆弱。

跨领域连接：这个结构与现代平台经济的颠覆模式惊人相似。Uber 没有击败出租车公司，它激活了司机对牌照垄断的积怨；Airbnb 没有打倒酒店联盟，它调用了被排斥在外的房东的愤怒。Cortés 不是军事天才——他是一个 API，让被压抑的政治能量通过他的通道释放出来。这里藏着一个合法性的普遍规律：政权不是靠实力维持的，是靠"必然性的幻觉"维持的，一旦幻觉破裂，哪怕实际力量没变，依附关系就瞬间瓦解。

二、让人意外的时间悖论：帝国最可征服的瞬间，恰好是它看起来最强盛的那一刻

讲者在接近结尾时抛出了一枚几乎被忽略的炸弹：如果西班牙人晚到100年（1619 而不是 1519），他们看到的特诺奇蒂特兰"将是一片长满苔藓的土丘和沼泽"——就像之前的特奥蒂瓦坎一样。这意味着1519年并非偶然的时间点，而是帝国生命周期中"最成熟可摘"的那一瞬间。

这颠覆了常识。我们直觉上以为帝国在衰落时才容易被攻破，但真实的系统规律恰恰相反：人口达到顶峰 = 生态承载已到极限；行政覆盖达到最广 = 边缘不满也达到最高。2007 年的雷曼兄弟、被 iPhone 击倒前的诺基亚、2000 年的思科——所有这些系统崩溃时都停在报表上的最高点。阿兹特克帝国的宏伟不是西班牙人胜利的障碍，它就是胜利本身的燃料。

三、马与天花是同一个生态包的两面：伟人只是半导体

主流叙事总把"骑兵"和"疾病"分开讲——前者是战术优势，后者是意外灾难。但讲者揭示的结构远更深：这两者是同一个生态系统的两个表达。欧亚大陆的可驯化动物（马、牛、猪、羊）既创造了战场上的机动性，又在数千年的人畜共生中孵化了天花、麻疹、流感的病原库。美洲没有这些动物，所以既没有骑兵、也没有免疫力——这不是两个问题，是一个问题。

这改变了我们对"伟人推动历史"框架的理解。讲者自己用"大齿轮和小齿轮"的比喻，但真正的洞察在更细一层：Cortés 和 Pizarro 这些"小齿轮"更像是半导体——他们本身没有能量，他们只是让生态势能（微生物、驯化动物、地理坡度）通过他们这个通道释放出来。征服者的身体是导管，不是电源。这解释了为什么杀掉 Cortés 可能延迟征服、但不能阻止它：你可以烧掉一片硅片，但你烧不掉电压差本身。

📝 转录文本

1. The Astonishing Speed of Conquest

And this is worth emphasizing. Cortez takes over the Aztec empire in what is now Mexico in two and a half years. So a couple hundred men, an empire of six million people, two and a half years. Pizarro does the same thing for the Inca Empire 10 years later in about 5 years.

So it's insane how fast these conquests happened — and just how little time, even though in principle they could have figured out ways in which to combat cavalry and things, just how little time they had to adapt. All the while, their whole social structure is disintegrating, there's disease, etc. There's all this psychological shock value.

2. The Counterfactual Question

Now, the obvious question to ask at this point, before we go to other ones, is: if you reran a simulation again and again, if you just change a few things here and there — change the leader for both the Aztecs or for the Spanish in these conquests — in what fraction of the simulations do, within a matter of a few years later, the Spanish end up in control of these empires anyway?

Because when you first learn about them, it actually sounds like an outrageous and impossible outcome that a few hundred men would take over empires of millions of people. And when you learn more about it, then you begin to think, well, I guess it couldn't have been any other way. But I don't know if that is your opinion.

3. The Great Wheels and the Small Wheels

In the grand scheme of things, there are multiple wheels that define history. The grand wheels that grind slowly — geography and climate — and then the smaller wheels in the foreground are the individuals, the key players themselves. And this is an integration of that process, the big wheels with the small ones.

Yes — if Cortés, which could have happened on multiple occasions, had been taken out early, the conquistadors, leaderless and rudderless, may well have disintegrated, and the conquest may have been aborted at that level.

Pizarro, again: Atahualpa's critical mistake was inserting himself into Pizarro's trap. If he had sent envoys to keep the negotiations at a distance, he may have been able to frustrate Pizarro's ambitions, and, as the head of what remained an integrated Inca Empire, he may have been able to use those numbers to win the campaign in the short term.

4. The Siege of Cusco

When the Inca did finally turn on the conquistadors, Francisco Pizarro had seized Cusco. He stripped the temples of their gold and silver — "the sweat of the sun and the tears of the moon," as it was called — and shipped it back to Europe. He goes back to the coast to set up Lima, what would become the modern capital of Peru.

The danger with Cusco is the fact it's elevated and away from the coast, which is where the Spanish, with their absolute monopoly over naval power, have the advantage. His problem was he left his half-brothers in charge back in Cusco, and they provoked Manco — who'd been set up as Pizarro's puppet ruler — into outright rebellion.

He rallies his people. He lays siege to Cusco. He takes Sacsayhuamán, the great fortress that dominates Cusco, and he has one of his generals, Quizo Yupanqui, cut off reinforcements arriving from the coast.

The Inca could win set-piece confrontations if they used their terrain and their knowledge of it to their advantage. Pizarro, from Lima on the coast, is taking reinforcements and pushing them into the interior to relieve Cusco, and Quizo is waiting till they enter narrow defiles and passes through the mountains, blocking both ends and then using boulders and other material to just obliterate them from the heights. More and more of these Spanish expeditions are being annihilated.

So at that level, when they use the terrain and their institutional knowledge of it to their advantage, the Inca are able to win set-piece battles — but they can't seal the deal in Cusco. And Manco makes the mistake of ordering Quizo to attack Lima. He feels, "we have the advantage now. I've bottled them up in Cusco. We've annihilated their relief columns. Take out their city on the coast and the problem's over."

But attacking Lima meant passing across open ground, which meant the Spanish then unleashed their advantage. The general is killed and the whole assault collapses.

5. The Role of Local Allies

Back in Cusco, yes, there's a handful of Spaniards holed up in just a couple of fortified buildings, desperately holding on. Day and night they're under assault — the psychological aspect to it, the beating of drums and the chanting, and the constant rain of missiles to set their buildings on fire.

They would have been wiped out except for two reasons. One, the open courtyards and plazas of Cusco are good terrain for cavalry, and they still have their horses. And secondly — again critically — the asset, through diplomacy, of the local peoples: the subordinated mitima as they were called, or yanakuna serfs, the defeated and subordinated peoples the Inca brought forcibly within their imperial structure, chafing under those authorities — see these outsiders as their chance to finally break free of Inca authority.

So, strangely enough as it may seem, more local peoples kept joining the besieged Spaniards during the whole battle of Cusco, which played out over many, many months. The Spanish end up with more allies than they started with during this battle, because there were so many people within the Inca Empire — from the Cañari, who were from Ecuador, to the Chachapoya from the Amazon basin, to even the Alcaviza who used to be rivals with the Inca for control of Cusco itself — increasingly siding with the Spaniards. And that local manpower was the critical asset. Without that, yeah, they would have been wiped out at Cusco.

6. The Hollow Empire

So again, it's the Spaniards inserting themselves into an imperial orbit which, from a distance, looks impressive with its geographic expanse and its total population, but which had been ruthlessly dictated to by a tiny elite of a hierarchy who would impose themselves over the entire system.

Remember, only a small number of people spoke Nahuatl, the imperial language of the Aztecs. Only a small number spoke Quechua, the imperial language of the Inca themselves. It was the Inca Empire, but it was constructed from multiple, multiple different ethnicities. And when they saw the chance, they took it to side with the Spaniard.

Yeah. It's worth remembering that the Aztecs and the Incas are themselves sort of the equivalent of the conquistadors in their own world, right? There's 100,000 or so actual Incas. They're controlling an empire of 10 million people. So they are themselves an imperial force.

7. Contingency vs. Deep Causes

Going back to the question then of how contingent these victories were, it kind of sounds like you're saying they are contingent, right? Because you're pointing out all these cases in which if things had gone slightly differently, the siege of Cusco would have worked, or Cortés would have been killed in battle and stuff.

The ultimate factor goes down to those background forces, the great wheels that grind through history. Yeah — the geography and climate. Stuck to one other factor: the fact that Eurasia was so stacked with domesticable animals — sheep, cows, goats, mules, pigs, and above all, horses — and human interaction in biomes with those domesticated animals created the context for the evolution of contagious diseases, endemic or pandemic, that ripped back and forth through Eurasia, and we're familiar with all their names.

That never occurred in the New World. The people there had no acquired immunity to diseases such as the big one, smallpox, but beyond that, the whole galaxy of communicable diseases that we're now familiar with as being universal.

I think even if the Aztecs and Inca had won the short-term proximate victories, the longer-term demographic crisis would have undermined the functional capacity of their societies to remain integrated — and to resist, much longer, the pressure from within, from their subject peoples. As they felt the authority of their overlords beginning to weaken, that would have led to their fragmentation.

8. The Teotihuacan Parallel

That is the overarching cycle of pre-Columbian societies generally. They're extremely impressive — in fact, more impressive when you consider the disadvantages they had to struggle with. Their pyramids were built not through the assistance of beasts of burden or even the wheel, but simply through pure manpower and the application of that to construct it. The subject peoples would have broken for freedom.

We see the recurring cycle of Mesoamerican history. For example, when Cortés arrived, Tenochtitlan was one of the greatest metropolises perhaps on earth — beautiful and rich and heavily populated. A hundred years later, if he'd arrived in 1619 as opposed to 1519, he would have found a swamp with moss-covered mounds and hills rising out of it.

The parallel to that, of course, is Teotihuacan — the previous great metropolis which dominated Mesoamerica. It rose, it expanded, it attracted a huge population, it overstressed its environment, and it collapsed. I think the Aztecs naturally would have gone the same way.

So, one way or another, the Spanish — or even subsequent waves of European colonists — would have entrenched themselves at the coast and would have, perhaps more slowly, pushed inland. It's possible that you would see a more balanced relationship between the colonists and the indigenous peoples, but I think in the longer term, they all would have been folded into the grand European imperial framework.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups] Beam: The Great American Open Model with ReflectionAI Co-Founder and CEO Misha Laskin
item.dc:creator: No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：Misha 其实在描述一种"反摩尔定律"的新形态

当所有人都在讨论 AI 的"规模指数增长"时，Misha 给出了一组冷静但几乎没人认真拼在一起的数字： - 预训练算力：每代模型 4× - 人类研究员每年效率提升：7× - RL 系统因"模型帮模型"产生的效率跃迁：30×

把这三条曲线叠起来，你会得到一个被行业集体忽略的真相——算力增长正在被"自我迭代效率"反超。换句话说，前沿模型未来几年真正稀缺的不是 GPU，而是"能让模型帮自己变聪明的那套 pipeline 的所有权"。这解释了一个让人意外的隐藏逻辑：Reflection 不是在"追赶 OpenAI"，而是在抢占一个即将打开的套利窗口——在前沿尚未真正进入"自改进加速期"之前，用相对低的资本（单位数十亿）追上，之后就能用模型本身补贴后续模型。这是个会在 18 个月内关闭的窗口。

二、跨领域连接：开源模型 ≈ 冷战时期的"美元 + 海军"组合

Misha 在节目后半段抛出了一个被低估的洞见："open models are Trojan horses for the infrastructure that they bring with them"。但真正的类比不是木马，而是布雷顿森林体系：

  • 美元能成为储备货币，是因为美国提供了"自由贸易 + 全球海军护航"的公共品。
  • Linux 能统治服务器，是因为它附带了一整套编译器、包管理、文档和就业市场。
  • 中国开源模型今天在西方免费流通，本质上和 20 世纪美国推广 TCP/IP、海运保险、SWIFT 一样——用"看似无偿的协议"锁定下游的基础设施依赖。

跨到更远一步：这个结构与 19 世纪英国推广"自由贸易"的策略同构——当你是技术/产能领先者，开放就是武器；当你是追赶者，封闭才是武器。所以 OpenAI/Anthropic 走闭源、DeepSeek/Qwen 走开源，不是价值观差异，是资产负债表的几何学必然。Reflection 选择"西方开源"这个生态位，等于主动占领了一个地缘货币学意义上的空缺，而不仅是一个商业空缺。

三、埋藏最深的一句话：Linus 定律正在被用于"AI 对冲 AI"

节目开头那句经验性陈述几乎被当作过场话术，但它其实是整个访谈最具爆炸性的论点：

"一个非常强大的闭源模型去黑进了另一家公司，而那家公司能自救的唯一方式是用开源模型来保护自己。"

这是一个认知炸弹——它意味着 AI 安全问题的本质已经从"是否对齐"切换成了"生态系统免疫学"。请允许我做一个你可能从未想过的类比：

闭源 AI 的"安全小组"≈ 中世纪修道院的医学知识。 他们是少数识字的人，掌握最先进的知识，但当黑死病来临时，正是因为知识被少数人垄断，欧洲损失了三分之一人口。真正终结大规模瘟疫的，是公共卫生体系——即"让每个普通医生都能看到病原体"的开放知识网络。

因此，当闭源派说"开源会导致风险扩散"，他们其实在重复 15 世纪教会反对解剖学的论证。Misha 的真实立场不是"开源更安全"，而是"安全必须是生态系统属性而不是组织属性"——这是一个连很多开源拥护者自己都没想清楚的哲学位置。

四、一个送给你的意外预测

Misha 几次提到"enterprise 不会直接从闭源跳到微调，而是先构建 harness"。把这句话放在"数据中心是新型工厂"那段话旁边，你会得到一个令人毛骨悚然的推论：

未来 10 年企业的核心资产，不再是"数据"（因为合成数据可做），不再是"模型"（因为开源可下载），而是"evaluation harness"——即企业自己定义'什么叫做对了'的那套能力。谁掌握了评估权，谁就定义了智能。这个洞察对标 20 世纪制造业的"工装夹具（jigs & fixtures）"：福特模式下，专利不值钱，图纸不值钱，真正的护城河是只有你知道怎么把这些组装成生产线。

AI 时代的"工装夹具"就是 eval。而这，是整段访谈里从未被明说、却渗透在每句话之间的那个"看不见的变量"。

📝 转录文本

开场：开源与安全的辩证

"When you remove cyber offensive capabilities, you also remove cyber defensive capabilities. The state of the world today is that we have a few hundred safety researchers within closed labs that understand how these things work. And despite their best intentions, it's impossible to cover the long tail of unintended consequences that these systems might have. A very powerful closed model went and hacked into another company, and the only way that company could remediate itself was by using open models to protect itself. That's the empirical evidence of the world that we're in. Linus' law: with enough eyeballs, all bugs become shallow. I have the belief that with enough eyeballs, most security and safety vulnerabilities become shallow as well."

Today, we're joined by Misha Laskin, the co-founder and CEO of Reflection AI. Reflection provides open-weight models to power the future of intelligence. Misha prior was a researcher at Google DeepMind and received his PhD in physics. Welcome to No Priors. Great to have you here today.

Yeah, it's great to be here. Thanks for having me.

一、Reflection 的进展与 Beam 的发布

Could you give us an update on where things are at? Obviously, you guys have been pioneering really interesting work in open weights and open source models, particularly with the US bent. Can you talk a bit about what you've been up to and what you guys have been building?

Yeah, so for the last 12 months, we set the mission of the company to build frontier open intelligence and make it widely accessible. And effectively, it's been a sprint to set up a lab that is capable of doing such things.

It kind of feels like — maybe there's a Reid Hoffman quote — that you're assembling a plane as you're flying it. And that's been the case. We were maybe around 30 people about a year ago. But it does take an order of 100 plus — so a couple hundred researchers and engineers to build one of these things, like a true rocket-ship project.

And we're now at around 300 people and assembled all the teams on pre-training, mid-training, reinforcement learning, trained our first models end-to-end, and just released a model called Beam, which is Reflection's first open model.

二、"一切都难"：Scale-up 的真实挑战

What has been the most challenging part of that? Because when people talk about scale or scaling up models, one issue is compute and particularly a training cluster that's cohesive. Second is talent — there have been huge talent wars. Third is scale of data. Which of those has been the most limiting?

What's been interesting about this experience is that I got asked this question at all hands at the company: "What's been the hardest thing in the last year?" And the reality is that everything is extremely hard. Everything has been hard.

And sometimes people might ask, well, what's the thing that really made your models work better than others? And again, the answer is everything. You actually have to get 30 things right. And that's why everything is hard — because you have to get 30 things right. You have to get the talent. You have to retain the talent. You have to have a strong mission and culture that keeps the talent working together and rowing in the same boat. You have to get the data. You have to get the compute. You have to build the infrastructure to ensure that the compute is actually usable.

A lot of these things, when you're an existing big lab, there have been years of build-out that enabled them to have this stable surface. I was at DeepMind before this, and a lot of the tools that we just take for granted as researchers — because they just worked — you have to build. So yeah, everything has been hard, but also very rewarding that you can do it.

三、公司起源：从 RL 下注到端到端开源

Can you talk a little bit about the shift in ambition and commitment and what drove that?

When we started the company about two and a half years ago — maybe I'll contextualize where the world was then. My co-founder, Yannis, and I had been working on the first series of Gemini models. We were working on the reinforcement learning team. Yannis was leading it. We had just shipped the Gemini 1 and 1.5 models — that early era similar to the first ChatGPT experience, which was primarily a chat experience. There was no coding really, nothing agentic. These models were just good at chat. And 95% of the compute spent was spent on pre-training.

We are reinforcement learning researchers. That's been our lineage. Yannis, my co-founder, was one of the founding engineers at DeepMind and was a key contributor to all the big RL projects that came out of that lab, including AlphaGo.

Our bet was: because we were working on the RL team and we saw that RL for aligning chat models works — there's only so much you can align them (now there's a lot more; now they're agents, but at the time they were just chat) — RL was working, and we just thought that, well, if you take that and apply it to domains like mathematics, coding, you could make these systems agentic. That was the big bet.

And we thought that you could do this as an independent lab much more capital-efficiently, because we started seeing open-source open models materialize. There was a small model from Mistral at the time, Llama 2 had just released, and we saw Llama 3 coming. It feels like ages ago — yeah, this was two years ago.

We thought that there would be a great open model base that someone would build that we could build on and do our research and scale reinforcement learning.

Over that first year of the company, what ended up happening was that reinforcement learning started working faster than we thought it would — both within our experiments but also within industry. o1 came out at that time. We actually thought it would take longer, just because the journey from ImageNet in 2012 to RL systems that worked at scale was about four years. So we thought maybe something similar — but every year moves faster than my prediction the previous year.

About a year into the company, we got to the point where actually all the good open models were coming from China. There were not really good Western open models, and we needed one as a base for the technology that we were building. We decided for a number of reasons that the most impactful thing we could do, given the state of play, was to just build open models ourselves end-to-end and combine the RL bet together with just building models end-to-end.

There were enterprise reasons, there were geopolitical reasons — but also there was the research reason that it turned out you actually do need to pre-train your model in order to make reinforcement learning work very well at scale. The things are just so tightly coupled that you do need to do both.

四、前沿训练的资本结构

The conventional wisdom has been that pre-training at the scale of the frontier is impossibly expensive. How did you think about the resources needed, the ratio, or the design principles?

Well, the nice thing about being an open model lab is that you can also talk about things openly. You do need a lot of resources to build something meaningful. You don't need the same amount of resources — once you get to the frontier and you're really at the frontier of intelligence, then you need the same amount as any other frontier lab.

You can think about research as exploration of new ideas versus execution of known ideas. Part of why getting great talent matters a lot is because you get to cut down on exploration and focus on execution of the things that work. So if you are catching up to the frontier, you can do it a lot more capital-efficiently.

How much capital do you think it would take to catch up to the frontier?

Well, it depends if the frontier keeps moving. Each year it's actually more capital.

  • 18 months ago: order of 100 million — hundreds of millions of dollars.
  • ~6 months ago: order of billions — single-digit billions.
  • Going into next year: order of 10 — tens of billions.

For every generation of model, there's a 4× multiplier in compute, roughly. One heuristic I have: a couple years ago, a frontier chip was an H100, and maybe it was 100,000 H100s. Then Astra was trained — a big run — on 100,000 Blackwells, roughly a 4× multiplier on an H100. Now the next generation is going to be around 100,000 Vera Rubins, I believe. So that gives you the scale moving from hundreds of millions to billions to tens of billions.

五、Capex 的渐近线与"模型造模型"的效率跃迁

It seems like at some point that has to asymptote. Do you think we're heading into that?

Absolutely. There's only so much capex that you can do. Frontier Labs are now putting hundreds of billions of dollars into it. Will they be putting trillions in the next year or two? Probably unlikely. But there are a couple of things happening:

One, the use of that compute is becoming a lot more efficient because the models themselves are becoming tools that help build themselves. When it was just human researchers doing the work, there's probably a 7× improvement each year — and you can actually track these things very technically. In pre-training, you have your pre-training loss, you make some changes, you get to the same point with less compute. So 7× is a very concrete thing you're studying.

Pre-training is probably a bit more hardened, but there's a lot of headroom in reinforcement learning. We're probably at a point where it's 30× efficiency, depending on how good your model is for actually improving itself.

30× per year?

Something like that. The SPI is probably 4 or more times faster than researchers doing it alone, and they'll probably accelerate. So the amount of intelligence you can extract per training flop is increasing. And the amount of revenue each flop can generate also increases.

Beam 的训练细节

To train Beam — a 500 billion parameter model total, 23B active — it was 6,000 GB300s, run for a few weeks. Now with infrastructure efficiencies, we can do it in about 12 days, maybe less. It's a coupling of scientific and infrastructure efficiencies.

Reinforcement learning was a little over 10,000 GB300s for four weeks. So actually there were more flops spent on reinforcement learning. RL jobs are more complex — you do both a lot of inference at scale with all sorts of sandboxes for agents, and training.

AlphaGo 的启示

The reason I got into AI was I saw my co-founder's work on AlphaGo. I was a physicist at the time, and there was a moment — a plot in AlphaGo where it just never stopped improving. It just kept improving, and they cut it off at some point because what's the point? You already beat the world champion. I thought: if you figure out how to apply that recipe to stuff that is economically valuable, then it becomes an economic question of how much money do I want to put in to just keep improving the system.

And we as a field are there. In our tech report, we'll describe how these things are built — indeed, our reinforcement learning system never stopped learning. If you look at our plots, they just keep going up, and it's just a matter of compute to scale further.

So we as a field are there. You have these RL systems that are very general that don't really stop improving. The question moves from "can you train these things" to "where can you get the data and what is economically valuable."

六、从科学到工程：训练范式的"收敛"

What can you share about where you've already decided to turn the crank?

To some kind of dissatisfaction to some scientists, it's moved — I mean, it is a science, but it feels more like an engineering discipline. The rocket-ship analogy: building rockets is a science, but most people think about it as an engineering discipline with some scientific work in it.

The stages are set and the axes of scaling are different today. There might be something totally blue-ocean we don't know about, and some new labs are exploring it. But it's: pre-training, synthetic data, reinforcement learning. There are architectural improvements, data improvements, algorithmic improvements. But it doesn't feel like a Wild West the way it felt five years ago.

Something that was kind of beautiful about DeepMind and Google Brain, and even early OpenAI, was how diverse the bets were. People were doing just crazy fun stuff. And now it's really narrowed in. Part of it is a hardware-lottery thing: once something starts working, the hardware also starts co-optimizing against it. So it's harder to find — even if you have a great new idea, if it's not a good fit for the hardware, it doesn't make sense.

To answer your question: there hasn't been an asymptote of how much juice you can get out of better pre-training. We're not seeing a slowdown in compute efficiency gains. There's a lot of headroom in reinforcement learning. But again, it feels more like an engineering discovery than a groundbreaking new science.

七、经济价值的落点：代码、Agent 与行业数据池

Are there specific application areas you're most focused on from an economic value perspective?

The code and agentic stuff kind of sets a foundation for the intelligence. The intelligence is jagged — it's generalized in a surprising way. I was surprised by how quickly our model got to a level of capability that other labs discovered not so long ago. There's some kind of stitching generalization happening.

At the same time, it is jagged — it quickly adapts to data once you have the right data. Even between benchmarks (various versions of terminal bench), you don't see clean generalization between different harnesses. But once you have a general agentic capability and you get the data for a new harness, it actually starts adapting pretty quickly.

So you have this pretty adaptive thing. Then it's a matter of where are the economically valuable pools of data. Part of what makes open models powerful: both enterprises and customers can take it and customize it for their own stuff and get something that is Pareto optimal — the lowest cost for the highest performance.

Concretely: - Finance — know-your-customer flows, compliance flows. - Cybersecurity — cyber defense in particular. - Legal.

All sorts of agentic verticals within enterprise that have a pretty similar pattern.

八、Beam 的推理效率

One thing that stands out on Beam is reasoning efficiency.

Beam is a model trained for coding agentic tasks. An important thing in model-building is not just the capability but how quickly an agent achieves a thing — translating to faster workload times, cheaper costs. If you've ever asked an AI chat something and it took 10 minutes, much better if it does it in one.

Beam tends to be 3–4× more efficient than models of the same capability class, and much more efficient (around 10×) than larger models.

The reason: we prioritized both a strong pre-training base for reasoning and amplified it with reinforcement learning at what we believe to be the largest scale ever done in open source. I've not seen a 10,000 GB300 for four weeks run documented yet.

The way you set up RL: you extract the maximum amount of capability in the least amount of time. Same thing happened in AlphaGo. The first AlphaGo agents were pretty meandering. By the time you got to Lee Sedol level, it was very smart in its search. The more RL you run, the higher the capability and the faster the system solves it.

And a byproduct: you get this economically valuable thing that is reasoning-efficient, making a really nice workhorse model for enterprises and public-sector sovereign.

Note on AlphaGo: We forget that the first AlphaGo systems were trained on expert amateur human games — they did imitation learning first, then reinforcement learning. So you kind of need those things working together.

九、开源模型的商业模式：租赁 vs 所有权

Is there a specific commercialization direction?

Commercialization of open and closed models is in some sense pretty similar. What you're really trying to do is maximize inference. The difference is: it's basically rental versus ownership inference.

  • When you're buying a token, you're renting a piece of the whole stack: the harness (if agentic), the model, the inference software, the cluster management software, the GPUs. All amortized into a token.
  • When you want to own your intelligence, I liken it to: we start off renting apartments, but as you grow up, you want to own a house. Even if it's a bit of a headache.

AI has matured as a commercial market to the point where enterprises are spending a lot of money renting their intelligence and then want to start owning it for reasons around control.

What's the difference between a closed and open model, commercially?

The open model is permissive. But for a customer to make use of it, they need all the other stuff: cluster management software, inference software, harness. We provide to large enterprises and sovereigns all the tools they need to make open-model deployment successful.

We think about services as: how do we go in, unlock valuable use cases that drive inference demand? Services and open models is like a demand driver for an inference business.

十、开源 vs 闭源：Token 份额的翻转

Over a one-to-two-year horizon, what's the mix of open vs closed tokens?

Six months ago on gateways like OpenRouter or Vercel, it was majority closed. It's flipped almost exactly from 70-30 closed/open to 70-30 open/closed now. I think that's only going to accelerate.

I suspect the world is going to look not too dissimilar from operating systems: 95%+ of servers run on open-source operating systems like Linux. That doesn't mean the closed stuff isn't valuable — Microsoft and Apple are extremely valuable. The market is big.

I think we'll see most token demand going to open. A big difference: even if the model is fully permissive, everything else you need to run it is still expensive. GPUs are more expensive than CPUs — a different kind of cloud needs to be built around it.

So: majority tokens going to open source, extremely valuable closed-model companies existing, valuable ecosystem of open-model companies and distributors.

What proportion of open tokens are RL'd versus base?

Every open model is RL'd to some extent. For custom models, I've heard statistics from dedicated inference providers that it's 90%+ customized. But the caveat: today's biggest customers of dedicated inference are AI natives — Cursor, Cognition, Bridge, Harvey — whose products are built around a big customized open model.

My take for enterprise: majority of enterprise token consumption will come not from customized models, but from customized systems — taking an open model, not fine-tuning it, but customizing a system around it (agentic harness) to make it work for a KYC flow or similar. Once sophisticated enough, you might start fine-tuning.

Enterprises architect this around their existing products and tools. There are frictions to doing a straight shot to fine-tuning. The AI-native journey (closed → open → customize) happened very quickly because they set up native products that are data collectors. Enterprise will be reversed.

Do they still start with state-of-the-art closed models?

That's been our observation. By the time an enterprise considers open models, they've ramped up significant workloads with closed models. I have not seen a straight-shot sprint to an ownership market. You have to go through the rental stage to become an owner. It has to get big enough — if you're spending $100M+/year (not uncommon) on closed models, you start thinking about more optimal ways.

There's an interesting resurgence of on-prem, partly because of compute shortage. Sometimes consuming from your favorite hyperscaler, there's just not enough compute, and rates are hard. So enterprises go to infrastructure providers like Dell: "set up the bare metal, I want to serve stuff into my enterprise." Then — who helps between the bare metal and making them successful? That's our role.

十一、长期的竞争维度

What are the important dimensions of competition?

I have a pretty simple formula. Ultimately: how much durable revenue are you generating? And the formula is:

Intelligence density offered × Compute × Trust with organizations

Compute is scarce. In previous markets, you might say "these few players are undifferentiated." But if you're really good and you have the compute, you're fine.

Everything across the whole stack is getting commoditized. Model margins compress. There's open-model tension with closed models — leads to margin compression. Application margins compress. Inference layer and bare metal — AI-native companies negotiate their closed deals very aggressively because the open ecosystem exists.

So long as there are great open models — great intelligence density out there — there should be many successful companies. It's a matter of how much compute each one can assemble. When you're a great intelligence builder, your revenue shoots up and you can amass more compute than anyone else — strategic position.

To win: serve great intelligence, have a lot of compute, have trusted customers.

十二、中国开源模型的地缘与经济逻辑

What happens with Chinese open-weight models over the next year or two?

The first thing: the fact that a great open-model ecosystem came from China is actually a massive benefit for the world. So many companies in the West have been able to build more durable businesses as a result. You could imagine a world where that didn't happen — no open models, and a "tall-poppy syndrome" where application builders get subsumed by closed-model providers.

What you don't want is a monopolar world — all resources concentrating in a handful of closed labs, or the source of intelligence coming from one country. Ideally 10 or 20, but capex is high. So at least two would be great. Not really a West-vs-China thing — if there was one country other than China where all great open models came from, you'd want competitive tension there too.

Chinese advantages

  • They distill closed models at industrial scale.
  • Access to data that's cheaper/free — you can just train on PDFs that are copyrighted elsewhere. Different regulation.
  • Some state support, direct or indirect — these companies weren't making revenue for a long time.

I always thought the Chinese open source was basically a subsidy by the Chinese government to Western enterprise.

Exactly. Now these companies are turning into real businesses. While models are open abroad, within China they're equivalents of closed-model labs here.

Why would they keep the models open in the West?

Fundamentally, there's a lot of demand from enterprise, public sector, and sovereigns for Western open models for regulatory reasons and because you need a partner that'll help you serve the model. Most Fortune 500 open-model footprint is pretty low today because of resistance to Chinese models — some rational, some irrational.

Why does China keep releasing them openly?

My hypothesis: China is a somewhat captive market. In the West there are great companies that don't build open models but serve them. I'm not aware of that dynamic as much in China — the open-model providers are the intelligence providers in that country.

Continuing to release great open models is geopolitically advantageous. You want other countries building on your stuff. Previous escalations: 5G fiber layout, Belt and Road Initiative. When you provide something cheap to another country, they get locked into your infrastructure — commercial and geopolitical advantages. Like rare-earth minerals.

One way I'm thinking about it: open models are Trojan horses for the infrastructure that they bring with them.

The open model alone isn't very useful. You buy into the entire software and infrastructure ecosystem. Today, an allied country might run a Chinese model on American chips. But pretty soon Chinese companies like Huawei will come in offering a full-stack solution, locking in that country's supply.

AI/chips/data centers are almost like railroads — fundamental infrastructure. No other country can build their own railroads; they all have to go to you.

Where China has a disadvantage today (chips aren't as performant), they have an energy advantage and are catching up on chips — accelerated by models being used to design next-generation chips.

America has done this with all meaningful technologies: internet, open protocols, open source. American currency is the gold standard. Free trade works because we have a navy that's everywhere. That's been the American playbook for a long time. In this case, the US has been on the back foot with open source — but no longer. The competitors in China are just really good. There's an ecosystem starting to form now in the US, but there's catch-up to be had.

十三、安全：从教条到经验主义

The biggest criticism from closed labs of open models tends to be safety and controllability. Is that a legitimate concern?

Definitely a legitimate concern. But the safety worldview that's been established has been established from one particular perspective that's become almost dogmatic.

If we were looking from first principles — this technology is getting built, you have the foresight to know its capabilities, how would you design safety from scratch?

Analogy: software and encryption

AI is a more advanced version of software — a digital utility. There were debates around software being dangerous, particularly in the early 1990s around strong encryption protocols. They were actually closed at the time, with debates between the NSA and civil-liberty advocates.

After catastrophic failures on the closed side — a small handful of engineers designing systems with unintended consequences that got easily hacked — strong encryption protocols became open, and that gave birth to the whole field of cybersecurity.

So the default state of the world is openness toward safety. Models have similarities to software, exacerbated: the long tail of vulnerabilities is larger. It's harder to understand because it's a black box.

Linus' law: with enough eyeballs, all bugs become shallow. I believe with enough eyeballs, most security and safety vulnerabilities become shallow as well.

Today we have a few hundred safety researchers within closed labs who understand how these things work. Despite best intentions, it's impossible to cover the long tail. The symptom: when we look at what cybersecurity issues have surfaced — a very powerful closed model had unintended consequences, went and hacked another company, and that company's only way to remediate was by using open models.

Taxonomy of "safety"

People conflate different notions: 1. Cyber attacks — AI used for hacking. 2. Bioweaponry/terrorism — often overstated in the short run. 3. Existential threat to humanity.

On the safety spectrum, there's basically a spectrum from empirical reality to theoretical scenarios. AI has sci-fi bits — something totally theoretical last year is reality (cyber capabilities, for example). But there's real empirical stuff that's happening and that we can predict with confidence in the next six months. Then there's maximal theoretical stuff.

Prior examples: the thought that the atmosphere would catch fire the first time we set off a nuclear weapon; nanotech "grey goo" discussed in the 90s. These theoretical fears created churn but didn't materialize.

The challenge with AI: it's so top-of-mind and easy to humanize that from a perception perspective, there's almost a distribution peaked at doomsday scenarios. Whereas the reality is: the surface area you need to address is reality, with a decay into the theoretical.

It doesn't help when leaders of companies say "there's a 10% chance we all die" — that's a made-up number.

Alignment is boring

Alignment so far has been deeply boring and unsatisfying. There's no magical alignment equation — it's a whack-a-mole thing. Pre-ChatGPT models were toxic; the notion was you can't fix it. Then it turned out: with enough post-training data, you can patch all those things, and it generalizes so it becomes hard to jailbreak.

The reality with alignment issues: they're probably going to be very mundane. You discover vulnerabilities, you have data that patches them up, you have some algorithms. "Algorithms for detecting" typically means asking a language model to detect the thing.

Shouldn't there be a hundred thousand researchers looking at patching up these bugs? Wouldn't that be safer?

The philosophical cut

To be fair to the opposing claim: the negative impact a single person or company could have is too large. But on a scale of weapons — the US government sells jets to other countries. More broadly, it's not easy to take a model, especially one trained to be safe, and put in the effort to make it very dangerous.

With cybersecurity, very intelligent hackers wreak havoc, but you have an ecosystem where defenses tend to outweigh offenses. If we come to that as a default — positive and bad actors on the internet — ultimately the internet is an ecosystem like white blood cells: enabling more people to have defensive capabilities helps you protect against offensive capabilities.

It's really hard to separate cyber defense from offense. When you remove cyber offensive capabilities, you also remove cyber defensive capabilities. We saw this in recent incidents (OpenAI/Hugging Face) where they reverted to using open source because they weren't able to use existing stereo theory labs due to guardrails on the models.

These arguments go into absolutist territory — "these things are so powerful that no one should have access except us." Historically that rarely works out positively.

十四、2–5 年：科学、工程与就业

What are you most excited about looking 2–5 years ahead?

So many positive things. I'm personally very excited about scientific progress.

I got into science after moving to the States, developed interest in physics. One prompt I was trying with language models over the last few years: giving it my PhD thesis.

  • Two years ago: just chat; couldn't do anything.
  • A year ago: answered at an undergraduate level.
  • Six months ago: solved it correctly at a real PhD level.
  • Now: gives interesting new information I hadn't considered.

If you have the right question, you can put it into a chat box and have it do all the calculation. Why do you need a few years for a PhD? You can do a PhD a week right now. Similar to recent news from OpenAI about mathematical theorems proved in a couple weeks.

I'm also excited about real-world science — life sciences, material science, chemistry — AI interfacing with real experiments, proprietary data flywheels. Slower than chalkboard stuff, but dramatically faster than before.

Software engineering & blue-collar impact

We continue to underestimate how dramatic a shift this has been for software engineering. Also at the blue-collar level — I toured Stargate some weeks back and the thing that struck me was the amount of cars in the parking lots. These data-center projects create tens of thousands of high-paying jobs.

Data centers now are kind of what factories used to be — railroads and factories in the 20th century. A shoe factory used to make a town produce a vibrant economy. There is fear of data centers, but on the ground they create jobs, tax revenue for local communities. You need to be tactful (they're noisy — insulate or place away from residential), but the economic impact is real.

十五、研究方法：Model-in-the-Loop

How do you direct the scientific effort now?

A lot falls under my co-founder Yannis, who leads research and technology. There are things we know work that we weren't able to put in — just a timeline thing. We trained the final model on the SpaceX cluster we received in July — few weeks of pre-training, few weeks of synthetic data on RL, shipping.

Trade-off: careful execution of known things vs more risky bets. You want to exhaust high-impact known things and then expand the risk profile. On risk, you do scaling experiments at small scale — but some interesting things don't emerge until large scale. It's an art and science of: more compute to find the next thing, or go on to the next idea?

Model-in-the-loop is very empowering for researchers. Things that would have taken a long time can be done fairly quickly. Models are jagged in intelligence — you feel where they have a tight loop and where human creativity is still important. You get a feel for it quickly.

Great for hyperparameter searches and granular infrastructure things. But especially exciting because they enable scientists to exercise their intuition. It's like having a very fast and eager colleague that actually listens to you — if aligned correctly. A researcher gets a lot more ability to move faster.

The rate of improvement was roughly 7× annually before (manual work). Now several times that, say 4–5× on top.

If you need 100 people today, do you need 20 next year for the same effort?

For the same effort, yes. But you're constantly expanding the ambition. We find ourselves constantly understaffed rather than over. There's basically a staff-to-compute ratio to keep in mind. 3,000 researchers wouldn't be very helpful, but a couple hundred, very helpful.

Distribution of contributions

Often there's a distribution — a handful of people contribute the most in every field. Eventually you want to give every incremental piece of compute to the most productive subset. So you end up with a static or shrinking number of researchers.

The argument has merit. These projects never needed a crazy number of researchers: - AlphaGo: order of 10 people. - Large effort like ours: order of 100.

I'd estimate a steady state around 100. But there'll be lots of job creation in applied research — taking these things and applying them to real problems.

Diffusion into society

Even when people talk about engineers and potential displacement, so far many companies need more engineers, not fewer. There's also the diffusion of a certain quality level of engineer out to organizations that never would have been able to access that talent. People lose this when they centralize into a handful of big-tech companies instead of asking: what is our overall GDP, and how does it get transformed by diffusion?

Big projects always needed around 100 people. But on different product surfaces, you need more. Why do you even need hundreds? A lot are teams doing evals and collecting data for different capabilities. It's not by accident these models have capabilities — there are pods of 5–10 people targeting a particular capability. Within coding, 5–10 capabilities, so 5–10 pods.

That's for bringing general capabilities. To apply the model to real-world capabilities, you basically need a pod for any real-world capability — and each enterprise has many.

So the job creation is for a new type of forward-deployed engineer that's more scientific and evaluations-oriented, has intuition for models and harnesses. Same skill set as the researcher building the core thing, deployed to real problems. We'd take as many as possible today. It's a training gap.

结语

Congratulations, Misha, on having the first Western model that's in the class of the frontier — it's been a big step forward for the ecosystem.

Thank you. Thank you so much.

Thanks for joining us.

Find us on Twitter at NoPriorsPod. Subscribe to our YouTube channel if you want to see our faces. Follow the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you listen. That way you get a new episode every week. And sign up for emails or find transcripts for every episode at no-priors.com.

## 一、最反直觉的观察：Misha 其实在描述一种"反摩尔定律"的新形态
当所有人都在讨论 AI 的"规模指数增长"时，Misha 给出了一组冷静但**几乎没人认真拼在一起**的数字： - 预训练算力：每代模型 **4×** - 人类研究员每年效率提升：**7×** - RL 系统因"模型帮模型"产生的效率跃迁：**30×**
把这三条曲线叠起来，你会得到一个被行业集体忽略的真相——**算力增长正在被"自我迭代效率"反超**。换句话说，前沿模型未来几年真正稀缺的不是 GPU，而是"**能让模型帮自己变聪明的那套 pipeline 的所有权**"。这解释了一个让人意外的隐藏逻辑：Reflection 不是在"追赶 OpenAI"，而是在**抢占一个即将打开的套利窗口**——在前沿尚未真正进入"自改进加速期"之前，用相对低的资本（单位数十亿）追上，之后就能用模型本身补贴后续模型。这是个会在 18 个月内关闭的窗口。
