item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、瓶颈迁移的隐秘定律：AI 让设计变易，物理世界却开始反扑

Pat 在访谈中说出了一句看似寻常却极深的话："当技术让某件事变简单时，瓶颈就会迁移到别处。" 真正令人意外的是迁移的方向——AI 让"软"的部分（RTL、kernel、编译器）接近零摩擦，瓶颈反而退回到最"硬"、最 19 世纪的物理环节：九个月的流片、HBM 的 shoreline 带宽、40% 被 guard banding 白白浪费的功率预算、八年起步的燃气轮机交付周期。

这里有一个几乎没人指出的悖论：AI 越聪明，硬件越回到热力学原理。Pat 顺口提到"我得重新翻书看 Carnot 卡诺循环"，这不是玩笑——这意味着当代最前沿的工程师在被迫回到 1824 年的教科书。类似的模式在金融里出现过：量化交易让 alpha 消失后，所有竞争退回到物理层——光缆到交易所的毫秒距离。AI 行业正在经历同构的"下沉"：当认知层被抹平，决胜点回到土地、铜、水、热。

二、"最糟糕的行业"反转：memory 的二十年屈辱与它正在成为的护城河

这是整段对话中最反直觉的事实：过去三十年零次重大内存创新。DRAM、SRAM、Flash——就这三样。Optane 死了，几十种新内存全部死了。memory 行业因此被 Pat 称为"一年赚钱四年亏钱的行业"。

然后请注意数字：memory 板块过去四年市值增加了约 2.5 万亿美元，三大 memory 厂商全部进入全球市值 Top 20。这不是增长，这是行业格式塔的翻转。

跨领域连接——这个模式在历史上出现过多次：航运业从 1970-2005 一直是毁灭价值的行业，直到中国的出现把它变成了战略资源；1980 年代被嘲笑的"烟囱产业"稀土矿，今天是地缘政治武器。规律是：长期被商品化循环折磨到无人投资的行业，一旦遇到不可替代的新需求，会因为供给侧的三十年荒芜而形成最深的护城河。memory 行业现在就处于这个"复仇时刻"。Pat 隐晦地暗示他刚种子投了一家新 memory 公司——如果你相信他的历史判断力，这是未来十年最被低估的信号之一。

三、Edison 的复仇与 Nick McKeown 悖论：被遗忘的技术决定正在被 AI 推翻

两个看似无关的细节，拼起来是一张震撼的图：

第一个倒转：1890 年的"电流战争"中，Tesla 的交流电击败了 Edison 的直流电——因为长距离传输交流更经济。整整 135 年后，Pat 一句"Edison 的复仇就在眼前"，说的是 800V 直流在数据中心即将取代传统 AC 配电。为什么？因为 AI 数据中心本质上不是城市电网，而是极度集中的化学反应堆——短距离、单一用途、每一步 AC/DC 转换都在烧钱。整个工业电气化历史的默认假设被颠覆了。

第二个倒转：Nick McKeown 的洞察被 Pat 复述得极美——"我们建网络是为了让任何一个数据包能去任何地方，不知道它去哪儿。AI 却正好相反：流动是巨大的、可预测的。" 这意味着半个世纪前以太网/IP 对电路交换的胜利，正在被 AI 工作负载逆转。光学 OCS 回归，circuit switching 复活。

把这三件事（memory 复兴 + Edison 复仇 + 电路交换回归）放在一起，一个让人头皮发麻的模式浮现：AI 不是在创造未来，而是在系统性地回滚过去 50-100 年里为通用性做出的工程折中。每一个"通用化、商品化、抽象化"的胜利——通用内存、交流电网、分组交换——都因为 AI 工作负载的极端专用性而被重新审视。这不是科技进步的直线叙事，这是一个巨大的 U-turn。

四、意外彩蛋：代理的虚拟机，不是人的虚拟机

Guido 在最后抛出一个几乎被忽略的问题，但它可能是整场对话最深远的提问："如果今天重建 VMware，是为 agent 建还是为人类建？" Pat 的回答泄露了一个尚未被业界明说的转向：虚拟化的服务对象从"硬件↔操作系统↔人"变成了"硬件↔操作系统↔agent 集群"。

这暗含一个产业预言：整个 1998-2015 年期间构建的云/虚拟化栈，正在悄悄被重写成一个"非人类优先"的基础设施。agent 没有耐心等待启动、不需要图形界面、需要宪法式的护栏而不是密码管理——这是比"iOS 之于 PC"更根本的 UI/UX 范式转移。谁搞定"agent 的 vMotion"，可能就是下一代 VMware。

📝 转录文本

Opening Hooks

"In an AI digital age, energy capacity equals economic capacity. Why build a new data center and buy the million GPUs if I can't power them? You're going to see more and more defaults happening on many of those data center projects cuz the energy won't be there."

"Whenever you have the technology to make something easy, that means the bottleneck moves somewhere else."

"Nothing's a chip anymore. It's a rack. It took me 3 months to design it, but it's 9 months until I can actually start to use it."

"How many major new memories have we had over the last 30 years? Zero. Zero. Memory innovation for the first time in 30 years is nigh upon us."

"I declared the death of copper about 25 years ago. Eventually, I'll be right. For all of us hardware guys, this is like renaissance in front of us."

"AI inference accelerator chips — I'm sure I don't even know them all. Why are you guys funding so many of those?" — "You funded your fair share, too."

"Historically, there have not been a 100 competing processor vendors in any industry ever. This is a temporary thing. It'll converge back."

Introduction

Host: I'm here with our esteemed guest and dear friend and former boss, Mr. Pat Gelsinger. Welcome Pat. Pat is currently the general partner at Playground Global, but you're very very well known in the industry for leading Intel, for being the CTO of Intel, of course, leading VMware and many other things. So, welcome.

Pat: Hey, thank you, Rayu. Great to be with you and Guido, right? And to me, this feels just a little bit like old home. It's like we superimposed a year of change, but you both look the same. I feel energetic. So let's dive in.

Host: There has never been a day when you stopped being energetic. So there's no news there.

Part 1 — From Tech School to Intel: An Accidental Career

Host: Let's start from your Intel career. Recently Andreessen Horowitz created the Horowitz-Recrent Academy, which was to find talented people between 16 and 22 and then put them into a modern educational setting so they'd be well prepared for either doing things on their own or joining the companies of today. You had a similar experience — you went to a regular trade school and then jumped into Intel.

Pat: Yeah. When we were what, 18 or 19? You know, it was really a sort of magical period. I'm 16 years old. I accidentally win a scholarship. I go to tech school, skipped my last year and a half of high school, and Intel comes recruiting when I'm 18 years old. I'd never been on an airplane. I had already fallen in love with computers at tech school.

The interviewer, Ron Smith was his name, he writes on his page — I was number 12 that he interviewed that day. And if you've interviewed 12 people in a row, you can't tell male from female by the end of it. I'm number 12. He says, "Smart, aggressive, arrogant. He'll fit right in." So, I got invited to come to Intel.

Starting as a technician, moved into the design team at the end of the 286, engineer number four on the 386, architect and design manager for the 486 — all of that while doing my bachelor's, master's and PhD work. It was the best career that you could possibly have. You're learning by day and you're putting it to practice at night.

Host: You're creating completely new eras of chips. I bet most of what you learned and what you built there was a big gap because you're breaking new ground.

Pat: In a lot of ways. One of my professors at Stanford postulated a new carry-look-ahead adder design in one of my classes. I said, well, I'm working on the 386 carry-look-ahead adder, so let me try it. I come back two days later and I said, it doesn't work — and I started arguing with my professor at Stanford. The next two class periods were just me and the professor arguing over why his design didn't work.

He had a book being published with that design in it. So he was very annoyed — it was very time sensitive for him.

We started built-in self test. Ed McCluskey at Stanford was my professor, sort of the father of that, and we had wonderful arguments around why most of his ideas were bad — they weren't practical for real chips, but I was putting built-in self test to work on the 386. John Hennessy was my thesis advisor, and obviously he did okay. I helped his career — he became president and he's done okay since then.

Guido: I had the same experience when I was teaching at Stanford. You come with something that you think is the truth and then the student comes who works in industry and says, well, actually not quite. The next lecture you come back with, okay, I looked this up. You're right. This is outdated.

Pat: That interaction is part of what makes Silicon Valley so unique. You have so many companies, entrepreneurship is in the water here — starting things up, new ideas, challenging the professors. You can't be a professor at a place like Stanford and not expect to get challenged and enjoy it.

Host: There's good foot traffic in and out of that ivory tower.

Part 2 — The 486 and the Birth of Modern EDA

Host: The 486 was your big accomplishment — obviously lots of people worked on it. You guys broke some new ground in chip design, and increased what functions the chip was supposed to do.

Pat: It was a pretty magic period because it was before what you would think of as the EDA industry. The 486 was really the first chip to implement what you would think of as modern EDA techniques. We did a high-level design — a description and RTL description — but there was no Verilog.

So, we invented HDL — the Intel Hardware Description Language. I wrote my own language. Well, you had to build a compiler for that language, so we created the compiler. There was no automatic place and route, so we had to invent that. We worked with Alberto Sangiovanni-Vincentelli at Berkeley and some of his students for the first placement, the first routing, the first automated timing management.

That was really one of the hallmarks — not only was the 486 a pipelined compatible microprocessor, but we ushered in many of the foundations of what became the modern EDA industry.

Part 3 — Is AI the Next 486 Moment for Chip Design?

Host: Will people look back at Blackwell saying, this was the last generation done before AI took over the design process for micros? Are we in a similar transition right now?

Pat: I think there are certainly aspects of that. When you look at things like Jalapeno today, that's a first-principles use of AI in the chip design process where you throw out a lot of those things. Pieces of design are still really hard — a lot of the analog aspects (SerDes is probably the best example) are still not AI-able. You just need lots of silicon data. So you either get so conservative in your analog design that you're able to AI it, or you've got to do those the hard way.

But many of the logic functions can really be done with AI tools and techniques in pretty incredible ways. Your transistor budgets are big enough, the design tools are getting smart enough, a few experts guiding the tools in how to apply it. I think it will be somewhat like the 486 that way — you'll look back and say, yep, that was the beginning of a new era of chip design.

The Bottleneck Migrates

Guido: Whenever you have the technology to make something easy, that means the bottleneck moves somewhere else. Can we guess at this point where the bottleneck will be in the future? There are some things which it seems like AI is incredibly good at — creating the software layers, writing kernels, being able to specify the objectives at a higher level which then gets translated into Verilog. So what is the new frontier?

Pat: Let's say Guido and Pat are off to do a great new chip together. We have understanding of the 486, understanding of the AI workloads, understanding of how to compose that into the right multiply-accumulate, register structures. Perfect visibility into the model workloads of tomorrow.

We turn our AI tools loose. Within three months we have an awesome design. We've been a little conservative on all the analog components.

Now, we still have a couple of really major bottlenecks. One is — we still have nine months of silicon processing time. I can design the thing in three months but I can't actually get it into real silicon at scale for 9 months. That sucks. We have to see that bottleneck improve.

  • First, I can't get anything out of fab in less than three months, and that's with supercharged design flows.
  • Then I've got to get into advanced packages. 3D packages are getting complex — that's another three months.
  • Then I have to put it into a rack-scale solution because nothing's a chip anymore. It's a rack.

So — nine months. It took me 3 months to design it, but it's 9 months until I can actually start to use it. How do we compress that?

I think we need new forms of lithography. We need design flows that don't require $50 million of mask cost until I can get things into prototyping. How do you compress that to a month or two? Because if it takes me a year and a half until I actually get scale and software on it, my understanding of the AI workloads is no longer applicable to the chip that I designed.

Guido: You see that play out live right now with AI.

Pat: Historically — Graphcore wasn't a bad design, but the world moved on. All of those aspects somewhat obviate the fact that AI has made the design piece easy. The manufacturing scale issues become a huge bottleneck.

Memory, Power, Thermals

Another bottleneck is memory. Memory bandwidth. As I've described, HBM is a hideous memory. It's just the best one we have.

  • Terrible bit density
  • Limited to shoreline bandwidth
  • Power issues, thermal issues
  • DRAM doesn't like to be hot — concentrating everything in one spot is terrible

AI is a memory-compute workload. So I need to fix memory. That's another critical bottleneck.

And power — power in, thermals. Most of the power simulation tools today are bad. You don't have good 3D modeling tools for power dissipation, hotspots, etc. My voltage in — I'm essentially guard-banding almost my full power envelope. I'm losing roughly 40% of my power to guard-banding. I've got to get much better at power modeling, and my power dissipation techniques are bad. The delivery model has to change too.

Those are the next big bottlenecks. Thank you for those great AI tools — but I've got big challenges even when those are fully deployed.

Part 4 — A Hundred AI Chips: Will They All Survive?

Host: We've seen a rebirth in the number of chips and chip architectures thanks to these workloads. There's a hundred AI inference accelerator chips and I'm sure I don't even know them all.

Pat: Why are you guys funding so many of those?

Host: You funded your fair share too. They're all, to their credit, making different design assumptions. Do you think there's room for all of these, or are we in a world where — partly because of AI tooling — we now have the ability to build more different kinds of chips? Historically, there have not been a hundred competing processor vendors in any industry ever. Is this a more heterogeneous future, or temporary?

Pat: I see it as temporary, and it will converge. Three reasons:

Reason 1 — Workload drift. You see emerging heterogeneity in the compute environment: specialized prefill versus decode. People are saying we need a specialized tier for midfill. So I have early prefill and midfill. Maybe speculate and verify if we listen to OpenAI. My compute fleet becomes more and more granular across the workload. Anytime you've seen that in history, it's not sustainable.

Then as I go to reasoning models, I want something that looks more like a CPU again. All of a sudden that didn't become the predominant portion of my compute capacity — I needed more over here. Model workflows.

Also, today's models are about to go through evolutionary breakthroughs. The LLM is reaching the limits. As people look at how to model 3D — molecules, chemicals, imaging — a flattish LLM doesn't work well. We'll see algorithmic shifts.

Some of the most interesting workloads bring HPC-like things back into AI-like things, where 64-bit precision counts again. Imagine my AI model is now inducing the five most interesting domains for chemical analysis — those chemical algorithms are going to run with high precision, and that'll be the dominant piece of the workload.

Reason 2 — Capital gravity. There are a hundred of them now: multiple optical ones, probabilistic ones. They're not all going to win. You have to get scale, and scale requires capital and workloads. It defies logic that you're going to have a hundred of these.

Reason 3 — Winners pick winners. Open AI, Nvidia, Anthropic will say, I like this one, because it isn't just hardware — it's how the hardware and software co-evolve. There's going to be, here's ten I could pick for this. I like that one. And it requires investment in software and workload evolution.

Software Complexity as the Historical Gatekeeper

Guido: Let me try to stir a little controversy. Historically, we standardized on one or two architectures because different instruction sets were hard — software complexity dictated that you can only have a small number of hardware platforms. That part seems to be changing with AI. Writing an optimized kernel — humans can't really program this thing anymore, but an agent swarm overnight can do it. If you can build a chip that has a certain capability, it's now much easier to build the software layers on top. Could the result be more heterogeneity?

Pat: It changes where the bottleneck lands. The first bottleneck is still: it takes a year and a half to build these things. The second: to make them useful, could I borrow $50 billion? You're talking about very large capital expenditures, data centers, power commitments. That's going to defy a lot of heterogeneity.

Big players — like Nvidia with Groq — will own some of that heterogeneity. Two years from now, you're not going to tell what Groq is inside of Nvidia. Architectures will hide the heterogeneity. That's what abstraction has always done.

Part 5 — Memory: The 30-Year Drought Ends

Host: Earlier you talked about HBM being hideous memory —

Pat: By far the best one we have today. Exactly. It's like the thing about democracy.

Host: We can't recall when there was the last memory innovation. It might have been Optane. I think you probably had something to do with it.

Pat: Yeah, that one died.

Host: We killed it.

Pat: We killed it.

Host: Do you think memory innovation is around the corner?

Pat: Let's look at that history. I've personally been associated with at least five different new memory architectures — Optane just being one. I'm probably familiar with close to a hundred that have happened in the industry over the last 30 years.

How many major new memories have you had over the last 30 years?

Zero. Zero.

DRAM, SRAM, flash. What else is there? It's been a disappointing lack of new physics that enables low-cost, high-performance, resilient, manufacturable memory.

Over the last 30-40 years, memory was a terrible industry. You'd make money one year and lose money for the next four. R&D in an industry that makes money one out of five years? Driven by violent commoditization cycles.

Host: That has changed recently. Over the last 5 years. Happy days.

Pat: All three big memory vendors are in the top 20 most valuable companies on the planet. Crazy change, isn't it? Anybody who looks at the AI workloads — it's a memory wall.

Two Domains to Watch

Domain 1 — Compute-in-memory / stacked integration. HBM's shoreline bandwidth limitations are a fundamental issue. Companies like D-Matrix are doing this; Cabrris and their techniques. Somehow you've got to bring memory and compute together into fundamentally new structures.

Domain 2 — New physics for memory itself. Given the capital being deployed against AI workloads, we'll break through some of those physics challenges. I've just seed-invested in a new memory company — still stealth — but I'm quite excited.

You're going to see new materials: - Ferroelectrics - Non-capacitive high-density memories - Memories that can be high performance, high density, and stackable

Low-cost flash — I'm not particularly enthusiastic. Speed and performance of the underlying cell are problematic with flash or MRAM structures. But memory innovations are coming for the first time in 30 years.

Host: It's amazing what a couple of $10 billion of market cap — I don't even know, you say a trillion…

Pat: The memory industry has increased by market cap by $2.5 trillion over the last four years.

Guido: We could have just invested there and not done any venture stuff.

How Tall Will Chips Get?

Guido: On stacking — how quickly will our chips get taller? Will we go to two and sit there, or will we have the 16-layer sandwich, mixing logic, memory?

Pat: The problem with stacking: the value of the stack grows with dimensionality, which means the yield of any individual layer has to go up exponentially. When you get to 8- or 16-high stacks, it's so hard. Your manufacturing flows have to be so close to perfect.

Yes, you can design in redundancy — DRAMs always had bad-block replacement, spare lines. But if I have a cracked die, I don't care how much resilience you've built in — it's a bad die.

I'm not a crazy 16- or 32-stack guy. I think there'll be nice three-, four-, five-stacks that end up being the sweet spot. The mid-rises.

Even then — I have a great compute tile. Everything's reticle-limited now. Can I go to more chiplets with better yield and thermals? Then a memory stack — two-stack, four-stack, not an eight-stack. Power delivery needs to be integrated in the Z-dimension. Intelligent RDL layers to distribute signals.

My canonical thing is already about eight layers thick when you add up all those pieces. That's about all you can do as we understand manufacturing today.

Then optics come in. More III-V material structures that are closer to this complex because I want my IO deeply integrated. That is an engineering feat and a manufacturing nightmare.

Thermals & Materials

You can't have the physics hotspots you have today. You have to be more intelligent about how you use and spread the heat. If I can get much more efficient power in at the voltages I want with better voltage regulation, I don't create as many thermal chimneys. Diamonds and other new materials have been postulated for thermal cooling. Better liquid cooling techniques sitting right on it.

Pat: We engineers are becoming plumbers, right?

Optics vs. Stacking for Memory

Host: Some people have said, let's get the memory off the package and go all-optical between compute and memory. What's your view on that versus stacking?

Pat: The more OEO interfaces you have — optical to electrical to optical — the more of those you demand in your core compute complex, enmity is just hard. You always have losses. I'm not a fan because it gives you access to large pools of memory, but I burn a lot of power getting there.

The femtojoules per compute is amazingly good. The femtojoules per bit of communication is comparatively a thousand times worse. If I'm spending that much to go get to large pools — I don't like those approaches.

Processing-in-Memory

Guido: Can we actually integrate compute and memory directly — shift some compute into the memory? Some of the PIM approaches?

Pat: Not a fan either. I have to take my workload and push little pieces of compute into the memory. That puts constraints on workloads. Most PIM ideas have been around for 25-30 years. I think 25-30 years from now, they'll still be hanging around.

Give me great memory bandwidth that I can have at high density, high performance, close to the real compute engines. That's a more generalizable solution across evolving workloads.

Part 6 — Optical Everywhere, and the Death of Copper

Host: So we're still stuck with denser chips, more compute, more logic, more power —

Pat: And much better IO. I am a huge fan of moving to optics for all IO function. I declared the death of copper about 25 years ago. Eventually, I'll be right.

Host: When does it go all optical? What's the application driver?

Pat: The workload driver is the one in front of us. Today, our scale-up environments — we're putting tons of copper. Copper is becoming a waveguide that's getting shorter and shorter. To make copper work at 5 meters is more expensive than making optical work at 100 meters. The physics is driving us there today.

Host: Why haven't we moved there already?

Pat: It's a complex supply chain that has never been tested at scale. Everybody is looking at some form of NPO/CPO in the 2028-2029 timeframe, because I can't scale up to large radix compute clusters for my scale-up environment without that move. Nvidia has indicated that. Everybody else in the industry expects that's the conversion point.

In reality, I should have never built an NVL72. It's an engineering marvel and a manufacturing nightmare. It took the industry an extra year and a half to digest that beast. Had we had a more mature optical supply chain, we'd be much more advanced today — better scale-up, better power, better cost, better energy.

Guido: We're gaining a lot of experience in how in-package optics work in networking. Much of that will translate to GPUs.

Pat: But these things have to work at 10 million GPU scale. They have to fit in packages. Many forms of optical don't like bad thermals — and bad thermals is the nature of the game. Package integration problems. We didn't have enough laser capacity. But I don't see anything fundamental. It's just a lot of hard work.

Circuit Switching Returns

Guido: In terms of network architecture, will this also mean a switch towards more circuit-switched networks?

Pat: Nick McKeown — another Stanford professor, good friend — describes it well: we built networks to handle any packet going anywhere with no knowledge of where it might go. When you think about AI, it's almost exactly the opposite. We're doing flows that are large and predictable. Just the description says — that looks more like a switch than like a packet.

Confluence: moving to optical plus workloads that are far more predictable, manageable, large in flow. We will go all the way to bringing optical into the compute complex, and we will go all the way to OCS or some form of optical switching with more predictable flows.

Scale-Up vs. Scale-Out — the Boundary Dissolves

Pat: Is that scale-up or scale-out? To some degree it dissolves the boundary. If my scale-up is big enough — what's the radix of my scale-up environment, and when do I want to hook it up to other clusters?

Guido: I always found scale-up versus scale-out an artificial distinction. One is front-end, one is back-end network. From a system architecture perspective it achieves the same goal with slightly different flavors. Over time I think they'll converge, especially for the AI training workload.

Pat: Training and inference actually look fairly similar.

Continuous Learning Erases Another Boundary

Pat: Does your brain stop learning? No. The separation of training and inferencing is going to become less so, not more so. That's a bit of the argument against more heterogeneous architectures. I think there'll be algorithmic domains that say continuous learning becomes the nature of the algorithm — I want my inference environment updating my model weights because that's giving me more refinement.

Workloads moving into environments that are less formalized training, smaller data sets. The number of nodes you need to be useful is a smaller diameter for inference than for training. That remains.

Host: Different types of AI workloads require very different underlying hardware — some more compute-limited, some more memory-bandwidth. A small diffusion workload looks very different from a 15-trillion-weight LLM.

Pat: You're talking about putting a million GPUs to work in my data center. For that diffusion workload I should put something optimized this way — a thousand of those. For another workload, 2,000 of these. All of a sudden you don't get the flexibility of scale. How much does it cost me to manage, upgrade, connect, fault-domain?

Guido: The agents will do all the upgrades — no longer a problem.

Pat: Everything gets easy. Good out there. Fleet management is done.

Part 7 — Power: The Renaissance of Hardware

Host: We talked about compute, memory, networking. Power is next. You touched on vertical delivery inside the chip. But there's 800V DC, there's power delivery to the data center, an entire ecosystem all the way to power generation — and the socio-political dimensions. Where does innovation come in, and where is it pure execution?

Pat: Let's start at first principles. Our nation has done a terrible job with energy capacity. For 10-15 years we were taking coal offline at the rate we were adding renewables. The nation was flat-lined in overall energy capacity. Not good — because in an AI digital age, energy capacity equals economic capacity. My economic capacity as a nation flat for 15 years.

Even over the last 5 years with the influx, we've gone to maybe increasing our national energy capacity 4% per year. 4%. Bad situation. We need more energy capacity.

Nuclear, Gas Turbines, and Supply-Chain Reality

  • Nuclear as baseload — fabulous thing we want to build more of. When was the last nuclear reactor to come online in the US? 20 years ago. We stopped a very capable industry.
  • Renewables — deep dependencies in China. Very unfortunate for us.
  • Gas turbines — lead times are only eight years at this point.

We have a difficult environment to scale up rapidly. Energy capacity somewhat dampens how euphoric we can get on AI. Why build a new data center and buy a million GPUs if I can't power them? You're going to see more and more defaults happening on data center projects because the energy won't be there.

Host: You think it'll be a significant headwind?

Pat: The Oracle-Comet thing was just the first indicator. People will start saying — do I really have the energy to underwrite the capital commitments I'm making for cement, data center racks, GPU purchases?

The Revenge of Edison

We need to get more efficient at delivering the power networks. Moving to 800V DC data centers — absolutely. Eliminating so many conversion steps that exist for historical standardization reasons. 800V DC — the revenge of Edison is upon us.

Playground has a company called vertical GaN — vertical gallium nitride — that can do 800V to 48V, 800V to 12V, or even 800V to 5V in one conversion step. Solid-state transformers. Switches. Rebuilding the power delivery network.

Power's cool again. All of those are needed in the cooling systems. Turbines and refrigerants get to be exciting new technologies again. For all us hardware guys, this is like renaissance in front of us. After 25 years, I had to go back and read about Carnot efficiencies. How does the first law of thermodynamics work again?

Changing the Physics

We also need to change the physics. CMOS hasn't improved. The essential power per teraflop for the last five generations of Nvidia chips has flat-lined. Not okay. That's where companies like SnowCap — superconducting — can fundamentally change the physics. A thousand times better power performance. Some of those innovations are upon us.

Part 8 — VMs Are Back: VMware for Agents

Host: I've been a terrible time manager. So many topics yet to cover — but one before we leave. VMs are back. How do you think about that as a former CEO of VMware?

Pat: I feel excluded from this conversation. Every innovation has always led to the next abstraction. What's new in our world today? Data structures, algorithms, abstractions. The virtual machine abstraction — whether done from the infrastructure level or the application level — is still a foundational abstraction model that deserves to always have a place in the compute hierarchy.

Host: Should one of us go back and run VMware again?

Pat: I told you — it's time to go back and run VMware again.

Managing the Agent Swarm

At VMware we essentially managed every aspect of the computing hierarchy — the workload, the network, the storage system. How do you abstract those?

In the AI context, we think about agent swarms. Who's going to manage the agents? Who's going to create the security profiles around the agents? Who's going to manage the performance of the agents? Every fundamental element of virtualization and management needs to get recreated in this next computing hierarchy. There'll be lots of wonderful companies that break through for how those things will be done.

VMware for Agents, Not Humans

Guido: The most interesting thing is that we're now building VMs so they're usable for agents as opposed to usable for humans. That changes the form factor, how you market them — you want the agent to make the pick for your VM offering. It changes how much complexity you can have, how quickly the startup should be. Humans are a lot more patient than agents. If you had to rebuild VMware today, how would it look different?

Pat: Does there need to be a VMware for agents and a VMware for humans? I think there needs to be — using Dario's "constitution," guard rails, being able to set policies.

Every aspect of the virtual machine as we know it will be servicing agents — as opposed to servicing hardware and humans. That becomes your fundamental design constraint. How do I make agents great? How can I make them secure, performant? How do I abstract them, migrate them? V-Motion for agents. Every one of these will have the new embodiment.

But I also need to think about how humans set the policies, describe the constitutions, get the dashboards. That's where the interesting thing is — you need to do both.

The hard design stuff we did for virtual machines was abstracting the hardware in a performant way for applications or operating systems. Here, it's abstracting the hardware and the operations for agents. That's the fundamental thing you're serving.

Closing

Host: It was great discussing this. Thank you so much, Pat, for coming in — we'll do it again.

Pat: Two of my favorite people. Anytime.

Host: Thanks.

Pat: That was awesome. Thank you.

Host: Thank you.

item.description:
## 一、瓶颈迁移的隐秘定律：AI 让设计变易，物理世界却开始反扑
Pat 在访谈中说出了一句看似寻常却极深的话："当技术让某件事变简单时，瓶颈就会迁移到别处。" 真正令人意外的是迁移的方向——**AI 让"软"的部分（RTL、kernel、编译器）接近零摩擦，瓶颈反而退回到最"硬"、最 19 世纪的物理环节**：九个月的流片、HBM 的 shoreline 带宽、40% 被 guard banding 白白浪费的功率预算、八年起步的燃气轮机交付周期。
这里有一个几乎没人指出的悖论：**AI 越聪明，硬件越回到热力学原理**。Pat 顺口提到"我得重新翻书看 Carnot 卡诺循环"，这不是玩笑——这意味着当代最前沿的工程师在被迫回到 1824 年的教科书。类似的模式在金融里出现过：量化交易让 alpha 消失后，所有竞争退回到物理层——光缆到交易所的毫秒距离。AI 行业正在经历同构的"下沉"：当认知层被抹平，决胜点回到土地、铜、水、热。
## 二、"最糟糕的行业"反转：memory 的二十年屈辱与它正在成为的护城河
这是整段对话中最反直觉的事实：**过去三十年零次重大内存创新

item.title: [Business of Sport] Man City’s Etihad Problem, LA Clippers Sanctioned, More Chaos at Celtic, & LIV 2.0 $100m Franchises
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最意外的观察：Bulma 与 Mansour 的"俱乐部成员悖论"

真正值得玩味的，不是 LA Clippers 案与 Man City 案在违规本质上的相似，而是两位违规者面对最终悬崖时所做出的身份选择完全相反。

Steve Bulmer 走到悬崖边，往下看了一眼——他看到的是"被 billionaires club 开除"的风险。他是 Microsoft 的前 CEO，他的身份认同建立在"美国资本精英俱乐部成员"之上。于是他认输了，解雇了律师，把自己从反抗者缩回成"club member"。

而 Abu Dhabi 皇室家族看向悬崖下，看到的是截然不同的东西：那不是"失去俱乐部席位"，而是"国家尊严受损"。对一个主权实体来说，EPL 的会员资格远不如 Microsoft 对 Bulmer 的身份意义重大。

这里有一个跨领域的隐藏联系：这其实是博弈论中"退出成本"的经典问题。但更深层的是——当一方的身份认同锚点在俱乐部之外（主权），另一方的身份认同锚点在俱乐部之内（资本精英圈层），同一套惩戒机制对两者的威慑力完全不对称。这意味着联盟规则对非主权投资者天然有效，对主权投资者天然失效。NBA 之所以能"快、准、狠"，部分原因恰恰是它从未真正接纳过主权资本——这是一个被忽视的、却决定性的结构优势。

二、"Kirsty 法则"：组织失败的通用诊断工具

节目中那个俏皮的词"pulling a Kirsty"（甩锅给下属以逃避责任），其实是一个值得严肃对待的组织病理学指标。

Bulmer 挨了罚之后开除自己的律师，Celtic 董事会把 AGM 转到线上以回避股东质询，WTA 用"Billie Jean King 的精神"包装一个连基本商业逻辑都站不住脚的决定——这三件事表面毫无关联，但本质是同一种动作：当权者在面对系统性失败时，用一个象征性的替罪羊/修辞来替代真正的问责。

跨领域连接：这与心理学中的"替代攻击"（displaced aggression）以及中世纪的"替罪羊仪式"（scapegoat ritual）在结构上完全一致——组织无法消化真实责任时，必须找到一个仪式性的出口。所以 Celtic 把 Dermot Desmond 的脸印在网球上扔向他，并不是"过激"，而是球迷直觉地把仪式反向使用了——他们在为管理层制造一个无法回避的替罪对象（Desmond 本人），迫使组织无法再 pull a Kirsty。

这是球迷抗议作为一种治理机制而非情绪宣泄的罕见案例。

三、LIV 2.0 与 WTA：两种"价值叙事通胀"的镜像

LIV 2.0 对球员说："团队估值将很快达到 1 亿美元"——用一个未来的虚拟数字替代当下真实的现金义务。WTA 对世界说："我们实现了男女同酬"——用一个道德高地话术替代"我们亏损、现金见底、商业能力不足"的真实处境。

这两件事看起来一个在高尔夫、一个在网球；一个是私募 PE 推动、一个是道德平权推动——但它们结构上完全同构：用叙事通胀对冲财务失能。

最让我意外的发现：这其实是量化宽松的组织学版本。QE 时代央行用货币印刷替代真实生产力增长；LIV 2.0 和 WTA 用估值叙事与道德叙事替代真实商业价值创造。两者都在"透支未来的信任"，两者都依赖"故事能跑得比现实快"。

但有一个关键差异：QE 由主权信用背书，可以撑很久；而体育组织的"叙事 QE"由球员信任背书——而球员，正如节目中那位匿名 LIV 球员的愤怒所显示的，信任消耗殆尽的速度远比央行信用快得多。

这给我们一个反直觉的预测：LIV 2.0 不会死于资金断裂，而会死于"球员叙事挤兑"——某一天，一个 Pot 4 的严肃球员公开拒绝接受股权替代现金，然后雪崩开始。

四、彩蛋级观察：Tattersalls 的 4.6 million 与整件事的隐喻

节目中那匹 460 万英镑的一岁小马——它从未赛跑，可能永远不会跑，Sheikh Mohammed 买的其实不是"马"，而是血统的未来期权。

而 LIV 球员被要求接受的"团队股权"、WTA 要求球迷接受的"同酬承诺"、Man City 希望留住的"冠军合法性"——本质都是在交易未来的血统权。

区别在于：赛马业有 400 年的血统登记制度做背书，这个期权有真实的可验证价值链。而体育组织的治理失败告诉我们——当缺乏可验证的血统制度（即独立、迅速、透明的仲裁机制），一切"未来价值"叙事都会退化为庞氏结构。

NBA 的 Adam Silver 之所以是"Leviathan"，Richard Masters 之所以终于赢得尊重——他们的本质工作，是在为自己的联赛建立血统登记簿。

📝 转录文本

Business of Sport 本期要点

开场：几大主题预告

I wanted to start off this week with the story of a major sports club that has been found guilty of contravening cost control regulations. We're not talking about Man City. We are talking about the LA Clippers. It's the harshest draft related punishment in league history. That is how a serious professional competition deals with misdemean.

The reputation of Celtic and its fans do not belong to any self-appointed group. This statement has absolutely poured more fuel on the fire. These guys don't want to be questioned. There's a profound hubris and arrogance about it where they basically say, "We're not even going to engage with our shareholders, let alone the fans."

Scott O'Neal and Ted Goldthorp, who is the head of VC Partners, sat on a panel about Live 2.0. It's not grounded in reality. All of this is just fanciful. We're going to very quickly get to 100 million valuations. It's bollocks.

I was kind of like beused when I saw this week the WTA announcing that they were now going to move to genuine pay equality next year. This is not saying that equal pay is the wrong ambition to have. What it's saying is that to achieve equal pay, you have to earn it as an organization.

寒暄与上周回顾

Good afternoon, Charlie. Hi, Charlie. Um, horrible rainy day outside. It's the first one we've had in a long time, isn't it? It is. It is. It's not going to bring me down from the highs though of our week. It's been a great week. Do tell the viewers.

I think it's been fantastic for the viewers and listeners who recognized that the show last week was on Manchester City and the verdict was um one of great thought and reflection on on the situation. So that's what many people said. Not all people.

Well, not all. No, of course of course. But you're never going to you're never going to please all the people. Never going to please everyone. And if you do, then there's something worrying.

But in all seriousness, thank you seriously to everyone that has got involved with that. It's been an incredible response and reaction to I know probably a huge amount of content that you've engaged and consumed over that time. So yeah, I just want to say a big thank you for that.

Thank you indeed. But we've got a lot to get through today. Um it's not like last week one topic. This is um a smorgish board. This is lots of different topics.

一、LA Clippers 案：另一场"成本管控违规"

开场悬念

I kind of wanted to start off this week which will surprise people. This is going to surprise people. I wanted to start off this week with the story of a major sports club that has has been found guilty of contravening um cost control regulations and which has engendered an explosive response from the owners of that organization and indeed threats of massive sanctions and punishments. Not even threats. It's actually in this case it has actually happened because we're not talking about Man City. We are talking about the LA Clippers.

The naughty LA Clippers. The naughty LA Clippers. a naughty Steve Bulmer um their owner um who uh has been caught um really on a quite sort of personal level here. He's been absolutely pinged himself by the NBA for being at the heart of this.

事件背景：Steve Ballmer 其人

I'll read it out. I've written I've written a nice little like chronology of it because it's it's going to ring true to a few of you based on what we talked about last week.

Just to give a bit of that context to anyone that doesn't know, Steve Bulma is a former chief executive of Microsoft. Uh he's the biggest biggest single shareholder in Microsoft actually I think he has about 4%. He's worth 155ish billion dollar um which if you're looking at individuals who own sports assets firmly places him right at the top of that um and yes him and the team have been um being a bit naughty.

违规机制详解

So, to break down what what they've done: every NBA team has a salary cap and there's also a cap on how much a single star can earn. They call that kind of a maximum contract. Now, a team can't get around those limits by finding a player extra money on the side. That would be called circumvention, and it's banned under the deal between the league and the players union, which is these collective bargaining agreements. You know, we've talked about where it's a split between the revenue of um the leagues that goes to the players and then back into the system.

Now, a player called Kawhi Leonard, one of the biggest stars in the NBA who joined the Clippers in 2019, there's been found that payments have gone beyond that salary cap and manufactured, created, come to him through means that do not fit within the existing regulations.

The Clippers went to four companies that were already doing business with the club. That includes Aspiration, uh, Boeing Wireless, uh, Dacttronics, and Locked in Insurance. They got those companies to give Leonard endorsement deals. The companies were persuaded by being offered more business from the team. So in effect like sponsor our player and then you'll get more from us.

The club also paid the personal expenses for Leonard and his people. So they failed to report the improper solicitations for the off-court income opportunities made um on Leonard's behalf through the business manager that he had, a guy called Dennis Robertson. Leonard through the conduct of Robertson um violated those circumvention rules by pressuring the Clippers to assist him in obtaining the off-court income opportunities and when he successfully did get those opportunities failed to reimburse the payments that the Clippers had paid for the personal expenses.

The NBA calls this a pattern of misconduct and notes that the Clippers are prior offender uh on these rules. Interestingly, in the statement, they didn't actually develop what they meant by that.

调查效率对比

The investigation was run by an independent law firm called Watchel Lipton.

How long did it take? Uh, I don't actually know. Uh, not long is the answer. How did you know? It it was not long. Wow. So, they were clean. Clean and effective, were they? Um, so it was definitely not um 8 years from original discovery through until final verdict. Um I'd have to go back and check exactly how long it was, but it was obviously much swifter.

处罚内容

Punishments. Well, they've been they've been pretty severe, haven't they? Quite chunky. Yeah, quite Lay them out or have you got them? I've got them in front of me here.

The loss of five future first round draft picks. So, the problem then is that the WTA commercial lady goes out and tries to find a jewelry partner for the WTA tour as a whole. And she goes and pitches out at one of the big jewelry firms. The jewelry firm says, "Yeah, but hang on a second. Your biggest stars are wearing their own clobber, right? They're not going to be wearing my stuff. They're gonna be wearing their own stuff. So, all of the cameras and eyeballs are on the jewelry that the players are wearing. And meanwhile, we've got a logo up there in the stadium saying that we're the WTA Tours official jewelry partner."

牺牲文化的消失

So, if the players were truly behind this, really behind this, they would have a conversation with WTA which said, "Right, we're going to pull our rights here, right? So we know that overall the tour will make much more money if all of us leading players agree that in these seven or eight categories — jewelry, cars, travel, whatever it might be — that we will all agree not to sign individual sponsorships in those particular categories and we will then ask the WTA to go to one of the big agencies and say right find us the biggest potential sponsor in all those categories and we will all wear the jewelry from that company. We will all drive the car from that company etc."

But that would require a degree of sacrifice from these players, right? And what strikes me about this generation of tennis player as compared to the Billie Jean Kings and Martinas is they just aren't willing to sacrifice anything. All they do is say — the WTA tour, we expect you to achieve equality of pay for us whilst we pull in endorsements that are bigger than the men's endorsements. That's what's going on here. So, we want to get the same level of prize money as the men whilst reserving the right to get bigger sponsorships than the men. It's absolutely mad.

But unfortunately, it seems like the WTA is effectively controlled by those senior players. I noticed in this statement that Jessica Pegula, the American player, who I think is head of the players committee and is probably on the board of the WTA, was very much involved in that whole statement. And they're all invoking Billie Jean King. Billie Jean King was paying 500 bucks. You ladies have been paid $20 million. We're not talking about a group of impoverished people here, right? There are all sorts of good causes that they could get involved in to do with equality. That doesn't mean playing, as you say, a particular random tournament Miami. Well, in that one, we definitely have to be equally paid. Even though the following week we're being paid half as much.

反事实场景

If you had a situation where those three tournaments that I listed out, right, Wuhan, Doha, and Dubai all had the same revenue as those ATP Shanghai. And then when they get into the combined tournaments, there was a disparity in prize money. You'd have a — of course that's your argument, right? You're making an assumption. But we can show you, we can prove on the side that these tournaments are worth X, so how could you pay less? But that's not the case. So these tournaments have just been reacting to how the WTA has valued itself, which is why again the WTA then having to top this up and it just doesn't make sense and it's creating really dangerous problem.

数学验证

The mathematics on it are, by the way, that the gap between the $4 million bucks and the $9 million bucks is $5 million bucks. Yeah. Okay. That $5 million bucks being filled over seven tournaments is $35 million bucks, right? And the CVC investment is $30 million a year. There you go.

开放邀请

We await comment from the WTA. Um, and we welcome it. Um, and if we are wrong about this and this is being generated by new sponsorships and by new media rights deals that we are unaware of, we will happily hold our hands up and say that on the show. I say well done. Well done.

结尾

Right guys, thanks very much. Um, that was an awful lot of topics to cram into one session. Tell you what, I could do with um I could do with a couple of beers.

Oh, just two. Oh, well, I've actually got a story to tell you about a couple of beers. I won't reveal it to everyone else. Can you tell me that story over a couple of beers? I'll tell you over just a couple of beers.

Anyway, uh guys, as always, thank you. Thanks, Charlie. Thanks a lot, guys.
