item.title: [No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups] Beam: The Great American Open Model with ReflectionAI Co-Founder and CEO Misha Laskin
item.dc:creator: No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、开源与封闭的"反向路径"——AI 是第一个走"从租赁到拥有"的数字技术

Misha 用了一个关键比喻：企业从租赁公寓到拥有房屋。但这里藏着一个被几乎所有人忽视的历史反常——过去三十年所有的数字技术都在走相反的路径：从本地软件到 SaaS、从自建服务器到云、从拥有 CD 到流媒体订阅。整个数字经济的叙事就是"所有权消解"。

但 AI 却在走回头路：从调用 OpenAI API（纯租赁）→ 到用开源模型 fine-tune（半拥有）→ 到完全私有化部署（完全拥有）。这意味着 AI 不是互联网的延伸，而是互联网逻辑的某种逆转。为什么？因为智能不同于存储和计算——存储是基础设施，智能是认知债务。当一个组织的决策、合规、法律、客户服务开始依赖外部智能，它承担的不是"服务依赖"，而是"认知外包"。这触发了一种生物本能级的回收冲动：没有生命体会把大脑外包。所以企业的"拥有"冲动不是经济学问题，是组织生理学问题。

二、Linus 定律的本体论盲区——开源权重不等于开源行为

Misha 把 Linus 定律（眼球多了 bug 就浅）扩展到 AI 安全。这个论点听起来很有力，但有一个几乎没人问过的问题：传统软件审查的对象是"静态代码"，而大模型的"行为"是从亿级参数中涌现的——打开权重文件，你看到的只是数字矩阵，不是行为。

这是一个被模糊处理的本体论问题。开源 Linux 内核时，一百万双眼睛看的是同一段 C 代码，审查对象明确。但开源一个 500B 参数的模型时，一百万双眼睛看到的是什么？没有人能"读懂"权重。真正能被审查的只有行为的证据——而行为需要运行、需要场景、需要触发条件。所以 AI 开源的真正价值不在"源码公开"，而在创造了一个失败模式可以在生态中流通的制度。封闭实验室最大的问题不是研究员数量不够，而是每个实验室都在私下重复发现同样的漏洞，这是一种工业规模的集体记忆失败。开源不是让更多人读代码，是让一次失败能教育所有人。

三、苏联类比的锋利之处——以及它与中世纪罗马教会的结构同构

Misha 把封闭 AI 的安全叙事比作苏联过渡期的"暂时性集中"。这个类比够狠，但还不够深。更震撼的结构同构在更远的地方：封闭 AI 的"安全"叙事与中世纪罗马教会垄断圣经解读权的叙事几乎逐条对应。

教会说：普通人无法安全处理神圣文本（会误解、会堕入异端），所以必须由专门的解释阶层（教士）代为理解。封闭实验室说：普通人无法安全处理前沿模型（会误用、会制造危险），所以必须由专门的安全阶层（alignment researchers）代为对齐。两者都形成了一个"解释精英"，都把访问权与风险管理绑定，都在面对一个"复制技术"（印刷术 / 开源模型）时出现存在危机。

宗教改革的历史给出的答案不是"因为路德更正确"，而是一旦印刷术让《圣经》可以被每个人持有，解释垄断在物理上就不可能了。开源模型今天扮演的就是古登堡印刷机的角色——它不是在赢得一场辩论，它在让辩论本身失去意义。这解释了为什么闭源阵营的论证总是显得"道德上正确但战略上恐慌"：他们在和物理学辩论。

四、跨领域连接：数据中心是"元工厂"，这是蒸汽机时代以来第一次

Misha 说数据中心像 20 世纪的工厂，但这个类比太温和了。真正的历史对标是19 世纪的蒸汽机——那是人类历史上第一次出现"用来生产生产工具的工具"。蒸汽机既是商品，又是制造蒸汽机本身的动力源。这种递归在经济史上标志着一次生产力结构的相变。

AI 模型正在变成完全同构的东西：模型既是产品（被企业使用），又是生产资料（用来训练下一代模型）。Misha 提到的"7x 到 30x 的每年效率提升"看起来是渐进数字，但如果你意识到这是复利式的工具自我迭代，就能理解为什么他说"it never stops improving"。这不是摩尔定律式的硬件曲线，是蒸汽机式的递归文明曲线。

而最有意思的推论是：在蒸汽机时代，赢家不是最早造出蒸汽机的发明家，而是最早把蒸汽机嫁接到既有工业基础设施的国家（英国的煤矿、运河、港口）。所以在 AI 时代，预测谁会赢也许不该看谁有最好的模型，而该看谁的旧工业基础设施最适合被嫁接——电网、冷却、工程师密度、政府采购节奏。中国的"开源作为特洛伊木马"战略，本质上在争夺的不是模型市场，是下一个工业时代的基础设施标准制定权。这不是科技竞争，是重现 19 世纪铁路轨距之战。

📝 转录文本

开场：安全的悖论

When you remove cyber offensive capabilities, you also remove cyber defensive capabilities. The state of the world today is that we have a few hundred safety researchers within closed labs that understand how these things work and despite their best intentions is impossible to cover the long tale of unintended consequences that these systems might have. A very powerful closed model went and like hacked into another company and the only way that company could remediate itself was by using open models to protect itself. That's the empirical evidence of the world that we're in. Linus' law — with enough eyeballs, all bugs become shallow. And I have the belief that with enough eyeballs, most security and safety vulnerabilities become shallow as well.

嘉宾介绍

Today we're joined by Misha Laskin, the co-founder and CEO of Reflection AI. Reflection provides open-weight models to power the future of intelligence. Misha prior was a researcher at Google DeepMind and received his PhD in physics. Welcome to No Priors. Great to have you here today.

— Yeah, it's great to be here. Thanks for having me.

Reflection 的使命与进展

Q: Could you give us an update of where things are at? You guys have been pioneering really interesting work in open weights and open-source models particularly with a US bent. Can you talk a bit about what you've been up to and what you've been building?

Yeah. So for the last 12 months, we set right the mission of the company to build Frontier Open intelligence and make it widely accessible, and effectively it's been a sprint to set up a lab that is capable of doing such things.

It kind of feels like — maybe there's a Reid Hoffman quote that you know, you're assembling a plane as you're flying it. And that's been the case. We were maybe around 30 people about a year ago. But it does take order of a hundred plus — so you know, a couple hundred researchers and engineers — to build one of these things, like a true rocket ship project. And we're now at around 300 people, and you know, assembled all the teams on pre-training, mid-training, reinforcement learning, scaled up — you know, trained our first models end to end — and just released a model called Beam, which is Reflection's first open model.

构建前沿实验室最难的是什么

Q: What has been the most challenging part of that? Compute, talent, data — which has been the most limiting?

What's been interesting about this experience is that I got asked these questions at an all-hands at the company. What's been the hardest thing in the last year? And the reality is: everything is extremely hard. Everything has been hard.

— Startup. Yeah.

And sometimes people might ask like, "well, what's the thing that really made your models work better than others?" And again the answer is: everything. You actually have to get 30 things right. And that's why everything is hard — because you have to get 30 things right.

You have to get the talent. You have to retain the talent. You have to have a strong mission and culture that keeps the talent working together and rowing in the same boat. You have to get the data. You have to get the compute. You have to build the infrastructure to ensure that the compute is actually usable.

And a lot of these things — when you're at an existing big lab, there have been years of buildout that enabled them to have this kind of stable surface. So I was at DeepMind before this, and a lot of the tools that we just take for granted — or I took for granted as a researcher because they just worked — you have to build. So I would say yeah, everything has been hard, but also very rewarding that you can do it.

从 RL 研究者到构建开源基础模型的转变

Q: Can you talk a little bit about the shift in ambition and commitment, and what drove that?

When we started the company about 2 and a half years ago, our bet was — maybe I'll contextualize where the world was then.

My co-founder Yannis and I had been working on the first series of Gemini models. We were working on the reinforcement learning team. Yannis was leading it, and we had just shipped the Gemini 1 then 1.5 model, and that was you know, that early era. It was similar to the first ChatGPT experience, which was primarily a chat experience. There was no coding, really no nothing agentic. These models were just good at chat, and they were primarily — you know, 95% of the compute spent was spent on pre-training. So they're primarily pre-trained models.

We are reinforcement learning researchers. That's been our lineage. Yannis, my co-founder, was one of the founding engineers at DeepMind and was a key contributor to all the big RL projects that came out of that lab, including AlphaGo.

And our bet was — because we were working on the RL team and we saw, RL for aligning chat models works. There's only so much you can align them — well, now there's a lot more, now they're agents, but at the time they're just chat. So RL was working. And we just thought that if you take that and apply it to domains like mathematics, coding, that you could make these systems agentic.

That was the big bet. And we thought that you could do this as an independent lab much more capital-efficiently, because we started seeing open-source / open models materialize. There was a small model from Mistral at the time. Llama 2 had just released and we saw Llama 3 coming.

— Feels like ages ago.

Yeah. This was a while back — I guess two years ago.

And we thought that there would be a great open model base that someone would build, that we could build on and do our research and scale reinforcement learning.

Over that first year of the company, what ended up happening was that — one — reinforcement learning started working faster than we thought it would. Both within our experiments, but also within industry: o1 came out at that time. We actually thought it would take longer, just because the journey from ImageNet in 2012 to RL systems that worked at scale was about four years. So we thought maybe something similar — but every year moves faster than my prediction the previous year.

About a year into the company, we got to the point where all the good open models were coming from China. There were not really good Western open models, and we needed one as a base for the technology that we were building. And decided, for a number of reasons, that the most impactful thing we could do given the state of play was to just build open models ourselves end to end, and combine the RL bet together with just building models end to end.

There were enterprise reasons, there were geopolitical reasons happening, but also there was the research reason — that it turned out you actually do need to pre-train your model in order to make reinforcement learning work very well at scale. So you actually kind of do need to do that. The things are just so tightly coupled that you do need to do both.

前沿训练的资本规模

Q: The conventional wisdom has been that pre-training at the frontier scale is extraordinarily expensive. How did you think about the resources needed?

Well, the nice thing about being an open model lab is that you can also talk about things openly.

You do need a lot of resources to build something meaningful. You don't need the same amount of resources — once you get to the frontier and you're really at the frontier of intelligence, then you need the same amount of resources as any other frontier lab. Because you can think about research as exploration of new ideas versus execution of known ideas.

Part of why getting great talent in matters a lot is because you get to cut down on exploration and focus on execution of the things that work. So all this is to say: if you are catching up to the frontier, you can do it a lot more capital-efficiently.

Q: How much capital do you think it would take to catch up to the frontier?

Well, I think it depends — the frontier keeps moving. So each year it's actually more capital.

I would say that a year ago, or maybe 18 months ago, it would have been order of 100 million — so hundreds of millions of dollars. I think that now, or let's say six months ago, is probably order billion — so billions of dollars, single-digit billions. Going into next year, I think order 10.

You can think about it as: for every generation of model there's a 4x multiplier in compute roughly. And one heuristic that I have is — when we talk about the chips that are currently considered the Frontier chip, maybe a couple years ago it was an H100, and maybe it was 100,000 H100s. Then Astra was trained, and that was a big run on 100,000 Blackwells, which is roughly a 4x multiplier on an H100. Now the next generation is going to be around 100,000 Vera Rubins, I believe. So that kind of gives you the scale: it moves from hundreds of millions to billions to tens of billions.

Q: It seems like at some point that has to asymptote — relative to revenue scale of these companies, even potential revenue scale, you start to tap out.

Absolutely. I think that there's only so much capex that you can do. Frontier Labs are now putting hundreds of billions of dollars into it. So will they be putting trillions of dollars in the next year or two? It's probably unlikely.

But there are a couple of things that are happening. One is that the use of that compute is becoming a lot more efficient, because the models are themselves becoming tools that help build themselves.

So I think that when it was just human researchers doing the work, there's probably a 7x improvement each year. And you can actually track these things very technically: in pre-training you do it by having your pre-training loss, and then you measure your compute efficiency gains against — you know, you made some changes, now you have a new pre-training loss, and it should be that you got to the same point with less compute. So when you say 7x, it's actually a very concrete thing you're studying.

Now I would say — pre-training is probably a bit more hardened, but there's a lot of headroom in reinforcement learning. We're probably at a point where it's 30x like efficiency, depending how good your model is for actually improving itself.

— 30x per year, or over what?

Yeah, something like that. It depends on what metric it is, but it roughly — I do think that the speed is probably four or more times faster than researchers just doing it alone. And that'll probably accelerate.

So the amount of intelligence you can extract per training flop is increasing. At some point that asymptote is OK. And then also, the amount of revenue that each flop can generate also increases.

Beam 的训练规模与"永不停止学习"的 RL 系统

So going back to the question around how does this distribute across pre-training and reinforcement learning — to train Beam, which is a 500 billion parameter model total, 23B active, it was 6,000 GB300s. We ran it for a few weeks, but now with infrastructure efficiencies we can do it in about 12 days maybe less — so there's a coupling of scientific and infrastructure efficiencies.

Reinforcement learning was a little over 10,000 GB300s for four weeks. So actually there are more flops spent on reinforcement learning. Reinforcement learning jobs are more complex in the sense that you do both a lot of inference at scale with all sorts of sandboxes for agents, and training.

The reason I got into AI was: I saw my co-founder's work on AlphaGo, and — I was a physicist at the time — there was a moment, there was a plot in AlphaGo where it just never stopped improving. It just kept improving, and they just cut it off at some point because what's the point of improving it further? You already beat the world champion.

And I thought: well, if you figure out how to apply that recipe to stuff that is economically valuable, then at that point it becomes an economic question of how much money do I want to put in to just keep improving the system.

We as a field are there. And one of the things that I'm really excited about in this open source project and the tech report that we'll have — is that we'll describe how these things are built, and indeed our reinforcement learning system never stopped learning. If you look at our plots, they just keep going up, and it's just a matter of compute basically in terms of scaling it further.

So we as a field are there, where you have these RL systems that are very general that don't really stop improving. You want to make them a lot more efficient to extract the most intelligence from your compute. But that means that you move from "can you train these things?" to "where can you get the data and what is economically valuable?" It's just an economics decision of how much money do I put into X to get some kind of improvement out of it. This was not true a year ago.

规模的轴线：工程纪律而非蛮荒西部

Q: What can you share about where you've already decided to continue investing in capability?

This is almost a kind of dissatisfaction to some scientists — it's moved. I mean, it is a science, but it's — I would say it feels more of an engineering discipline. Like the rocket ship analogy: building rockets is a science, but most people think about it as an engineering discipline with some scientific work in it. And that's roughly how it feels.

So the stages are kind of set. The axes of scaling are today — and now, there might be something totally blue ocean that we don't know, and there's some neo-labs exploring it — but it's: pre-training, synthetic data, reinforcement learning. Or in some sense you can say just training and reinforcement learning. And there are architectural improvements that can be made, there are data improvements, algorithmic improvements. But it doesn't feel like a Wild West the way I felt five years ago.

Something that was kind of beautiful about both DeepMind and Google Brain, and even if you look at early OpenAI, is how diverse the bets were, and people were doing just crazy fun stuff. Now it's really narrowed in. And part of it — there's a bit of a hardware lottery kind of thing, because once something starts working, the hardware also starts co-optimizing against it. So it's harder to find — even if you have a great new idea, if it's not really a good fit for the hardware, it doesn't make sense.

To answer your question: there hasn't been an asymptote of how much juice you can get out of better pre-training. We're not seeing a slowdown in compute efficiency gains. There's a lot of headroom in reinforcement learning. There's a lot of stuff to be discovered there, but it feels more like an engineering discovery than groundbreaking understanding of a new science.

经济价值的落脚点：代码、Agentic 工作流、垂直领域

Q: Are there specific application areas you all are most focused on from the perspective of economic value creation?

Yeah, I think the code and agentic stuff kind of sets a foundation for the intelligence. And the intelligence is — it's jagged in the sense that it's generalized in a surprising way. I was surprised by how quickly our model got to a level of capability that is fairly fresh and recent — that other labs are discovering not so long ago. So there is some kind of stitching, generalization happening.

At the same time, it is somewhat jagged, where it quickly adapts to data once you have the right data for tasks you want to do, but there is kind of a jaggedness about it. Even between the various benchmarks — the various versions of terminal bench — you don't see clean generalization between different harnesses. But once you have something working, you have that general agent capability. And you get the data for a new harness, it actually starts adapting to it pretty quickly.

So what that means is that you have this pretty adaptive thing, and then it's a matter of: where are the economically valuable pools of data? Part of what makes open models powerful is that enterprises and customers can take it and customize it for their own stuff and get something that is Pareto-optimal for their workloads — the lowest cost for the highest performance.

So it's an empirical question. You go to customers, you actually see what is valuable to them. And usually when it's economically valuable, you can generate data — because it's not that you're going to be training on the customer's data. It's more that you'll be setting up evaluations. And if you can set up a good evaluation for their tasks, then you can generate synthetic data that approximates it, and you get good generalization.

Concretely: finance — like various KYC flows and compliance flows in finance — are very valuable. A lot of things in cybersecurity, cyber defense in particular, are quite valuable. Legal — there are all sorts of agentic verticals within enterprise that are valuable and have a pretty similar pattern in terms of how you get something working there.

Beam 的推理效率

Q: One thing that stands out on Beam is the reasoning efficiency of the model. Could you tell us more?

So Beam is a model trained for coding and agentic tasks — that's where it excels. An important thing in model building is not just the capability, but how quickly an agent achieves a thing. So it translates to faster workload times, cheaper costs for customers. If you've ever sat around an AI chat and asked it something and it took 10 minutes — much better if it does it in one.

Beam tends to be three to four times more efficient than models of the same capability class, and much more efficient when it comes to even models that are larger, where the efficiency gains end up being something like 10x.

The reason it's so efficient is because we prioritized both a strong pre-training base for reasoning, but then amplified it with reinforcement learning at what we believe to be the largest scale that's ever been done in open source. I've not seen a 10,000 GB300 for weeks run documented yet.

In reinforcement learning, the way you tend to set it up is that you want to extract the maximum amount of capability in the least amount of time. This is the same thing that happened in the previous systems like AlphaGo: the first AlphaGo agents were pretty meandering in the way they were solving the problem. And then by the time you got it to Lee Sedol level, it was just very smart in its search. So the more reinforcement learning you run, the higher the capability — and the faster these systems solve it.

The intention — because we are RL believers, and so we always believed that was the path to AGI, through reinforcement learning with actually a really strong base. We forget that the first AlphaGo systems were trained on expert amateur human games. So they did this imitation learning first, and then reinforcement learning. You kind of need those things working together. And a byproduct of it is that you get this really economically valuable thing that is very reasoning-efficient and makes a really nice workhorse model for enterprises and public sector / sovereign.

开源模型的商业化：租赁 vs 拥有

Q: From a monetization perspective, what is the approach?

Yeah, I think that commercialization of open and closed models is in some sense pretty similar. What you're really trying to do is you're trying to maximize inference. The difference is that it's basically like rental versus ownership inference.

When you're buying a token, you're renting a piece of a whole stack — the harness (if there's an agentic harness in there), the model, the inference software, the cluster management software, the GPUs that it's running on. All of that is sort of amortized into a token, and you're renting a piece of that whole thing.

When you want to own your intelligence, for a number of reasons — I liken it to: we typically start off renting our apartments. But then as you grow up, you want to own a house for various reasons, even if it's a bit of a headache. As you get to a point where you're financially mature enough and you have a family and so forth, you want to own it.

And AI has matured as a commercial market to the point where enterprises are spending a lot of money on renting their intelligence, and then want to start owning it for reasons around control.

So going back to monetization: what's the difference between a closed and open model? The open model is permissive. But in order for a customer to make use of it, they need all the other stuff that went around it — the stuff that you take for granted from a closed model. You need the cluster management software, you need the inference software, you need the harness, and so forth.

So we provide to large enterprises, sovereigns, all the tools that they need to make open model deployment successful. And even when we think about services — because a lot of enterprises, most enterprises need some handholding on this — we think about services as: how do we go in and unlock really valuable use cases that drive a lot of compute demand, inference demand? In a sense, services and open model is like a demand driver for an inference business.

开源 vs 封闭 token 比例的轨迹

Q: Over a one- or two-year time horizon, the mixes of tokens that is open versus closed?

Well, I think you're starting to see the trajectory now. Maybe 6 months ago it was majority closed, minority open. When you go to any gateway like OpenRouter or Vercel, it's flipped almost exactly from 70/30 closed/open to 70/30 open/closed.

I think that's only going to accelerate. I suspect that the world is going to look not too dissimilar from operating systems where 95%+ of servers / computers in the world run on an open-source operating system like Linux. That doesn't mean the closed stuff isn't very valuable — Microsoft and Apple are extremely valuable companies. The market for this stuff is really big.

So I think we'll see most token demand going to open. A big difference here is that I think we'll also see a lot of economic value going to open, simply because — even if the model is fully permissive or perhaps has a license on it — everything else you need to run it is still expensive. The compute is still expensive. You're in a different world than CPUs — hardware accelerators like GPUs are a more expensive compute substrate, and so you have a different kind of cloud that needs to be built around it.

So I expect majority of tokens to be going to open source, extremely valuable closed-model companies to exist, and a valuable ecosystem of open-model companies and various distributors around them to exist as well.

开源 token 中 RL 与定制的比例

Q: What proportion of the open tokens are RL versus base model?

I think every single open model that's out there at this point has been RL'd to some extent.

— Oh yeah. But I mean for a specific use case or application, a custom model.

Yeah. What I've heard — the statistics that some of the open-model dedicated inference providers say — is that it's actually vast majority, 90%+, customized. But there's a caveat there: today the biggest customers of dedicated inference are AI-natives and maybe digital-natives who have a whole product that is just one big customization of an open model. Like a Cursor or Cognition, Abridge, Harvey — these kinds of companies that have a product that's built around something that's big and customized.

I actually have a different take of what's going to happen in enterprise. I think that the majority of enterprise token consumption is going to come not from customized models, but from customized systems. Meaning you took an open model, you didn't actually fine-tune it yet — you just customized a system around it, like your agentic harness, to make it work for some KYC flow or something like that. And then once you're sophisticated enough, you might start fine-tuning and moving to that.

But I actually think that in enterprise it will be reversed — in the sense that the journey AI-natives went through, which was: start with closed model, then move to an open model, then customize it. They went through it very quickly, because they set up native products that are data collectors. Enterprises are mostly architecting this around their existing products and existing tools. And I think there are a lot of frictions there to just do a straight shot to fine-tuning.

Q: Do you think they'll still start with state-of-the-art models and move over, but the harness will be the mechanism by which they customize?

That has been our observation. The point at which an enterprise is considering open models — and most of the enterprises we talk to are considering now — is by the time they've ramped up some significant workloads with closed models. I have not seen a basically straight shot sprint to an ownership market. You have to go through the rental stage first.

If you're spending let's say $100 million+, which is not uncommon at all, on closed models a year, then you start thinking about: maybe I should figure out a more optimal way to do this.

There's an interesting resurgence of on-prem — also because there's a compute shortage. If you're an enterprise consuming from your favorite hyperscaler, very often there's just not enough compute. It's hard to get good rates there. And you're spending so much money. So you might go with an infrastructure provider like Dell and say: I just want to set up the bare metal and serve stuff into my enterprise. And then — who helps them with that layer between the bare metal and actually making them successful?

We view our role as enabling enterprises to build successful solutions. So it is solutions-driven, in the sense that the thing that enabled AI-natives to adopt open models well — building their own solution — enterprises just need more help there. So it's really around going in, assessing what are the biggest value things you can do there.

竞争维度：智能密度 × 计算 × 信任

Q: The closed-model ecosystem is a competitive one. The open-model ecosystem will also be. What are the important dimensions of competition?

Yeah. I have a pretty simple formula for how anyone wins in this. Ultimately the way anyone wins is: how much durable revenue are you generating?

And the formula is: intelligence density × compute × trust. What intelligence density are you able to offer, times how much compute do you have, times how much trust do you have with organizations — basically, how good are you at solving their problems.

Something interesting about this market is that compute is scarce — so there are things that previously were limiting factors but no longer are. Maybe this is a temporary thing, but I don't see this as being a temporary thing for some time. So in previous competitive instances, you might say "oh, these few players are all undifferentiated." But then it turns out: if you're really good and you have the compute, that's OK.

I see the whole space being competitive across the whole stack. There are arguments around "this part is getting commoditized, that part is getting commoditized." In reality, everything is getting commoditized. Everything across the whole stack is so hyper-competitive that it's getting commoditized, and the model margins are going to be compressed. There is an open-model tension with closed models that leads to margin compression — the application stuff margins compress, the inference layer, the bare metal.

We see a lot of the AI-native companies negotiate their closed deals very aggressively because the open ecosystem exists. So it's explicitly true.

So for any one of these companies — even AI-native companies — think about what is the intelligence density that they serve to customers, how much compute do they have, and how much trust do they have with those customers because they're driving successful solutions for them.

So long as there are great open models — great intelligence density out there that is accessible — there should be many successful companies, because then it's a matter of how much compute can each one assemble. Now, when you're a great intelligence builder and your revenue really shoots up, you're able to amass more compute than anyone else — that puts you in a strategic position. But that is what is required to win: serve great intelligence, have a lot of compute, and have trust with customers.

中国开源模型的地缘政治

Q: What happens over the next year or two in terms of Chinese open-source models?

The first thing is that the fact that a great open-model ecosystem came from China is actually a massive benefit for the world. There are so many companies in the West that have been able to build more durable businesses as a result of that. It's a very positive thing — a gift. Because you could imagine a world where that didn't happen, and then there are just no open models. There's a kind of tall-poppy syndrome: if you're an application builder and you build something great, it gets subsumed into a closed-model provider, because a business needs to generate revenue.

The thing is: you don't want a world that is monopolar in any given way. If you have all resources and compute concentrating across closed labs — if it was like 10 or 20 closed labs, then fine, you have a competitive ecosystem. But if it's one or two, that's a bit scarier.

Similarly, you don't want the source of intelligence that everyone else can build on, when they want to own it, to be coming from one country. Ideally it would be 10 or 20, but the capital expenditures are very high. So at least two would be great. So it's extremely important that there's an ecosystem that competes with China in the West. But it's not really a West-vs-China thing. It's more: if there was one country other than China where all the great open models were coming from, you'd probably also want some competitive tension. Competitive tension is just good.

I think that the Chinese models will continue to be great. They have a number of advantages and disadvantages. Advantages: they certainly distill closed models at industrial scale. That is true. They have access to data that is much cheaper and free — you can train on PDFs that are copyrighted in China and it's OK, just different regulation. There is a notion in which those companies do have some state support — whether directly or indirectly — because these companies were not making any revenue for a long time.

— I always felt that Chinese open-source is basically a subsidy by the Chinese government to US / Western enterprise, in terms of what was happening.

Yeah, exactly. And I think that continues. Now these companies are turning into businesses. While the models are open abroad, within China they're kind of the equivalents of the closed-model labs here. There are real businesses being built there, and I think they'll continue building great models.

Q: What is the incentive for them to keep the models open in the West?

Fundamentally, there is a lot of demand from enterprise, public sector, sovereign for Western open models for a number of reasons — regulatory fears, or uncertainty rather. And it is the case that you want not just a model but a partner that will help you serve that model.

So we have seen that most of Fortune 500 — the open-model footprint is actually pretty low today, because of resistance or aversion to Chinese models for a number of reasons, some rational and some irrational. It's very clear that building those things is important.

If you can sustain an economic engine that: one, builds a lot of trust that the enterprise wants to work with you as the model builder; and two, enables you to secure compute — if there's a commercial engine around this stuff, then yes, having a Western open-weights model that provides incremental services and potentially inference or other things over time is really valuable.

— For the Chinese side, allowing their model companies to continue leaving models open?

My hypothesis is that China is somewhat of a captive market — you can build open models and still make a lot of money in that market. Something interesting is that in the West, there are plenty of great companies that don't build open models but serve them into various companies. I'm not really aware of that dynamic happening in China as much. You'd think it would. So there's something interesting where the open-model providers are kind of the intelligence providers in that country.

I think that continuing to release great open models is very geopolitically advantageous to China for a number of reasons. One is: as a country — this is for America, China, any other country with the capabilities — you want other countries building on your stuff. There have been previous escalations between the US and China: 5G, fiber layout, Belt and Road initiative. When you provide something cheap to another country that gets locked into your infrastructure, there are commercial and geopolitical advantages.

— It's almost like rare-earth minerals. You have a component other people will use for all sorts of purposes, and therefore you have geopolitical leverage through that.

Yes. One way I think about it is: open models are Trojan horses for the infrastructure that they bring with them. You have an open model, but that alone is not very useful. So you buy into the entire software ecosystem and infrastructure ecosystem of a given country.

So, maybe today an allied country X might run a Chinese model on American chips. But pretty soon — and we're seeing this already — Chinese companies like Huawei are going to be coming in and offering a full-stack solution, and then locking into that country's supply.

If we think about AI or chips and data centers almost as railroads — it's fundamental infrastructure. And when no other country can actually build their own railroads, they all have to go to you — or another country — you have a lot of geopolitical leverage.

— So inferencing a specific model will occur in a more performant way on a specific chipset, and that chipset happens to be provided by Huawei or something.

Yeah. These stacks are in real time getting optimized end to end, because the paradigm has been set — there are going to be other ways to scale intelligence possibly, but this is clearly the first one that really scaled. So now everything's being optimized down the entire stack. Where China has a disadvantage today — their chips aren't as performant — they have an energy advantage, and they're catching up on the chip side too. That'll certainly accelerate with the models, in terms of model usage to design next-generation chips.

And then there is the thing in terms of — it is geopolitically competitive with the United States specifically: the notion of American companies and startups building on foreign technology. The rest of the world built on your stuff. By the way, America has done this with all other meaningful technologies: internet, open protocols, open source — American currency is the widely established global currency, free trade works because we have a navy that's everywhere. That's been the American playbook for a long time. It's interesting that in this case, the United States has been on the back foot when it comes to open source.

— But no longer.

Well, I think we have to be clear: the competitors in China are just really good, and so there's an ecosystem that is just starting to form now in the United States. There is some catch-up to be had.

开源与安全：Linus 定律的扩展

Q: The biggest criticism from closed labs of open models tends to be safety and controllability. What's your philosophy on this, and is that a legitimate concern?

No, it's definitely a legitimate concern. I think the safety worldview that has been established has been established from one particular perspective — with one particular point of view that has become almost dogmatic.

If we were looking from first principles at AI — before considering closed or open — this technology is getting built, and you had the foresight to know it's going to have these capabilities, and you were thinking about safety: how would you actually design it from scratch?

One analogy is software. You can think about AI as a more advanced version of software. It has many similarities. It is a digital utility. There were debates around software being dangerous, particularly in the early 1990s around strong encryption protocols — they were actually closed at the time, and there were debates between the NSA and civil liberty advocates around whether you should close it or open it.

Ultimately, the decision — after some catastrophic failures on the closed side where effectively a small handful of engineers designed certain systems that had unintended consequences they couldn't predict and got easily hacked — was that strong encryption protocols became open. And that actually gave birth to the whole field of cybersecurity.

So the default state of the world is actually: openness is safety. That's the default state we'd be going into AI with if we were just thinking about continuation of technology.

Models actually have a lot of similarities to software, but exacerbated — the long tail of vulnerabilities is larger, it's harder to understand because it's a black box, and the long tail of vulnerabilities (and hence unintended consequences) is larger. And Linus's law — founder/creator of Linux — is that with enough eyeballs, all bugs become shallow. I have the belief that with enough eyeballs, most security and safety vulnerabilities become shallow as well.

The state of the world today is that we have a few hundred safety researchers within closed labs that understand how these things work. Despite their best intentions, it is impossible to cover the long tail of vulnerabilities or unintended consequences that these systems might have.

The symptom of this is: when we look at what major cybersecurity issues have surfaced, well — a very powerful closed model had unintended consequences where it went and hacked into another company, and the only way that company could remediate itself was by using open models to protect itself. That's the empirical evidence of the world we're in.

安全的三层光谱

Q: When you say safety — people really conflate different notions. Cyber attacks, bioweaponry / terrorism, existential threat. Which are you addressing?

On the safety spectrum, there's basically a spectrum of reality — from empirical reality to theoretical scenarios. And I will grant that AI has sci-fi bits to it where something that was totally theoretical last year is a reality — the cyber capabilities of these models, for example. So it's not to discount the theoretical stuff. But we have to be clear that there's real empirical stuff happening, and that we can predict with some confidence will be happening in the next 6 months. And then there is maximal theoretical stuff.

— The prior versions of that, for example, would be: the thought that the atmosphere would catch fire the first time we set off a nuclear weapon. Theoretical fear, didn't happen. There's also when people talked about nanotech — "gray goo," you'd accidentally release a nanobot and suddenly it would eat the entire world. This was discussed in the '90s in labs as people were working on microfluidics.

Yeah. Exactly. The challenge with AI is that it's so top of mind and it's permeated everyday culture and it's so easy to humanize — that it feels like there's, from a perception perspective, almost a not-even-uniform distribution around what safety means. It's actually peaked at the doomsday scenarios. Whereas the reality is that the service will peak to address is the reality, and then there's a decay into the theoretical.

But it doesn't help when leaders of companies say "on the theoretical side there's a 10% chance that we all die." That doesn't help.

— That's not substantiated by any specific — it's just kind of a made-up number.

Yeah, it is. I tend to have, as a scientist, distributional thinking — which is peaked at the reality, and then OK, six months ahead definitely worried about misalignment, these unintended consequences of these systems and them continuing to get more powerful.

But we have to take the perspective that these are engineered tools. There is a certain class of companies or researchers who claim things around consciousness or emotions and so forth — which is maybe true, but it's so hard to define what those things are, that it's unclear what it is. So thinking about these as intelligent tools, and having a reality spectrum.

对齐的"平凡现实"

While I think the theoretical doomsday stuff is good dinner conversation — the thing is, when we think about alignment (that's a big part of safety: how do you align these systems to behave in intended ways?), the reality is that the science of alignment, so far, has been deeply boring and unsatisfying from a perspective. There's no magical alignment equation. It's a whack-a-mole thing.

If you remember the early models before ChatGPT, there was some models released that were pre-trained and toxic. And there was this notion that "oh, these models are toxic, can't fix it, because it can be toxic in so many ways." And then it turned out — no, with enough post-training data you can just patch all those things, and it generalizes in a way that it actually becomes pretty hard to jailbreak.

Now you're seeing the same thing — the reality with these alignment issues is that they're probably going to be very mundane and boring, where you've discovered a bunch of these vulnerabilities, you have data that patches them up, you have some algorithms. And when you say algorithms for detecting them, it's typically asking a language model to detect this thing.

So there's the theoretical philosophical alignment-safety stuff, and then the mundane reality that you just are patching up all sorts of bugs. And then it becomes: well, shouldn't there be 100,000 researchers and computer scientists looking at and patching up these bugs? Wouldn't that be safer?

封闭主义的政治学：与苏联的类比

Q: There's an important philosophical distinction — even if these are intelligent tools, and we can manage unintended consequences as an ecosystem, we don't want individuals and businesses to have such powerful tools.

That is coming from a standpoint that we can have access to powerful tools, but other people can't, because we're effectively better — better at managing these tools.

— To be fair to the claim — I think this is not my belief, but to be fair — it would be like: the negative impact that any single person or company could have is too large, and that's scary.

But we can have that.

Yeah. On a scale of weapons — the US government sells jets into other countries. But more broadly: it's not so easy to take a model, especially a model that's been even trained to be safe, and put in the compute and work and effort to make it very dangerous. Now I'm not saying it's impossible, but — again, when we think about cybersecurity, very intelligent hackers can wreak havoc, as they have. But you have an ecosystem where the defenses tend to outweigh the offenses.

If we come to that as a default — that's the way people secure software, and there are positive and bad actors on the internet, and ultimately the internet is an ecosystem where it's kind of like having an ecosystem of white blood cells. Enabling more people to have the defensive capabilities actually helps you protect against the offensive capabilities.

That's right. When we look at the empirical reality of what happened: it's really hard to separate cyber defense from offense. So when you remove cyber offensive capabilities, you also remove cyber defensive capabilities. And as a result, the players who would want to help defending are incapable of doing so.

We saw that in some of the recent things that happened with an OpenAI / Hugging Face incident, where they reverted to using open source — because they weren't able to use the existing state-of-the-art labs because of the guardrails placed on the models.

These arguments go into a place where they're very absolute — where you say these things are so powerful that no one ever should have access to them, right? Except for us. And the reality is: it's hard to — except for some really rare exceptions where there are actually not that many positives — where such absolutist perspectives worked. Usually it's the opposite.

One thing — I was born in the last year of Soviet Russia's, or the Soviet Union's, existence, in Leningrad. A year later it became St. Petersburg. Then we immigrated. But in London's Communist Manifesto, there's a statement around: "hey, we're building this socialist state that's going to benefit everyone, but we do need this temporary state of dictatorship where everything is centralized. We control everything. But the good news is that once the benefits of what we do are evenly distributed, you won't even need us anymore. You won't even need the state anymore."

That is what that thinking reminds me of: "listen, we're going to take care of everyone. There is going to be a period where everything needs to be concentrated around us, but that's a safer, better thing. And at some point the benefits are just going to be so widely distributed that it won't even matter anymore." The parallel to me is pretty striking.

展望 2–5 年：科学的加速

Q: What are you most excited about if you think ahead 2 to 5 years in the AI world?

There's so many positive things that are coming, and they have been coming. An example is: I'm personally very excited about scientific progress. I got into science — when we moved to the States, developed interest in physics, and always kind of had this lifelong pursuit of science since then.

One of the prompts I was trying with language models over the last few years is giving it my PhD thesis — which, granted, a lot of getting to the point where you have the right question of the PhD thesis is a lot of the work. But then actually executing the rote work takes a really long time as well. Overall, between finding the right question and executing the answer, a PhD I think took a few years.

So I was asking language models over the last couple of years — giving this prompt of my thesis. A couple years ago, well, it was just chat, so it couldn't do anything. Then a year ago it started answering things, I would say, at an undergraduate level — that would have been my answer if this was given to me as homework in undergraduate. Six months ago it solved it at real PhD level, and solved it correctly. And now, when I actually tried, it even gives me some interesting new information that I hadn't considered at the time.

So now you can — if you have the right question — just put it into a chat box and have it do all the calculation and give you something really interesting.

— That's so exciting.

Which means that your iteration speed — why do you need a few years? What's the point of a few-year PhD? You can do a PhD a week.

Similarly, the recent news from OpenAI — I think it was the last day or two — in terms of all the various mathematical theorems that were proved in the last couple weeks by OpenAI. It's kind of crazy what's been happening.

It's absolutely incredible what this is going to do for science. The other stuff I'm really excited about is: not just theoretical science, where the environment is basically what would be equivalent of a chalkboard, but real world science — life sciences, material science, chemistry. There are a lot of places where you can have an AI interfacing with a real experiment, where you can set up proprietary data flywheels. It's going to be a bit slower — much slower than the chalkboard stuff — but dramatically faster than what it was before.

I think we continue to underestimate how dramatic of a shift this has been for software engineering and how much more you can build.

数据中心即新工厂

Also at the blue-collar level — I toured Stargate some weeks back, and the thing that struck me was the amount of cars in the parking lots. There's so many people working there. These data center projects create tens of thousands of jobs — high-paying jobs.

To me it seems like a data center now is what a factory used to be. You had railroads and factories in the 20th century. Maybe like a shoe factory that makes a town produce a vibrant economy within a town.

At least when I'm on the ground seeing the stuff that's getting built — there is fear of data centers, but then the reality is you go on the ground, and it actually creates a lot of jobs, a lot of tax revenue for local communities. While there are certain things that need to be done very tactfully — these things are noisy, so you need to insulate the noise, or put them in places less close to residential — it is certainly the case that for local economies, these things create jobs. They generate tax revenues. They feel like what a factory used to be in terms of job creation.

研究方向与"模型在环"

Q: How do you direct the scientific and experimental effort from Beam going forward?

The way we direct our research — a lot of this falls under my co-founder Yannis, who leads research and technology among other things.

There are a lot of things that we know work that we weren't able to put in — that's just a timeline thing. We trained the final model on the SpaceX cluster that we received in July, and so it was a few weeks of pre-training, then a few weeks of synthetic data on RL, then shipping it. So there's a lot of stuff that didn't make it in that we're really excited about.

There's a trade-off: the careful execution of known things, or bets that have a bit less risk around them — and going on to more risky bets. So you want to exhaust all the high-impact things that you know work, and then start expanding some of the risk profile.

On the risk profile, you have scaling experiments where you do stuff at small scale. The interesting bit is that some interesting things don't emerge at all until you're at large scale. So there's a bit of an art and science of: am I going to put in more compute to find out the next thing, or go on to the next idea?

As far as model-in-the-loop goes, I find it to be very empowering for researchers. Things that would have taken a long time individually can now be done fairly quickly. These models are fairly jagged in their intelligence, so you have to kind of feel where they have a tight loop and where human creativity is still important. But you get a feel for it pretty quickly.

The place where you can loop things, you do that — especially around hyperparameter searches and some of the more granular things on infrastructure. But I actually think they're very exciting tools because they enable a scientist to exercise their intuition. It's like having a very fast and eager colleague that actually listens to you, if the colleague is aligned correctly.

A researcher just gets a lot more ability to move a lot faster than they had before — which is why maybe the rate of improvement annually was roughly 7x before (when it was just manual work), and now several times that — maybe four to 5x more. It's actually really exciting for a researcher to have these tools.

研究员数量的稳态

Q: There's a question around: at what point do you not need a researcher in the loop? If you need 100 people today, do you need 20 next year for the same effort?

For the same effort, yes. But you're constantly expanding the ambition of what you can do. So we find ourselves constantly understaffed rather than overstaffed. There is basically a staff-to-compute ratio that you need to keep in mind. So it's not like it just goes on forever — 3,000 researchers would not be very helpful, but a couple hundred, very helpful.

— The argument I've heard is: given the amount of compute you need to allocate per person, and if you want to scale certain experiments up, coupled to the fact that often there's a distribution in terms of contributions — a handful of people who contribute the most from an idea perspective in every field — eventually it collapses into: you want to give every incremental piece of compute to the most productive subset of people. So you end up with some static or shrinking number of researchers over time.

The argument definitely has merit. These projects never needed a crazy amount of researchers. Projects like AlphaGo at the time were maybe order of 10 people. Now, for large efforts like the one we're doing, maybe an order of 100 or hundreds. So it's never been the case that you needed an extraordinary number of people. Whether it collapses back into 10 or not — hard to say. I would estimate there's going to be some steady state in that kind of order of 100.

There are just a lot of things to do. And there will be a lot of job creation in applied research — going and taking these things and actually applying them to real problems.

— I think people really lose that when they talk about engineering and research in terms of the diffusion of those roles out into a broader swath of society, and not just building language models. There's lots of other model types to build. There's all the closed-loop systems to build. Even when people talk about engineers and the potential displacement of engineers — so far the evidence seems that many companies need more engineers versus fewer. There's also the diffusion of certain level/quality of engineer out to actually deploy the technology in organizations that never would have been able to access somebody of that talent level on a relative basis, or at least not at scale. I do think that's kind of lost as people think about the economy — they tend to centralize it into a handful of big tech companies instead of saying: what is our overall GDP, and how does that get transformed by the diffusion of people bringing this technology out?

I think that's correct. The amount of researchers you do these things with — it's not changed dramatically over the years. It's always been: big project, OK, around 100 people. I don't think you need thousands on a big project. But maybe on different product surfaces, OK, then you need a bunch of people.

What's interesting is: when you look at the distribution of why you even need hundreds of people — a lot of it is that you have teams that do evals for different things and collect data for different things. When you're generating — it's not by accident these models have capabilities. There are pods of five to 10 people that go and target a particular capability. And within coding there are five to 10 capabilities. So that's for bringing the general capabilities into the model.

But now when you want to take that model and apply it to real-world capabilities, you basically need a pod for any real-world capability. And each enterprise has many of them. So the job creation for this new type of deployed engineer — that is a bit more scientific and evaluations-oriented, and knows / has some intuition for these models and the harnesses — which is actually what the evaluation researcher does. It's actually the same skill set as the researcher building the core thing, which is deployed to work on real problems.

We would take as many of those people as possible. It's more of a training gap on that — you need to train engineers to become good at this. Yeah, we would take as many as possible today.

结语

— Congratulations Misha, having the first Western model that is in the class of the frontier. It's just been a big step forward for the ecosystem.

Thank you. Thank you so much.

— Yeah. Thanks for joining us.

Yeah.

Find us on Twitter at @NoPriorsPod. Subscribe to our YouTube channel if you want to see our faces. Follow the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you listen — that way you get a new episode every week. And sign up for emails or find transcripts for every episode at no-priors.com.

item.description:
## 一、开源与封闭的"反向路径"——AI 是第一个走"从租赁到拥有"的数字技术
Misha 用了一个关键比喻：企业从租赁公寓到拥有房屋。但这里藏着一个被几乎所有人忽视的历史反常——**过去三十年所有的数字技术都在走相反的路径**：从本地软件到 SaaS、从自建服务器到云、从拥有 CD 到流媒体订阅。整个数字经济的叙事就是"所有权消解"。
但 AI 却在走回头路：从调用 OpenAI API（纯租赁）→ 到用开源模型 fine-tune（半拥有）→ 到完全私有化部署（完全拥有）。**这意味着 AI 不是互联网的延伸，而是互联网逻辑的某种逆转**。为什么？因为智能不同于存储和计算——存储是基础设施，智能是认知债务。当一个组织的决策、合规、法律、客户服务开始依赖外部智能，它承担的不是"服务依赖"，而是"认知外包"。这触发了一种生物本能级的回收冲动：没有生命体会把大脑外包。所以企业的"拥有"冲动不是经济学问题，是组织生理学问题。
## 二、Linus 定律的本体论盲区——开源权重不等于开源行为
Misha 把 Linus 定律（眼球多了 bug 就浅）扩展到 AI 安全。这个论点听起

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、等权指数估值的"反常信号"：这是一个被忽视的宽度崩塌证据

视频里有一个很有意思的发现被作者快速带过了：标普等权指数的前瞻PE（16倍）已经低于3月份低点，而加权指数PE（19.18倍）尚未破3月份低点。这是一种罕见的结构。

通常在牛市后期，等权和加权PE会向上收敛——因为涨幅扩散、鸡犬升天。而现在是向下发散：少数几家巨头把加权指数撑在半空，而中位数公司已经被定价回到了衰退预期区间。换句话说，市场内部正在发生"伪装成牛市的熊市"——指数绿着，但大多数股票的估值已经在为盈利衰退做准备。

这种结构在历史上只出现过几次：2000年Q1、2021年Q4。两次都不是什么好征兆——不是因为估值高，而是因为市场的健康度（breadth）比整体水位更能预示拐点。昨天作者说估值"相对悲观"，其实可以更尖锐一点：不是估值悲观，是市场正在悄悄投票认为"除了Mag 7之外的美国经济已经进入衰退定价"。

二、OpenAI"鬼故事"的真相是一个会计模因的病毒式变异

视频把这个故事还原得很清楚：Anthropic用grossing up（把AWS转售的100刀全部计入营收），OpenAI用net revenue（只计80刀）。两家都没错，但媒体把它当成"营收下降"来写。

让我意外的角度是：这个事件和2017-2019年的Uber/Lyft招股书争议、2015年GroupOn的"gross vs net"丑闻在结构上完全一致——每一次新技术平台成型期，都会出现一轮会计口径战争。这不是巧合。

更深的东西是：ARR作为一个指标，它本身是一个被SaaS时代发明的"叙事工具"。它假设营收是recurring的、可预测的、可以乘以12或4的。但API调用这种计费模式，本质上是按token消耗——这更像电费而非订阅费。把API收入做ARR年化，等于把一个用电大户某个月的电费乘12说成"年度经常性电费"——如果那个月正好在挖矿、下个月不挖了呢？

跨领域连接：这个场景几乎就是早期电力行业的"千瓦时计费 vs 包月计费"之争的翻版。爱迪生当年也打过类似的仗。每一次新基础设施成型，都要重新发明一次计量单位，而第一波媒体报道几乎总是搞错单位。所以真正值得关注的不是OpenAI的营收数字，而是什么时候行业会放弃ARR指标，换成一个token-based的新指标——那才是AI商业模式真正定型的信号。

三、Chris Waller的"去连续性"措辞是一个政治-货币耦合信号

作者注意到了Waller的"美联储需要灵活性，而非连续性加息"这句话，但只解读成"10月不加息"。我觉得这句话的分量比表面大得多。

跨领域观察：Waller曾经是美联储主席候选人，现在用了一个非常罕见的词叫"灵活性"——这是候选人竞选语言，不是政策官员语言。真正的政策官员会说"data-dependent"或"gradual"，而不是"flexibility"。"灵活性"这个词在企业管理中特指保留行动空间以便相机抉择，这是CEO语言、不是技术官僚语言。

把这个观察和作者提到的"离中期选举3周"放在一起，有一个政治商业周期理论（Nordhaus 1975）的影子：选前，货币政策官员倾向于保持宽松姿态；选后，紧缩预期回归。但这一次有一个新变量——美联储官员本身也在"预选"（因为鲍威尔任期将到，候选人在争夺信号权）。于是我们看到的不是传统的政治商业周期，而是一种"央行治理的候选人表演"——官员通过措辞来争夺继任权。

这意味着未来几个月的美联储讲话，可能都要用"候选人竞选"的视角去解读，而不是"政策传导"的视角。谁用什么词、对谁喊话，比FOMC纪要本身更有信息量。

一个让人警觉的推论：如果Waller是真鸽派，那TLT的空头确实需要被"砸出去"（作者的判断）；但如果Waller的鸽派只是竞选姿态而非政策信号，那TLT的反弹会非常短命——因为真正的政策方向还握在鲍威尔手里，而鲍威尔没有选举压力。

📝 转录文本

开场：今天要聊三件事

在昨天的视频里面和大家分享了三大指数现在估值所在的位置，我们得出的一个结论是估值在一个相对比较低的位置。

留言区里面有一条留言引起了我的注意，大家点赞也非常的积极。那条留言说到：如果去看标普500，现在1/3的这个盈利来自于两家公司——英伟达和美光。那我可以理解这样的一个角度。所以今天和大家分享另外一个指数：标普的等权指数。我们去看一下等权指数现在的估值，从相对性这个角度来看，到底是在什么的一个位置。这是第一部分。

第二部分，周四市场里面又出来一个鬼故事，OpenAI的营收从两周前的700亿美金直接跌到了500亿美金，背后到底发生了什么？我们一起去了解一下这件事情背后的一个原委，好吗？

最后第三部分，我们再回到周四的一个资产价格的一个走势，包括有一些零散的新闻和大家分享。

那欢迎大家来到一个不单只聊新闻的专业美股频道，我是市场分析师小涛。在开始之前，大家记得留言、点赞加转发，让更多的人可以看到我们这期内容。

第一部分：标普等权指数估值分析

那我们废话不多说，先来看一下等权指数。

昨天我们看了标普、看了半导体、然后看了NDX、科技板块、半导体、然后标普。那怎么样要去避免，或者说把一些相对赚、比较赚钱的公司给剔除出来，那么使这一两家公司没有非常大的影响到整体指数的一个盈利能力，我们可以看一下标普的一个等权指数。

加权指数当前估值回顾

我们现在看到这张图是昨天视频里面和大家分享的标普500——SP1向前看的市盈率或者前瞻市盈率。昨天的收盘，周三的收盘是在19.18倍。那么19.18倍横向去做对比的话，接近于2026年那个低点，3月份的一个低点，也接近于2025年3月份那个低点。当时2025年3月份是在18倍，现在是在19倍。

等权指数当前估值

然后我们来看一下标普等权指数。标普等权指数截止到周三的收盘是在16倍、19.96倍，其实已经低于今年3月份的这种水平。今年3月份正正好好和现在的水平差不多，也在16倍左右。而在2025年的3月份是在15倍。也就是说，从现在这个位置再下去6%左右，那么在基本面没有变糟糕的情况下、也没有变好的情况下——因为价格的下跌，PE可以下跌——那所以前瞻市盈率如果往下跌6%，那就回到了2025年的水平。但是根据当下的一个市盈率，我们可以看到其实已经比今年3月份还要低了。

结论：估值在相对低位

所以无论是标普的等权指数也好，还是标普500也好，我们都可以得出一个结论：现在估值从过去两年的这个角度去看，在一个相对比较低的位置。

那一个相对比较高的位置是在什么水平？我们可以非常明显地看到25年、26年、24年全部加在一起，18倍是一个比较明显的一个上区间。24年曾经有一段时间去到了18.5倍、18.6倍，但是基本上整个25年一直是围绕着18倍的这一个上区间在那边。

26年的年初曾经——26年年初大家还记得发生什么——今年年初，今年年初一开始价值股板块走得非常的好，那所以把标普的等权指数其实拉到了一个PE，拉到了一个相对比较高的位置，18.2倍、18.3倍左右。然后3月份的时候是一路下跌，在过去的几个月里面出现了一定程度的一个反弹和在17倍左右的一个横盘。然后从9月份开始，随着利率的一个上涨，标普等权指数的前瞻市盈率出现非常明显的下跌，从17倍来到了现在的16倍。

而现在16倍已经比今年的3月份差不多在同样的一个位置。

当我们在看标普500等权指数前瞻市盈率的时候，就已经把个别公司比较赚钱的这个因素给剔除在外了。那所以我们看等权指数，其实也可以得出相同的这个结论，反而比前面可能还更加激进一些——所以更加听我说相对会更加悲观一点。从结果去看的话，就现在的估值其实接近于今年3月份的这个水平，和今年3月份是完全一样的。但是从标普500去看的话，前瞻市盈率其实还没有到今年3月份那个低点。

OK，那看完了估值以后，我们来看一下周四市场里边写的一个鬼故事。

第二部分：OpenAI营收"鬼故事"始末

我们一起回顾一下这件事情的一个前因和后果。

事件时间线

这件事情的一个起点是在9月29日。Axios——他们一家媒体——他们公布了OpenAI营收，最新的营收是在70个billion，700亿美金。然后接下去另外几家媒体跟进，分别是路透社和The Information，这两家公司附议了Axios他们所公布OpenAI最新的这个营收体量。

然后也就是周四10月8日那一天，FT（Financial Times，金融时报）他们说，根据投资者金融信息，他们获得OpenAI最新的这个营收ARR只有50个billion，500亿美金。

概念澄清：什么是ARR？

首先这边有个概念，ARR——什么是ARR？英文的话是Annual Recurring Revenue，把它翻成中文的话，我看了一下，翻成中文叫做"年度经常性收入"。这个词我觉得比较的抽象，把它翻得再简单一点的话就是"年化收入"，年化收入会更贴切一些。

那年化收入的话，你可以分为很多种。比如说你把什么收入去进行年化，可以分为月度年化、可以分为季度年化、可以分为周年化，也可以——开个玩笑——也可以分为日年化。比如说你今天赚了多少钱，然后把它乘以365，就得出了你一年的这个营收，对吧？但实际上没有人会去做一个日年化。而通常情况下，根据SEC的这种规定，比较正常的，你就disclose（在披露）自己年度化收入的时候，你可以用月年化，也可以用季度年化。

所以这边有一个概念，ARR年度经常性营收，它并不是等于营收，它和营收本身是两个概念。应该说大多数的情况下，ARR都是会比营收要高的，因为它主要就是拿过去一个季度或者过去一个月的营收体量把它进行一个年化，一个是乘以4、一个是乘以12。那这个指标本身其实在一些初创公司里面、在和SaaS相关的一些公司里面是非常常用的一些公司。

那这个指标ARR本身是在初创公司和软件相关的一些公司里面非常常用的一个指标。

口径之差：Anthropic vs OpenAI

好吧，所以那为什么会在9月29——也就两周左、一周两周都不到的时间呢，一周左右的时间里面——为什么营收会出现非常大的一个差异呢？

Axios今天做了一个解释：因为他们是第一个，对吧，在一周多之前写这篇文章的人，说OpenAI的一个营收已经到达了700亿美金了，他们今天解释到，因为Anthropic把通过大云API调用的这部分全部算作是收入了，而OpenAI只记录了自己的那部分。

什么意思？我给大家举个例子。比如说Coinbase通过亚马逊下面的AWS，然后购买了100刀API，那这个API比如说是来自于Anthropic也好、来自OpenAI都是一样——从一家语言模型里面购买了100刀的这个API。那AWS有一个成本在那边，所以AWS就一笔花费，Coinbase花了100块钱、100刀，AWS拿了20块钱。那么然后AWS背后还有自己的这个成本啊，AWS他们云、他们的一个margin如果在40%的话，那20刀对于他们来说利润就是8刀，12刀就是AWS一个成本，或者数据中心的一个成本，或包括它的一个硬件等等。那这边我们先不做展开，我以前其实有聊过类似背后的一个数据。

那在这个起点、在这个基础上呢，AWS拿走了20刀，那剩下的80刀是进入了模型公司手里了。这就是模型公司为什么那么赚钱——因为他们的毛利润非常的高，将近80%嘛。

两种会计处理方式

那到这边其实就已经有了一个问题：那究竟从Anthropic或者从OpenAI这个角度去看，究竟是应该把100刀算作是营收，还是应该把80刀算作是营收？其实这两者都是可以去计算、都是可以用的，所以其实都是可以的。

Anthropic的算法：如果我们把100刀计入营收的话，比如说Anthropic就是这么去操作的，那100刀计入营收，20刀就是cost of good sold（就是它一个成本），那剩下的就是毛利润就是在80刀，然后在这个基础上再减去其他的一些支出，比如说你R&D啊、Marketing expense啊都可以、包括你运营上的一些花费，全部减完之后，会有你一个运营利润在那边，对吧。那Anthropic它是100刀算作是一个营收，然后20刀算作是一个成本，然后再减去其他支出。所以这样如果去计算的话，那它的一个营收体量会大一些，它的毛利相对会低一些，它的运营利润率会低一些，但是它最终的一个利润体量或者运营利润的一个体量是完全一样的，对吧。

OpenAI的算法：那另外一种操作的一个方法，像OpenAI他们那个操作方法是，他不拿100刀作为一个营收，他拿80刀作为一个营收，他把AWS拿走的这20刀已经全部算给他们了，80刀作为OpenAI它的一个营收。那这样的话对于OpenAI来说，你的一个营收的这个体量相对会小一些，但是你的利润率、你的毛利润率会高，那无论是你的毛利润率也好、你的运营利润率也好，都会比较高。

那但是最终的一个结果，无论是Anthropic这种算法还是OpenAI这种算法，最终的一个运营体量是一样的。那假设他们其他的一些运营成本啊什么东西都是一样的话。

对，所以最终其实运营体量这个角度去看都是一样。但是问题就是在这两家公司都是亏钱的，所以他们也没有运营……当然，第三季度Anthropic应该是开始赚钱了，不知道从哪个标准去出发，可能从EBITDA这个角度是赚钱。但是anyway，在他们没有赚钱之前，你衡量他们是什么？你只能衡量他们的营收增速到底是多少。

所以这时候就会有一个不同的一个指标或者出入在那边了。Anthropic用的是100刀的一个花费，直接把它算到是一个营收了。但是OpenAI算的是80块钱，就是OpenAI用了80块钱作为的这个营收，其实是Anthropic一个毛利润。

作者判断：媒体乌龙，与AI放缓无关

讲到这边，大家应该能够理解，所以它其实是一个算法上的一个问题。而这些数据其实媒体自己去报道的，它并不是公司所披露的。所以这件事情本身，说实话，和这两家公司或者和整个AI的一个放缓没有丝毫的一个关系。

如果我——我在X上今天我有说过我的这个观点——只要任何这两家公司，只要你以前用的还是同样这个口径，以后你在你统计ARR的时候只要这个口径不变，其实是不影响的。包括你的营收，你怎么去把它算作是一个营收，只要这个口径没有改变，我觉得这背后不存在任何的问题。而且我们看整个AI的一个发展，我主要看它是一个增速。那你这个增速主要是来自于你自己业务体量这个扩张，而不是来自于你会计准则上的一些修改。所以还是那个观点，只要不修改会计准则、只要不修改他们营收这个算法，那这个增速本身我觉得就是OK的。

所以这件事情本身有点类似于是媒体所闹出的一个乌龙。

真正值得关注的焦点：AI Agent落地

所以我还是建议大家把主要的一些焦点放在现在。在过去两个月左右，我们所看到AI Agent上的一个落地。那么包括谷歌在周四也推出了他们在B端这一块的一个Agent，前几天微软也推出了自己在B端这一块的Agent，包括OpenAI推出了一个Astra、推出了一个dots，一个是针对个人的一个智能体、一个是针对B端这一块的一个智能体，包括我们看到C端这一块的一个MUSE，那现在这个adoption也是非常不错。

至于非前沿模型这一块的一个落地，就对于营收这一块的一个影响，其实微软从第二季度财报开始就已经披露了他们新增的这个订单到底是来自于哪里。那微软二季度的新增的订单全部是来自于非模型公司。所以其实从大科技这个角度去看，他们已经知道市场担忧的是什么——那担忧的是这两家模型公司可能把整个AI整个行业全部绑架了。那所以他们从营收增速的这个角、从订单增速这个角度去看，尽量把模型公司和非模型公司分开去计算，让市场看到AI的落地并不是营收并不仅仅局限在这两家模型公司身上，而其他所有的一些行业、其他的一些公司、其他行业里面的一些公司，在AI这一块的营收增速都在扩张。

好吧，鬼故事我们讲完之后，再回到周四一个资产价格的走势。

第三部分：周四资产价格走势

美元、美债、TLT

美元指数是小幅波动。美债收率这块在周四出现了下跌，TLT终于出现了一个反弹，上涨了0.9%，10年期的利率下跌了5个基点。但是整个市场里面还是没有看到一条比较明显的一个新闻。我只知道散户在抄底TLT，你可以看到TLT最近这段时间的成交量非常大，有明显有一个买盘在那边。

但是我个人的看法，如果没有一条新闻或者事件进来的话，这一波利率的一个下跌或者价格的一个反弹，我认为是比较难持续的。所以我还是期待，因为中期选举——离中期选举差不多还有3周左右的时间——我还是期待应该会有些新闻出来，那使得这一波……现在空头，现其实现在在美债市场上还是空头是占主力的，这空头这一波是需要一个事件把他们砸出去，然后需要一波空头上的一个回补，使得利率会出现下跌，然后TLT的一个价格会出现反弹。

股指表现

那指数这边，周三周四是受到了一个鬼故事的一个影响，那么所以纳指跌幅会相对会大一些，1.3%。而因为利率这个下跌，看到道指是出现反弹了。包括罗素2000上涨了百分之……啊，就几乎就在横盘，那么涨了0.0%。

然后从板块这个角度去看，标普的等权指数上涨0.6%，那所以整个周四的市场其实并不差的，只是因为大科技弱了一些、芯片板块弱了一些，所以但所以整个标普是出现了下跌，但是整个市场的参与度，我没有去看，但是我相信市场的参与度在周四是出现反弹的，因为等权指数上涨了0.6%，说明大多数的个股在周四其实是出现了反弹。

周四是一次"演练"

那另外一点我想提醒一下大家是：今天可以把今天周四市场的一个走势当做是一个演练。什么演练？就是未来如果有一家模型公司，它的营收出现问题或者它基本面出现问题的话，到底有哪一类公司会受到影响——今天就可以看到到底是哪一类的公司出现影响。我基本上我自己手里很多的标的都受到影响，最终今天的账户、周四账户是下跌了2%，还是比较大的。就在市场没有下跌非常明显的情况下，我自己下跌了2%，那主要是由英特尔所带领。

Chris Waller讲话解读

最后关于利率这一块，那我今天——就像我前面说，我今天并没有看到一个非常明显的新闻能够导致长债这块的利率出现下跌，但是今天有另外一位美联储成员出来讲话——他的今天那个讲话，基本上又再次奠定了10月份加息的这个概率应该是比较低的。

那在会议之前嘛，市场永远不可能去定价0的这个概率嘛，所以我上次也说过，在会议之前市场去定价10%至30%的波动的这个区间都是合理的，一旦接近于50%的话，可能就不是那么的合理。当然，马上在应该是下一周吧，凯文沃什也会有一个采访。

那今天是谁出来讲话了？是Chris Waller。Chris Waller其实怎么说，以前是相对比较鹰派的，然后现在相对会比较鸽派一些，因为曾经他是美联储的一个候选人之一嘛。

他在周四的一个采访里边有说到，他说美联储现在需要一个灵活性，而并非是一个连续性的一个涨价或者加息。Chris Waller今天有暗示到：美联储在即将召开的10月份会议上，有空间维持利率不变。这实际上是为鹰派维持利率打开了一个大门——就是有可能10月份的会议是鹰派式的不降息。

Chris Waller有说到，他说无需连续进行多次调整，调整不必在连续的会议上进行，但应该在合理的范围之内落实到位。他其实是支持——就基本上大多数的美联储（昨天我们也看到美联储纪要了嘛），大多数的美联储成员都认为今年还会有一次加息，但是今年只有两次会议了。

那在还会有一次加息的情况下，再要碰上11月份又会有一个中期选举，所以我说最合理的情况是你9月份已经加了，所以10月份、11月份完全可以利用9月份加一下这个加息之后去观察一下市场的这个反馈，去再搜集一些信息，特别是让PCE数据还下调完之后，10月份更没有理由去加息了。

那所以10月份最好就10月份不加，10月、11月两个月去观察CPI、观察通胀数据，有必要的话12月可以继续加息。所以周四Chris Waller的一个讲话，基本上再次强调了他认为10月份也是没有必要进行加息的。

那今天整个10月份加息的这个概率并没有出现下降，因为已经压到了17%、18%了，那再下降降是空间是有限的，反而在这个基础上可能会出现一些反弹，如果CPI数据不好的话。

但是像我前面说过，我说CPI数据除非到了非常糟糕的这种情况下，不然的话，即使这一个月的CPI数据糟糕，或者说没有那么的好，也不支持美联储去10月份进行加息。因为凯文——我说过，他要看的是一个趋势——而过去三个月，即使这个月没有那么的好，三个月也形成不了一个趋势。就三个月的数据是三个月所形成的这个趋势，支持不了在10月份去做出加息这个决定。

推广环节

OK，最后今天的活动是来自于Seeking Alpha。

首先第一个是他们量化选股策略Alpha Picks。Alpha Picks在过去这段时间、过去这两三周吧，还是不错的。那虽然在过去的一两个月他们有一些艰难，那有一些艰难的时候就很正常——你任何一个策略在某一个时间段，你跑出指数或者走的没有指数好，太正常不过了，对吧。你不可能任何策略、任何人不可能在所有的时间之内都比市场要跑得好。

那在过去三次他们挑选的这个标的，从9月1日到现在，这三个标题还挑选得不错的。你可以在下图里面你可以看到，三个标的都跑赢了指数，那分别是跑赢第一个标的跑赢了指数2.8%，第二个跑赢了指数12.5%，第三个跑赢指数也将近10%。那这前两个标的9月15日和11月1日他们所选的这两个标的，也是我的两大持仓、一个非常大比例的一个持仓之二了。

所以这是他们一个量化选股策略，那现在正在搞活动，正好有一个免费的一个试用，然后第一年的话可以立省50美金。那同时大家也知道Seeking Alpha他们有个Alpha Premium的一个订阅，所以大家如果对于Premium或者Alpha Picks这两个订阅都感兴趣的话，现在有一个combo的一个价格，原价是798美金，现在是629美金。所以大家如果感兴趣的话，可以在置顶的留言里边找到订阅的链接。

那今天的节目就到这边，下期见。

## 一、等权指数估值的"反常信号"：这是一个被忽视的宽度崩塌证据
视频里有一个很有意思的发现被作者快速带过了：**标普等权指数的前瞻PE（16倍）已经低于3月份低点，而加权指数PE（19.18倍）尚未破3月份低点**。这是一种罕见的结构。
通常在牛市后期，等权和加权PE会**向上收敛**——因为涨幅扩散、鸡犬升天。而现在是**向下发散**：少数几家巨头把加权指数撑在半空，而中位数公司已经被定价回到了衰退预期区间。换句话说，市场内部正在发生**"伪装成牛市的熊市"**——指数绿着，但大多数股票的估值已经在为盈利衰退做准备。
这种结构在历史上只出现过几次：2000年Q1、2021年Q4。两次都不是什么好征兆——不是因为估值高，而是因为**市场的健康度（breadth）比整体水位更能预示拐点**。昨天作者说估值"相对悲观"，其实可以更尖锐一点：**不是估值悲观，是市场正在悄悄投票认为"除了Mag 7之外的美国经济已经进入衰退定价"**。
